title: Observability Analysis of Joint Steering and Extrinsic Calibration
summary: This technical report studies the local weak observability of a planar bicycle-model vehicle when vehicle pose, planar LiDAR extrinsic calibration, and steering-angle bias are estimated jointly. A Lie-derivative-based nonlinear observability analysis is used to examine stationary, straight-line, constant-curvature, and combined straight-plus-arc motion. The resulting observability matrices and nullspaces describe how pose, LiDAR translation and yaw offsets, and steering bias become coupled under different motion primitives. Stationary motion and individual motion primitives retain unobservable directions, whereas the combination of straight and curved motion removes the identified degeneracies and yields full local weak observability of the seven-state system. The analysis provides a theoretical basis for selecting calibration trajectories that sufficiently excite both steering and sensor-extrinsic parameters.

AI.tldr: This technical report presents a local weak observability analysis of a planar bicycle-model vehicle jointly estimating vehicle pose, LiDAR extrinsic calibration (translation and yaw), and steering-angle bias. Using Lie-derivative-based nonlinear observability analysis, it examines stationary, straight-line, constant-curvature, and combined straight-plus-arc motions, showing that only the combination of straight and curved motion achieves full local weak observability of the seven-state system by removing degeneracies present in individual motion primitives.
AI.motivation: To provide a theoretical basis for selecting calibration trajectories that sufficiently excite both steering and sensor-extrinsic parameters, by rigorously analyzing under which motion conditions the joint estimation problem becomes observable.
AI.method: Lie-derivative-based nonlinear observability analysis applied to a planar bicycle model, examining stationary, straight-line, constant-curvature, and combined straight-plus-arc motion primitives. Observability matrices and nullspaces are derived to characterize how pose, LiDAR translation/yaw offsets, and steering bias couple under different motions.
AI.result: Stationary motion and individual motion primitives preserve unobservable directions, while the combination of straight and curved motion removes all identified degeneracies, yielding full local weak observability of the seven-state system.
AI.conclusion: Combined straight-plus-arc trajectories provide sufficient excitation for full observability of the joint pose-LiDAR extrinsic-steering bias estimation problem, offering a principled foundation for designing calibration trajectories.

title: Multi-robot Learning-based Informative Path Planning Using Spatio-Temporal Gaussian Process Kalman Filter
summary: Multi-robot informative path planning (IPP) for persistent target monitoring requires robots to reason about spatial uncertainty, temporal evolution, and practical sensing and communication constraints. Recent learning-based multi-robot IPP methods use Gaussian Processes (GPs) for target uncertainty, but often rely on simplified sensing models and centralized belief updates. We propose a grid-based spatio-temporal GP-Kalman filtering framework for learning-based multi-robot IPP. Instead of maintaining one GP per target, we represent anonymous target presence as a single latent field over a discrete workspace grid. The proposed recursive update considers all visible cells inside a camera footprint and supports arbitrary fields of view and range-dependent noise. A GP-consistent temporal process update accounts for moving targets and stale information by inflating uncertainty over time. For decentralized deployment, each robot maintains its own mapper and exchanges compact belief summaries rather than raw measurements. Received beliefs are fused using diagonal covariance intersection to remain conservative under unknown inter-robot correlations. We integrate the mapper with a reinforcement-learning policy for graph-based neighbor selection. Simulation benchmarks show about 20% lower average target uncertainty and improved target visitation compared with learning-based and classical auction/coverage baselines. Real-world two-UAV experiments demonstrate transfer to outdoor multi-robot search over a large field of more than 7000 square meters.

AI.tldr: A grid-based spatio-temporal GP-Kalman filtering framework for learning-based decentralized multi-robot informative path planning (IPP) in persistent target monitoring, achieving ~20% lower target uncertainty than baselines and validated in real-world two-UAV experiments over a 7000+ m² field.
AI.motivation: Existing learning-based multi-robot IPP methods rely on Gaussian Processes for target uncertainty but are limited by simplified sensing models (e.g., one GP per target), centralized belief updates, and constraints that fail to account for practical camera footprints, range-dependent noise, moving targets, and decentralized deployment.
AI.method: The paper proposes a grid-based spatio-temporal GP-Kalman filtering framework where anonymous target presence is represented as a single latent field over a discrete workspace grid. The recursive update processes all visible cells within arbitrary camera footprints with range-dependent noise. A GP-consistent temporal process update inflates uncertainty over time to handle moving targets and stale information. For decentralization, each robot maintains its own mapper and exchanges compact belief summaries, fused via diagonal covariance intersection to remain conservative under unknown inter-robot correlations. The mapper is integrated with a reinforcement-learning policy for graph-based neighbor selection.
AI.result: Simulation benchmarks demonstrate about 20% lower average target uncertainty and improved target visitation compared to learning-based and classical auction/coverage baselines. Real-world two-UAV experiments validate transfer to outdoor multi-robot search over a field exceeding 7000 square meters.
AI.conclusion: The proposed decentralized, learning-based spatio-temporal GP-Kalman mapping framework improves multi-robot IPP performance in terms of uncertainty reduction and target visitation, and successfully transfers from simulation to real-world outdoor multi-robot search settings.

title: Robots Influencing Humans to Reveal their Goals during Collaboration and Competition
summary: We propose a unified strategy for fast goal inference in human-robot interaction. The core idea is to drive the human toward Critical Decision Points (CDPs)-states where competing human strategies prescribe different next actions and thus maximally reveal the goal. We formalise CDPs using a goal-conditioned policy divergence measure and incorporate them into a Receding-Horizon Planner that explores future action sequences while optimizing a cost function balancing task progress and information gain. We evaluate this approach in both a collaborative, fully observable cooking task and a competitive, partially observable hide-and-seek game, each in simulation and on real robots. In both scenarios, our method infers human goals more accurately and earlier than baseline strategies.

AI.tldr: A unified framework for fast goal inference in human-robot interaction that actively steers humans toward Critical Decision Points (CDPs), where divergent policies maximally reveal their intent, using a Receding-Horizon Planner that balances task progress against information gain.
AI.motivation: Goal inference in human-robot interaction is often slow or passive; the robot needs to actively gather information about human intent early and accurately to enable efficient collaboration or competition.
AI.method: Formalizes Critical Decision Points (CDPs) as states where competing goal-conditioned policies prescribe different actions, quantified by a policy divergence measure. These CDPs are incorporated into a Receding-Horizon Planner that explores future action sequences and optimizes a cost function trading off task progress and information gain.
AI.result: The approach outperforms baseline strategies in two distinct settings: a collaborative, fully observable cooking task and a competitive, partially observable hide-and-seek game, both in simulation and on real robots, achieving more accurate and earlier goal inference.
AI.conclusion: Actively steering humans toward informative decision points enables faster, more accurate goal inference across both collaborative and competitive human-robot interaction scenarios, suggesting a broadly applicable unified strategy.

title: Situation Awareness for Intelligent Data Distribution in Connected Vehicles
comment: Peer-reviewed and Published in the 2025 IEEE 101st Vehicular Technology Conference (VTC2025-Spring)
summary: The limitations of on-board sensors and blind spots caused by occlusion cause the reduction of perception quality in autonomous vehicles. In such cases, cooperative perception provides additional data via Vehicle-to-Everything communication to enhance local perception, causing a large volume of data transmission. The vehicle can focus on acquiring and utilizing relevant data according to the prevailing road context by identifying the current traffic situation. To achieve this, we propose a concept for the situation identification of the vehicle using Bird's-Eye-View images. Firstly, the situation around the vehicle is identified using object detection with semantic segmentation, followed by understanding the context of the traffic using a situation identification module consisting of an open-source projective transformation network Cam2BEV and a situation identification neural network. The concept was evaluated and validated by running the software on the CARLA simulator using the in-built RGB camera and the semantic segmentation camera. Additionally, the portability of the situation identification module for real-world applications was verified on Cityscapes and nuScenes urban driving datasets. Overall, the proposed situation identification approach enables efficient sensor data management by prioritizing relevant data to the current traffic situation. The source code is available in the following link: https://github.com/akshaynarla/DySi_Select

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a situation identification concept for autonomous vehicles using Bird's-Eye-View (BEV) images to enable context-aware data prioritization in cooperative perception. The system uses object detection with semantic segmentation, followed by a situation identification module combining the Cam2BEV projective transformation network and a situation identification neural network. It was validated in the CARLA simulator and verified for real-world portability on Cityscapes and nuScenes datasets.
AI.motivation: On-board sensors suffer from limitations and occlusion-induced blind spots, degrading perception quality in autonomous vehicles. Cooperative perception via V2X communication addresses this but generates large volumes of data transmission. Vehicles need to identify the current traffic situation to selectively acquire and utilize only relevant data, improving efficiency of sensor data management.
AI.method: The approach first identifies the situation around the vehicle using object detection combined with semantic segmentation. Subsequently, a situation identification module—comprising the open-source Cam2BEV projective transformation network and a situation identification neural network—is used to understand the surrounding traffic context from BEV images. Evaluation was conducted using the CARLA simulator with an RGB camera and semantic segmentation camera, and portability was verified on Cityscapes and nuScenes datasets.
AI.result: The proposed situation identification approach was validated in simulation (CARLA) and demonstrated portability to real-world urban driving datasets (Cityscapes and nuScenes). It enables efficient sensor data management by prioritizing data relevant to the current traffic situation.
AI.conclusion: The situation identification approach improves cooperative perception efficiency by enabling context-aware prioritization of relevant data, reducing unnecessary data transmission while maintaining perception quality. Source code is publicly available.

title: Beyond Right and Wrong: Evaluating Second-order Social Reasoning in Large Language Models
summary: Previous AI alignment efforts have focused primarily on first-order social norms -- teaching models what is socially acceptable or unacceptable (e.g., `do not steal'). However, social intelligence depends not only on norm recognition, but also on anticipating who will enforce it and how (e.g., public shame or even imprisonment). These second-order expectations, known as metanorms, govern how people respond when social rules are broken. We introduce a novel framework for evaluating metanorm reasoning in Large Language Models (LLMs) along two dimensions: emotional appraisal and behavioral response, and propose new classification tasks, namely, predicting self-regulation in violators, and other-regulation in observers. We release a multi-perspective dataset, NormReact, of 450 norm violation scenarios, hand-annotated for emotions and behavioral responses across norm violators' gender and observers' social closeness. Current LLMs portray a harsher social world: across six models, they overpredict negative sanctions where humans would expect inaction, and alignment with human judgments deteriorates as social distance increases. These findings suggest that AI systems in norm-sensitive domains from conflict mediation to policy simulation, may risk producing a distorted picture of social regulation: one that over-represents punishment and under-represents the tolerance, restraint, and relational calibration that characterize actual norm enforcement in real world.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces NormReact, a framework and dataset (450 norm violation scenarios) for evaluating metanorm reasoning in LLMs—i.e., how models predict emotional appraisal and behavioral responses to norm violations, including self-regulation (violators) and other-regulation (observers). Findings reveal that six LLMs systematically overpredict negative sanctions where humans expect inaction, with alignment degrading as social distance increases, producing a distorted picture of real-world social regulation.
AI.motivation: Prior AI alignment has focused on first-order social norms (what is acceptable/unacceptable), but ignores second-order expectations (metanorms)—how people respond when norms are broken, such as who enforces them and how. This gap matters because social intelligence requires anticipating enforcement dynamics, not just rule recognition.
AI.method: The authors propose a framework evaluating metanorm reasoning along two dimensions: emotional appraisal and behavioral response. They introduce new classification tasks predicting self-regulation in violators and other-regulation in observers, and release NormReact, a hand-annotated dataset of 450 norm violation scenarios covering violator gender and observer social closeness.
AI.result: Across six LLMs, models overpredict negative sanctions relative to human expectations (humans more often expect inaction), and model-human alignment degrades as social distance between observer and violator increases.
AI.conclusion: Current LLMs risk producing a distorted picture of social regulation in norm-sensitive applications (e.g., conflict mediation, policy simulation)—over-representing punishment while under-representing the tolerance, restraint, and relational calibration that characterize real-world norm enforcement.

title: Information-Guided Safe Reinforcement Learning for Autonomous Gas Source Localization using sUAS
comment: 8 pages, 5 figures, 2 tables. Submitted to the 2026 IEEE Conference on Decision and Control (CDC). Code: https://github.com/sachingirime/Info-guided-safe-RL
summary: The autonomous localization of fugitive gas emissions using small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (sUAS) constitutes a fundamentally ill-posed inverse problem. In turbulent atmospheric boundary layers, highly intermittent scalar concentration fields violate the assumptions of classical gradient-based navigation, causing data-driven estimators to suffer from severe noise and spurious local minima. To address these challenges, we introduce an Information-Guided Safe Reinforcement Learning framework evaluated within a custom, GPU-accelerated 3D simulation environment coupling an Eulerian wind solver with a Lagrangian puff dispersion model. We identify a critical vulnerability in deterministic information-seeking planners - a Gramian bias where agents act greedily upon flawed early estimates, starving the estimator of spatial diversity. To systematically break this degeneracy, our architecture integrates a classical empirical observability Gramian (EMGR) planner with a learned Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) exploratory policy. A deterministic meta-supervisor actively monitors estimator reliability via Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence, dynamically blending deterministic exploitation with learned exploration to steer the sUAS into high-information zones. Trained via a progressive curriculum and safeguarded by a strictly enforced Robust Control Barrier Function (RCBF), our RL framework achieves nearly 80% localization success on complex, mobile sources - drastically outperforming classical baselines (~30%) - while ensuring zero safety violations.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces an Information-Guided Safe Reinforcement Learning framework for autonomous sUAS-based localization of fugitive gas emissions in turbulent atmospheric boundary layers. The approach combines an empirical observability Gramian (EMGR) planner with a Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) exploratory policy, dynamically blended by a meta-supervisor using KL divergence, and safeguarded by a Robust Control Barrier Function, achieving ~80% localization success versus ~30% for baselines with zero safety violations.
AI.motivation: Autonomous localization of fugitive gas emissions with sUAS is an ill-posed inverse problem where turbulent atmospheric boundary layers produce highly intermittent scalar concentration fields that violate gradient-based navigation assumptions, causing data-driven estimators to suffer from severe noise and spurious local minima. Additionally, deterministic information-seeking planners exhibit a Gramian bias—acting greedily on flawed early estimates and starving the estimator of spatial diversity.
AI.method: The framework uses a GPU-accelerated 3D simulation coupling an Eulerian wind solver with a Lagrangian puff dispersion model. The architecture integrates a classical empirical observability Gramian (EMGR) planner with a learned Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) exploration policy. A deterministic meta-supervisor monitors estimator reliability via KL divergence and dynamically blends deterministic exploitation with learned exploration. Training employs a progressive curriculum, and safety is enforced via a strictly enforced Robust Control Barrier Function (RCBF).
AI.result: The RL framework achieves nearly 80% localization success on complex, mobile sources, drastically outperforming classical baselines (~30%), while ensuring zero safety violations.
AI.conclusion: By systematically breaking the Gramian bias degeneracy through hybrid deterministic-exploration planning and maintaining strict safety guarantees via RCBF, the proposed framework demonstrates that learned exploratory policies can be effectively and safely integrated with classical information-seeking planners for autonomous gas source localization in turbulent environments.

title: CriticGen: Generation-Aware Evaluation as Actionable Feedback
summary: Current evaluation methods for large language models are coarse-grained and decoupled from generation, producing generic explanations that fail to provide actionable feedback for model improvement. We propose CriticGen, a fine-grained, generation-aware evaluation framework that turns evaluation into actionable control for answer improvement. CriticGen first generates sample-specific evaluation dimensions and scoring criteria under high-level categories such as subjective, objective, and self-derived constraints. These criteria then serve as a dynamic rubric for jointly producing a score, a reason, an executable refinement suggestion, and a refined answer. This rubric-conditioned refinement process enables models to diagnose flaws and perform targeted answer improvement. Experimental results show that fine-grained evaluation should be both instance-specific and actionable. CriticGen induces higher-quality rubrics, improving relevance/coverage from 3.33/4.03 to 3.97/4.24. CriticGen also achieves the best score correlations, with 0.9556 Pearson and 0.9560 Spearman, and raises the F1 of criterion-grounded reasons and executable suggestions from 0.6369/0.5994 to 0.7554/0.7900. Crucially, its feedback translates into reliable answer improvement, improving 73.17% of answers with a 93.28% non-degradation rate.

AI.tldr: CriticGen is a fine-grained, generation-aware evaluation framework for LLMs that generates instance-specific rubrics (dimensions + scoring criteria) and uses them to jointly produce scores, reasons, executable refinement suggestions, and refined answers. It outperforms baselines in rubric quality, score correlation, criterion-grounded feedback quality, and answer improvement reliability.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM evaluation methods are coarse-grained and decoupled from the generation process, producing generic explanations that cannot provide actionable feedback for model improvement.
AI.method: CriticGen first generates sample-specific evaluation dimensions and scoring criteria under high-level categories (subjective, objective, self-derived constraints). These criteria serve as a dynamic rubric for jointly generating a score, a reason, an executable refinement suggestion, and a refined answer via rubric-conditioned refinement, enabling diagnosis and targeted improvement.
AI.result: CriticGen achieves relevance/coverage of 3.97/4.24 (up from 3.33/4.03), best score correlations (0.9556 Pearson, 0.9560 Spearman), improves F1 of criterion-grounded reasons and executable suggestions from 0.6369/0.5994 to 0.7554/0.7900, improves 73.17% of answers with a 93.28% non-degradation rate.
AI.conclusion: Fine-grained evaluation should be both instance-specific and actionable. CriticGen demonstrates that turning evaluation into actionable control enables reliable answer improvement and higher-quality, more useful feedback compared to coarse-grained evaluation methods.

title: Benchmarking Dexterity of Multifingered Robot Hands: A Review and Perspective
comment: To be published in the $Annual$ $Review$ $of$ $Control$, $Robotics$, $and$ $Autonomous$ $Systems$, Volume 10, 2027
summary: Robot hands are a key interface between AI and the physical world, making advances in robotic dexterity essential to realizing the vision of physical AI. While impressive dexterity has been demonstrated with simple grippers, multifingered hands offer the potential for substantially greater versatility, precision, and adaptability in manipulation. In this review, we survey the state of the art in benchmarking the dexterity of multifingered robot hands. Recognizing dexterity as a complex and multifaceted concept, we present the perspective of the U.S. National Science Foundation HAND Engineering Research Center, with a particular focus on fine in-hand manipulation. We introduce a framework consisting of three benchmark levels that correspond to increasing system complexity, review representative benchmarks at each level, and propose new benchmarks and metrics to address limitations in the literature. More information can be found at https://hand-erc.github.io/benchmarking/.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a framework for benchmarking the dexterity of multifingered robot hands from the perspective of the U.S. NSF HAND Engineering Research Center, introducing three benchmark levels corresponding to increasing system complexity and proposing new benchmarks and metrics to address gaps in existing literature.
AI.motivation: Robot hands are a critical interface between AI and the physical world, and multifingered hands offer greater versatility, precision, and adaptability than simple grippers. However, dexterity is a complex, multifaceted concept lacking comprehensive benchmarking standards, motivating the need for a systematic framework to evaluate and advance fine in-hand manipulation.
AI.method: The paper surveys the state of the art in multifingered robot hand dexterity benchmarking, introduces a three-tier benchmark framework aligned with increasing system complexity, reviews representative benchmarks at each level, and proposes novel benchmarks and metrics to overcome limitations in current literature.
AI.result: The framework provides a structured categorization of benchmarks across three levels of system complexity, identifies gaps and limitations in existing dexterity evaluations, and introduces new benchmark proposals and metrics, with supporting resources available online.
AI.conclusion: A systematic, multi-level benchmarking framework is essential for advancing robotic dexterity, and proposed new benchmarks and metrics aim to better capture the complexity of fine in-hand manipulation with multifingered hands, supporting the broader vision of physical AI.

title: When Does Memory Help? A Cost-Aware Evaluation of Long-Term Memory in Tool-Using LLM Agents
summary: Long-term memory for LLM agents is evaluated today by conversational recall benchmarks (LoCoMo, LongMemEval), which measure question answering over dialogue history, not whether remembered facts change what a tool-using agent does. We present MERIT (Memory Evaluation for Realistic Instrumented Tasks), a benchmark and harness that measures the marginal utility of memory for task-executing agents under explicit cost accounting. MERIT provides episodic tool-use tasks in three domains whose dependence on earlier-episode facts is verified by an automated leak check; a difficulty ladder ending in updated-fact recall; controlled memory corruption; and full token and dollar metering of every memory operation. Across 23,440 scored episodes ($42.57), a two-generation pilot on gpt-4.1-mini and a preregistered 3-model x 3-seed grid (GPT-4.1, Claude Haiku 4.5; memory side held fixed), memory lifts dependent-task success from a leak-verified floor of 0.00 to 0.55-1.00. On updated facts, embedding retrieval collapses unpredictably (0.30-0.95 across models; max seed gap 0.45), and agents act on a correctly retrieved value only 55% of the time, while update-on-write stores (a structured fact store and, notably, LLM summarization) remain at 0.70-1.00; the hybrid is worse than the fact store alone. A latest-generation spot-check (Claude Sonnet 5, gated on a clean full-replay control) reproduces the pattern. Swapping a memory's implementation moves task success by up to 60 points, and full replay is never economical: the best condition per domain delivers 2.7-3.9x its marginal utility per dollar. We release the benchmark, harness, and all traces.

AI.tldr: MERIT is a benchmark and harness that measures the marginal utility of long-term memory for tool-using LLM agents under explicit cost accounting. Across 23,440 scored episodes, memory lifts dependent-task success from 0 to 0.55-1.00, but embedding retrieval collapses on updated facts (agents act on correct values only 55% of the time), while structured and LLM-summarization stores remain robust. Memory implementation choice can shift task success by up to 60 points.
AI.motivation: Existing long-term memory evaluations for LLM agents rely on conversational recall benchmarks (e.g., LoCoMo, LongMemEval) that measure question answering over dialogue history rather than whether remembered facts actually change what a tool-using agent does. The paper aims to address this gap by measuring the marginal utility of memory for task-executing agents under explicit cost accounting.
AI.method: MERIT provides episodic tool-use tasks across three domains with verified dependence on earlier-episode facts (via automated leak checks), a difficulty ladder ending in updated-fact recall, controlled memory corruption, and full token/dollar metering of every memory operation. Experiments include a two-generation pilot on gpt-4.1-mini and a preregistered 3-model x 3-seed grid (GPT-4.1, Claude Haiku 4.5) with memory held fixed.
AI.result: Memory lifts dependent-task success from a leak-verified floor of 0.00 to 0.55-1.00. On updated facts, embedding retrieval collapses unpredictably (0.30-0.95 across models; max seed gap 0.45), with agents acting on correctly retrieved values only 55% of the time. Update-on-write stores (structured fact store, LLM summarization) remain at 0.70-1.00, while the hybrid underperforms the fact store alone. A spot-check with Claude Sonnet 5 reproduces the pattern. Swapping memory implementation changes task success by up to 60 points, and full replay is never economical: the best condition delivers 2.7-3.9x its marginal utility per dollar.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that memory implementation is not interchangeable—its choice substantially affects agent task performance and economics. It suggests that update-on-write memory strategies are more reliable than embedding retrieval for updated facts, and that full replay-based memory access is economically suboptimal. The benchmark, harness, and all traces are released publicly.

title: GE-Act 2.0: Pretraining and Scaling a World-Action Model for Robotic Manipulation
comment: Technical report by the AgiBot Research Team. Project page: https://ge-act-v2.github.io/
summary: World-action models (WAM) predict future states to guide robot actions, enabling learning from both action-free video and action-labeled interaction. Most inherit pretrained video generators, leaving WAM pretraining and scaling underexplored. We introduce Genie Envisioner Act 2.0 (GE-Act 2.0), a world-action model whose trainable generative and action components are all initialized from scratch on manipulation data. It combines a control-oriented autoencoder (CoAE), a single-step visual planner (SVP), and an inverse dynamics model (IDM). CoAE retains action- and instruction-relevant information under aggressive compression, while SVP produces a complete future state in one differentiable pass, so visual planning and inverse dynamics can be pretrained separately on complementary data. The components are then jointly trained with knowledge-aligned selective optimization (KASO), which reduces mismatched supervision by selecting only predicted futures judged behaviorally compatible with the recorded action. We evaluate pretrained checkpoints directly, without per-task fine-tuning, on 100 tasks across 20 manipulation skill groups with held-out scenes, backgrounds, lighting, and object instances. Scaling co-training data from 300 to 30,000 hours raises success from 17.1% to 44.1% on G1-OP and from 13.4% to 31.1% on G2-90D; despite comprising less than 2% of the co-training data, G2-90D improves by 17.7 points, suggesting cross-embodiment transfer. Gains span 19/20 and 18/20 skill groups, and skill-specific coverage strongly correlates with zero-shot out-of-distribution (OOD) success (Pearson r=0.80; Spearman rho=0.85). Under the same protocol, the model grounds object, color, shape, and position references in at least 90% of trials and follows explicit instructions even when they conflict with an already-committed behavior or a conventional scene association.

AI.tldr: GE-Act 2.0 is a world-action model built entirely from scratch on manipulation data, combining a control-oriented autoencoder, single-step visual planner, and inverse dynamics model. Scaling co-training data from 300 to 30,000 hours improves success from ~17% to ~44% on manipulation benchmarks, demonstrates cross-embodiment transfer, strong OOD generalization, and robust instruction following even under conflicting contexts.
AI.motivation: Most world-action models inherit pretrained video generators, leaving WAM pretraining and scaling underexplored. The authors aim to investigate whether a WAM trained entirely from scratch on manipulation data can achieve strong task performance, while enabling separate pretraining of visual planning and inverse dynamics on complementary data sources.
AI.method: GE-Act 2.0 introduces three components: (1) a control-oriented autoencoder (CoAE) that preserves action- and instruction-relevant information under aggressive compression; (2) a single-step visual planner (SVP) that produces a complete future state in one differentiable pass; and (3) an inverse dynamics model (IDM). These are pretrained separately then jointly trained using knowledge-aligned selective optimization (KASO), which filters predicted futures by behavioral compatibility with recorded actions to reduce mismatched supervision.
AI.result: On 100 tasks across 20 manipulation skill groups with held-out scenes and object instances, scaling co-training from 300 to 30,000 hours improves success from 17.1% to 44.1% (G1-OP) and 13.4% to 31.1% (G2-90D). Despite being <2% of co-training data, G2-90D improves 17.7 points, indicating cross-embodiment transfer. Gains span 19/20 and 18/20 skill groups, with skill-specific coverage strongly correlating with zero-shot OOD success (Pearson r=0.80). The model grounds object/color/shape/position references in ≥90% of trials and follows instructions conflicting with committed behaviors or conventional scene associations.
AI.conclusion: GE-Act 2.0 demonstrates that world-action models can be effectively pretrained and scaled from scratch on manipulation data rather than relying on video generators, achieving strong scaling behavior, cross-embodiment transfer, and instruction-following robustness under out-of-distribution conditions.

title: AutoFyn Technical Report: Non-Parametric Expert Iteration for Long-Horizon Agents
summary: We introduce AutoFyn, an agent harness inspired by the Expert Iteration algorithm, adapting a frozen model across many rounds by updating persistent state from verified reward signals rather than model weights. Each round begins from a fresh model session, and durable information is reintroduced only through explicit interfaces such as persistent memory files, reports, and repository state. Within a round, an orchestrator explores, plans and builds many alternative approaches with specialized agents, while a task-grounded verifier verifies the work and supplies an objective reward for measuring progress. This reward is distilled back into the persistent state, which updates the effective policy for the next round. In this technical report, we formalize this loop and describe its persistent state and verification interfaces. We then demonstrate its use in three domains, namely olympiad mathematics, data science, and cybersecurity. On the six fresh problems of the 2026 International Mathematical Olympiad, every model with room to improve scores higher under AutoFyn than in its provider's own coding agent. AutoFyn also built the top-ranked agent on the Spider 2.0 dbt benchmark, and has produced $16$ maintainer-confirmed vulnerability advisories in Next.js, MetaMask, pnpm, Warp, LiteLLM, Langflow, and Open WebUI.

AI.tldr: AutoFyn is an agent harness based on Expert Iteration that improves a frozen model's performance across rounds by updating persistent state (memory files, reports, repository state) from verified reward signals instead of updating model weights. It demonstrates success across olympiad mathematics (outperforming provider coding agents on 2026 IMO problems), data science (top-ranked on Spider 2.0 dbt), and cybersecurity (16 maintainer-confirmed vulnerability advisories across major open-source projects).
AI.motivation: To enable continuous improvement of foundation models without costly weight updates, by leveraging verified reward signals to iteratively refine an agent's persistent state and effective policy across rounds.
AI.method: AutoFyn formalizes an Expert Iteration-style loop: each round starts a fresh model session; an orchestrator explores, plans, and builds multiple approaches with specialized agents; a task-grounded verifier checks work and produces an objective reward; and that reward is distilled into persistent state (memory files, reports, repository state) that shapes the next round's effective policy.
AI.result: AutoFyn outperforms provider coding agents on all six fresh 2026 IMO problems for every model with room to improve, achieved the top-ranked agent on the Spider 2.0 dbt benchmark, and produced 16 maintainer-confirmed vulnerability advisories in Next.js, MetaMask, pnpm, Warp, LiteLLM, Langflow, and Open WebUI.
AI.conclusion: A frozen model can be adaptively improved via persistent state updates from verified rewards, enabling competitive performance across mathematics, data science, and security domains without modifying model weights.

title: Adaptive Cost-Sensitive Machine Learning for Autonomous Robot Navigation Failure Prediction: When Not All Errors Are Equal
summary: Autonomous robot navigation failures differ not only in categorical severity but also in the physical context in which they occur. A near-miss at low speed under reliable sensing is not equivalent to the same event during rapid motion, close obstacle approach or degraded perception. This paper reframes navigation failure prediction as consequence-sensitive forecasting. We first establish a fixed baseline in which training weights are modulated by categorical severity, then introduce an adaptive extension defining a state-dependent consequence function combining severity with normalised velocity, obstacle proximity and sensing uncertainty, together with a risk-sensitivity term that rises as conditions deteriorate. We evaluate on 2,000 simulated differential-drive episodes (~1,000,000 timesteps) using episode-level GroupKFold, with external validation on the UCI SCITOS G5 dataset. Fixed weighting raises Logistic Regression high-severity recall from 0.851 to 0.985 and reduces missed consequence cost from 1,940 to 313; the adaptive extension reaches 0.998 and 82. Under matched false-positive conditions, however, the discriminative advantage is modest (0.986 versus 0.984), so most of the gain reflects a more conservative operating point rather than better ranking. The effect is consistent across all five folds and stable across a threefold span of context coefficients. Because the primary simulation produced no collisions, we add a controlled extension in which 108 of 600 episodes terminate in contact: collision recall rises from 0.850 to 0.966 (fixed) and 0.984 (adaptive), with missed collision cost falling from 1,000 to 105, at false-positive rates of 0.413 and 0.799, respectively. Context-dependent consequence modelling thus provides a principled mechanism for allocating conservatism by physical risk.

AI.tldr: This paper reframes autonomous robot navigation failure prediction as consequence-sensitive forecasting, introducing a state-dependent consequence function that combines categorical severity with velocity, obstacle proximity, and sensing uncertainty. Evaluations on 2,000 simulated episodes show fixed weighting raises high-severity recall from 0.851 to 0.985 and cuts missed consequence cost from 1,940 to 313, with an adaptive extension reaching 0.998 and 82. In a controlled collision extension, collision recall rises to 0.984 with missed collision cost dropping from 1,000 to 105, though discriminative gains over mere conservative operating-point shifts are modest under matched false positives.
AI.motivation: Navigation failure prediction must account not only for categorical severity but also physical context — a near-miss during rapid motion, close obstacle approach, or degraded perception is not equivalent to the same event under safe conditions. Existing methods ignore this state-dependence when allocating conservatism.
AI.method: The paper first establishes a fixed baseline where training weights are modulated by categorical severity. It then introduces an adaptive extension defining a state-dependent consequence function combining severity with normalized velocity, obstacle proximity, sensing uncertainty, plus a risk-sensitivity term that grows as conditions deteriorate. Evaluation uses episode-level GroupKFold on 2,000 simulated differential-drive episodes (~1,000,000 timesteps) with external validation on UCI SCITOS G5, plus a controlled collision extension with 108/600 contact episodes.
AI.result: Fixed weighting raises Logistic Regression high-severity recall from 0.851 to 0.985 and reduces missed consequence cost from 1,940 to 313; adaptive reaches 0.998 and 82. Under matched false positives, discriminative advantage is modest (0.986 vs 0.984), indicating gains are largely from a conservative operating point. In collision extension, recall rises 0.850→0.966 (fixed) and 0.984 (adaptive), with missed collision cost 1,000→105 at FPR 0.413 and 0.799. Results stable across five folds and threefold context-coefficient span.
AI.conclusion: Context-dependent consequence modelling provides a principled mechanism for allocating conservatism according to physical risk, offering a practical framework for consequence-sensitive failure prediction in autonomous navigation. The main benefit is calibrated conservative operating-point selection rather than dramatically improved ranking.

title: Damage-Aware Bandit Pruning for Vision and Language Transformers
summary: Structured post-training pruning of transformers requires selecting complete functional units whose suppression causes limited degradation. We formulate structured-unit selection for language and vision transformers as a damage-aware multi-armed bandit problem under a fixed candidate-evaluation budget. Attention heads and MLP channel groups are temporarily masked on calibration batches. Paired damage is the masked loss minus the base loss on the same batch, reducing batch-to-batch variation. A smooth bounded reward drives either a UCB-style policy or fractional-Beta Thompson Sampling, and the final mask is constructed sequentially by adding one unit at each step. The selected units are functionally zeroed in the original dense checkpoint; therefore, the reported parameter effects represent effective structural suppression rather than physical compression or measured speedup. Experiments on WikiText-2, LAMBADA, and Imagenette cover GPT-2, OPT, Pythia, Qwen2.5, SmolLM2, ViT-B/16, DeiT-Tiny, and Swin-Tiny, with comparisons against random, magnitude, static-saliency, and budgeted-greedy selection. Across five seeds, the bandit methods usually reduce degradation relative to budgeted greedy in the paired language-model comparisons. Of 28 comparisons highlighted in the paper, 23 bootstrap confidence intervals exclude zero and 11 paired tests have p < 0.05; six have q < 0.05 after Benjamini-Hochberg correction across the full family of 116 dataset-wise tests. Matched-evaluation results for ViT-B/16 and Swin-Tiny indicate that their gains are not explained solely by a larger candidate-evaluation budget.

AI.tldr: This paper frames structured post-training pruning of transformers as a damage-aware multi-armed bandit problem, selecting functional units (attention heads and MLP channel groups) via sequential UCB or fractional-Beta Thompson Sampling policies under a fixed evaluation budget. Experiments across multiple language and vision models show bandit methods generally reduce degradation compared to budgeted greedy selection, though only a subset of comparisons reach statistical significance after multiple-testing correction.
AI.motivation: Structured pruning of transformers requires selecting complete functional units whose removal causes minimal performance degradation, but existing methods lack an efficient, damage-aware decision framework under limited candidate-evaluation budgets.
AI.method: The approach formulates unit selection as a multi-armed bandit problem. Attention heads and MLP channel groups are temporarily masked on calibration batches; paired damage (masked loss minus base loss per batch) reduces variance. A smooth bounded reward drives either UCB-style policy or fractional-Beta Thompson Sampling. The final mask is built sequentially one unit at a time, with selected units functionally zeroed in the original dense checkpoint.
AI.result: Experiments on WikiText-2, LAMBADA, and Imagenette across GPT-2, OPT, Pythia, Qwen2.5, SmolLM2, ViT-B/16, DeiT-Tiny, and Swin-Tiny show bandit methods usually reduce degradation relative to budgeted greedy in paired language-model comparisons. Of 28 highlighted comparisons, 23 bootstrap confidence intervals exclude zero, 11 have p<0.05, and 6 survive Benjamini-Hochberg correction across 116 tests. Matched-evaluation results for ViT-B/16 and Swin-Tiny indicate gains are not solely explained by larger evaluation budgets.
AI.conclusion: Bandit-based structured pruning provides a viable and generally superior alternative to budgeted greedy selection for transformer structured pruning, with statistically meaningful (though not universally significant after multiple-testing correction) improvements across diverse model architectures and modalities.

title: Closed-Loop Evaluation of Bird's-Eye-View Maps from Cross-View Transformers as Inputs to Behavior-Cloning Policies
summary: In autonomous driving, Bird's-Eye View (BEV) representations provide a structured, top-down abstraction of the vehicle's surroundings and have become a key input modality for Behavioral Cloning (BC) policies. While ground-truth BEV maps are readily available in simulation, real-world deployment requires replacing them with camera-predicted counterparts - a substitution that introduces perceptual errors whose downstream impact on closed-loop driving performance is not well understood. In this work, we investigate the use of Cross-View Transformer (CVT)-predicted BEV maps as direct policy inputs for a BC agent in the CARLA simulator. We propose a six-channel BEV representation covering road surface, planned route, lane boundaries, vehicles, pedestrians, and traffic lights, and introduce a Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) weighting scheme that rebalances the segmentation loss towards underrepresented driving maneuvers such as curves and intersections. Closed-loop evaluation across two CARLA towns shows that the KDE-weighted model is the only predicted-BEV agent to complete a full episode without infractions, despite not achieving the highest aggregate IoU. This discrepancy reveals that global segmentation metrics are poor proxies for driving performance: what determines navigation success is prediction quality at geometrically critical locations, and the route channel emerges as the primary bottleneck for reliable agent navigation under predicted BEV inputs.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates using CVT-predicted BEV maps as direct inputs for behavioral cloning agents in autonomous driving. They propose a six-channel BEV representation and a KDE-based loss reweighting scheme targeting underrepresented maneuvers. Closed-loop CARLA evaluation shows the KDE-weighted model alone completes a full episode without infractions, despite not having the highest IoU, revealing that geometric-critical prediction quality—not aggregate segmentation metrics—determines driving success.
AI.motivation: Real-world autonomous driving with BEV-based behavioral cloning requires replacing ground-truth BEV maps (available in simulation) with camera-predicted counterparts. The downstream impact of these perceptual errors on closed-loop driving performance is poorly understood, motivating an investigation into how predicted-BEV inputs affect BC policy behavior.
AI.method: The authors use CVT-predicted BEV maps as direct policy inputs for a BC agent in CARLA. They design a six-channel BEV representation (road surface, planned route, lane boundaries, vehicles, pedestrians, traffic lights) and introduce a KDE-based weighting scheme that rebalances the segmentation loss toward underrepresented driving maneuvers such as curves and intersections. Closed-loop evaluation is conducted across two CARLA towns.
AI.result: The KDE-weighted model is the only predicted-BEV agent to complete a full episode without any infractions. Notably, it does not achieve the highest aggregate IoU, demonstrating that global segmentation metrics are poor proxies for closed-loop driving performance. The route channel is identified as the primary bottleneck for reliable navigation under predicted BEV inputs.
AI.conclusion: Prediction quality at geometrically critical locations—not overall segmentation accuracy—determines navigation success. Loss reweighting toward underrepresented maneuvers can mitigate the impact of perceptual errors, and the route channel specifically requires more reliable prediction for robust autonomous driving.

title: Compiling VGDL into Causal Models
comment: To be published at IEEE Conference on Games 2026
summary: Reinforcement learning and large language models often struggle to accurately capture the causal mechanics of game environments. Standard reinforcement learning agents tend to rely on spurious correlations, while large language models are prone to hallucinating game rules. Although causal reinforcement learning improves interpretability, there is currently no formal methodology to map complex game mechanics directly into causal models. To address this, we propose a deterministic framework that compiles games specified in the Video Game Description Language into Dynamic Structural Causal Models. Rather than inferring causal structures from gameplay traces or noisy large language models' outputs, our methodology directly translates game components, including sprite dynamics, interaction rules, and termination conditions, into explicit structural equations. Each game tick represents a causal transition from state variables at time $t$ to $t+1$. By establishing this grounded mapping, the approach guarantees absolute causal fidelity to the ground-truth game mechanics. The resulting models offer transparent causal pathways that support counterfactual reasoning, causal reinforcement learning agent training, and procedural content validation. This framework provides a principled bridge between symbolic game descriptions and causally grounded game AI.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a deterministic framework that compiles Video Game Description Language (VGDL) games into Dynamic Structural Causal Models (DSCMs), providing a principled bridge between symbolic game descriptions and causally grounded game AI.
AI.motivation: Reinforcement learning agents rely on spurious correlations and large language models hallucinate game rules, and there is no existing formal methodology to map complex game mechanics directly into causal models.
AI.method: The framework directly translates VGDL game components—sprite dynamics, interaction rules, and termination conditions—into explicit structural equations, where each game tick represents a causal transition of state variables from time t to t+1.
AI.result: The approach guarantees absolute causal fidelity to ground-truth game mechanics, producing models with transparent causal pathways that support counterfactual reasoning, causal RL agent training, and procedural content validation.
AI.conclusion: This framework provides a principled and deterministic bridge between symbolic game descriptions and causally grounded game AI, eliminating the need for causal structure inference from noisy data sources.

title: CR-VLA-Force: Learning Control-aware Compliance VLA Model for Robust Contact-rich Robotic Manipulation
comment: 14 pages, 8 figures. Accepted by IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RA-L)
summary: Integrating visuomotor policies or Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models with force/torque (F/T) perception has demonstrated significant progress in imitation learning for robotic manipulation. However, existing force-aware VLA models frequently exhibit limited capability in precise force tracking and rapid successive adjustments. This deficiency stems from the limitations of action-chunk execution strategies and the substantial latency between perception and real-time control. Such limitations can lead to task failures and safety risks, particularly when the execution of an action chunk exerts excessive interaction forces without timely adjustment. To overcome this challenge, we propose the Control-aware Compliance VLA (CC-VLA) framework for reactive control. The CC-VLA model employs a multimodal mixture-of-experts (MoE) to encode force signal sequences and vision-language fused feature. Furthermore, it utilizes a multi-stage training strategy to ensure robust perception within the visual-semantic space and effective force perception under sparse sampling conditions. Additionally, a VLA-guided adaptive compliance controller is designed to facilitate precise position tracking during contact-free motion and optimal force-position tracking for contact-rich tasks. To facilitate high-precision F/T data acquisition, we also implement an adversaria shared teleoperation strategy for contact-rich demonstrations that bolsters system safety and interactivity. Extensive real-world experiments demonstrate that CC-VLA significantly improves success rates in challenging force-perception tasks and enhances force-control precision, while providing multi-level safety and robustness under the tested partial-OOD pose-shift settings.

AI.tldr: CC-VLA is a Control-aware Compliance Vision-Language-Action framework that integrates force/torque perception into VLA models for robotic manipulation, addressing limitations in precise force tracking and rapid adjustments through multimodal mixture-of-experts, multi-stage training, an adaptive compliance controller, and adversarial shared teleoperation for data collection.
AI.motivation: Existing force-aware VLA models struggle with precise force tracking and rapid successive adjustments due to action-chunk execution strategies and perception-to-control latency, leading to task failures and safety risks when excessive interaction forces are exerted without timely correction.
AI.method: The CC-VLA framework includes: (1) a multimodal mixture-of-experts (MoE) encoder for force signal sequences and vision-language fused features; (2) a multi-stage training strategy for robust visual-semantic perception and effective force perception under sparse sampling; (3) a VLA-guided adaptive compliance controller for position tracking during contact-free motion and force-position tracking in contact-rich tasks; and (4) an adversarial shared teleoperation strategy for collecting high-precision F/T contact-rich demonstrations.
AI.result: Extensive real-world experiments show CC-VLA significantly improves success rates on challenging force-perception tasks, enhances force-control precision, and provides multi-level safety and robustness under partial out-of-distribution pose-shift settings.
AI.conclusion: CC-VLA effectively overcomes the limitations of prior force-aware VLA models by enabling reactive, control-aware compliance behavior, improving both task success and safety in real-world robotic manipulation.

title: ARC-Bench: Closed-Loop Replanning Masks Broken Action Ranking in Frozen JEPA World Models
summary: Reward-free latent world models plan by scoring candidate actions with distances in a frozen latent space: an action is preferred if its predicted future embedding lands closer to the goal embedding. This silently assumes that latent closeness is action-rankable, i.e., that ordering candidates by latent distance agrees with ordering them by true cost. We audit this assumption directly. We introduce ARC-Bench, a no-leak, fixed-candidate protocol that measures whether frozen JEPA-style objectives rank candidate actions correctly, and apply it to official released JEPA-WM checkpoints across navigation and manipulation-style control. The assumption fails, severely and structurally: on the official manipulation audits the top-scored candidate is almost always suboptimal, and the same inversion appears in the maze domains. A controlled visual-backbone extension shows that the defect persists when DINOv2 is replaced by video-pretrained V-JEPA 1 and V-JEPA 2 encoders at ViT-L/ViT-G scale. Provenance, undertraining, matched-budget backbone controls, and metric-circularity controls rule out trivial explanations. We then explain why this defect has stayed invisible: closed-loop replanning masks it. When we reduce the planner's replanning frequency, success collapses in both a navigation and a manipulation domain, and the episodes rescued by frequent replanning are enriched for severe first-plan ranking failures in the PointMaze first-plan diagnostic. Closed-loop success rates therefore systematically overstate the rankability of frozen latent representations. ARC-Bench supplies the measurement, and the masking mechanism the explanation, for methods that adapt, amortize, or replan around latent-space planners without directly auditing released JEPA-WM action rankability.

AI.tldr: This paper audits whether frozen JEPA-style latent world models can correctly rank candidate actions by latent distance, proposing ARC-Bench—a no-leak, fixed-candidate protocol that reveals severe and structural rankability failures in official JEPA-WM checkpoints across navigation and manipulation domains. The authors show closed-loop replanning masks these failures: when replanning frequency is reduced, success rates collapse, demonstrating that closed-loop metrics systematically overstate latent-space action rankability.
AI.motivation: Reward-free latent world models (JEPA-WM) plan by ordering candidate actions according to latent-space closeness to a goal embedding, implicitly assuming that latent distance agrees with true cost ordering. This fundamental assumption—action rankability—has never been directly audited. Since these models are increasingly deployed and adapted, verifying this assumption is critical, especially given the lack of any published evaluation of released JEPA-WM action rankability.
AI.method: The authors introduce ARC-Bench, a fixed-candidate, no-leak protocol that measures whether frozen JEPA-style objectives (InfoNCE, VICReg, etc.) rank candidate actions correctly against ground-truth optimality. They apply ARC-Bench to official released JEPA-WM checkpoints across maze navigation and manipulation-style control tasks. They also perform a controlled visual-backbone study replacing DINOv2 with V-JEPA 1/2 encoders at ViT-L/ViT-G scale, plus controlled experiments to rule out provenance, undertraining, matched-budget backbone, and metric-circularity explanations. Finally, they conduct closed-loop replanning-frequency ablation experiments to test the hypothesis that frequent replanning masks rankability failures.
AI.result: The latent-closeness action-ranking assumption fails severely and structurally: on official manipulation audits, the top-scored candidate is almost always suboptimal, with the same inversion appearing in maze domains. The defect persists when DINOv2 is replaced by video-pretrained V-JEPA encoders at large scale. Trivial explanations (provenance, undertraining, backbone budget, metric circularity) are ruled out. When replanning frequency is reduced, success collapses in both navigation and manipulation domains, and episodes rescued by frequent replanning are enriched for severe first-plan ranking failures.
AI.conclusion: Closed-loop success rates systematically overstate the rankability of frozen latent representations in JEPA-style world models. ARC-Bench provides a direct measurement of this failure, and the masking mechanism (closed-loop replanning) explains why it has remained invisible. Methods that adapt, amortize, or replan around latent-space planners must directly audit action rankability rather than relying on closed-loop performance.

title: A4A: Cross-Embodiment Transfer of Action-Oriented 4D Affordances from Human Demonstrations
summary: Human demonstrations contain rich manipulation knowledge, but it remains unclear what information can be transferred effectively to robot control. Existing affordance representations are typically formulated as 2D masks, 3D regions, contact points, or actionability scores, and therefore primarily identify where interaction may occur. However, effective manipulation also requires modeling how interaction-relevant geometry evolves during task execution. To bridge this gap, we introduce action-oriented 4D affordances, which represent the language-conditioned future trajectories of interaction-relevant 3D points. These trajectories capture task-conditioned geometric evolution rather than embodiment-specific actions, enabling transferable interaction priors across humans and robots. Based on this representation, we construct a large-scale action-oriented 4D affordance dataset from existing human--object interaction video data and complementary RGB-D demonstrations, and introduce A4A, an affordance-to-action framework that uses 4D affordance trajectory prediction to pretrain robot policies before manipulation fine-tuning. Experiments in both simulation and the real world validate the effectiveness of A4A, showing that pretraining with action-oriented 4D affordance data consistently improves the manipulation performance of diverse VLA policies. These results establish action-oriented 4D affordances as an effective cross-embodiment representation for transferring manipulation knowledge from human demonstrations to robot control.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces action-oriented 4D affordances, which represent language-conditioned future trajectories of interaction-relevant 3D points, capturing task-conditioned geometric evolution rather than embodiment-specific actions. They build a large-scale dataset from human-object interaction videos and RGB-D demonstrations, and propose A4A, an affordance-to-action framework that pretrains robot policies via 4D affordance trajectory prediction before manipulation fine-tuning, showing consistent improvements across diverse VLA policies in simulation and real-world experiments.
AI.motivation: Existing affordance representations (2D masks, 3D regions, contact points, actionability scores) primarily identify where interaction may occur but fail to model how interaction-relevant geometry evolves during task execution, which is essential for effective manipulation.
AI.method: The authors propose action-oriented 4D affordances representing language-conditioned future trajectories of interaction-relevant 3D points, construct a large-scale dataset from human-object interaction videos and RGB-D demonstrations, and introduce A4A — an affordance-to-action framework using 4D affordance trajectory prediction to pretrain robot policies before manipulation fine-tuning.
AI.result: Experiments in simulation and the real world demonstrate that A4A pretraining with action-oriented 4D affordance data consistently improves the manipulation performance of diverse VLA (vision-language-action) policies.
AI.conclusion: Action-oriented 4D affordances serve as an effective cross-embodiment representation for transferring manipulation knowledge from human demonstrations to robot control.

title: RAPID: Reliability-Aware Pair Importance Distillation
summary: Inter example relational distillation transfers a teacher's representation geometry by matching relations among examples within a mini batch. Computing all pairs has quadratic complexity in the batch size, whereas uniform subsampling may use a limited relation budget inefficiently. We introduce Reliability Aware Pair Importance Distillation, or RAPID, which separates a reliability gated relational target from a full support adaptive pair proposal. Reliability determines which teacher relations are emphasized, while calibrated teacher entropy and detached student-teacher residuals determine which relations are evaluated. Exact inverse proposal correction makes the loss and gradient estimators conditionally unbiased with respect to the gated mini batch target. We evaluate RAPID in two text classification settings: AG News with BERT-to-DistilBERT distillation using three paired seeds and a relation budget of 256, and SST-2 with DistilBERT to DistilBERT distillation using three paired seeds and a relation budget of 64. Reliability gated relational distillation achieves the highest observed mean student accuracy on both datasets: 94.285 plus or minus 0.054 percent on AG News and 88.800 plus or minus 0.532 percent on SST-2. RAPID ranks second, achieving 94.241 plus or minus 0.025 percent and 88.685 plus or minus 0.462 percent, respectively, compared with 94.154 plus or minus 0.124 percent and 87.271 plus or minus 0.162 percent for the cross entropy baseline. Pilot evaluations are counted toward the same total budget as the main relation evaluations. Across both settings, the gated target yields the highest mean accuracy, while the adaptive proposal remains within seed-level variation. These results support the modular view that target reliability and evaluation priority are separable design dimensions.

AI.tldr: RAPID (Reliability Aware Pair Importance Distillation) improves inter-example relational distillation by separating a reliability-gated relational target from an adaptive pair proposal. It uses calibrated teacher entropy and detached student-teacher residuals for adaptive sampling with exact inverse proposal correction for unbiased estimation, achieving top mean student accuracy on AG News (94.285%) and SST-2 (88.800%) text classification benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing inter-example relational distillation methods face a key efficiency problem: computing all pairs within a batch has quadratic complexity, while uniform subsampling wastes a limited relation budget on uninformative pairs. The paper aims to address how to spend a fixed relation budget effectively by determining which relations matter (reliability) and which relations to evaluate (priority).
AI.method: RAPID decomposes relational distillation into two orthogonal components: (1) a reliability-gated relational target that determines which teacher relations are emphasized, and (2) an adaptive pair proposal mechanism that uses calibrated teacher entropy and detached student-teacher residuals to select which relations are evaluated. Exact inverse proposal correction ensures the loss and gradient estimators remain conditionally unbiased with respect to the gated mini-batch target.
AI.result: Evaluated on AG News (BERT-to-DistilBERT, 3 paired seeds, relation budget 256) and SST-2 (DistilBERT-to-DistilBERT, 3 paired seeds, relation budget 64). Reliability-gated relational distillation achieves highest mean accuracy: 94.285±0.054% on AG News and 88.800±0.532% on SST-2. RAPID ranks second at 94.241±0.025% and 88.685±0.462%, both outperforming the cross-entropy baseline (94.154±0.124% and 87.271±0.162%).
AI.conclusion: The results support a modular design view where target reliability (which relations matter) and evaluation priority (which relations to spend budget on) are separable dimensions. The gated target consistently yields the highest mean accuracy, while the adaptive proposal stays within seed-level variation, suggesting reliability gating is the more critical factor for relational distillation performance.

title: GIF: Agentic Generation of Interactive and Functional Object Compositions for Robot Learning
summary: Robot manipulation foundation models require scalable evaluation and data generation across diverse scenarios, with simulation providing an environment for both. Automated scene generation offers a promising path, yet prior work has largely emphasized coarse-grained scene layouts rather than fine-grained functional object compositions. Motivated by this gap, we present GIF, an agentic Generation framework for Interactive and Functional object compositions. In this framework, we recast this problem as disentangled reconstruction followed by relative pose recovery. CoGen produces instance-disentangled meshes with coarse initial poses leveraging complementary strengths of 2D and 3D generative models. GPRM refines the relative pose under joint geometric and physical guidance, and a VLM verifier selects the candidate that best matches the structured specification. We further construct a benchmark spanning eight representative contact-geometry classes and compare with state-of-the-art generators; GIF improves both asset quality and relation matching, while reducing collision rate to below 1%. Finally, we synthesize data for policy learning, revealing diversity scaling in both simulation and real-world deployment.

AI.tldr: GIF is an agentic generation framework for interactive and functional object compositions, combining CoGen (disentangled reconstruction with 2D/3D generative models), GPRM (physical-geometric guided pose refinement), and a VLM verifier. It reduces collision rate below 1%, improves asset quality and relation matching, and demonstrates diversity scaling in policy learning across simulation and real-world deployment.
AI.motivation: Robot manipulation foundation models need scalable evaluation and data generation across diverse scenarios. Prior automated scene generation work has emphasized coarse-grained scene layouts rather than fine-grained functional object compositions, motivating the need for a framework that generates precise, physically plausible, and functional object arrangements.
AI.method: GIF decomposes the problem into (1) instance-disentangled reconstruction by CoGen, which generates meshes with coarse initial poses by leveraging complementary strengths of 2D and 3D generative models, followed by (2) relative pose recovery via GPRM, which refines poses under joint geometric and physical guidance, and (3) a VLM verifier that selects candidates best matching the structured specification.
AI.result: Evaluated on a benchmark spanning eight contact-geometry classes, GIF surpasses state-of-the-art generators in both asset quality and relation matching, reducing collision rate to below 1%. Synthesized data additionally reveals diversity scaling for policy learning in simulation and real-world deployment.
AI.conclusion: GIF demonstrates that an agentic, multi-stage framework combining generation, physically guided pose refinement, and VLM-based verification can produce high-quality, functional object compositions at scale, enabling improved robot policy learning through diverse synthetic data.

title: PGP-Clinical-TimeKAN: Prior-Guided Joint Probabilistic Forecasting of Clinical Trajectories
summary: Clinical deterioration unfolds through coupled, partially observed trajectories, not a single diagnostic label. We introduce PGP-Clinical-TimeKAN, a trajectory-first framework for joint probabilistic forecasting of multivariate physiology. It combines missingness-aware temporal encoders, a soft organ-system prior, patient-specific relations, nonlinear Kolmogorov-Arnold messages, and a low-rank multivariate Student-t head. We evaluate 24-hour histories and six-hour forecasts on a frozen MIMIC-IV-derived cohort of 6,882 patients and 54,694 windows. Across five seeds and 13 models, PGP-Clinical-TimeKAN obtains the second-lowest normalized MAE (0.37727 +/- 0.00029) and the lowest RMSE (0.52656 +/- 0.00034). It reduces MAE by 0.52% relative to deterministic TimeKAN. For probabilistic forecasting, it reaches a marginal NLL of 0.66380 and a CRPS of 0.27301. Empirical coverage is 0.533, 0.831, and 0.958 for nominal 50%, 80%, and 95% intervals. Removing relational structure causes the largest ablation loss. Increasing covariance rank improves joint likelihood but has little effect on point accuracy. A trajectory-derived risk score remains weaker than a dedicated GRU-D classifier (AUROC 0.603 versus 0.650), which limits the present clinical claim. Joint trajectory forecasting therefore provides an inspectable intermediate task, but accurate physiology forecasts alone do not ensure a calibrated event detector.

AI.tldr: PGP-Clinical-TimeKAN is a trajectory-first framework for joint probabilistic forecasting of multivariate physiology on MIMIC-IV, achieving strong point and probabilistic accuracy but limiting clinical utility as an event detector.
AI.motivation: Clinical deterioration is fundamentally a coupled, partially observed process across multiple physiological trajectories rather than a single diagnostic label. Existing approaches overlook this trajectory-first nature, motivating a framework that models joint probabilistic evolution of multivariate physiology.
AI.method: The framework combines missingness-aware temporal encoders, a soft organ-system prior, patient-specific relations, nonlinear Kolmogorov-Arnold message passing, and a low-rank multivariate Student-t output head for joint probabilistic forecasting of physiology.
AI.result: On a frozen MIMIC-IV cohort (6,882 patients, 54,694 windows, 24-hour histories, 6-hour forecasts), across five seeds and 13 models, PGP-Clinical-TimeKAN achieves the second-lowest normalized MAE (0.37727 ± 0.00029) and lowest RMSE (0.52656 ± 0.00034), reducing MAE by 0.52% over deterministic TimeKAN. It reaches marginal NLL of 0.66380 and CRPS of 0.27301 with empirical coverage of 0.533/0.831/0.958 for nominal 50/80/95% intervals. Removing relational structure yields the largest ablation loss; increasing covariance rank improves joint likelihood but not point accuracy. The trajectory-derived risk score underperforms a dedicated GRU-D classifier (AUROC 0.603 vs 0.650).
AI.conclusion: Joint trajectory forecasting provides an inspectable intermediate task with accurate physiology predictions, but accurate forecasts alone do not guarantee a calibrated event detector, limiting the present clinical claim.

title: Moment-Matching Probabilistic Data Association for Optimization-Based SLAM
summary: Optimization-based simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) makes it possible to reduce accumulated navigation errors of sensing platforms by returning to known areas (loop closure). In this paper, we present an approach to combine probabilistic data association (PDA) with optimization-based SLAM. Instead of associating a single measurement with each landmark, we follow the PDA paradigm from the multiobject tracking community. In particular, in a processing stage performed in addition to the nonlinear least-squares solver of optimization-based SLAM, our method (i) assigns multiple measurements to landmarks probabilistically, (ii) computes the mean and covariance of landmark distributions via moment matching by taking multiple measurement-to-landmark associations into account, and (iii) establishes a virtual landmark measurement and a corresponding linear-Gaussian measurement model that leads to the mean and covariance matrix as moment-matching PDA in (ii). By converting the PDA update step into an equivalent linear-Gaussian measurement update step, PDA can be performed effectively within any optimization-based SLAM method. Our preliminary numerical evaluation in a scenario with false negatives and false positives indicates that incremental smoothing and mapping 2 (iSAM2), combined with the proposed PDA approach, can improve agent localization performance compared to conventional iSAM2.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a method to integrate probabilistic data association (PDA) into optimization-based SLAM by converting the PDA update step into an equivalent linear-Gaussian measurement update, enabling robust loop closure under ambiguous data associations.
AI.motivation: Optimization-based SLAM reduces accumulated navigation errors via loop closure, but relies on hard (single) measurement-to-landmark associations, which struggle under false positives/negatives and ambiguous data. The authors seek to bring the probabilistic data association paradigm from multiobject tracking into optimization-based SLAM to handle measurement uncertainty more gracefully.
AI.method: The proposed approach adds a processing stage alongside the nonlinear least-squares solver that (i) assigns multiple measurements to landmarks probabilistically following the PDA paradigm, (ii) computes the mean and covariance of landmark distributions via moment matching over multiple measurement-to-landmark associations, and (iii) constructs a virtual landmark measurement with a linear-Gaussian measurement model that reproduces the moment-matching PDA mean and covariance. This transforms the PDA update into an equivalent standard measurement update, allowing it to be plugged into any optimization-based SLAM framework such as iSAM2.
AI.result: Preliminary numerical evaluations in a scenario with false positives and false negatives show that iSAM2 augmented with the proposed PDA approach improves agent localization performance compared to conventional iSAM2.
AI.conclusion: The PDA-based association strategy can be effectively embedded within optimization-based SLAM through an equivalent linear-Gaussian virtual measurement, yielding improved robustness and localization accuracy under imperfect data association conditions.

title: SciLitBench: Benchmark and Design Principles for LLM-Powered Systematic Literature Reviews
comment: 22 pages, 6 figures, and 5 tables. Data and code are available at https://github.com/linlab/SciLitBench
summary: Systematic reviews require sustained human judgment across thousands of records, yet existing evaluations of large language models (LLMs) typically examine review stages in isolation. We introduce SciLitBench, a multi-stage benchmark spanning title and abstract screening, full-text screening, and schema-guided data extraction, with 42,981 retrieved records, 1,012 full texts, and annotations for 888 included papers. Across 22 open-weight LLMs from six model families, explicit inclusion and exclusion criteria improve title and abstract screening $F_2$ by 28.8\%, while researcher-authored rationales improve full-text screening by 15\%. Data extraction reveals a different reliability regime: performance declines from 0.97 accuracy for publication year to 0.37 Jaccard overlap for computational approach, while the strongest models recover only 30\% of annotated evaluation evidence and 25\% of limitations. SciLitBench identifies a practical boundary between high-recall screening and evidence-complete extraction and provides a reproducible resource for evaluating LLM-assisted evidence synthesis.

AI.tldr: SciLitBench is a multi-stage benchmark for evaluating LLMs across systematic review processes (title/abstract screening, full-text screening, and data extraction), built on 42,981 records, 1,012 full texts, and 888 annotated papers. Results show criteria improve screening by 28.8% F2, rationales improve full-text screening by 15%, but extraction reliability varies dramatically (0.97 accuracy to 0.37 Jaccard), revealing a boundary between where LLMs achieve high-recall screening and where they fall short on evidence-complete extraction.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of LLMs for systematic reviews examine review stages in isolation rather than the full workflow, which requires sustained human judgment across thousands of records.
