AI.method: The authors construct SciLitBench, a multi-stage benchmark spanning title/abstract screening, full-text screening, and schema-guided data extraction, with 42,981 retrieved records, 1,012 full texts, and annotations for 888 included papers. They evaluate 22 open-weight LLMs from six model families across all stages.
AI.result: Explicit inclusion/exclusion criteria improve title and abstract screening F2 by 28.8%. Researcher-authored rationales improve full-text screening by 15%. Data extraction accuracy ranges from 0.97 (publication year) to 0.37 Jaccard overlap (computational approach). The strongest models recover only 30% of evaluation evidence and 25% of limitations.
AI.conclusion: SciLitBench delineates a practical boundary between high-recall screening tasks where LLMs perform well and evidence-complete extraction where they fall short, providing a reproducible resource for evaluating LLM-assisted evidence synthesis.

title: Observation Design for Certified Control Authority: Projection--Estimability Separation and Active-Face Equivalence
summary: A sound runtime admission gate executes only actions it can certify, and certifies only what its observations support. This paper asks how observations should be designed to maximize the set of actions that can be safely admitted, and shows the question is not a re-vocabulary of classical design problems. First, a projection--estimability separation: decomposing a constraint normal as $c=c_{\mathrm{Range}}+c_{\ker}$ relative to an information matrix, two-point discrimination along $c$ becomes arbitrarily reliable as the budget grows whenever $c_{\mathrm{Range}}\neq 0$, while robust admission of an action with normal $c$ is impossible at every budget whenever $c_{\ker}\neq 0$; such mixed directions are generic at any deficient rank, and at full rank the decoupling is bounded by the Kantorovich ratio and diverges with the condition number. Discrimination-optimal designs, being corner solutions of a linear criterion, land in exactly this regime. Second, an active-face equivalence theorem: the permissiveness-optimal design is $L$-optimal for a target matrix generated endogenously by the action faces that become certification bottlenecks, weighted inversely by their remaining slack; single-face collapse recovers $c$-optimal and goal-oriented design exactly, and a Caratheodory argument yields a bottleneck certificate of at most $r(r+1)/2+1$ faces. Around these we assemble exact certifiability per convex contract mode, for which $κ\approx 3.29$ is derived rather than calibrated, the $\sqrt{r}$ price of contract-agnostic design, an information-to-slack transfer theorem with a curvature-budget corollary, and a two-part audit in which a design meeting every margin requirement still leaves an action face at a certification cost above ten times its testing cost, in every probe library tested.

AI.tldr: This paper studies how observation designs should be constructed to maximize the set of actions a runtime admission gate can safely certify, proving that the design problem is fundamentally distinct from classical statistical design problems. Key results include a projection–estimability separation theorem showing the interplay between constraint-normal components in the range vs. kernel of the information matrix, and an active-face equivalence theorem establishing that the permissiveness-optimal design is L-optimal for an endogenously generated target matrix, with a Carathéodory bottleneck certificate of at most r(r+1)/2+1 faces.
AI.motivation: A sound runtime admission gate must only execute actions it can certify based on its observations, yet existing work has not systematically addressed how the observation design itself should be chosen to maximize the set of safely admissible actions. The authors aim to show this is not merely a reformulation of classical experimental design problems but introduces genuinely new structural questions.
AI.method: The paper develops a theoretical framework decomposing constraint normals relative to the information matrix into range and kernel components, proving a projection–estimability separation: two-point discrimination becomes arbitrarily reliable as budget grows whenever the range component is nonzero, while robust admission is impossible at any budget if the kernel component is nonzero. It further proves an active-face equivalence theorem showing permissiveness-optimal designs correspond to L-optimality for an endogenously generated target matrix, weighted inversely by remaining slack on bottleneck constraint faces, with a Carathéodory-based bottleneck certificate.
AI.result: The results include: mixed (range+kernel) directions are generic at any deficient-rank information matrix; at full rank the decoupling is bounded by the Kantorovich ratio and diverges with condition number; discrimination-optimal designs fall into the deficient regime as corner solutions; the permissiveness-optimal design recovers c-optimal and goal-oriented design under single-face collapse; the constant κ ≈ 3.29 is derived (not calibrated) for exact certifiability per convex contract mode; a √r price is paid for contract-agnostic design; and a two-part audit demonstrates a real design can meet margin requirements yet admit an action face with certification cost over ten times its testing cost in every probe library tested.
AI.conclusion: Observation design for runtime admission gates is a structurally novel problem with its own geometry, characterized by range/ker separations, active-face optima, and sharp cost constants. The derived results provide exact certifiability bounds and reveal that even well-marginalized designs can fail to make certification economically viable, underscoring the need for design principles tailored to admission rather than discrimination alone.

title: SCAFFOLD: Self-Improving Web Agents via Recursive Parametric Skill Abstraction
summary: Web agents need to navigate visually rich, long-horizon interfaces that change across sites, yet most previous agents still learn each task in isolation and discard the procedural knowledge they accumulate. Recent skill-augmented frameworks take an important first step, but they treat the skill library as a flat or two-tier prompt-side cache and offer no principled mechanism for compressing redundancy or composing skills recursively. We introduce \textsc{Scaffold}, a self-improving framework for visual web agents that (i) induces parametric, executable skills from successful trajectories under a multi-instance abstraction constraint, (ii) maintains a recursively composed hierarchy in which higher-level skills invoke lower-level ones, (iii) compacts the library via a minimum-description-length (MDL) criterion and behavioral equivalence checking, and (iv) periodically distills skill-augmented trajectories back into model weights to internalize the abstractions. Across WebArena, VisualWebArena, and a held-out split of Online-Mind2Web, \textsc{Scaffold} improves success rate by $11.1$--$17.2$ absolute points over the strongest skill-augmented baseline and shows monotonic gains across five self-improvement iterations without library collapse. We release the code and documents in the Github \href{https://github.com/BokwaiHo/SCAFFOLD}{repository}.

AI.tldr: Scaffold is a self-improving framework for visual web agents that induces parametric executable skills from successful trajectories, organizes them into a recursively composed hierarchy, compresses the library via an MDL criterion with behavioral equivalence checking, and periodically distills skill-augmented trajectories into model weights. It outperforms strong skill-augmented baselines by 11.1-17.2 absolute points across WebArena, VisualWebArena, and Online-Mind2Web, with monotonic improvements over five self-improvement iterations without library collapse.
AI.motivation: Existing web agents learn each task in isolation and discard accumulated procedural knowledge. Prior skill-augmented frameworks treat the skill library as a flat or two-tier prompt-side cache, lacking principled mechanisms for compressing redundancy or composing skills recursively.
AI.method: Scaffold operates via four components: (i) inducing parametric, executable skills from successful trajectories under a multi-instance abstraction constraint; (ii) maintaining a recursively composed skill hierarchy where higher-level skills invoke lower-level ones; (iii) compacting the library using minimum-description-length (MDL) criterion plus behavioral equivalence checking; and (iv) periodically distilling skill-augmented trajectories back into model weights to internalize the learned abstractions.
AI.result: Across WebArena, VisualWebArena, and a held-out split of Online-Mind2Web, Scaffold improves success rate by 11.1-17.2 absolute points over the strongest skill-augmented baseline and shows monotonic gains across five self-improvement iterations without library collapse.
AI.conclusion: Skill-based self-improvement with recursive composition and principled compression yields robust, scalable gains for visual web agents, avoiding the library-collapse and redundancy problems of prior flat/2-tier caching approaches.

title: A Brain-inspired Hierarchical Framework for Zero-Shot Robot Task Reasoning and Execution
summary: Robots that follow open-ended language instructions need to connect semantic intent to visual scene understanding, geometric feasibility, object states, and physical interaction conditions. End-to-end Vision-Language-Action policies have improved cross-task generalization, but they typically map visual and language inputs directly to robot actions, leaving limited explicit structure for long-horizon decomposition, physical verification, and recovery. We present \method, a zero-shot hierarchical framework functionally inspired by the division of roles in the human brain, comprising visual perception and state inference, language grounding and action-sequence generation from a shared atomic action library, cost-based plan selection, and real-robot execution and verification. The framework grounds commands in explicit object states, composes reusable atomic actions into task-conditioned sequences, ranks alternative sequences by execution cost, and verifies intermediate physical outcomes from refreshed observations. In the evaluation, \method{} completes 10/10 clean board trials, 10/10 pick-and-place trials, and 4/5 pyramid stacking trials for both the flat and irregular initial-layout conditions; the corresponding mean task progress is $99.03\%$, $100.00\%$, and $96.67\%$ respectively. Across all evaluated conditions, \method{} achieves higher success rates than ReKep, Dream2Flow, and $π_{0.5}$ benchmarks, demonstrating the effectiveness of combining explicit object-state reasoning, compositional atomic actions, cost-based plan selection, and closed-loop execution verification.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a zero-shot hierarchical framework for robot instruction following that decomposes tasks via explicit object-state reasoning, reusable atomic actions, cost-based plan selection, and closed-loop execution verification, outperforming benchmarks across board clearing, pick-and-place, and pyramid stacking tasks.
AI.motivation: End-to-end Vision-Language-Action policies lack explicit structure for long-horizon decomposition, physical verification, and error recovery when following open-ended language instructions, which limits robustness in tasks requiring geometric feasibility assessment and physical interaction reasoning.
AI.method: A zero-shot hierarchical framework inspired by the functional division of roles in the human brain, comprising: (1) visual perception and state inference, (2) language grounding and action-sequence generation from a shared atomic action library, (3) cost-based plan selection to rank alternative sequences, and (4) real-robot execution with closed-loop verification of intermediate physical outcomes from refreshed observations.
AI.result: The framework completes 10/10 clean board trials, 10/10 pick-and-place trials, and 4/5 pyramid stacking trials under both flat and irregular initial-layout conditions, with mean task progress of 99.03%, 100.00%, and 96.67% respectively. It outperforms ReKep, Dream2Flow, and π0.5 across all evaluated conditions.
AI.conclusion: Combining explicit object-state reasoning, compositional atomic actions, cost-based plan selection, and closed-loop execution verification effectively improves success rates over end-to-end baselines for instruction-following manipulation tasks.

title: Reasoning-Aware Compression: Identifying and Protecting Vulnerable Reasoning Circuits for Energy-Efficient LLM Deployment
summary: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) impose substantial energy costs during deployment, yet current compression methods apply uniform quantization across all components, risking damage to critical reasoning circuits. We present a reasoning-aware compression framework that benchmarks quantization conditions across five reasoning benchmarks, GSM8K, FOLIO, MATH-500, ProofWriter, and MuSiQue, with hardware-level GPU energy measurement; profiles per-module INT4 vulnerability across all 196-224 (layer, projection) pairs via a perturbation sweep on a held-out calibration split, then selectively restores the most sensitive circuits to FP16. Three findings emerge. First, INT4 quantization can increase energy by extending reasoning chains; a 25% power reduction becomes a net energy increase on GSM8K. Second, vulnerability is task-dependent: attention projections are more critical for mathematical reasoning, and sensitivity patterns differ by architecture in logical inference. Third, selective compression achieves Pareto-optimal points inaccessible to uniform methods: R1-Qwen-7B Top-10% on ProofWriter gains +12 pp over FP16 at -9.7% energy, validated on held-out data across five reasoning benchmarks.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a reasoning-aware compression framework for Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) that profiles per-module INT4 vulnerability across 196-224 (layer, projection) pairs and selectively restores the most sensitive circuits to FP16. It finds that INT4 quantization can paradoxically increase energy by extending reasoning chains, that vulnerability patterns are task-dependent and architecture-sensitive, and that selective compression achieves Pareto-optimal energy-accuracy trade-offs unattainable by uniform quantization methods.
AI.motivation: LRMs incur substantial energy costs during deployment, but current compression methods apply uniform quantization across all components, which risks damaging critical reasoning circuits. The paper addresses the need for compression strategies that respect the heterogeneous sensitivity of different model components while preserving reasoning capability and achieving energy efficiency.
AI.method: The framework benchmarks quantization conditions across five reasoning benchmarks (GSM8K, FOLIO, MATH-500, ProofWriter, MuSiQue) with hardware-level GPU energy measurements. It profiles per-module INT4 vulnerability across all 196-224 (layer, projection) pairs via a perturbation sweep on a held-out calibration split, then selectively restores the most sensitive circuits to FP16 precision.
AI.result: Three findings: (1) INT4 quantization can increase total energy despite reducing power, because it extends reasoning chains—a 25% power reduction becomes a net energy increase on GSM8K. (2) Vulnerability is task-dependent: attention projections are more critical for mathematical reasoning, and sensitivity patterns differ by architecture for logical inference. (3) Selective compression achieves Pareto-optimal points unavailable to uniform methods—R1-Qwen-7B Top-10% on ProofWriter gains +12 pp over FP16 at -9.7% energy, validated on held-out data across all five benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Reasoning-aware selective compression, which restores only the most critical circuits to higher precision, yields Pareto-optimal energy-accuracy trade-offs that uniform quantization cannot achieve, while also revealing that quantization impacts reasoning energy through chain length dynamics and task- and architecture-dependent sensitivity patterns.

title: GLoRI: Closed-Loop Whole-Body Tracking with Global-Local Reference Interaction for Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
summary: Humanoid loco-manipulation requires accurate whole-body motion tracking in the world frame for physical interaction. While local references preserve motion structure, they lack explicit constraints on absolute spatial placement, leading to accumulated global errors. Existing globally aware approaches augment teleoperation policies with global observations but do not explicitly integrate global correction with local motion guidance, limiting autonomous tracking accuracy. We present GLoRI, a closed-loop whole-body controller that integrates structured global reference and feedback with local motion guidance. Its GLoRI-Net uses Global-Local Cross Attention(GLCA) to refine local keypoint features with global target and pose-difference features, preserving motion structure while correcting world-frame placement. GLoRI achieves 100% completion and a g-MPJPE of 6.44cm on held-out HuMoTo motions. This accuracy remains robust under direct Isaac Gym-to-MuJoCo transfer without fine-tuning, demonstrating strong generalization. Furthermore, such accuracy and generalization enable autonomous loco-manipulation with a single policy on a real Unitree G1 interacting with diverse unseen objects, extending beyond prior systems that primarily rely on teleoperation or focus on single-object interactions.

AI.tldr: GLoRI is a closed-loop whole-body controller for humanoid loco-manipulation that integrates structured global reference and feedback with local motion guidance via a Global-Local Cross Attention network, achieving 100% completion, 6.44cm g-MPJPE, robust sim-to-real transfer without fine-tuning, and enabling autonomous single-policy manipulation on a real Unitree G1 with diverse unseen objects.
AI.motivation: Humanoid loco-manipulation requires accurate whole-body motion tracking in the world frame, but existing methods face a trade-off: local references preserve motion structure yet accumulate global errors, while globally aware approaches do not explicitly integrate global correction with local motion guidance, limiting autonomous tracking accuracy.
AI.method: GLoRI is a closed-loop whole-body controller whose GLoRI-Net employs Global-Local Cross Attention (GLCA) to refine local keypoint features with global target and pose-difference features, thereby preserving local motion structure while simultaneously correcting world-frame placement.
AI.result: GLoRI achieves 100% completion and a g-MPJPE of 6.44cm on held-out HuMoTo motions. It remains robust under direct Isaac Gym-to-MuJoCo transfer without fine-tuning, demonstrating strong generalization. It also enables autonomous loco-manipulation with a single policy on a real Unitree G1 interacting with diverse unseen objects.
AI.conclusion: GLoRI demonstrates that explicitly fusing structured global reference and feedback with local motion guidance yields accurate and generalizable whole-body control for humanoid loco-manipulation, extending beyond prior teleoperation-based systems or single-object-focused approaches to enable real-world autonomous manipulation across diverse objects.

title: When and What to Teach: Budget-Aware Online Adaptation for Web Agents
summary: Web agents have achieved significant success in automating complex internet tasks but deploying them in real-world environments requires continuous online adaptation. Given that deploying powerful proprietary models remains commercially cost-prohibitive, practitioners must rely on lightweight local models that evolve post-deployment via online teaching from a stronger teacher. However, standard interactive feedback imposes prohibitive costs. We show that conventional trajectory-level preference optimization wastes budget on both unresolvable episodes and redundant execution turns. To resolve these inefficiencies, we propose \textbf{Score-Guided Online Teaching with Budgeted Trajectory Trimming}, a budget-aware framework that systematically orchestrates \textbf{when} and \textbf{what} to teach. Specifically, our framework integrates a solvability-aware teacher gate to dictate \textbf{when} to query the teacher model and a score-guided turn selection mechanism to decide \textbf{what} informative turns to retain. Extensive experiments on MiniWoB and TimeWarp demonstrate that our method achieves comparable first-pass success while reducing teacher calls by 22.6\% and student training compute by 52.1\% on average. Our code is available at https://github.com/zjw131f1fc/budgeted-online-teaching.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a budget-aware framework called Score-Guided Online Teaching with Budgeted Trajectory Trimming for efficiently adapting lightweight web agents online from a stronger teacher model. The framework uses a solvability-aware teacher gate to decide when to query the teacher and a score-guided turn selection mechanism to trim trajectory turns, achieving comparable success rates while cutting teacher calls by 22.6% and student training compute by 52.1% on MiniWoB and TimeWarp benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Deploying web agents in real-world environments requires continuous online adaptation, but relying on powerful proprietary models is commercially prohibitive. Practitioners must use lightweight local models that evolve via online teaching from a stronger teacher. However, standard interactive feedback is costly, and conventional trajectory-level preference optimization wastes budget on unresolvable episodes and redundant execution turns.
AI.method: The proposed framework integrates two key components: (1) a solvability-aware teacher gate that dictates when to query the teacher model, avoiding wasteful queries on unresolvable episodes, and (2) a score-guided turn selection mechanism that decides which informative turns to retain during training, eliminating redundant execution turns. Together these orchestrate both when and what to teach under a fixed budget constraint.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on MiniWoB and TimeWarp benchmarks show the method achieves comparable first-pass success rates while reducing teacher calls by 22.6% and student training compute by 52.1% on average compared to baselines.
AI.conclusion: Budgeted trajectory trimming combined with solvability-aware teaching gating effectively addresses the cost inefficiencies in online web agent adaptation, making it feasible to deploy lightweight local agents that learn from stronger teachers under constrained budgets.

title: How to Learn from What a Human Would Avoid? Intervention-Aware World Models with Real-World RL for Dexterous Manipulation
comment: 15 pages, 8 figures, 3 tables. Accepted by CoRL 2026. Project page: https://whirl-dexterous.github.io/
summary: Multi-fingered dexterous manipulation remains a frontier for real-world reinforcement learning (RL) due to the high-dimensional action space and the prohibitive cost of hardware failures. While human-in-the-loop (HIL) RL allows operators to intervene before failures occur, current pipelines often treat these interventions as reactive corrections, discarding the rich safety signal inherent in the operator's decision to take control. In this paper, we ask: How can we learn from what a human would avoid? We present WHIRL, a safety-aware RL framework that transforms binary human interventions into forward-predictive signals for proactive risk avoidance. Our approach centers on an intervention-aware latent world model with four prediction heads: dynamics, reward, termination, and a novel per-state intervention-probability head that learns to predict the likelihood of a human takeover at future states. This head provides an actor-side risk-shaping term that discourages the policy from entering "intervention-prone" regions, modeling the operator's internal safety threshold. We evaluate our framework on a 16-DoF LEAP Hand across tasks spanning convex and irregular object grasping, prismatic manipulation, and long-horizon multi-stage tasks. Our results show that predictive risk-shaping enables the system to achieve a 96.7 percent success rate on complex grasping tasks while reducing the operator intervention burden by up to 84 percent in step-weighted terms. By closing the loop between human intuition and predictive world modeling, this work provides a practical safety-aware recipe for training complex dexterous agents in the real world while reducing operator fatigue and hardware-risk exposure.

AI.tldr: WHIRL is a safety-aware RL framework for multi-fingered dexterous manipulation that converts binary human interventions into forward-predictive risk signals via an intervention-aware latent world model with a novel per-state intervention-probability prediction head, achieving 96.7% success on complex grasping tasks while reducing operator intervention burden by up to 84%.
AI.motivation: Multi-fingered dexterous manipulation with RL suffers from high-dimensional action spaces and hardware failure costs. Human-in-the-loop RL allows intervention before failures, but current pipelines treat interventions as reactive corrections and discard the rich safety signal in the operator's decision to take control—the question of learning from what a human would avoid remains unaddressed.
AI.method: WHIRL introduces an intervention-aware latent world model with four prediction heads: dynamics, reward, termination, and a novel per-state intervention-probability head that predicts the likelihood of human takeover at future states. This head produces an actor-side risk-shaping term that discourages the policy from entering intervention-prone regions, modeling the operator's internal safety threshold.
AI.result: Evaluated on a 16-DoF LEAP Hand across convex/irregular object grasping, prismatic manipulation, and long-horizon multi-stage tasks. Achieves 96.7% success rate on complex grasping tasks while reducing operator intervention burden by up to 84% in step-weighted terms.
AI.conclusion: Predictive risk-shaping from human intervention signals enables proactive risk avoidance in real-world dexterous manipulation. By closing the loop between human intuition and predictive world modeling, the work provides a practical safety-aware recipe for training complex dexterous agents while reducing operator fatigue and hardware-risk exposure.

title: The Failure Happens Before the Drift: The Social Dynamics of Values in LLM Agent Societies
summary: Large Language Model (LLM)-based agents are increasingly used as proxies for human participants in social science research, yet it remains unclear whether they can faithfully simulate diverse and conflicting human value systems. We present a World Values Survey (WVS)-grounded simulation framework where culturally diverse agents with different communication styles engage in longitudinal, value-laden discussions. Across approximately 4,000 conversations involving 1,200 personas, 15 topics, and three models (GPT-4o, Gemini-2.5-Flash, and Gemma-4-E4B), we evaluate value faithfulness, value drift, and conversational realism. We find that more than 50\% of personas fail to express their assigned WVS profiles from the outset, while 2-7\% drift after repeated conversations. Ablations removing demographic details improve faithfulness for some models but do not change the broader trend: simulated value distributions still systematically deviate from the assigned WVS profiles. Compared to human discussions, simulated dialogues show a different trade-off between stylistic consistency and semantic diversity, often producing content-wise varied but stylistically repetitive exchanges. These findings suggest that current LLM agents can generate plausible conversations, but remain limited proxies for representing and preserving diverse human value profiles over time.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates whether LLM-based agents can faithfully simulate diverse human value systems using a WVS-grounded framework with culturally diverse personas engaging in longitudinal value-laden discussions. Across ~4,000 conversations with 1,200 personas across three models, over 50% of personas fail to express assigned value profiles, 2-7% drift over time, and simulated dialogues show different stylistic-semantic trade-offs than human discussions, concluding that current LLM agents remain limited proxies for representing diverse human values.
AI.motivation: LLM-based agents are increasingly used as proxies for human participants in social science research, but it is unclear whether they can faithfully simulate diverse and potentially conflicting human value systems, which is essential for their validity as research proxies.
AI.method: The authors build a World Values Survey (WVS)-grounded simulation framework where culturally diverse agents with varied communication styles engage in longitudinal, value-laden discussions. They conduct approximately 4,000 conversations involving 1,200 personas, 15 topics, and evaluate three models (GPT-4o, Gemini-2.5-Flash, and Gemma-4-E4B) on value faithfulness, value drift, and conversational realism. Ablation studies removing demographic details are also performed.
AI.result: More than 50% of personas fail to express their assigned WVS profiles from the outset, while 2-7% drift after repeated conversations. Demographic ablations improve faithfulness for some models but do not change the broader trend of systematic deviation from assigned WVS profiles. Simulated dialogues differ from human discussions in the trade-off between stylistic consistency and semantic diversity, often being content-wise varied but stylistically repetitive.
AI.conclusion: Current LLM agents can produce plausible conversations but remain limited proxies for representing and preserving diverse human value profiles over time, suggesting caution in their use for social science simulation.

title: FALCON-S: Fixed-wing ground-effect Aerodynamics Simulator and Flight Control Learning Suite
comment: Index Terms: Robot Learning, Flight Control, Reinforcement Learning, Autonomous Navigation, Control and Dynamics, Modeling and Simulation, Wind In Ground Vehicles
summary: We present a modular, high-fidelity simulation framework for the development and benchmarking of flight control strategies in fixed-wing aerial robots operating near the ground. Unlike existing simulators that rely on simplified or hover-oriented dynamics, our framework models full 6DoF rigid-body physics, semi-empirical ground-effect aerodynamics, actuator dynamics, sensor noise, and environmental disturbances. This physical realism, combined with modular component design, enables systematic analysis of low-altitude flight behavior under realistic conditions. The simulator supports both CPU and GPU backends via Torch and NVIDIA Warp, enabling high-throughput parallel execution suitable for large-scale reinforcement learning training and optimal control rollouts. A unified interface accommodates a range of controllers (both RL and optical control algorithms) across tasks such as altitude regulation and trajectory tracking. Cross-validation with X-Plane and JSBSim is also supported to facilitate engineering integration and visual fidelity.

AI.tldr: A modular, high-fidelity 6DoF fixed-wing flight simulation framework for near-ground operation, featuring ground-effect aerodynamics, actuator/sensor modeling, CPU/GPU parallel backends, and support for RL and optimal control benchmarking.
AI.motivation: Existing flight simulators rely on simplified or hover-oriented dynamics that fail to capture the complexities of fixed-wing aircraft operating near the ground, where ground effect, full rigid-body physics, and realistic disturbances matter for developing robust control strategies.
AI.method: The framework models full 6DoF rigid-body dynamics, semi-empirical ground-effect aerodynamics, actuator dynamics, sensor noise, and environmental disturbances with modular components. It uses Torch and NVIDIA Warp backends for CPU/GPU parallelism, offers a unified controller interface across tasks, and supports cross-validation with X-Plane and JSBSim.
AI.result: The simulator enables high-throughput parallel execution for large-scale RL training and optimal control rollouts, supports systematic low-altitude flight behavior analysis across altitude regulation and trajectory tracking tasks, and integrates with established simulators for engineering validation.
AI.conclusion: The framework addresses the gap in low-altitude fixed-wing flight simulation by providing physically realistic, modular, and scalable tooling suitable for training and benchmarking both learning-based and classical flight controllers.

title: Beyond "AI Helps Humans": Decision-Targeted Evaluation Design for Human-Agent Teams in the Agentic Era
summary: Wherever a coding agent works under engineer supervision, or a clinical model assists a radiologist, the deployment question is whether to keep the human-AI workflow or replace it with the human alone or the agent alone. The human-AI workflow is worth keeping only if it beats both of those alternatives. Yet once it is deployed, neither alternative outcome is observed: recovering one means replaying the task under that alternative, and every replay costs expert time or compute. Under a fixed replay budget, the design question is therefore which tasks should be more likely to receive a human-only replay, and which an agent-only replay. Existing methods do not directly target this decision. Agent benchmarks do not choose which missing baseline to measure, variance-based sampling ignores which of the two comparisons is closer to failing, and Bayesian information methods focus on learning model parameters instead of making the deployment decision. We propose TEAM-Design, a rule that gives every task two replay probabilities, one per baseline. It raises a probability where the missing baseline outcome is hard to predict from what is already known about the task and where that comparison is harder to establish, and lowers it where replay is expensive. We prove that the rule solves this budgeted design problem, and that drawing the replays at random from recorded probabilities still controls the chance of wrongly declaring that the workflow beats both. We reanalyze 6 clinical settings, where no human-AI workflow beats both alternatives, and a coding benchmark, where one does, then evaluate TEAM-Design on synthetic designs and on a semi-synthetic design built from a real chest X-ray reader study. TEAM-Design works best when one of the two comparisons is clearly harder to settle than the other, and can do worse than variance-based allocation when the two are similarly difficult.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes TEAM-Design, a rule that allocates a fixed replay budget between human-only and agent-only baseline evaluations to decide whether a human-AI workflow should be deployed, by assigning each task two replay probabilities (one per baseline). It prioritizes replays where the missing baseline outcome is hard to predict and where the comparison is harder to establish, while accounting for replay costs. The rule provably solves the budgeted design problem and controls error rates under randomized replay selection. Evaluations on clinical settings, a coding benchmark, synthetic designs, and a chest X-ray semi-synthetic study show TEAM-Design excels when one comparison is much harder, but can underperform variance-based allocation when both are similarly difficult.
AI.motivation: When deploying a human-AI workflow, it must outperform both the human-alone and agent-alone alternatives, but only one of these outcomes is observed in deployment. Estimating the missing baselines requires costly replays, and under a fixed budget, the key question is which tasks should receive which type of baseline replay. Existing methods (agent benchmarks, variance-based sampling, Bayesian information methods) do not directly target this deployment decision.
AI.method: TEAM-Design assigns each task two replay probabilities—one for the human-only baseline and one for the agent-only baseline. The rule increases a replay probability when the missing baseline outcome is hard to predict from existing task information and when that specific comparison is harder to settle, while decreasing it when replay is expensive. The paper provides proofs that this rule optimally solves the budgeted design problem and that randomized replay sampling based on these probabilities controls the probability of falsely declaring the workflow superior to both alternatives. Evaluation spans reanalysis of 6 clinical settings and a coding benchmark, plus synthetic and semi-synthetic (chest X-ray reader study) experiments.
AI.result: TEAM-Design is most effective when one of the two baseline comparisons is distinctly harder to settle than the other. When the two comparisons are of similar difficulty, TEAM-Design can perform worse than variance-based allocation. The reanalysis found no clinical human-AI workflow that beats both alternatives, while one coding benchmark workflow did.
AI.conclusion: The paper addresses a previously unformulated but practically important budgeted design problem: allocating replay budget across two missing baseline types for deployment decisions of human-AI workflows. TEAM-Design provides a principled, provably correct solution, with performance varying by problem structure—best when one comparison dominates in difficulty, and less competitive when comparisons are symmetric in difficulty.

title: SCoCaT: Success Conditioned Constrained Reinforcement Learning for Spacecraft Docking
summary: Termination-based constrained reinforcement learning is attractive for safety-critical robotic deployments: it avoids online optimization at inference, scales easily to many constraints via a single scalar per constraint, and is simpler to implement than commonly used Lagrangian methods. Instead of pricing violations through summed cost penalties, this approach makes violations structurally unprofitable by shortening the effective horizon for each violation. We identify a structural failure mode of this method class on terminal-navigation tasks: reaching a precise goal configuration while satisfying safety constraints that tighten along the final approach. When the goal sits inside the region close to where the constraints become active, the survival-weighted objective makes dwelling outside the goal region strictly preferable to entering, producing high constraint compliance with low task completion. We formalize this pathology and show that a minimal augmentation to off-the-shelf RL algorithms like PPO resolves this ``feasibility collapse''. We empirically demonstrate that adding a dense per-step success signal via an auxiliary value critic improves the task completion rate while maintaining safety-critical constraint compliance. Validation across two representative spacecraft platforms: a 6U-CubeSat spanning the mass and degree-of-freedom envelope of operational proximity operations, and a floating platform testbed for zero-shot sim-to-real transfer in our laboratory, supports the generality of these findings.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies a structural failure mode ("feasibility collapse") in termination-based constrained reinforcement learning for terminal-navigation tasks, where survival-weighted objectives make dwelling outside the goal region strictly preferable to entering when safety constraints tighten near the goal. The authors show that adding a dense per-step success signal via an auxiliary value critic to standard RL algorithms like PPO resolves this pathology, improving task completion while maintaining constraint compliance. Validation on a 6U-CubeSat and a floating platform testbed supports generality.
AI.motivation: Termination-based constrained RL is attractive for safety-critical robotics (no online optimization, scalable to many constraints, simpler than Lagrangian methods), but the authors identify a critical structural failure mode: when the goal lies inside the region where safety constraints become active (tightening along the final approach), the survival-weighted objective makes it strictly more profitable to dwell outside the goal region than to enter it. This produces high constraint compliance at the cost of low task completion, a pathology they term "feasibility collapse."
AI.method: The authors formalize this pathology analytically, then propose a minimal augmentation to off-the-shelf RL algorithms such as PPO: adding a dense per-step success signal via an auxiliary value critic. This dense success signal counteracts the survival bias that makes dwelling outside the goal preferable, without complicating the constrained optimization framework or requiring Lagrangian methods.
AI.result: Empirical results demonstrate that the auxiliary value critic augmentation improves task completion rates while maintaining safety-critical constraint compliance. Validation across two representative spacecraft platforms — a 6U-CubeSat spanning the mass and degree-of-freedom envelope of operational proximity operations, and a floating platform testbed for zero-shot sim-to-real transfer — supports the generality of these findings.
AI.conclusion: Termination-based constrained RL suffers from "feasibility collapse" on terminal-navigation tasks where safety constraints tighten near the goal. A simple dense per-step success signal via an auxiliary value critic resolves this failure, offering a practical and general fix that preserves the attractive properties of termination-based methods (simplicity, scalability, no online optimization) while restoring task completion.

title: EdgeMem: LLM-Free Agent Memory Construction and Retrieval via Evidence-Preserving Multi-Anchor Hypergraph
comment: 10 pages, 5 figures, and 5 tables. An earlier implementation is available at https://github.com/Soullesskid/edgemem ; it differs substantially from the version described in this paper. The repository will be updated with the corresponding implementation after peer review
summary: Agent memory allows LLM agents to use earlier interactions when answering new queries. Existing methods often compress interaction histories into summaries or other LLM-generated representations. Repeated generation adds cost and can discard answer-bearing details before the system knows what a future query will require. We propose EdgeMem, an agent-memory method built around a simple principle: preserve original interaction turns and organize them through complementary content, temporal, and episodic cues. EdgeMem realizes this principle with a multi-anchor hypergraph constructed by lightweight local processing. Retrieval directly returns source evidence and reserves LLM use for final answer generation, combining structured access to multi-session histories with faithful retention of the original conversation. Experiments on LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S show strong retrieval and memory-grounded question answering; on LoCoMo, EdgeMem achieves the highest strict-judge score among seven reproduced systems under a shared prompt (61.01 versus 58.70), while construction and retrieval require no generative-LLM calls. Overall, EdgeMem shows that preserving and organizing source evidence provides an effective and efficient foundation for agent memory without generative memory management.

AI.tldr: EdgeMem is an agent-memory method that preserves original interaction turns and organizes them via a multi-anchor hypergraph built with lightweight local processing, avoiding LLM-based memory compression. It retrieves source evidence directly and returns state-of-the-art results on LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S without any generative-LLM calls during construction or retrieval.
AI.motivation: Existing agent-memory methods compress interaction histories into summaries or LLM-generated representations, which incurs repeated generation costs and risks discarding answer-bearing details before future query requirements are known.
AI.method: EdgeMem preserves original interaction turns and organizes them through complementary content, temporal, and episodic cues using a multi-anchor hypergraph constructed by lightweight local processing. Retrieval directly returns source evidence, reserving LLM use solely for final answer generation.
AI.result: On LoCoMo, EdgeMem achieves the highest strict-judge score among seven reproduced systems under a shared prompt (61.01 versus 58.70 for the runner-up), and shows strong retrieval and memory-grounded QA on both LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S without requiring generative-LLM calls during construction or retrieval.
AI.conclusion: Preserving and organizing source evidence provides an effective and efficient foundation for agent memory, demonstrating that generative memory management is unnecessary when original turns are retained and structured accessibly.

title: Where Success Breaks: Failure-Boundary Learning for Robust Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models adapted through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) inherit a structural asymmetry: expert demonstrations teach the policy where success behavior lies, but provide no signal about where it ceases to be reliable. We argue that robust VLA adaptation should therefore be viewed not as further demonstration fitting, but as **Failure-Boundary Learning**---the problem of *Discovering*, *Localizing*, and *Shaping* the boundary between recoverable deviations and task failure. To instantiate this view, we propose **DLS**: built on a **real-grounded behavioral prior** from few real demonstrations and simulated co-training, DLS *discovers* failure boundaries at scale through on-policy digital twin rollouts. Rather than reducing each rollout to a binary label, **semantic progress localization** uses privileged simulator states to assign progress-aware signals that capture *where* the failure boundary is crossed, not merely *whether*. These signals drive **directional boundary shaping** in the flow dynamics---reinforcing success-producing denoising directions and suppressing failure-producing ones, without action likelihoods or auxiliary critics. Across real-robot manipulation tasks, DLS improves robustness over SFT and online RL baselines, especially under randomized initial states and unseen visual conditions.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes DLS (Discover-Localize-Shape), a framework for robust VLA model adaptation that frames the problem as learning failure boundaries rather than merely fitting demonstrations. It uses real-grounded behavioral priors with simulated co-training to discover failures via digital twin rollouts, localizes failure crossings through semantic progress signals from privileged simulator states, and shapes the flow dynamics by reinforcing success-producing denoising directions while suppressing failure-producing ones.
AI.motivation: Supervised fine-tuning of VLA models only teaches where successful behavior lies but provides no signal about where the policy becomes unreliable. This structural asymmetry limits robustness under distribution shift. The authors argue for reframing VLA adaptation as Failure-Boundary Learning—discovering, localizing, and shaping the boundary between recoverable deviations and task failure.
AI.method: DLS consists of three components: (1) Discovering failure boundaries at scale via on-policy digital twin rollouts built on a real-grounded behavioral prior learned from few real demonstrations with simulated co-training; (2) Semantic progress localization that uses privileged simulator states to assign progress-aware signals capturing where (not just whether) the failure boundary is crossed; (3) Directional boundary shaping in flow dynamics that reinforces success-producing denoising directions and suppresses failure-producing ones, without requiring action likelihoods or auxiliary critics.
AI.result: Across real-robot manipulation tasks, DLS improves robustness over supervised fine-tuning and online RL baselines, with particularly notable gains under randomized initial states and unseen visual conditions.
AI.conclusion: Framing robust VLA adaptation as failure-boundary learning, coupled with progress-aware localization and directional flow shaping, yields more robust policies than demonstration fitting or generic RL fine-tuning, especially under distribution shift in initial states and visual conditions.

title: Deep belief networks are exact
summary: We prove that every strictly positive probability distribution on \(\{-1,1\}^n\) is represented exactly by a sigmoid belief network with finite parameters. This answers a question of Sutskever and Hinton. The proof upgrades their probability-sharing approximation to exact representation using Brouwer's fixed-point theorem.

AI.tldr: This paper proves that any strictly positive probability distribution on the Boolean hypercube {-1,1}^n can be represented exactly by a sigmoid belief network with finite parameters, resolving an open question posed by Sutskever and Hinton, using Brouwer's fixed-point theorem to upgrade a probabilistic approximation into an exact representation.
AI.motivation: Sutskever and Hinton posed the question of whether sigmoid belief networks can exactly represent all strictly positive distributions on the Boolean hypercube. Prior work only established approximate representation via probability-sharing, leaving the exact representability question open.
AI.method: The proof leverages Brouwer's fixed-point theorem to upgrade the existing probability-sharing approximation approach of Sutskever and Hinton into an exact representation result, showing that finite parameters suffice to represent any strictly positive distribution on {-1,1}^n.
AI.result: It is proven that every strictly positive probability distribution on the n-dimensional Boolean hypercube can be exactly represented by a sigmoid belief network with finite parameters, thereby answering Sutskever and Hinton's question affirmatively.
AI.conclusion: Sigmoid belief networks are universal approximators in the exact sense for strictly positive distributions on the Boolean hypercube, with finite parameters guaranteed. This establishes a fundamental theoretical result about the expressive power of this class of probabilistic models.

title: RefGuard: Identity-Aware Language-Guided Robot Manipulation via Joint Target-Anchor-Frame Grounding
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have substantially advanced language-guided robot manipulation, yet reliable execution still hinges on identifying which physical object an instruction refers to. In cluttered scenes containing repeated objects, ambiguous anchors, or frame-dependent spatial terms, a robot can execute a geometrically valid action on a semantically compatible but unintended instance; we call this failure an identity switch. The referent is jointly determined by three coupled latent variables: the target, the anchor, and the reference frame, so committing to any one of them before execution turns residual ambiguity into a silent and irreversible error. We propose RefGuard, an identity-aware grounding framework that delays commitment by maintaining a joint posterior over all three variables. RefGuard builds a frame-conditioned object-centric scene graph from RGB-D observations, separating frame-independent geometry from directional relations, and routes the posterior through a decision policy that executes, clarifies, reobserves, or aborts. On a real UF850 arm, RefGuard records no identity switch on any ambiguity-stress trial and executes correctly on 90.0% of them, whereas fine-tuned VLA and LLM (Large Language Model)-based baselines switch identity in 33-46% of the same trials, while retaining 93.3% success on unambiguous scenes and recovering from post-grounding scene changes in 86.7% of trials. On a 3200-episode procedural suite, it raises correct execution on solvable instructions from 56.6% to 80.5% over the ablation that commits to the anchor and frame before the target, while deferring less often (19.5% vs. 43.4%).

AI.tldr: RefGuard is an identity-aware grounding framework for VLA robot manipulation that delays commitment by maintaining a joint posterior over three coupled latent variables—target, anchor, and reference frame—preventing "identity switches" (executing on the wrong instance of a semantically compatible object) via a frame-conditioned object-centric scene graph and a decision policy that executes, clarifies, reobserves, or aborts.
AI.motivation: VLA models struggle with referent disambiguation in cluttered scenes containing repeated objects, ambiguous anchors, or frame-dependent spatial terms. Existing approaches commit to target/anchor/frame independently before execution, which turns residual ambiguity into silent, irreversible errors called identity switches. A joint, deferred-commitment framework is needed to ensure reliable grounding.
AI.method: RefGuard constructs a frame-conditioned object-centric scene graph from RGB-D observations, separating frame-independent geometry from directional relations, and maintains a joint posterior over the target, anchor, and reference frame. The posterior is routed through a decision policy that can execute, clarify, reobserve, or abort, delaying commitment to any single interpretation until sufficient evidence is gathered.
AI.result: On a real UF850 arm: zero identity switches on ambiguity-stress trials with 90.0% correct execution (vs. 33-46% identity-switch rates for fine-tuned VLA and LLM baselines), 93.3% success on unambiguous scenes, and 86.7% recovery from post-grounding scene changes. On a 3200-episode procedural suite: correct execution on solvable instructions improved from 56.6% to 80.5% over the anchor/frame-committing ablation, while deferring less often (19.5% vs. 43.4%).
AI.conclusion: Jointly reasoning over target, anchor, and reference frame with deferred commitment substantially reduces identity-switch failures in language-guided manipulation while retaining high performance on unambiguous scenarios and robustness to scene changes, outperforming both fine-tuned VLA and LLM-based baselines.

title: EnvCraft: Synthesizing Executable Environments in Agentic RL for Claw-like Agent
summary: The paradigm of LLMs has rapidly shifted from passive language interfaces to autonomous Claw-like agents that execute long-horizon tasks across stateful workspaces. While Agentic Reinforcement Learning (Agentic RL) provides a promising path to optimize these agents, its scaling is heavily bottlenecked by the severe scarcity of interactive training environments. Existing synthetic environments are strictly limited to tool-calling endpoints, rendering them insufficient for accommodating the end-to-end real-world demands of claw-like agents. To bridge this gap, we introduce EnvCraft, an automated framework for synthesizing executable environments and scalable training data. Specifically, EnvCraft employs an environment synthesis engine to build sandbox-isolated workspaces, alongside a topology-aware data generation engine to produce coherent task trajectories. Overall, we synthesize 139 interactive environments comprising approximately 20K complex tasks for Agentic RL training. Experiments on Qwen3/3.5 models (8B-32B) show that our method yields gains of up to +11.9% on Claw-style benchmarks and +8.0% on general tool-use benchmarks, with concurrent reductions in inference token cost. The results confirm that synthesized executable environments provide robust and generalizable learning signals for training.

AI.tldr: EnvCraft is an automated framework that synthesizes executable, sandbox-isolated interactive environments and topology-aware training data for Agentic Reinforcement Learning, producing 139 environments and ~20K complex tasks. Training Qwen3/3.5 models (8B-32B) with this data yields up to +11.9% gains on Claw-style benchmarks and +8.0% on general tool-use benchmarks while reducing inference token costs, demonstrating that synthesized executable environments provide robust, generalizable learning signals.
AI.motivation: Agentic RL for LLM-based agents is bottlenecked by the severe scarcity of interactive training environments. Existing synthetic environments are limited to tool-calling endpoints and cannot accommodate the end-to-end, stateful, long-horizon demands of claw-like agents operating in real-world workspaces.
AI.method: EnvCraft consists of two key components: (1) an environment synthesis engine that builds sandbox-isolated, executable workspaces; and (2) a topology-aware data generation engine that produces coherent task trajectories within these environments. Together they synthesize 139 interactive environments with approximately 20K complex tasks suitable for Agentic RL training.
AI.result: Experiments on Qwen3/3.5 models ranging from 8B to 32B demonstrate gains of up to +11.9% on Claw-style benchmarks and +8.0% on general tool-use benchmarks, with concurrent reductions in inference token cost.
AI.conclusion: Synthesized executable environments provide robust and generalizable learning signals for training autonomous claw-like agents, effectively bridging the gap between limited tool-call simulation and real-world end-to-end agentic tasks.

title: GloVLA: Let Geometry Move and Local VLA Interact for Robust Object-Centric Manipulation in Unstructured Environments
comment: 9 pages, 7 figures. Submitted to IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RA-L)
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have shown promising generalization for language-conditioned robot manipulation, but deploying them in unstructured environments remains challenging. A single end-to-end VLA policy must simultaneously solve long-range transport of the end effector to task-relevant regions and short-horizon, contact-rich interaction upon arrival. This formulation is inefficient and brittle: small visual shifts, distractors, clutter, occlusions, or unfavorable initial gripper poses can push the policy outside the local state distribution in which it was trained, leading to task failure. We introduce GloVLA, a hybrid framework that explicitly separates object-centric manipulation into two complementary regimes: a geometric transport controller moves the end-effector into interaction-centric handoff regions, and local VLA policies handle only the short-horizon interaction phases. GloVLA is model-agnostic and can be integrated with different VLA backbones with no additional demonstrations and no changes to the action space or success predicate. Experiments on standard LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus Object tasks together with a newly introduced LIBERO-Challenge benchmark ettings with clutter, distractors,illumination changes, visual shifts, and obstruction show that GloVLA improves task success and substantially lowers VLA inference cost compared with full end-to-Challenge, full-trajectory GR00T N1.6execution degrades to 20.9% average success while GloVLA retains 88.5%; on a physical UR10e, overall success improves from 35.6% to 90.0% while mean inference time is more than halved. Videos and additional results are available at https://glovla-project.github.io/

AI.tldr: GloVLA is a hybrid framework for robot manipulation that splits object-centric tasks into two regimes: a geometric transport controller for long-range end-effector movement and local VLA policies for short-horizon, contact-rich interactions. It is model-agnostic, requires no extra demonstrations, and significantly improves task success and reduces inference cost over end-to-end VLA baselines on LIBERO benchmarks, including a new LIBERO-Challenge setting, and on a physical UR10e robot.
AI.motivation: End-to-end VLA policies must simultaneously solve long-horizon transport and short-horizon contact-rich interaction, which is inefficient and brittle. Small perturbations in the environment (visual shifts, distractors, clutter, occlusion, unfavorable gripper poses) push the policy outside its trained local state distribution and cause task failure.
AI.method: GloVLA explicitly decomposes object-centric manipulation into two complementary regimes: a geometric transport controller moves the end effector into interaction-centric handoff regions, while local VLA policies handle only the short-horizon interaction phases. It is model-agnostic and integrates with different VLA backbones without additional demonstrations or changes to the action space or success predicate.
AI.result: On the new LIBERO-Challenge benchmark (with clutter, distractors, illumination changes, visual shifts, obstruction), full-trajectory end-to-end GR00T N1.6 degrades to 20.9% average success while GloVLA retains 88.5%. On a physical UR10e, overall success improves from 35.6% to 90.0% and mean inference time is more than halved.
AI.conclusion: GloVLA demonstrates that decoupling geometric transport from local interaction dramatically improves robustness and efficiency for VLA-based manipulation, achieving strong performance gains over end-to-end execution in both simulated benchmarks and physical robot experiments while reducing inference cost.

title: Planning and Scheduling Business Processes under Control-Flow Uncertainty
summary: Scheduling activities in business processes can improve efficiency (e.g., reduce makespan), but is challenging because the exact sequence of activities required to complete a case is often uncertain due to decisions based on data that emerges during execution. Nevertheless, probabilistic information regarding such decisions can often be estimated or derived from historical execution logs, and can help anticipate which execution paths are likely to lead to successful completion. Planning with particular execution paths affects feasibility, i.e., the probability of successful completion, and the expected number of superfluous activities that are planned but never executed. We frame the problem as a chance-constrained optimization problem and present two formulations: A decomposed approach with two stages, a planning stage that minimizes the expected number of superfluous activities subject to a feasibility constraint, and a scheduling stage that minimizes the makespan over the planned activities; and an integrated approach that combines planning and scheduling into a single formulation. Evaluation on two real-world and one synthetic dataset shows that the integrated approach yields superior makespans but is intractable at scale, while the decomposed approach scales to large settings.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the challenge of scheduling business processes under uncertainty in activity sequences by framing it as a chance-constrained optimization problem. The authors propose two approaches: a decomposed two-stage approach (planning to minimize expected superfluous activities under a feasibility constraint, then scheduling to minimize makespan) and an integrated single-formulation approach. Evaluations on two real-world and one synthetic dataset show the integrated approach produces better makespans but is intractable at scale, while the decomposed approach scales well.
AI.motivation: Scheduling business process activities improves efficiency but is complicated by uncertainty in the exact activity sequence required to complete a case, since decisions depend on data emerging during execution. The authors aim to plan and schedule activities under this uncertainty while considering both feasibility (probability of successful completion) and superfluous activities (planned but never executed).
AI.method: The problem is formulated as a chance-constrained optimization problem. Two formulations are presented: (1) a decomposed two-stage approach with a planning stage minimizing expected superfluous activities subject to feasibility constraints, followed by a scheduling stage minimizing makespan over the planned activities; and (2) an integrated approach combining planning and scheduling into a single formulation.
AI.result: Evaluation on two real-world and one synthetic dataset demonstrates that the integrated approach achieves superior makespans but suffers from intractability at scale, whereas the decomposed approach scales effectively to large settings.
AI.conclusion: There is a trade-off between solution quality (makespan) and scalability: the integrated approach is better for small problems, while the decomposed approach is preferable for large-scale settings where tractability is essential.

title: Bundle Length Tradeoffs in Decentralized Multi-Robot Task Allocation Under Degraded Communications
summary: Bundle length B is commonly fixed when configuring multi-task multi-robot task allocation (MRTA) algorithms. MinSum and MinMax are known to favor different task distributions, but the role of B in this objective tradeoff has not been systematically characterized. Additionally, degraded-communication evaluations also often retain settings selected under ideal communication, leaving whether nominal bundle-length tuning transfers under message loss unresolved. We examine both questions for ACBBA, PI, and HIPC across six bundle lengths in 300 paired ten-target Collaborative Visit scenarios under ideal communication and 25% Bernoulli packet loss. Under ideal communication, increasing B from 1 to 12 reduces MinSum cost by 19.0%, 23.0%, and 31.8% for ACBBA, PI, and HIPC, respectively, while increasing MinMax cost by 45.6%, 94.3%, and 67.6%. Under packet loss, the lowest-mean MinSum setting shifts from B = 12 to B = 2 for ACBBA and PI. Repeated paired cross-fitting shows that retaining the ideal-network setting incurs held-out MinSum penalties of 14.4% and 7.2%, respectively, and increases MinMax cost by 30.0% and 41.8% relative to the loss-conditioned MinSum setting. HIPC retains a deep MinSum operating region, while the MinMax setting remains stable for all three allocators. Experiments at two additional target loads reproduce the ACBBA and PI MinSum shifts.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically characterizes how bundle length B affects the MinSum/MinMax tradeoff in multi-task multi-robot task allocation (MRTA) under both ideal and degraded (25% Bernoulli packet loss) communication. Testing ACBBA, PI, and HIPC across six bundle lengths in 300 paired ten-target Collaborative Visit scenarios, the authors find that increasing B improves MinSum but worsens MinMax under ideal communication. Under packet loss, the optimal MinSum bundle length shifts from B=12 to B=2 for ACBBA and PI, making the ideal-network tuning choice incur significant penalties (7.2-14.4% MinSum, 30.0-41.8% MinMax). HIPC shows more robust behavior, and qualitative results reproduce at higher target loads.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses two unresolved questions in MRTA: (1) the systematic role of bundle length B in the MinSum vs. MinMax objective tradeoff has never been characterized, and (2) bundle-length settings tuned under ideal communication may not transfer to degraded-communication settings, yet evaluations under message loss typically retain ideal-network parameter choices.
AI.method: The authors conduct 300 paired ten-target Collaborative Visit scenarios across three allocators (ACBBA, PI, HIPC) and six bundle lengths, comparing performance under ideal communication and 25% Bernoulli packet loss. They perform repeated paired cross-fitting to assess the cost of transferring bundle-length settings between ideal and lossy regimes, and validate findings with two additional target loads.
AI.result: Under ideal communication, increasing B from 1 to 12 reduces MinSum cost by 19.0% (ACBBA), 23.0% (PI), and 31.8% (HIPC) while raising MinMax cost by 45.6%, 94.3%, and 67.6%, respectively. Under packet loss, the lowest-mean MinSum setting shifts from B=12 to B=2 for ACBBA and PI; retaining the ideal setting yields held-out MinSum penalties of 14.4% and 7.2% and MinMax increases of 30.0% and 41.8%. HIPC maintains a deep MinSum operating region, MinMax stability holds for all allocators, and additional target-load experiments reproduce the ACBBA and PI MinSum shifts.
AI.conclusion: Bundle length strongly mediates the MinSum/MinMax tradeoff in MRTA, and nominal bundle-length tuning does not transfer under packet loss for ACBBA and PI. Communication-robust allocators like HIPC and re-tuning B to the loss regime are therefore important for reliable deployment; MinMax-oriented settings remain stable across communication conditions.

title: Agents Trust Tools Too Much: Measuring Reliance on Unreliable Tools
summary: Existing evaluations of tool-using agents primarily measure whether an agent can successfully complete diverse tasks with tools. These evaluations generally assume that tools return reliable information. However, tool returns in real-world systems can be plausible yet incorrect. We investigate how agents respond to unreliable tool returns by evaluating fourteen LLMs using three tools-web search, LLM sub-agent delegation, and code execution. For each tool, we corrupt its returns and measure whether agents adopt the corrupted content in their final answers. Agents exhibit high levels of overtrust across all three settings: the mean adoption rate exceeds one third for every tool and reaches 68.0% for web search. Analysis of reasoning traces reveals a particularly concerning failure mode: agents often recognize conflicts and even recover the correct answer internally, yet present only the corrupted answer without warning the user. To mitigate agents' overtrust in tool returns, we intervene at three levels: prompting by the user, metadata from the tool provider, and post-training by the agent builder. Although some interventions help for particular models or tools, none consistently mitigates overtrust across tools. These findings identify overtrust in unreliable tools as a serious and persistent failure mode, motivating evaluations and interventions that enable agents to validate tool outputs and transparently communicate unresolved conflicts.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how LLM-based tool-using agents respond to unreliable (corrupted yet plausible) tool returns. Across fourteen LLMs and three tools (web search, sub-agent delegation, code execution), agents show high overtrust—mean adoption rates of corrupted content exceed one third for every tool and reach 68% for web search. A key failure mode is that agents often internally detect conflicts and recover correct answers yet present only corrupted content without warning users. User prompting, tool provider metadata, and post-training interventions help only inconsistently. Overtrust in unreliable tools is identified as a serious, persistent failure mode requiring new evaluation and intervention strategies.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks for tool-using agents assume tools return reliable information, but real-world tools can return plausible yet incorrect outputs. This discrepancy leaves a critical gap: we don't know how agents behave when tool returns are unreliable, nor whether their overtrust can be mitigated.
AI.method: The authors evaluate fourteen LLMs across three tools (web search, LLM sub-agent delegation, code execution). They corrupt each tool's returns and measure how often agents adopt the corrupted content in final answers. They analyze reasoning traces for failure modes and test three levels of intervention: user-level prompting, tool-provider metadata, and agent-builder post-training.
AI.result: Agents exhibit high overtrust across all settings: mean adoption rates exceed one third for every tool and reach 68% for web search. Reasoning trace analysis reveals agents often recognize conflicts and internally recover correct answers yet present only the corrupted answer without user warnings. None of the three intervention levels consistently mitigates overtrust across all tools and models.
AI.conclusion: Overtrust in unreliable tool returns is a serious and persistent failure mode of LLM agents. Current interventions are insufficient, motivating new evaluation paradigms and interventions that enable agents to validate tool outputs and transparently communicate unresolved conflicts to users.

title: IM-ENGINE: Image Editing for Embodied Data Generation
summary: Learning-based manipulation requires supervision that is both semantically meaningful and physically executable, but current data pipelines often provide only one of these properties. Human demonstrations capture intent but are costly to collect and constrained by the human-robot embodiment gap, while simulation can scale data generation but often under-specifies functional behavior. We present IM-ENGINE, a simulator-grounded pipeline that uses image editing as an intermediate representation for embodied data generation. Given a rendered scene with known geometry, depth, segmentation, and camera parameters, IM-ENGINE edits the image to inject task-relevant semantics, recovers explicit 3D state using simulator priors and an unchanged anchor object, refines the state in physics, and converts it into robot-executable supervision. We instantiate the pipeline for dexterous grasp synthesis and goal-state generation. For grasping, IM-ENGINE generates a human grasp in image space, recovers the hand-object interaction, retargets it to a robot hand, and refines it into physically validated robot grasps. For goal generation, it edits a rendered scene into a desired outcome, recovers the target-object pose, and refines it into physically valid, semantically meaningful goals and trajectories. This combination of generative semantic priors and simulator grounding enables scalable task-relevant supervision for robot learning.

AI.tldr: IM-ENGINE is a simulator-grounded data generation pipeline that uses image editing as an intermediate representation to generate robot-executable supervision that is both semantically meaningful and physically valid, demonstrated for dexterous grasp synthesis and goal-state generation.
AI.motivation: Existing data pipelines for learning-based manipulation provide either semantic meaning (human demonstrations) or physical executability (simulation), but rarely both. Human data is costly and limited by embodiment gaps, while simulation data often lacks functional semantics.
AI.method: IM-ENGINE takes a rendered scene with known geometry, depth, segmentation, and camera parameters, then: (1) edits the image to inject task-relevant semantics, (2) recovers explicit 3D state using simulator priors and an unchanged anchor object, (3) refines the state in physics simulation, and (4) converts it into robot-executable supervision. It is instantiated for grasp synthesis (editing human grasps in image space, recovering hand-object interaction, retargeting to robot hands, physics refinement) and goal-state generation (editing rendered scenes into desired outcomes, recovering target poses, refining into valid goals and trajectories).
AI.result: The pipeline combines generative semantic priors with simulator grounding to produce scalable, task-relevant supervision for robot learning, yielding physically validated robot grasps and semantically meaningful goals and trajectories.
AI.conclusion: Image editing serves as an effective intermediate representation that bridges generative semantic priors and physics simulation, enabling scalable generation of supervision that is both semantically meaningful and physically executable for robot learning.

title: The convergent laboratory: when AI reasoning, autonomous experiments, high performance and quantum computing reshape chemistry
summary: This Comment emerges from TPC26 (https://tpc26.org), a conference convening leaders from academia, national laboratories, and industry who are reshaping materials science discovery. The meeting explored how AI, autonomous agents, self-driving labs, higher performance and quantum computing converge to amplify their individual impact on materials science discovery. The perspectives here reflect the firsthand experiences of researchers at these frontiers and capture the essence of this global endeavor. As AI-driven reasoning, autonomous agentic frameworks, self-driving laboratories, and fault-tolerant quantum processors mature simultaneously, we offer this Comment as a reference at what we believe is a tipping point of transformative advances and productive disruption in the chemical sciences.

AI.tldr: This Comment presents perspectives from TPC26, a conference bringing together academia, national laboratories, and industry leaders, on how AI, autonomous agents, self-driving labs, high-performance computing, and quantum computing are converging to transform materials science discovery—positioned at a tipping point for the chemical sciences.
AI.motivation: To capture and share firsthand experiences of researchers at the frontiers of AI-driven materials discovery, documenting a pivotal moment where multiple advanced technologies are maturing simultaneously and amplifying each other's impact.
AI.method: A conference-derived Comment paper reflecting on the convergence of AI reasoning, autonomous agentic frameworks, self-driving laboratories, high-performance computing, and fault-tolerant quantum processors in materials science.
AI.result: No experimental results reported; the paper offers a forward-looking perspective identifying what the authors believe is a tipping point of transformative advances and productive disruption in chemical sciences.
AI.conclusion: The simultaneous maturation of AI-driven reasoning, autonomous frameworks, self-driving labs, and quantum computing signals a transformative inflection point in materials science discovery, with the paper serving as a reference for this global endeavor.

title: Geometric Distributional Control: Learning Progress with Partial Structural Knowledge
summary: Real-time control often sits between two limiting regimes. Predictive optimization and model-based control are powerful when dynamics, parameters, objectives, and online planning models are specified; reinforcement learning can relax this requirement, but must infer long-horizon value signals from sequential data and interaction, making training slow, high-variance, and hard to scale in large action spaces. This middle regime is common in systems including autonomous driving, warehouse robotics, traffic control, and delivery drones: partial geometry, physics, rules, or constraints are known, yet the local direction of task progress remains uncertain. Geometric Distributional Control (GDC) is designed for this partial-knowledge setting. It factorizes control into feasibility and progress: known geometry, rules, constraints, and response maps define an executable scaffold, while progress-weighted feasible data learns the missing directional signal on that scaffold. The learned score acts as a Bellman-like local value-gradient, selecting actions that make progress without requiring global Bellman recursion, a fully specified planner, or a black-box policy that absorbs both feasibility and preference. This knowledge can be lightweight and partial, such as simple dynamics, safety filters, local maps, constraint projectors, or lower-level response maps; it need not encode full dynamics or a long-horizon objective. Offline, GDC fits a progress-tilted distribution from short known-feasible snippets with weak signed progress certificates. Online, its score is projected through the scaffold and applied in receding-horizon feedback.
