We prove that this score descends a data-induced soft progress value and validate GDC on structured multilevel optimization and SUMO route-progress driving, where it improves over known-only solvers and learning baselines while preserving scaffold-enforced feasibility.

AI.tldr: GDC factorizes control into feasibility (known scaffold) and progress (learned from data), enabling real-time control in the middle regime between model-based optimization and pure RL where partial knowledge exists but direction of task progress is uncertain.
AI.motivation: Real-time control often sits between model-based optimization (requires full dynamics/objectives) and RL (needs long-horizon value inference, slow and high-variance). In many real systems—autonomous driving, warehouse robotics, traffic control—only partial geometry, physics, rules, or constraints are known, but the direction of task progress is uncertain. Neither existing paradigm is well-suited to this middle regime.
AI.method: GDC factorizes control into two components: (1) a feasibility scaffold constructed from known geometry, rules, constraints, and response maps; and (2) a learned progress score fitted from offline short known-feasible snippets with weak signed progress certificates. The learned score acts as a Bellman-like local value-gradient that selects progress-making actions without global Bellman recursion or full planning. Offline, GDC fits a progress-tilted distribution; online, the score is projected through the scaffold in receding-horizon feedback.
AI.result: GDC is proven to descend a data-induced soft progress value. Empirically validated on structured multilevel optimization and SUMO route-progress driving, where it outperforms known-only solvers and learning baselines while preserving scaffold-enforced feasibility.
AI.conclusion: GDC provides an effective framework for the partial-knowledge middle regime of real-time control, requiring only lightweight partial knowledge (dynamics, safety filters, local maps, constraint projectors) rather than full models, while avoiding the sample-inefficiency of end-to-end RL—achieving both feasibility guarantees and progress learning.

title: What LLM Trading Agents Actually Do in Production: A Six-Month, Population-Scale Record from Two Fleets
comment: 17 pages, 8 figures, 3 tables. Artifacts, figures, and aggregate data: https://github.com/ProjectDXAI/continuous-record-llm-trading-agents
summary: We present a continuous, population-scale measurement record of autonomous language-model trading agents operating in production across two systems with one design lineage: DX Terminal Pro (3,505 user-funded vaults trading real ETH in Base memecoin markets for 21 days, February to March 2026) and the DXAP live alpha fleet (500 to 599 user-created agents all-history, 91 to 117 concurrently active, trading Hyperliquid perpetuals, June to August 2026). The record spans roughly six months, 7.5M single-model invocations with about 300K onchain actions, and a further 231,638 multi-tool turns producing 14,596 fills. Four findings carry the paper. First, the operating layer determines behavior more than anything written in strategy text: a risk slider explains leverage (+0.425 per level), agent fixed effects absorb 60% of variance, and a leaderboard render boundary causally routes selection (regression discontinuity 1.75x at the top-3 cut). Second, sizing is volatility-blind: median leverage is 5.0x in every volatility sextile, and one posture-slider cell (11% of the book) holds 62% of liquidations. Third, agents capture almost none of the upside they reach: 43.2% of positions saw at least +300 bps of favorable excursion within 24h, yet 49.3% of those closed with a negative trade return; a mechanical bracket recovers +39.0 bps per position. Fourth, neither fleet shows a directional edge. The DXAP fleet is not profitable and trails a matched Hyperliquid retail benchmark (41% vs. 50% roundtrip win rate). A paired-replay league of frontier models on 416 captured production scenarios finds decision quality statistically indistinguishable at this horizon, while choice stability differs sharply across model families. Every headline survives day-clustered inference, permutation nulls, and a common-fee restatement; the paper closes with a 17-rule methodology canon bought with our own retractions.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a large-scale, population-level measurement record of autonomous LLM trading agents deployed in production across two systems (DX Terminal Pro and DXAP live alpha fleet), spanning ~6 months with 7.5M model invocations and ~300K onchain actions. Four key findings emerge: (1) the operating layer (UI/risk controls) shapes agent behavior more than strategy text; (2) agent sizing is volatility-blind, concentrating liquidation risk; (3) agents systematically fail to capture favorable price excursions, leaving rich mechanical improvement on the table; (4) neither fleet demonstrates directional alpha, performing at or below retail benchmarks with decision quality statistically indistinguishable across frontier models.
AI.motivation: To provide the first continuous, population-scale empirical record of real autonomous LLM trading agents operating with real capital in production, moving beyond simulations and single-agent case studies to quantify actual behavioral patterns, risk-taking, and economic outcomes of LLM-agent trading at scale.
AI.method: Analyzes production telemetry from two live systems (DX Terminal Pro: 3,505 vaults trading ETH in Base memecoin markets over 21 days; DXAP: 500+ user-created agents trading Hyperliquid perps over ~3 months). Uses agent-level fixed effects, regression discontinuity at leaderboard boundaries, volatility-sextile sizing analysis, favorable-excursion (MFE/MAE-style) dissection, matched retail benchmark comparison, and a paired-replay league of frontier LLMs on 416 captured scenarios. Robustness via day-clustered inference, permutation nulls, and fee-restatement checks.
AI.result: (1) Risk slider (UI) is the dominant behavioral driver (leverage +0.425/level; agent fixed effects explain 60% of variance; top-3 leaderboard cut creates a 1.75x causal selection effect). (2) Median leverage is constant at 5.0x across volatility sextiles while 11% of the book holds 62% of liquidations. (3) 43.2% of positions reach +300bps favorable excursion within 24h yet 49.3% of those close negative; a mechanical bracket recovers +39.0bps/position. (4) DXAP win rate (41%) trails retail benchmark (50%); frontier-model decision quality is statistically indistinguishable while choice stability varies sharply by model family. All findings survive multiple robustness checks.
AI.conclusion: LLM trading agents in production are behaviorally governed by interface and operating-layer design far more than by strategy specification, are systematically volatility-blind in risk management, fail to lock in favorable excursions, and collectively lack directional edge at current capability levels. The authors close with a 17-rule methodology canon developed through their own retractions, offering guidance for safe and honest evaluation of autonomous trading systems.

title: OcclusionCBF: Backup Control Barrier Functions for Safe Navigation Among Hidden Dynamic Obstacles
comment: The first two authors contributed equally to this work. Project page: https://www.taekyung.me/occlusion-cbf
summary: Robots navigating under occlusion may enter states from which no admissible input can avoid a dynamic obstacle once it becomes visible. We present OcclusionCBF, a safety filter that extends backup control barrier functions to reachable-occupancy predictions for potentially hidden dynamic obstacles in occluded regions. The method certifies a prescribed backup rollout against collision-inflated occupancy and a verified terminal set, yielding affine constraints for minimally invasive quadratic-program filtering. We establish recursive feasibility of the resulting safety filter, and collision avoidance for every hidden-obstacle motion covered by the occupancy prediction. Randomized benchmarks, MetaUrban simulations, and hardware experiments demonstrate improved task success over reactive and occlusion-aware predictive baselines with millisecond-scale computation.

AI.tldr: OcclusionCBF is a safety filter that extends backup control barrier functions to predict the reachable occupancy of potentially hidden dynamic obstacles, certifying backup rollouts against collision-inflated occupancy and a verified terminal set. It produces affine constraints for minimally invasive QP filtering, guaranteeing recursive feasibility and collision avoidance, with validated performance in randomized benchmarks, MetaUrban simulations, and hardware experiments.
AI.motivation: Robots navigating under occlusion can enter states from which no admissible input can avoid a dynamic obstacle once it becomes visible, creating a safety-critical gap in existing reactive and occlusion-aware predictive approaches.
AI.method: The method extends backup control barrier functions (CBFs) to reachable-occupancy predictions for hidden dynamic obstacles in occluded regions. It certifies a prescribed backup rollout against collision-inflated occupancy and a verified terminal set, producing affine constraints used in minimally invasive quadratic-program (QP) filtering.
AI.result: Randomized benchmarks, MetaUrban simulations, and hardware experiments demonstrate improved task success over reactive and occlusion-aware predictive baselines, with millisecond-scale computation.
AI.conclusion: OcclusionCBF guarantees recursive feasibility of the safety filter and collision avoidance for every hidden-obstacle motion covered by the occupancy prediction, offering a computationally efficient and practically validated solution for occluded navigation safety.

title: CUSP: Decomposable Collective Uncertainty for Multi-Agent Multimodal Reasoning
summary: Aggregating heterogeneous vision-language models (VLMs) can improve multimodal reasoning, but neither an individual model's confidence nor that of the aggregated answer measures reliability at the system level. We present CUSP (Collective Uncertainty through Semantic Opinion Pooling), a training-free uncertainty quantification framework that maps multiple VLM responses to a shared semantic response space, pools them into a pooled semantic opinion, and reports two complementary system-level signals: collective uncertainty, the dispersion of the pooled opinion, and Jensen-Shannon divergence (JSD), the conflict among the model-level opinions. Within this pooled semantic opinion, the unnormalized collective entropy decomposes exactly into the mean of the models' individual semantic entropies and the JSD, separating total dispersion from model conflict. Requiring neither token logits nor calibration labels, CUSP applies to open-weight and commercial VLMs alike. In static multi-VLM ensembles, collective uncertainty is the strongest signal in the small-model regime (0.764 AUROC for prediction-error detection, 0.889 AUARC for abstention), outperforming uncertainty baselines majority voting and naive selection by 4.7 to 15.8 points and widening its margin as the ensemble grows; JSD is strongest in the evaluated commercial regime (0.819 AUROC, 0.910 AUARC) and ranks hard-answer model conflict with AUROC up to 0.982. The pooled prediction also improves accuracy over the average single model by 5.6 to 13.0 points. Over the full trajectory of a multi-step, multi-agent system, subagent collective uncertainty ranks system failures above chance (0.619 AUROC) and gives the best abstention ordering among the evaluated signals (0.699 AUARC).

AI.tldr: CUSP is a training-free uncertainty quantification framework that pools responses from multiple vision-language models into a shared semantic space, decomposing collective entropy into individual semantic entropies (dispersion) and Jensen-Shannon divergence (conflict). It provides system-level reliability signals effective in both static ensembles and multi-agent trajectories.
AI.motivation: Aggregating heterogeneous VLMs improves multimodal reasoning, but neither individual model confidence nor aggregated-answer confidence reliably measures system-level uncertainty. Existing methods rely on token logits or calibration labels, which are unavailable for commercial VLMs and do not separate dispersion from inter-model conflict.
AI.method: CUSP maps multiple VLM responses to a shared semantic response space, pools them into a pooled semantic opinion, and computes: (1) collective uncertainty (dispersion of the pooled opinion) and (2) Jensen-Shannon divergence (conflict among model-level opinions). The unnormalized collective entropy exactly decomposes into the mean of individual semantic entropies plus the JSD.
AI.result: In static multi-VLM ensembles, collective uncertainty achieves 0.764 AUROC for prediction-error detection and 0.889 AUARC for abstention in small-model regimes, outperforming baselines by 4.7-15.8 points with margin widening as the ensemble grows. JSD is strongest in commercial regimes (0.819 AUROC, 0.910 AUARC) and ranks hard-answer conflict at up to 0.982 AUROC. Pooled prediction improves accuracy by 5.6-13.0 points over average single model. In multi-step multi-agent systems, subagent collective uncertainty ranks failures at 0.619 AUROC and gives the best abstention ordering at 0.699 AUARC.
AI.conclusion: CUSP provides complementary and effective system-level uncertainty signals—dispersion and conflict—without requiring logits or labels, making it applicable to both open-weight and commercial VLMs and to single-step ensembles as well as multi-agent trajectories.

title: LANTERN: A Closed-Loop Benchmark for VLM-Based Cooperative Driving with Temporally Grounded Warnings
comment: 19 pages, 11 figures, and 8 tables; includes supplementary material
summary: We present LANTERN, a closed-loop benchmark for temporally grounded cooperative warnings. LANTERN separates warning onset, hazard onset, warning termination, and post-hazard recovery, and evaluates each physical event under matched warning and no-warning executions so that the warning's contribution is measured in isolation rather than confounded with onboard vision. The benchmark spans six safety-critical scenario families and provides 3,272 sequences with 236,309 frames for training, together with 120 matched route pairs for closed-loop evaluation. Each hazard route is evaluated under the warning and no-warning conditions, while its no-hazard control penalizes unconditional braking. We further introduce the Cooperative Unified Score (CUS), a safety-gated metric that jointly rewards route progress, anticipation, clearance, and recovery. Fine-tuning a representative VLM driving model raises CUS from 34.6 without warnings to 75.5 with them, demonstrating both the value of cooperative warnings and the discriminative power of the paired protocol. All resources will be made publicly available.

AI.tldr: LANTERN is a closed-loop benchmark for evaluating temporally grounded cooperative warnings in driving. It separates warning onset, hazard onset, warning termination, and post-hazard recovery, and measures the warning's contribution via matched warning and no-warning executions. It provides 3,272 sequences (236,309 frames) for training and 120 matched route pairs for closed-loop evaluation across six safety-critical scenario families. A Cooperative Unified Score (CUS) is introduced, and fine-tuning a VLM driving model improves CUS from 34.6 to 75.5 with warnings.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks confound cooperative warnings with onboard vision capabilities, making it difficult to isolate the contribution of temporal warnings to driving safety and effectiveness.
AI.method: LANTERN decomposes warning events into distinct temporal phases (onset, hazard onset, termination, recovery) and evaluates each under matched warning/no-warning executions. It includes no-hazard control routes to penalize unconditional braking and introduces the Cooperative Unified Score (CUS) as a safety-gated metric combining route progress, anticipation, clearance, and recovery.
AI.result: Fine-tuning a representative VLM driving model raises CUS from 34.6 (without warnings) to 75.5 (with warnings), demonstrating both the value of cooperative warnings and the discriminative power of the paired protocol.
AI.conclusion: Cooperative warnings significantly improve driving performance when properly evaluated in isolation, and the LANTERN benchmark with CUS provides a discriminative framework for future cooperative driving research. Resources will be publicly released.

title: Recovering Temporal and Geographic Signals from Language Model Embeddings
summary: Understanding whether language-model embeddings encode structured real-world information is important for both representation analysis and information retrieval. We study this question for temporal and geographic signals using a simple projection-based method that operates directly on output embeddings. Given a small set of seed examples, the method defines an axis in embedding space and ranks texts or entities by their projection onto that axis. Our approach is fully black-box and model-agnostic: it requires only embeddings, without access to model weights, internal activations, auxiliary probes, or additional training. This makes it applicable to modern embedding models available only through APIs and provides a lightweight way to analyze whether temporal and spatial dimensions are present in their representation spaces. We apply the method to temporal and geographic datasets and find that embedding projections recover meaningful chronological and spatial structure. These results provide evidence that output embeddings encode signals relevant to time and space, while also offering a practical tool for interpretability and for downstream temporal and geographic information retrieval tasks, such as temporal ordering, geographic ranking, and tagging.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a simple, black-box projection-based method for probing whether language-model output embeddings encode temporal and geographic structure. Using only a small set of seed examples to define an axis in embedding space, the method ranks texts or entities by projection scores—requiring no access to model weights, internal activations, or additional training. Applied to temporal and geographic datasets, the method recovers meaningful chronological and spatial structure, with applications to temporal ordering, geographic ranking, and tagging.
AI.motivation: The authors aim to understand whether language-model embeddings encode structured real-world information, specifically temporal and geographic signals. This matters for both representation analysis and information retrieval, and they seek a lightweight, model-agnostic probing method applicable to modern embedding models available only through APIs.
AI.method: The method is a projection-based approach operating directly on output embeddings. Given a small set of seed examples, it defines an axis in embedding space and ranks texts or entities by their projection onto this axis. It is fully black-box and model-agnostic, requiring only embeddings without access to model weights, internal activations, auxiliary probes, or additional training.
AI.result: Applied to temporal and geographic datasets, the embedding projections recover meaningful chronological and spatial structure, providing evidence that output embeddings encode signals relevant to time and space.
AI.conclusion: The findings indicate that output embeddings encode temporal and geographic information, and the proposed method serves as a practical interpretability tool and supports downstream temporal and geographic information retrieval tasks such as temporal ordering, geographic ranking, and tagging.

title: OVMAN: A Task and Benchmark for Open-Vocabulary Motion-Aware Navigation
summary: Homes change between a robot's visits. Navigation benchmarks pose their goals in the world the agent currently sees, and the two-visit benchmarks that exist score recall or rearrangement rather than navigation. None of them can express go to the chair that was moved or go to where the vase used to be. OVMAN is a task in which an agent tours a scene, returns after a scripted change, and must navigate to a goal specified by the change itself. Two of its six change relations answer with a place an object has left, where nothing remains to be detected. We release 219 two-visit episodes, each certified solvable by an oracle agent that completes it three times. Two released systems fail as predicted. A zero-shot object-goal navigator reaches the change-defined target in 11.4% of episodes and essentially fails at vacated locations, 0.000 on former and 0.025 on removed. A self-maintaining open-vocabulary map answers past-tense queries at about a third of the rate of the same maps read as two visits, even when grounding is supplied. A simple two-visit reference agent reaches 45.2% when navigating, against an embodied oracle of 99.5%. An error decomposition places the remaining difficulty in open-vocabulary instance grounding rather than in geometry or in selecting the answer once positions are known.

AI.tldr: OVMAN is a new two-visit navigation task where an agent must navigate to a goal defined by changes that occurred between visits (e.g., a moved or removed chair). The paper releases 219 certified-solvable episodes and shows that existing systems (zero-shot object-goal navigation and open-vocabulary mapping) largely fail, especially at vacated locations, while a simple two-visit reference agent reaches 45.2% against a 99.5% oracle ceiling, with errors concentrated in open-vocabulary grounding.
AI.motivation: Existing navigation benchmarks only pose goals in the currently visible world, and two-visit benchmarks score recall or rearrangement rather than navigation. None can express change-based goals like "go to the chair that was moved" or "go to where the vase used to be," motivating a task that requires an agent to reason about scene changes across visits.
AI.method: OVMAN has an agent tour a scene, depart while a scripted change occurs, return, and navigate to a goal specified by the change. Six change relations define the goal types, two of which require navigating to vacated locations where nothing remains to detect. A dataset of 219 two-visit episodes is released, each certified solvable by an oracle that completes it three times. Two baseline systems (zero-shot object-goal navigator and self-maintaining open-vocabulary map) are evaluated, along with a simple two-visit reference agent, with an error decomposition analysis.
AI.result: The zero-shot object-goal navigator reaches the change-defined target in only 11.4% of episodes and essentially fails at vacated locations (0.000 on former, 0.025 on removed). The open-vocabulary map answers past-tense queries at roughly one-third the rate of two-visit map reads, even with grounding supplied. A simple two-visit reference agent achieves 45.2% on navigation, well below the 99.5% embodied oracle. The error decomposition shows the bottleneck lies in open-vocabulary instance grounding, not geometry or answer selection.
AI.conclusion: OVMAN is a challenging new benchmark that exposes a critical gap: current embodied agents cannot reliably handle temporal change-based goals, particularly those referencing vacated locations. The primary technical barrier is open-vocabulary instance grounding across visits, which future work must address to enable agents to reason about scene transformations over time.

title: Beyond Prompts: Measuring and Optimizing LLM Tool-Agent Harnesses
comment: Accepted to EMNLP 2026. 18 pages, 9 figures, 10 tables
summary: LLM tool agents can be improved without retraining by modifying the runtime harness around a fixed model: prompts, tool interfaces, middleware, state handling, and recovery logic. We study this setting as resource-bounded harness selection for fixed-model multi-turn tool agents, with the search surface scoped to prompts and tool-boundary middleware: edits are guarded intercepts at the tool boundary, not arbitrary rewriting of agent execution logic. Our optimizer-agnostic protocol reports mean held-out lift, worst-condition lift, repeatability, logged cost diagnostics, and RelLift95(B), a conservative estimate of the held-out gain of the harness selected under budget B. We instantiate the protocol with prompt-only and prompt-plus-middleware optimizers, including PRISM, which clusters failures and routes repairs to prompt, tool-boundary middleware, or joint edit surfaces within a Pareto search. On BFCL multi-round, tau2-Retail, and tau2-Telecom, PRISM obtains mean held-out lifts of 14.2, 14.9, and 10.1 percentage points and positive empirical RelLift95 on all three benchmarks, and a component ablation attributes the margin chiefly to failure-surface routing and the edit-pattern constraint. Across optimizers, the results show that some search procedures can occasionally find large gains but still choose brittle updates, so the reliability of the chosen harness should be reported alongside average held-out lift.

AI.tldr: This paper studies resource-bounded harness selection for fixed-model multi-turn tool agents, where the search surface is limited to prompts and tool-boundary middleware. The authors propose an optimizer-agnostic evaluation protocol and PRISM, a failure-clustering optimizer that routes repairs across prompt, middleware, and joint edit surfaces. PRISM achieves mean held-out lifts of 14.2, 14.9, and 10.1 percentage points on three benchmarks with positive RelLift95, and the paper highlights that reliability metrics must accompany average lift since some search procedures find large gains but choose brittle updates.
AI.motivation: LLM tool agents can be improved by modifying the runtime harness around a fixed model (e.g., prompts, middleware) without retraining, yet there is a lack of systematic methodology for searching and evaluating these harness modifications reliably under resource constraints.
AI.method: The authors formalize resource-bounded harness selection for fixed-model tool agents, restricting edits to prompts and tool-boundary middleware (guarded intercepts). They propose an optimizer-agnostic protocol reporting mean held-out lift, worst-condition lift, repeatability, cost diagnostics, and RelLift95(B). They instantiate prompt-only and prompt-plus-middleware optimizers, including PRISM, which clusters agent failures and routes repairs to prompt, middleware, or joint edit surfaces within a Pareto search.
AI.result: On BFCL multi-round, tau2-Retail, and tau2-Telecom, PRISM achieves mean held-out lifts of 14.2, 14.9, and 10.1 percentage points respectively, with positive empirical RelLift95 on all three benchmarks. A component ablation attributes the margin chiefly to failure-surface routing and the edit-pattern constraint.
AI.conclusion: Across optimizers, some search procedures discover large gains but still select brittle updates. Therefore, reporting both reliability metrics and average held-out lift is essential when evaluating harness search for tool agents. PRISM demonstrates that failure-aware routing and constrained edits yield robust held-out improvements without retraining.

title: Collision Snapshot Guided Time-Reversed Safety-Critical Scenario Generation
summary: The generation of safety-critical traffic scenarios is essential for training and evaluating autonomous vehicles. Prior approaches typically perturb the trajectories of existing agents in a traffic scenario using simplified adversarial objectives to induce safety-critical interactions, which can limit the plausibility and diversity of the generated scenarios. Although inserting new adversarial vehicles can alleviate this limitation, determining when and where to introduce them in a scenario-specific manner remains challenging. In this work, we introduce \underline{CO}llision \underline{S}napshot guided \underline{T}im\underline{E}-\underline{R}eversed safety-critical scenario generation (COSTER), a framework that leverages learned traffic priors to determine plausible collision times and locations. COSTER first constructs a collision snapshot by inserting a new vehicle in contact with the target vehicle at the identified collision state within a traffic scenario. Starting from this collision snapshot, a conditional variational autoencoder is used to perform a time-reversed rollout, reconstructing the trajectory of the inserted vehicle backward toward earlier timesteps. Experiments show that COSTER outperforms existing methods in plausibility, diversity, and data efficiency. Moreover, agents trained on COSTER-generated scenarios reduce collision rates by 31\% on safety-critical scenarios from the Waymo Open Motion Dataset while also improving ego task completion. The project website is available at https://anonym-121.github.io/COSTER/.

AI.tldr: COSTER is a framework that generates plausible and diverse safety-critical traffic scenarios by constructing collision snapshots (inserting a new vehicle in contact with the target at learned collision states) and using a conditional variational autoencoder to perform time-reversed rollouts. It outperforms existing methods in plausibility, diversity, and data efficiency, and reduces collision rates by 31% on safety-critical scenarios from the Waymo Open Motion Dataset.
AI.motivation: Prior adversarial scenario generation methods perturb existing agent trajectories with simplified objectives, limiting plausibility and diversity. Inserting new adversarial vehicles can help, but determining when and where to insert them in a scenario-specific manner remains challenging.
AI.method: COSTER first learns traffic priors to identify plausible collision times and locations, constructing a collision snapshot by inserting a new vehicle in contact with the target vehicle at the identified collision state. From this snapshot, a conditional variational autoencoder performs a time-reversed rollout to reconstruct the inserted vehicle's trajectory backward toward earlier timesteps.
AI.result: COSTER outperforms existing methods in plausibility, diversity, and data efficiency. Agents trained on COSTER-generated scenarios reduce collision rates by 31% on safety-critical scenarios from the Waymo Open Motion Dataset while also improving ego task completion.
AI.conclusion: The collision-snapshot-guided time-reversed framework effectively leverages learned traffic priors to generate safety-critical scenarios that improve downstream autonomous vehicle training and evaluation.

title: The Normalization of Deviance in AI Development
summary: Work on the risks of artificial intelligence has focused predominantly on capability risk: the danger that systems become too powerful, too autonomous, or too misaligned with human values. Far less attention has been paid to the organizational level---to whether the institutions building these systems are themselves predisposed to drift toward failure. This paper argues that they are. Regardless of how capable AI systems become, the organizations building them face the same structural dynamics that preceded past major technological disasters. Drawing on case studies of the Space Shuttle Challenger, the Three Mile Island accident, and the Boeing 737 MAX crashes, this paper identifies the common structural mechanisms preceding each failure and maps them onto contemporary AI development. The findings suggest that existing safety infrastructure may provide less protection than it appears, as organizations can complete safety processes in full compliance and still produce catastrophic outcomes. The pre-disaster period of AI development is still underway; the purpose of this paper is to make these dynamics legible while they can still be interrupted.

AI.tldr: This paper argues that risks from AI are not only capability-based but also organizational, drawing on historical disaster case studies (Space Shuttle Challenger, Three Mile Island, Boeing 737 MAX) to show that institutions building AI systems are structurally predisposed toward failure. It identifies common structural mechanisms preceding past disasters and maps them onto contemporary AI development, suggesting safety infrastructure can be fully complied with yet still produce catastrophic outcomes.
AI.motivation: AI risk research has overwhelmingly focused on capability risk (systems becoming too powerful or misaligned), neglecting the organizational level—whether the institutions building these systems are structurally prone to drift toward failure. The paper aims to fill this gap by examining organizational dynamics.
AI.method: The paper uses comparative case study analysis of three major technological disasters—the Space Shuttle Challenger, the Three Mile Island accident, and the Boeing 737 MAX crashes—to identify common structural mechanisms preceding each failure, then maps these mechanisms onto contemporary AI development organizations.
AI.result: The analysis finds that organizations building AI systems face the same structural dynamics that preceded past major disasters. Notably, existing safety infrastructure may provide less protection than it appears, as organizations can complete safety processes in full compliance and still produce catastrophic outcomes.
AI.conclusion: The pre-disaster period of AI development is still ongoing, and the paper's purpose is to make these dangerous organizational dynamics legible while they can still be interrupted or corrected.

title: \textbf{PLATO}: \emph{Preintegration Learning from Accurate Trajectory Observations} for Neural Inertial Odometry
summary: Neural inertial odometry has demonstrated strong potential for motion estimation in challenging environments, yet inertial-only preintegration remains sensitive to IMU bias and uncertainty. To this end, this paper introduces \textbf{PLATO}:~\emph{Preintegration Learning from Accurate Trajectory Observations}, a likelihood-based framework that leverages accurate trajectory observations to jointly learn IMU bias dynamics modeled by a neural ordinary differential equation~(NODE) and gyroscope and accelerometer noise covariances. Optimization exploits the sparse structure of the negative log-likelihood, with IMU noise-parameter gradients computed by forward differentiation. A tailored double-adjoint scheme couples a discrete invariant-error adjoint with a continuous-time adjoint for the bias NODE, enabling memory-efficient likelihood optimization over the nested bias-dynamics and IMU-preintegration rollouts. Validation on EuRoC shows improved performance, and underwater robot experiments demonstrate applicability under intermittent lighting failures and visual degradation.

AI.tldr: PLATO is a likelihood-based framework for neural inertial odometry that jointly learns IMU bias dynamics via a neural ODE and sensor noise covariances from accurate trajectory observations, using a memory-efficient double-adjoint optimization scheme.
AI.motivation: Inertial-only preintegration remains sensitive to IMU bias and uncertainty, limiting the accuracy and robustness of neural inertial odometry for motion estimation in challenging environments.
AI.method: PLATO jointly learns IMU bias dynamics (modeled by a neural ODE) and gyroscope/accelerometer noise covariances via likelihood-based optimization. The negative log-likelihood is optimized exploiting its sparse structure, with noise-parameter gradients computed by forward differentiation and a double-adjoint scheme coupling discrete invariant-error adjoints with a continuous-time adjoint for the bias NODE to enable memory-efficient training.
AI.result: Improved performance on the EuRoC dataset, and successful application in underwater robot experiments demonstrating robustness under intermittent lighting failures and visual degradation.
AI.conclusion: PLATO enhances inertial-only odometry accuracy by jointly learning bias dynamics and noise covariances from accurate trajectory observations, with demonstrated generalization to degraded visual environments.

title: From Monolithic Blending to Agentic Orchestration: Dynamic Response for Conversational Assistants at Scale
comment: Accepted to EMNLP 2026 Industry Track. 16 pages, 1 figure, 21 tables
summary: Conversational assistants can blend retrieval, action selection, escalation, and wording in a single model path, or separate those roles. We report a production migration of a customer-support assistant at a large accommodation marketplace (millions of conversations per month, 11 languages, 10-second P90). Dynamic Response (DR) replaces a single Qwen3-235B-A22B blended responder with a bounded ReAct orchestrator over typed tools plus a smaller generator that writes from a backend-validated context contract. Because the migration also changed prompts, alignment, and serving, we attribute each effect to its cause and claim as architecture effects only those measured on identical replayed turns: typed entity selection moves the reservation selector to a precision-first operating point (precision 8.3% to 89.1%, recall 75.2% to 67.3%), and typed action IDs with a membership check remove observed structured-action hallucination (2.14% to 0.0%). A low-ramp A/B test reproduces the replay escalation reductions: hard-escalation responses fall from 5.60% to 3.08% and soft-escalation responses from 9.56% to 2.49%, while production handoff volume holds roughly steady; self-solve is directional (+5.1 points, 95% CI [-2, +12]). Serving optimizations cut orchestrator P90 latency from 3.87s to 2.24s on a GPU footprint reduced by roughly one-third, and self-hosting reduces estimated annual model-serving cost by more than an order of magnitude.

AI.tldr: This paper reports a production migration of a customer-support assistant at a large accommodation marketplace (millions of conversations/month, 11 languages) from a single Qwen3-235B-A22B blended responder to a Dynamic Response (DR) architecture: a bounded ReAct orchestrator over typed tools plus a smaller generator writing from a backend-validated context contract.
AI.motivation: To improve reliability and controllability of a large-scale conversational assistant by separating concerns (retrieval, action selection, escalation, wording) instead of blending them in a single model path.
AI.method: The authors replace a single blended LLM responder with a bounded ReAct orchestrator that calls typed tools, paired with a smaller generator that writes from a backend-validated context contract. They attribute architecture effects via identical replayed turns and validate via a low-ramp A/B test.
AI.result: Typed entity selection improved reservation selector precision from 8.3% to 89.1% (recall dropping 75.2% to 67.3%); typed action IDs with membership check eliminated structured-action hallucination (2.14% to 0.0%); hard-escalation responses fell from 5.60% to 3.08% and soft-escalation from 9.56% to 2.49% in A/B testing; orchestrator P90 latency cut from 3.87s to 2.24s on roughly one-third smaller GPU footprint; self-hosting reduced estimated annual model-serving cost by over an order of magnitude.
AI.conclusion: Decomposing a blended conversational assistant into typed-tool orchestration with a smaller contract-validated generator yields substantial precision, hallucination, and escalation reductions while also improving latency, GPU footprint, and serving cost—at production scale across 11 languages.

title: VLA-Corrector: Stage-Aware Observable State Understanding for Prompt-Based Closed-Loop Recovery of Vision-Language-Action Policies
summary: Long-horizon robot manipulation with Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies remains vulnerable to execution-time deviations, as final task success provides little information for diagnosing and correcting failures caused by action noise, object displacement, or goal misalignment. We introduce a stage-aware failure verification and Prompt Recovery framework that enables closed-loop correction of a fixed VLA policy without parameter updates or privileged simulator states. The framework introduces an observable-history-based Learned Verifier that jointly estimates manipulation progress and execution risk by temporally modeling multi-view visual observations, proprioceptive states, and executed actions. To provide interpretable task understanding, we represent manipulation execution through semantic progress stages, including approach, alignment, grasp, transport, and placement, and identify stage-specific failure patterns. Upon detecting abnormal execution, the framework preserves the original instruction and generates a stage-conditioned recovery prompt, allowing the same frozen VLA policy to produce corrective actions. Extensive multi-round evaluations on LIBERO and LIBERO Plus demonstrate that the proposed approach substantially improves closed-loop reliability under diverse perturbations. Without access to privileged object or goal coordinates, the Learned Verifier achieves recovery performance close to that of the privileged rule-based verifier in the evaluated settings. These results show that observable visual-proprioceptive-action history is sufficient to infer latent task states and enable practical failure recovery for existing VLA policies.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a stage-aware failure verification and Prompt Recovery framework for long-horizon robot manipulation with frozen Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies. It uses a Learned Verifier that jointly estimates manipulation progress and execution risk from observable visual, proprioceptive, and action history, without parameter updates or privileged simulator states. The framework detects stage-specific failures and generates recovery prompts to enable closed-loop correction of the same frozen VLA policy.
AI.motivation: Final task success alone provides insufficient information for diagnosing and correcting execution-time deviations in long-horizon VLA robot manipulation, such as action noise, object displacement, or goal misalignment. There is a need for a closed-loop correction mechanism that does not require model retraining or access to privileged simulator state.
AI.method: The framework consists of (1) an observable-history-based Learned Verifier that temporally models multi-view visual observations, proprioceptive states, and executed actions to jointly estimate progress and risk; (2) a semantic progress stage representation (approach, alignment, grasp, transport, placement) for interpretable task understanding and stage-specific failure identification; and (3) a stage-conditioned prompt recovery mechanism that preserves the original instruction and generates corrective prompts for the frozen VLA policy upon detected anomalies.
AI.result: Multi-round evaluations on LIBERO and LIBERO Plus show substantial improvements in closed-loop reliability under diverse perturbations. The Learned Verifier achieves recovery performance close to that of the privileged rule-based verifier without accessing object or goal coordinates.
AI.conclusion: Observable visual-proprioceptive-action history is sufficient to infer latent task states and enable practical failure recovery for existing frozen VLA policies, offering a viable path toward robust closed-loop manipulation without model updates or privileged information.

title: Inference-Time Graph Engineering for Multi-Agent LLM Workflows
summary: Recent multi-agent LLM systems increasingly rely on graph-structured communication to coordinate specialized agents. We revisit multi-agent orchestration from a graph-engineering perspective: rather than optimizing a static topology, we synthesize a task-conditioned temporal workflow graph that jointly specifies agent connectivity and edge-level communication semantics. We introduce ReActNet, a training-free framework that compiles a query and a set of role-specialized agents into a sequence of directed communication graphs. Each graph snapshot corresponds to one reasoning stage, and each edge carries a natural-language instruction specifying the message that a source agent should provide to a target agent. The compiled temporal graph is then executed through structured message passing: agents update their reasoning states by integrating their previous states with messages from controller-assigned neighbors, and a final aggregator synthesizes the resulting states into the answer. This design separates graph compilation from graph execution, making multi-agent coordination explicit, inspectable, and task-conditioned without requiring reinforcement learning or gradient-based topology optimization. Across knowledge reasoning, mathematical problem solving, code generation, and GAIA-style assistant tasks, ReActNet consistently improves over fixed-topology and learned-topology baselines while maintaining competitive inference cost. These results suggest that effective multi-agent orchestration depends not only on which agents communicate, but also on engineering executable workflow graphs that encode when, why, and how information should flow during reasoning.

AI.tldr: ReActNet is a training-free framework that compiles a query and role-specialized agents into a task-conditioned temporal workflow graph, where each graph snapshot corresponds to a reasoning stage and each edge carries natural-language communication instructions. It separates graph compilation from graph execution via structured message passing, improving over fixed and learned-topology baselines on reasoning, math, code, and GAIA-style tasks.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent LLM systems rely on graph-structured communication, but existing approaches optimize static topologies. The authors argue orchestration should instead be viewed as graph engineering: synthesizing task-conditioned temporal graphs that jointly specify agent connectivity and communication semantics, without requiring reinforcement learning or gradient-based topology optimization.
AI.method: ReActNet compiles a query and role-specialized agents into a sequence of directed communication graphs (a temporal workflow graph). Each snapshot maps to one reasoning stage; each edge carries a natural-language instruction specifying what a source agent should send to a target agent. Execution uses structured message passing where agents update reasoning states by integrating prior states with controller-assigned neighbor messages, and a final aggregator produces the answer.
AI.result: Across knowledge reasoning, mathematical problem solving, code generation, and GAIA-style assistant tasks, ReActNet consistently outperforms fixed-topology and learned-topology baselines while maintaining competitive inference cost.
AI.conclusion: Effective multi-agent orchestration depends not only on which agents communicate, but also on engineering executable workflow graphs that encode when, why, and how information should flow during reasoning. Separating graph compilation from execution makes multi-agent coordination explicit, inspectable, and task-conditioned.

title: Knowledge-Guided Hierarchical Policy Learning for High-Precision Cylindrical Assembly under Tight Tolerances
comment: 25 pages, 14 figures. Submitted to Robotics and Computer-Integrated Manufacturing (Elsevier)
summary: A hybrid hierarchical learning framework is proposed to achieve high-precision assembly of 170mm cylindrical components with tolerance of 0.1mm. The lower-level network integrates expert experience through Behavior Cloning (BC), giving the robot human-like intuition, and incorporates the Twin Delayed Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (TD3) algorithm to enhance training stability and robustness. The upper-level network dynamically adjusts the lower-level decisions based on heuristic rules, ensuring flexibility in operations. A simulated model is constructed to learn before transferring to real world. An efficient and safe training is allowed. Comparisons show that the reward curve converges within 500 episodes, indicating high learning efficiency. It also demonstrates better adaptability to initial conditions and pose errors, achieving satisfactory success rates even under extreme conditions. Moreover, the method exhibits good stability under Gaussian noise interference. In the real world, the assembly trajectory of the cylindrical segment shows smoother motion and less fluctuation.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a hybrid hierarchical learning framework combining Behavior Cloning (BC) with Twin Delayed Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (TD3) at the lower level and heuristic rules at the upper level for high-precision assembly (0.1mm tolerance) of 170mm cylindrical components. The framework trains in simulation before real-world transfer, achieving convergence within 500 episodes, robust performance under extreme conditions and Gaussian noise, and smoother real-world assembly trajectories.
AI.motivation: High-precision robotic assembly of large cylindrical components (170mm with 0.1mm tolerance) is challenging due to the need for both human-like intuition and stable, adaptive control under pose errors and environmental disturbances.
AI.method: A hybrid hierarchical framework with: (1) a lower-level network combining BC (expert demonstration for human-like intuition) and TD3 (for training stability and robustness); (2) an upper-level network using heuristic rules for dynamic adjustment of lower-level decisions; and (3) a sim-to-real pipeline with model training in simulation prior to real-world deployment.
AI.result: Reward curve converges within 500 episodes indicating high learning efficiency; superior adaptability to initial conditions and pose errors with satisfactory success rates under extreme conditions; good stability under Gaussian noise; real-world assembly shows smoother motion and less fluctuation for the cylindrical segment.
AI.conclusion: The hybrid hierarchical learning approach effectively balances learning efficiency, robustness, and adaptability, enabling high-precision cylindrical assembly in both simulated and real-world environments.

title: DI-Bench: Systematically Generating In-Domain Data Intelligence Benchmarks for Enterprise Agents
comment: 19 pages, 3 figures, 13 tables. Accepted to the EMNLP 2026 Industry Track
summary: Evaluating enterprise agents on domain-specific benchmarks is critical, yet public benchmarks rarely evaluate whether agents can integrate business knowledge with analytical computation, and constructing such benchmarks manually is costly. We present DI-Bench, a pipeline for generating realistic benchmarks for data intelligence (DI), the practice of extracting insights from large volumes of enterprise data. To emulate realistic DI tasks that require both computation and knowledge retrieval, DI-Bench builds an artifact linkage graph over data tables, dimensions, metrics, and documents to form questions involving structured data and associated knowledge. Ground truth answers are derived via query execution, followed by LLM question generation and validation. Applied to two public datasets, the pipeline produces a 731-task benchmark covering knowledge retrieval, analytical computation, and rule-grounded reasoning. To show the discriminatory capability and difficulty of the benchmark, we evaluate four models, revealing a substantial finding: models achieve only 32% accuracy when doing computational tasks where retrieved business rules modify the computation.

AI.tldr: DI-Bench is a pipeline for automatically generating realistic domain-specific benchmarks for data intelligence (DI) agents, which require combining business knowledge with analytical computation. It leverages an artifact linkage graph over data structures to generate questions with ground-truth answers validated via query execution and LLM generation. Applied to two public datasets, it produces a 731-task benchmark revealing that current models achieve only 32% accuracy on computational tasks where business rules modify computations.
AI.motivation: Public benchmarks rarely evaluate whether enterprise agents can integrate business knowledge with analytical computation, and manually constructing such benchmarks is costly and impractical at scale.
AI.method: DI-Bench builds an artifact linkage graph connecting data tables, dimensions, metrics, and documents to formulate questions requiring both structured data access and knowledge retrieval. Ground-truth answers are derived via query execution, followed by LLM-based question generation and validation.
AI.result: The pipeline generates a 731-task benchmark covering knowledge retrieval, analytical computation, and rule-grounded reasoning. Evaluation of four models reveals that they achieve only 32% accuracy on computational tasks where business rules modify the computation, demonstrating the benchmark's discriminatory capability and difficulty.
AI.conclusion: DI-Bench provides an automated, scalable pipeline for constructing enterprise data intelligence benchmarks and reveals a significant gap in current models' ability to integrate business rules with analytical computation.

title: SHIFT: Surface-aware High-speed Integration For TSDFs
summary: Real-time 3D mapping is fundamental for autonomous robotic navigation, with Euclidean Signed Distance Fields (ESDFs) serving as the standard representation for online motion planning. While recent advancements in non- projective distance fields yield highly accurate maps, their computational overhead remains a severe bottleneck. Conventional integrators redundantly re-fuse millions of depth pixels every frame, even long after the corresponding voxels have converged, wasting significant computational resources in environments dominated by large planar surfaces. In this paper, we present SHIFT (Surface-aware High-speed Integration For TSDFs), an efficient mapping framework designed to reduce this per-frame update cost. By exploiting structural redundancy directly from 3D depth geometry, SHIFT compresses flat local regions into weighted super-rays and freezes flat-voxel gradients. A compact ESDF voxel layout further reduces the memory footprint of the remaining wavefront. Extensive evaluations across various RGB-D and LiDAR sequences show that SHIFT cuts TSDF cost by 1.42 to 4.07 times, while holding mesh error within millimeters, and reduces ESDF-layer memory by up to 28%

AI.tldr: SHIFT is an efficient 3D mapping framework that reduces per-frame TSDF integration cost by compressing flat local regions into weighted super-rays and freezing flat-voxel gradients, cutting TSDF cost by 1.42-4.07x while holding mesh error within millimeters and reducing ESDF-layer memory by up to 28%.
AI.motivation: Real-time 3D mapping via ESDFs is critical for robotic navigation, but existing non-projective distance field integration is computationally expensive. Conventional integrators redundantly re-fuse millions of depth pixels every frame even after voxels converge, wasting significant computational resources, especially in environments dominated by large planar surfaces.
AI.method: SHIFT exploits structural redundancy directly from 3D depth geometry by compressing flat local regions into weighted super-rays and freezing flat-voxel gradients. A compact ESDF voxel layout is also introduced to reduce the memory footprint of the remaining wavefront propagation.
AI.result: Across various RGB-D and LiDAR sequences, SHIFT cuts TSDF cost by 1.42 to 4.07 times while keeping mesh error within millimeters, and reduces ESDF-layer memory by up to 28%.
AI.conclusion: SHIFT demonstrates that exploiting surface structural redundancy can significantly accelerate TSDF integration and reduce memory overhead without compromising mapping accuracy, making it suitable for real-time robotic navigation in planar-dominated environments.

title: Distilling Vision-Language Models for On-Device Fire Understanding
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) offer a promising alternative to conventional fire detection systems by reasoning about the semantic context of a scene and thus reducing false alarms, yet their large model size makes deployment on embedded fire sensors impractical. In this paper, we study how domain-specialized VLMs can be compressed for fully on-device deployment without losing the safety-critical behavior required for fire detection. We develop a teacher-student knowledge distillation framework in which large VLMs fine-tuned for fire understanding can be distilled into lightweight students. Experiments across multiple VLM families and model scales show that compact students preserve most of their teachers' fire-understanding capability. We further deploy the distilled models on our commercial Detectium fire detection sensor and jointly evaluate reasoning accuracy, latency, and memory usage. The results show that compression and deployment affect not only accuracy but also model failure modes, with Qwen2.5-0.5B providing the strongest overall deployment trade-off. Our findings provide broader guidance for deploying domain-specialized VLMs in resource-constrained, safety-critical settings.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates compressing domain-specialized vision-language models (VLMs) for fire detection via teacher-student knowledge distillation, enabling fully on-device deployment on embedded fire sensors. Compact students retain most teacher capability, with Qwen2.5-0.5B offering the best trade-off across accuracy, latency, and memory on the commercial Detectium sensor, while also showing that compression affects not just accuracy but also model failure modes.
AI.motivation: Conventional fire detection systems suffer from false alarms, and while VLMs can improve accuracy through semantic scene reasoning, their large model size makes deployment impractical on embedded fire sensors. The authors aim to make safety-critical VLM-based fire detection feasible for on-device resource-constrained settings.
AI.method: The authors develop a teacher-student knowledge distillation framework where large VLMs fine-tuned for fire understanding are distilled into lightweight student models. They evaluate across multiple VLM families and model scales, then deploy the distilled models on the Detectium commercial fire detection sensor, jointly measuring reasoning accuracy, latency, and memory usage.
AI.result: Compact student models preserve most of the teachers' fire-understanding capability across multiple VLM families and scales. Deployment results show that compression affects both accuracy and model failure modes; Qwen2.5-0.5B achieves the strongest overall deployment trade-off on the Detectium sensor.
AI.conclusion: The work provides broader guidance for deploying domain-specialized VLMs in resource-constrained, safety-critical environments by demonstrating that knowledge distillation can effectively shrink VLMs for embedded fire detection without compromising safety-critical behavior.

title: Unifying Physics-Based Humanoid Interaction with a Context-Conditioned Interaction Prior
comment: Accepted at SIGGRAPH Asia 2026. Project page: https://jiann-li.github.io/chip-project/
summary: Developing unified physics-based humanoid controllers that can navigate complex 3D scenes and manipulate objects remains a longstanding challenge. Existing approaches are often specialized for either locomotion or object-centric manipulation, or rely on task-specific reward engineering that does not scale well across diverse behaviors. We present CHIP, a unified, physics-grounded framework for learning reusable humanoid interaction skills from heterogeneous motion data. Central to our approach is a conditional interaction prior that models a context-dependent distribution over these skills within a shared discrete space. Our method is trained in three stages. We first learn physics-based motion-imitation policies that acquire grounded teacher behaviors from heterogeneous interaction data. We then distill these behaviors into a context-conditioned interaction prior that captures reusable motion structure across locomotion and manipulation. Finally, we initialize downstream task policies from the pretrained prior and adapt them through prior-regularized online RL post-training. Experiments on a diverse suite of humanoid interaction tasks show that our approach supports scene-aware locomotion, contact-rich object manipulation, and compositional behaviors such as environment-aware object transport and long-horizon skill sequencing, while producing smooth transitions and physically plausible motion.

AI.tldr: CHIP is a unified physics-based framework for learning reusable humanoid interaction skills from heterogeneous motion data, using a conditional interaction prior over a shared discrete skill space, trained in three stages (motion imitation, prior distillation, and prior-regularized RL post-training) to enable both scene-aware locomotion and contact-rich manipulation.
AI.motivation: Developing unified physics-based humanoid controllers that can both navigate complex 3D scenes and manipulate objects is challenging. Existing approaches are typically specialized for either locomotion or object-centric manipulation, or require task-specific reward engineering that fails to scale across diverse behaviors.
AI.method: CHIP uses a conditional interaction prior that models a context-dependent distribution over reusable skills in a shared discrete space. Training proceeds in three stages: (1) learning physics-based motion-imitation policies from heterogeneous interaction data to acquire grounded teacher behaviors; (2) distilling these behaviors into a context-conditioned interaction prior capturing reusable motion structure across locomotion and manipulation; (3) initializing downstream task policies from the pretrained prior and adapting them via prior-regularized online RL post-training.
AI.result: Experiments across a diverse suite of humanoid interaction tasks demonstrate that CHIP supports scene-aware locomotion, contact-rich object manipulation, and compositional behaviors such as environment-aware object transport and long-horizon skill sequencing, while producing smooth transitions and physically plausible motion.
AI.conclusion: A unified interaction-prior framework trained from heterogeneous motion data can effectively support diverse humanoid interaction skills—including compositional and long-horizon behaviors—without requiring task-specific reward engineering, generalizing across both locomotion and manipulation.

title: More Than Mimicking Reviewers: Evaluating LLMs for Pre-Submission Peer Review
summary:
Peer-review feedback often arrives too late for authors to make meaningful revisions. We study an author-facing LLM system that moves part of this stress test before submission: it generates a broad pool of atomic concerns and compresses them into a short report. We evaluate agreement with historical reviews and, separately, the possible validity of concerns they omit.
  From 10,000 ICLR 2026 submissions, we use 3,398 manuscripts with accessible versions that predate review. On a ten-paper diagnostic, independent sampling covers 44.9% of historical issues; deduplication and refill reaches 78.7% strict and 84.9% seriousness-weighted coverage, at 3.6$\times$ more requests and 5.2$\times$ more tokens. A hidden Top-32 Oracle preserves the full 79.3% weighted coverage of a 256-candidate pool, but paper-only selectors retain only 40--44%. LLM review therefore provides broad coverage with a large candidate pool but compresses poorly; ablations identify representative selection and matcher sensitivity as the main sources of this gap.

AI.tldr: The paper studies an author-facing LLM system that generates a broad pool of atomic peer-review concerns before submission and compresses them into a short report. Using 3,398 ICLR 2026 submissions, they find that deduplication and refill achieves up to 84.9% seriousness-weighted coverage of historical review issues, but compression quality degrades substantially—paper-only selectors retain only 40-44% of coverage compared to an Oracle's 79.3%—identifying representative selection and matcher sensitivity as key bottlenecks.
AI.motivation: Peer-review feedback often arrives too late for authors to make meaningful revisions. The authors propose moving part of the review stress test before submission via an LLM-based pre-review system.
AI.method: The system generates a large pool of atomic concerns and compresses them into a short report. Evaluation measures agreement with historical reviews and the validity of omitted concerns. From 10,000 ICLR 2026 submissions, 3,398 manuscripts predating review were used. They compare independent sampling, deduplication+refill strategies, and a hidden Top-32 Oracle selector against paper-only selectors.
AI.result: Independent sampling covers 44.9% of historical issues; deduplication and refill reaches 78.7% strict and 84.9% seriousness-weighted coverage at 3.6x more requests and 5.2x more tokens. The hidden Top-32 Oracle preserves 79.3% weighted coverage of a 256-candidate pool, but paper-only selectors retain only 40-44%.
AI.conclusion: LLM review provides broad coverage with a large candidate pool but compresses poorly. Ablations identify representative selection and matcher sensitivity as the main sources of the compression gap.

title: MemCorr-DP: Counterfactual Correspondence Conditioning for a Diffusion Policy Guided by a Reference
comment: 12 pages, 6 figures. Tan Su, Haoxiang Yang, and Ruxin Wang contributed equally. Corresponding author: Binghui Xie
summary: Behavior-cloned visuomotor policies can remain accurate near their training distribution yet fail when object position and camera viewpoint change together. A successful reference trajectory contains the geometry needed to transfer the same interaction, but the policy must align that geometry with the current scene and remain sensitive to it during denoising. To address these challenges, we present MemCorr-DP, a diffusion policy that lifts frozen RoMa v2 matches into explicit 3D relations between the current scene and the reference trajectory. A counterfactual paired objective assigns opposite behaviors the same physical state and noisy action while retaining reference-specific denoising targets. Mixed-condition fine-tuning then adapts the policy from ground-truth geometry to measured correspondence errors. Our strongest evaluation places the Door in the outermost position bands beyond the training support and changes the query camera by $\pm15^\circ$. Under this combined shift, MemCorr-DP achieves 96.67% closed-loop success, compared with 88.00% for a visual Transformer with the same action architecture. Objective ablations and reference interventions show that behavior responds to the selected reference, while matched controls favor the complete relation set over future motion or centroid geometry alone. These results support explicit 3D reference relations as a robust conditioning interface when spatial and viewpoint changes are compounded in the evaluated task.

AI.tldr: MemCorr-DP is a diffusion policy that uses frozen RoMa v2 matches to establish explicit 3D relations between the current scene and a reference trajectory, enabling robust closed-loop visuomotor control under combined object position and camera viewpoint shifts. It achieves 96.67% success under extreme compounding shifts versus 88.00% for a visual Transformer baseline.
AI.motivation: Behavior-cloned visuomotor policies are accurate near their training distribution but fail when object position and camera viewpoint change together. Reference trajectories contain transferable interaction geometry, but policies must align that geometry to the current scene and remain sensitive to it during denoising—a challenge existing approaches do not adequately address.
AI.method: MemCorr-DP lifts frozen RoMa v2 feature matches into explicit 3D relations linking the current scene to a reference trajectory. A counterfactual paired objective assigns identical physical states and noisy actions to opposite behaviors while preserving reference-specific denoising targets. Mixed-condition fine-tuning then transitions the policy from ground-truth geometry to measured correspondence errors.
AI.result: Under the strongest combined shift (outermost object position bands beyond training support + camera changes of ±15°), MemCorr-DP achieves 96.67% closed-loop success versus 88.00% for a visual Transformer with identical action architecture. Ablations and reference interventions confirm behavior tracks the selected reference, and complete relation sets outperform future-motion or centroid-only geometry.
AI.conclusion: Explicit 3D reference relations serve as a robust conditioning interface for diffusion policies when spatial and viewpoint changes are compounded, supporting generalization beyond the training distribution in manipulation tasks.

title: Spillover-Aware Multi-Value Steering for Pluralistic LLM Alignment
summary: Activation steering controls LLM behavior at inference time by adding learned directions to hidden states, but existing methods handle one concept at a time. Pluralistic alignment, where different stakeholders need different value emphases, requires steering multiple dimensions simultaneously. We show that naive steering produces substantial spillover: the effect intended for one value leaks into others. This parallels the treatment-versus-spillover decomposition in causal inference. We trace spillover to geometric entanglement of steering directions, captured by their Gram matrix, and derive a zero-cost correction from an activation-norm-penalized objective that decouples each direction's contribution exactly. Our end-to-end pipeline requires no fine-tuning, no reward model, and no manual prompt engineering: given only domain questions, it automatically discovers value dimensions, extracts directions, diagnoses entanglement, and applies corrected steering. On climate discourse, the correction improves the net steering effect from +5.9% to +14.0%, validated over 100,000 pairwise judgments.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the problem of multi-dimensional activation steering for pluralistic alignment in LLMs. The authors show that naive multi-concept steering suffers from substantial spillover effects between value dimensions, traced to geometric entanglement of steering directions captured by their Gram matrix. They derive a zero-cost correction from an activation-norm-penalized objective that decouples steering directions exactly, and propose an end-to-end pipeline requiring no fine-tuning, reward model, or manual prompting. On climate discourse, the correction improves net steering effect from +5.9% to +14.0% over 100,000 pairwise judgments.
AI.motivation: Existing activation steering methods handle only one concept at a time, but pluralistic alignment—where different stakeholders need different value emphases—requires steering multiple dimensions simultaneously. Naive multi-concept steering produces substantial spillover where the effect intended for one value leaks into others, analogous to treatment-versus-spillover decomposition in causal inference. This motivates a principled approach to disentangle steering directions during multi-dimensional control.
AI.method: The method traces spillover to geometric entanglement of steering directions characterized by their Gram matrix. A zero-cost correction is derived from an activation-norm-penalized objective that exactly decouples each direction's contribution. The end-to-end pipeline automatically discovers value dimensions from domain questions, extracts steering directions, diagnoses entanglement, and applies corrected steering—without fine-tuning, reward models, or manual prompt engineering.
AI.result: On climate discourse, the proposed correction improves the net steering effect from +5.9% to +14.0%, validated over 100,000 pairwise human judgments, demonstrating significant reduction of spillover and improved efficacy of multi-dimensional steering.
AI.conclusion: Geometric entanglement of steering directions is the root cause of spillover in multi-concept activation steering, and a Gram-matrix-based zero-cost correction effectively decouples directions. This enables scalable pluralistic alignment across stakeholder value dimensions without resource-intensive fine-tuning, validated by substantial improvements in climate discourse steering.

title: CAVEAT: Recurrent Multimodal Diffusion Planning for Mapless Aerial Exploration
summary: Can exploratory UAV waypoint sequences be generated from multimodal onboard observations and a fixed-dimensional recurrent internal state without maintaining a persistent global map in the deployed policy? We investigate this question through CAVEAT, a diffusion policy conditioned on a recurrent internal state updated from fused LiDAR, visual, and pose features and trained from trajectories generated by the map-based FUELv2 expert. Rolling inference partially warm-starts consecutive predictions, while a temporary local signed distance field provides heuristic obstacle guidance. Simulation results evaluate both inference mechanisms and compare CAVEAT with its demonstration-generating expert. Proof-of-concept experiments on a Flyability Elios 3 demonstrate partial exploration of a previously unseen indoor environment and target-directed visual servoing using a separately trained policy.

AI.tldr: CAVEAT is a diffusion policy that generates exploratory UAV waypoint sequences using multimodal onboard observations (LiDAR, visual, pose) and a recurrent internal state, eliminating the need for a persistent global map during deployment. It is trained from map-based FUELv2 expert trajectories and validated in simulation and on a Flyability Elios 3.
AI.motivation: The paper investigates whether a UAV can perform exploration via waypoint sequences derived purely from onboard multimodal sensing and a fixed-dimensional recurrent internal state, without maintaining a global map in the deployed policy. This aims to address the computational and memory overhead of persistent map-based methods.
AI.method: CAVEAT uses a diffusion policy conditioned on a recurrent internal state updated from fused LiDAR, visual, and pose features. The policy is trained from trajectories generated by the map-based FUELv2 expert. During rolling inference, consecutive predictions are partially warm-started, and a temporary local signed distance field (SDF) provides heuristic obstacle guidance.
AI.result: Simulation results evaluate both the warm-started inference and local SDF guidance mechanisms, and compare CAVEAT's performance against its demonstration-generating expert (FUELv2). Proof-of-concept experiments on a Flyability Elios 3 demonstrate partial exploration of an unseen indoor environment and target-directed visual servoing via a separately trained policy.
AI.conclusion: The approach demonstrates feasibility of mapless exploration policies by distilling expert behavior into a recurrent diffusion policy, showing partial exploration and visual-servoing capability on real hardware, though the recurrent state alone appears to support partial rather than complete exploration of unseen environments.

title: Evidence-Aligned Local Composition of Discrete Experts for Sequence Restoration
summary: A document modeled as a discrete sequence of tokens can be thought of as being generated from a composition of texts from different domains; a README file, for example, moves between prose, code, and configuration. When such a document is corrupted and only frozen domain experts are available, restoring it requires deciding both what is missing and which expert to trust at each position, at test time and without region labels or a trained router. We introduce evidence-aligned local composition, which infers a soft, position-wise weighting over the experts from the marginal evidence of the corrupted observation under a given corruption model, estimating the evidence from the experts' own denoising losses and smoothing the weights across positions. Because the weighting is soft, it recovers a mixture when the true composition is mixed and concentrates on one expert when that suffices. Across a categorical simulator, byte-level experts, and experts fine-tuned from a $1.3$B discrete flow-matching model, the inferred weights track the true regions at $0.85$ field accuracy on naturally mixed scientific documents, and at $0.98$ on constructed mixtures whose regions are lexically disjoint. Restoration improves over a single global weight when the experts are genuinely distinct and reduces to it when they converge, tracking a measure of expert separation.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces evidence-aligned local composition, a method for restoring corrupted documents by inferring soft, position-wise weights over frozen domain experts at test time, without region labels or a trained router. The method estimates evidence from each expert's denoising loss and smooths weights across positions, achieving high field accuracy on both naturally mixed and constructed document mixtures while improving restoration over global weighting when experts are distinct.
AI.motivation: Documents like README files naturally mix content from multiple domains (prose, code, configuration). When such documents are corrupted and only frozen domain experts are available for restoration, one must simultaneously determine what is missing and which expert to trust at each position—at test time, without region labels or a trained router. This poses a challenging unsupervised composition problem.
AI.method: The proposed approach, evidence-aligned local composition, infers a soft position-wise weighting over available frozen experts. It estimates the evidence of the corrupted observation under a given corruption model from each expert's own denoising losses, then smooths the resulting weights across positions. The soft nature of the weighting allows recovery of mixtures when the true composition is mixed, yet concentrates on a single expert when that suffices.
AI.result: The inferred weights track true regions at 0.85 field accuracy on naturally mixed scientific documents and 0.98 on constructed mixtures with lexically disjoint regions. Restoration improves over a single global weight when experts are genuinely distinct and reduces to it when they converge, with performance tracking a measure of expert separation. Validation spans a categorical simulator, byte-level experts, and experts fine-tuned from a 1.3B discrete flow-matching model.
AI.conclusion: Evidence-aligned local composition provides an effective unsupervised approach to restoring corrupted mixed-domain documents by dynamically weighting frozen experts per position based on their denoising evidence. The method gracefully degrades to a global-weight baseline when experts are similar, and outperforms it when experts are genuinely distinct, making it broadly applicable without requiring trained routers or labeled regions.

title: SkillX: Unified Multi-Skill Policy Learning for Humanoid Soccer
comment: Accepted to CoRL 2026. Project page: https://yzc0731.github.io/SkillX/
summary: Humanoid soccer is a challenging testbed for dynamic whole-body control, requiring robots to coordinate balance, locomotion, object interaction, and skill switching over long horizons. Existing humanoid sports methods often rely on task-specific multi-stage pipelines, making it difficult to jointly learn and compose multiple object-interactive skills within a single deployable policy.
