To address this, we present SkillX, a unified reinforcement learning framework that learns and composes multiple atomic soccer skills through a single command-conditioned policy. SkillX integrates three core designs: skill-specific adversarial motion priors, skill-specific critics, and an object-aware temporal encoder, enabling the robot to execute atomic skills and transition among them such as dribbling, trapping, and shooting. Experiments in simulation and on a real Noetix E1 humanoid demonstrate robust multi-skill execution, long-horizon skill composition, and successful sim-to-real deployment.

AI.tldr: SkillX is a unified reinforcement learning framework that enables a single command-conditioned policy to learn and compose multiple atomic humanoid soccer skills (dribbling, trapping, shooting) via skill-specific adversarial motion priors, skill-specific critics, and an object-aware temporal encoder, validated in simulation and on a real Noetix E1 humanoid.
AI.motivation: Existing humanoid sports methods rely on task-specific multi-stage pipelines that make it difficult to jointly learn and compose multiple object-interactive skills within a single deployable policy. Humanoid soccer requires long-horizon coordination of balance, locomotion, object interaction, and skill switching, motivating a unified learning approach.
AI.method: SkillX integrates three core designs: (1) skill-specific adversarial motion priors to guide natural movement for each skill, (2) skill-specific critics to provide tailored value estimation per skill, and (3) an object-aware temporal encoder to capture ball dynamics and enable object-interactive control. These components are combined into a single command-conditioned RL policy that supports both atomic skill execution and seamless transitions between skills.
AI.result: Experiments in simulation and on a real Noetix E1 humanoid demonstrate robust multi-skill execution, long-horizon skill composition, and successful sim-to-real deployment.
AI.conclusion: SkillX demonstrates that a unified single-policy reinforcement learning framework can effectively handle multiple object-interactive soccer skills with long-horizon composition, achieving real-world deployment viability on a physical humanoid platform.

title: Exposing Weaknesses in Emotion Recognition in Conversations
summary: Emotion Recognition in Conversations (ERC) aims to identify speakers' emotions in multi-turn dialogue. Accurate emotion recognition can support a wide range of applications, including empathetic conversational agents, mental health support, and educational technologies. While many recent approaches rely on task-specific fine-tuning, such models may exploit dataset-specific cues. A central yet rarely questioned assumption in ERC is that each utterance can be assigned a single unambiguous emotion label. To investigate this assumption, we study ERC using Large Language Models (LLMs) in a zero-shot setting while incorporating preceding conversational turns as context. We show that aggregate metrics mask systematic failures. Errors concentrate around utterances containing negations, exclamations, and interjections. This pattern is consistent across all evaluated models, suggesting limitations in the benchmarks rather than model-specific weaknesses. A controlled re-annotation study involving four human annotators supports this finding: strong agreement is observed in only 35 percent of cases, with neutral utterances dominating high-agreement instances, while many emotional categories fall into low-agreement regimes. These findings suggest that many apparent model errors reflect genuine annotation ambiguity rather than poor emotion understanding. Standard single-label evaluation is therefore insufficient. To address this limitation, we introduce an LLM-as-Judge framework that evaluates each emotion independently according to its plausibility in the conversational context rather than enforcing a single-label decision.

AI.tldr: This paper challenges the single-label assumption in Emotion Recognition in Conversations (ERC) by showing that LLM errors in zero-shot settings often reflect genuine annotation ambiguity rather than model shortcomings, and proposes an LLM-as-Judge framework that evaluates each emotion independently by plausibility in conversational context.
AI.motivation: The authors question the central assumption in ERC that each utterance can be assigned a single unambiguous emotion label. They note that aggregate metrics mask systematic model failures, and hypothesize that these apparent errors may stem from annotation ambiguity in the benchmarks rather than poor emotion understanding by models.
AI.method: The authors evaluate LLMs in a zero-shot ERC setting with preceding turns as context, analyze error concentration patterns across utterances with negations, exclamations, and interjections, conduct a controlled re-annotation study with four human annotators, and introduce an LLM-as-Judge framework that evaluates each emotion independently based on its plausibility rather than enforcing single-label decisions.
AI.result: Errors systematically concentrate around utterances with negations, exclamations, and interjections, consistently across all evaluated models. Human re-annotation showed strong agreement in only 35% of cases, with neutral utterances dominating high-agreement cases while many emotional categories fell into low-agreement regimes.
AI.conclusion: Many apparent model errors in ERC reflect genuine annotation ambiguity rather than poor emotion understanding, making standard single-label evaluation insufficient. The proposed LLM-as-Judge framework addresses this by evaluating emotions independently according to their contextual plausibility.

title: OCTN: Neural OCT Representations for Robot-Guided Precision Intervention
summary: Optical coherence tomography (OCT) offers compact, contactless, micron-scale imaging suitable for intraoperative guidance, but native OCT volumes are discretely sampled, anisotropic, and currently inefficient for downstream geometric reasoning and robot integration. We present OCTN (pronounced "octane"), an implicit neural representation framework that converts volumetric OCT scans into a continuous, differentiable, and spatially faithful tissue-intensity field. OCTN uses a two-stage hybrid training strategy that combines supervision from acquired voxels with inter-slice interpolations, preserving B-scan fidelity while improving continuity in sparsely sampled regions. For versatility, we first show that OCTN enables fast volumetric reasoning by storing the learned tissue representation natively on the GPU, supporting intensity-based spatial queries with up to 43x speedup over conventional CPU processing. We then demonstrate OCTN-enabled OCT-guided robotic laser surgery where the continuous tissue representation supports implicit surface discovery and surface-constrained path planning via multiple optimization strategies, including Newton- and SGD-based optimization. Next, OCTN enables reconstruction of dense volumetric structure from sparsely acquired B-scans, while reducing acquisition time by 4x and preserving clinically relevant structures. Across the newly generated Duke TissueOCT dataset and public OCT datasets, OCTN achieves robust, high-fidelity reconstruction with PSNR > 30 dB and training time < 10 s, while preserving surface consistency within 10 $μ$m Chamfer distance relative to baseline reconstruction. The TissueOCT dataset and code are publicly available at raprakashvi.github.io/octn

AI.tldr: OCTN is an implicit neural representation framework that converts discrete volumetric OCT scans into continuous, differentiable tissue-intensity fields. It uses a two-stage hybrid training strategy with voxel supervision and inter-slice interpolation, enabling fast GPU-based volumetric queries (43x speedup), OCT-guided robotic laser surgery with implicit surface discovery, dense reconstruction from sparse B-scans (4x faster acquisition), achieving PSNR > 30 dB, sub-10s training, and sub-10μm surface consistency.
AI.motivation: Native OCT volumes are discretely sampled, anisotropic, and inefficient for downstream geometric reasoning and robot integration, limiting their use in intraoperative guidance despite OCT's compact, contactless, micron-scale imaging advantages.
AI.method: OCTN employs a two-stage hybrid training strategy combining supervision from acquired voxels with inter-slice interpolations to preserve B-scan fidelity while improving continuity in sparsely sampled regions. The learned representation is stored natively on GPU for fast intensity-based spatial queries. Applications include surface discovery and surface-constrained path planning using Newton- and SGD-based optimizations for robotic laser surgery, and dense volumetric reconstruction from sparse B-scans.
AI.result: OCTN achieves up to 43x speedup over conventional CPU processing for volumetric queries, enables OCT-guided robotic laser surgery, reconstructs dense volumes from 4x sparser B-scans, achieves robust reconstruction with PSNR > 30 dB, training time under 10 seconds, and surface consistency within 10 μm Chamfer distance on the new Duke TissueOCT dataset and public OCT datasets.
AI.conclusion: OCTN provides a versatile implicit neural representation framework for OCT that enables fast volumetric reasoning, robotic surgical guidance, and sparse-acquisition reconstruction, with publicly available dataset and code for the community.

title: Agentic BAIM-LLM Evaluation (ABLE): Benchmarking LLM Use of Protein Design Tools
comment: Last revised in February 2026; presented without further revision. An earlier revision at was presented at the NeurIPS 2025 Workshop on Biosecurity Safeguards for Generative AI; see https://openreview.net/forum?id=fDysOrWaGd
summary: We introduce ABLE, a benchmark for evaluating LLM agents' ability to use biological AI models (BAIMs), such as ProteinMPNN and AlphaFold3, in dual-use protein design workflows. ABLE assesses agent performance through a set of tasks spanning structure retrieval, sequence generation, and design validation. We evaluate 15 frontier models and find that seven refuse all tasks, while the remaining models exhibit substantial performance differences. Claude Sonnet 4 and Gemini 3 Pro achieve the highest scores across information retrieval, tool selection, and tool use. We further compare model performance on a subset of tasks against an expert human baseline. Our results suggest that current LLMs can substantially lower barriers to protein design, but remain inconsistent in planning, strategy generation, and integrating biological knowledge with tool use.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces ABLE, a benchmark for evaluating LLM agents' ability to use biological AI models (BAIMs) like ProteinMPNN and AlphaFold3 in dual-use protein design workflows. The benchmark covers tasks in structure retrieval, sequence generation, and design validation. Across 15 frontier models, seven refuse all tasks, with Claude Sonnet 4 and Gemini 3 Pro achieving the highest scores. Comparisons against expert human baselines reveal that while current LLMs lower barriers to protein design, they remain inconsistent in planning, strategy generation, and integrating biological knowledge with tool use.
AI.motivation: To address the lack of systematic evaluation of LLM agents' capabilities in dual-use protein design workflows that involve biological AI models (BAIMs), and to assess safety-relevant performance differences across frontier models.
AI.method: The authors construct ABLE, a benchmark with tasks spanning structure retrieval, sequence generation, and design validation. They evaluate 15 frontier LLM models on these tasks, assessing performance across information retrieval, tool selection, and tool use, and compare a subset of results against an expert human baseline.
AI.result: Seven of 15 models refuse all tasks. Remaining models show substantial performance differences, with Claude Sonnet 4 and Gemini 3 Pro achieving the highest scores in information retrieval, tool selection, and tool use. Models overall remain inconsistent in planning, strategy generation, and integration of biological knowledge with tool use compared to expert human baselines.
AI.conclusion: Current LLMs can meaningfully lower barriers to protein design, but their reliability in dual-use workflows is uneven. The findings highlight areas—planning, strategy generation, and biological knowledge integration—where further development is needed to improve agent capability and consistency.

title: RoboSense: Leveraging Robotaxi Fleets as Drive-by Sensors for Urban Traffic Monitoring
summary: Urban traffic monitoring plays a critical role in safety analysis, congestion management, and incident response. The growing deployment of robotaxis creates a new opportunity for network-level traffic monitoring. Although robotaxis are primarily designed to serve passengers, they can also be leveraged as drive-by sensors to collect traffic data. Compared to conventional infrastructure sensors or probe vehicles, a fleet of robotaxis forms a cooperative perception environment, which can collectively gather spatially and temporally continuous traffic information. This paper proposes a novel dynamic robotaxi routing framework that explicitly incorporates traffic monitoring tasks as an objective. The framework introduces: (1) a cell-based network representation that aligns with sensing capabilities of robotaxis; (2) a cell-level monitoring metric to quantify spatiotemporal robotaxi coverage; and (3) a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) formulation that jointly minimizes time-dependent travel time and maximizes traffic monitoring performance. A 5 by 5 urban grid network is built in SUMO to evaluate the framework under three robotaxi market penetration rates (2%, 5%, and 10%) with a range of objective weight combinations. Results show that incorporating spatiotemporal network coverage in the objective function can effectively improve the traffic monitoring performance. Interestingly, with appropriate weights between the two objectives, monitoring performance and robotaxi average speed can be improved simultaneously. This suggests better network monitoring leads to more accurate traffic state prediction and improved mobility. This win-win situation could incentivize robotaxi operators to contribute their vehicles as drive-by sensors for traffic monitoring.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a dynamic robotaxi routing framework that jointly optimizes passenger travel time and traffic monitoring performance by treating robotaxis as drive-by sensors. The framework uses a cell-based network representation, a spatiotemporal coverage metric, and a MILP formulation. Simulations in a 5x5 SUMO grid show that with appropriate objective weights, both monitoring performance and average robotaxi speed can be improved simultaneously.
AI.motivation: Conventional traffic monitoring relies on fixed infrastructure sensors or probe vehicles, which offer limited spatial and temporal coverage. With the growing deployment of robotaxis, there is an untapped opportunity to leverage their fleets as cooperative mobile sensors for network-level traffic monitoring, but existing routing frameworks do not explicitly account for monitoring objectives.
AI.method: The framework includes: (1) a cell-based network representation aligned with robotaxi sensing capabilities; (2) a cell-level spatiotemporal monitoring metric to quantify coverage; and (3) a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) formulation that jointly minimizes time-dependent travel time while maximizing traffic monitoring performance. Evaluation was conducted in a 5x5 urban grid network in SUMO under three robotaxi market penetration rates (2%, 5%, 10%) across various objective weight combinations.
AI.result: Incorporating spatiotemporal network coverage into the routing objective effectively improves traffic monitoring performance. With appropriately balanced objective weights, both monitoring performance and robotaxi average speed can be improved simultaneously across all tested market penetration rates.
AI.conclusion: Better network monitoring leads to more accurate traffic state prediction and improved mobility, creating a win-win scenario. This could incentivize robotaxi operators to voluntarily contribute their vehicles as drive-by sensors for traffic monitoring, benefiting both congestion management and robotaxi service quality.

title: Beyond Top-$k$ Skill Retrieval: Diversity-Aware Skill Routing for LLM Agents
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly rely on external skills, but routing user requests over large skill registries is difficult because many skills are functionally redundant while complex tasks often require complementary skill sets. Existing skill routers typically rank candidates independently by query relevance, which can waste context budget on redundant skills. We propose Diverse Skill Routing (DSR), a diversity-aware reranking framework that uses a Determinantal Point Process to balance relevance and non-redundancy. DSR introduces a query-residual diversity kernel that penalizes redundant skill overlap while reducing penalties caused only by shared query relevance. On the SkillRouter benchmark, DSR improves recall and full coverage over a strong pointwise reranking baseline, with larger gains on multi-skill queries. These results suggest that skill routing should be treated not only as relevance ranking, but also as complementary set selection.

AI.tldr: DSR, a diversity-aware reranking framework using Determinantal Point Process, balances relevance and non-redundancy for skill routing in LLM agents, improving recall and full coverage on the SkillRouter benchmark.
AI.motivation: LLM agents rely on external skills but routing over large skill registries is difficult due to functionally redundant skills and complex tasks requiring complementary skill sets. Existing routers rank candidates independently by query relevance, wasting context budget on redundant skills.
AI.method: DSR uses a Determinantal Point Process (DPP) for diversity-aware reranking, introducing a query-residual diversity kernel that penalizes redundant skill overlap while reducing penalties caused only by shared query relevance.
AI.result: On the SkillRouter benchmark, DSR improves recall and full coverage over a strong pointwise reranking baseline, with larger gains on multi-skill queries.
AI.conclusion: Skill routing should be treated not only as relevance ranking, but also as complementary set selection.

title: Diagnosing and Dynamically Filtering Occupancy World Models for Active Mapping
comment: Accepted by IEEE IROS 2026 Workshop on WORLDS: World Models and Spatial Intelligence for Physical AI
summary: Active mapping requires a robot to select camera viewpoints that efficiently reconstruct an unknown 3D scene. To reason about unobserved regions, recent systems use pretrained occupancy networks as world models that complete missing geometry. The predicted structure contributes to expected coverage gain and constrains feasible robot motion. Consequently, occupancy errors can change both what the robot chooses to explore and where it is able to move. We diagnose these effects by holding the planner fixed and varying only the occupancy representation provided to it. We consider planning without completion, with learned occupancy, with false positives removed by a ground truth oracle, with false negatives restored by an oracle, and with ground truth occupancy. Our experiments show that correcting false positives or false negatives alone does not consistently improve final coverage. This finding reveals a gap between occupancy accuracy and downstream planning performance. Ground truth occupancy provides a much larger improvement in coverage efficiency than in endpoint coverage, suggesting that planning and reachability remain important bottlenecks even when the geometric world model is accurate. Based on these findings, we introduce a dynamic filtering strategy that preserves predictions in unexplored space while suppressing repeatedly unsupported occupancy using online observations. Preliminary examples show that this strategy can redirect viewpoint selection toward reachable surfaces that would otherwise remain unobserved.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how occupancy prediction errors in learned world models affect active mapping performance. By systematically varying only the occupancy representation while holding the planner fixed, the authors find that correcting false positives or false negatives alone does not consistently improve final coverage, revealing a gap between occupancy accuracy and downstream planning. They propose a dynamic filtering strategy that preserves predictions in unexplored space while suppressing repeatedly unsupported occupancy, which redirects viewpoint selection toward reachable surfaces.
AI.motivation: Active mapping systems rely on pretrained occupancy networks as world models to complete missing geometry. These predictions influence both where the robot chooses to explore (via expected coverage gain) and where it can move (via feasible motion constraints). Since occupancy errors can fundamentally change both exploration choices and reachability, it is critical to understand the precise impact of these errors on downstream planning performance — a question not previously addressed in isolation.
AI.method: The authors hold the planner fixed and vary only the occupancy representation provided to it across five settings: planning without completion, with learned occupancy, with false positives removed by a ground truth oracle, with false negatives restored by an oracle, and with ground truth occupancy. This controlled ablation isolates the effect of occupancy errors. They additionally introduce a dynamic filtering strategy that preserves predictions in unexplored space while suppressing repeatedly unsupported occupancy using online observations.
AI.result: Experiments show that correcting false positives or false negatives individually does not consistently improve final coverage. Ground truth occupancy yields substantially larger improvements in coverage efficiency than in endpoint coverage, indicating that planning and reachability remain bottlenecks even with an accurate geometric world model. Preliminary tests of the dynamic filtering strategy demonstrate that it can redirect viewpoint selection toward reachable surfaces that would otherwise remain unobserved.
AI.conclusion: There is a meaningful gap between occupancy accuracy and downstream planning performance in active mapping: occupancy errors are not trivially reducible to better coverage, and even perfect geometry leaves significant room for improvement in planning and reachability. Dynamic filtering of occupancy predictions shows promise as a practical mitigation strategy to improve viewpoint selection toward reachable, unobserved surfaces.

title: Learning Counterfactual World Models for Embodied Reasoning under Partial Observability
summary: World models promise a general route to embodied intelligence: learn predictive dynamics once, then reason, plan, and act with them. Increasingly, the representations beneath such models are pretrained on large-scale video, interaction, and multimodal corpora, which raises a question prediction quality alone cannot answer: when is a learned representation actually actionable? We identify a failure mode we call counterfactual collapse: a model predicts visually plausible futures while failing to distinguish interventions with different behavioral consequences. This arises whenever a representation is optimized for perceptual similarity rather than intervention structure, which is precisely the objective under which most large-scale pretrained encoders are learned. We introduce Counterfactual Latent World Models (CLWM), which combine a recurrent belief-state encoder, action-conditioned latent dynamics, and a contrastive counterfactual objective that separates futures induced by distinct interventions even when their observations look alike. Across occluded manipulation, aliased navigation, and long-horizon manipulation, CLWM improves planning success over the strongest baseline (65.1% $\to$ 74.6% on Occluded Push and 67.3% $\to$ 78.9% on Aliased Maze) and reduces exploitative planning failures (18.4% $\to$ 9.7% on Deferred Kitchen), with ablations attributing the gains to hard counterfactual negatives, especially perceptual-alias negatives. Finally, our counterfactual separability metric, which tracks planning success across the five baseline model classes ($r \ge 0.94$), is representation-agnostic: given intervention-outcome labels, it can audit any encoder, pretrained or trained from scratch, before a planner trusts it. We do not yet measure it on large-scale pretrained encoders. Here we establish the metric and its relationship to planning success for world models trained from scratch.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies a failure mode called "counterfactual collapse" in world models—where representations predict visually plausible futures but fail to distinguish interventions with different behavioral consequences—and introduces Counterfactual Latent World Models (CLWM) that use contrastive counterfactual objectives to separate futures induced by distinct interventions. CLWM improves planning success across occluded manipulation (65.1%→74.6%), aliased navigation (67.3%→78.9%), and reduces exploitative planning failures (18.4%→9.7%). The paper also introduces a counterfactual separability metric (r≥0.94 across baselines) that audits any encoder's actionability for planning.
AI.motivation: World models offer a general route to embodied intelligence, but prediction quality alone cannot determine whether a learned representation is actually actionable for planning and reasoning. The authors identify that large-scale pretrained encoders optimized for perceptual similarity may exhibit "counterfactual collapse"—failing to distinguish between interventions with different behavioral consequences while still predicting visually plausible futures—which existing evaluation metrics fail to catch.
AI.method: CLWM combines a recurrent belief-state encoder, action-conditioned latent dynamics, and a contrastive counterfactual objective that separates futures induced by distinct interventions even when observations are perceptually similar. The paper also proposes a representation-agnostic counterfactual separability metric that audits any encoder (pretrained or trained from scratch) using intervention-outcome labels to predict planning success before deployment.
AI.result: CLWM improves planning success over the strongest baselines: 65.1%→74.6% on Occluded Push, 67.3%→78.9% on Aliased Maze, and reduces exploitative planning failures from 18.4%→9.7% on Deferred Kitchen. Ablations attribute gains to hard counterfactual negatives (especially perceptual-alias negatives). The counterfactual separability metric tracks planning success across five baseline model classes with r≥0.94.
AI.conclusion: Representations must be optimized for intervention structure, not just perceptual similarity, to be actionable for world-model-based planning. The counterfactual separability metric provides a practical way to audit encoders before a planner trusts them, though the authors note they have not yet measured it on large-scale pretrained encoders—this paper establishes the metric and its relationship to planning success for world models trained from scratch.

title: ContextFlow: In-Context Flow Matching for Robot Manipulation
summary: Although highly effective in vision and language domains, applying in-context learning to robotics remains challenging. Existing autoregressive in-context imitation methods discretize continuous actions and exacerbate the accumulation of early prediction errors through next-token prediction, limiting their generalization on unseen task configurations. Meanwhile, flow-matching policies have been explored for continuous robot control and can help mitigate compounding errors; however, in-context imitation learning within a flow-matching framework remains underexplored. To address these limitations, we introduce ContextFlow, a conditional flow-matching model that learns continuous action distributions for in-context imitation learning. ContextFlow conditions flow-based action prediction on demonstrations and observations, enabling robust generation from noisy action distributions. To better encode multimodal in-context demonstrations, we adapt perceiver-style multimodal context compressors that distill visual, proprioceptive, and action sequences into compact, task-relevant latent representations. On LIBERO, ContextFlow outperforms ICRT by 35 percentage points in average success rate on unseen task configurations, while matching the performance of the task-specific fine-tuned VLA model $π_0$ without any fine-tuning on unseen tasks. On real robots, it generalizes to unseen configurations of both single-arm and bimanual tasks, achieving 40% success on a new pen-uncapping configuration. Project Page: https://dingjiansw101.github.io/contextflow-page/.

AI.tldr: ContextFlow is a conditional flow-matching model that enables in-context imitation learning for robotics by learning continuous action distributions, avoiding the discretization and compounding error issues of prior autoregressive in-context methods. It outperforms ICRT by 35 percentage points on LIBERO unseen tasks and matches task-specific fine-tuned VLA models without fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Existing autoregressive in-context imitation methods discretize continuous actions and suffer from cascading prediction errors via next-token prediction, limiting generalization. While flow-matching policies excel at continuous robot control and mitigate compounding errors, in-context imitation learning within a flow-matching framework remains underexplored.
AI.method: ContextFlow is a conditional flow-matching model conditioned on demonstrations and observations for predicting continuous action distributions. It uses perceiver-style multimodal context compressors to distill visual, proprioceptive, and action sequences into compact task-relevant latent representations, enabling robust handling of multimodal in-context demonstrations.
AI.result: On LIBERO, ContextFlow surpasses ICRT by 35 percentage points in average success rate on unseen task configurations and matches the performance of the task-specific fine-tuned VLA model π0 without any fine-tuning. On real robots, it generalizes to unseen configurations of single-arm and bimanual tasks, achieving 40% success on a new pen-uncapping configuration.
AI.conclusion: ContextFlow demonstrates that flow-matching is an effective paradigm for in-context imitation learning, achieving strong zero-shot generalization on unseen task configurations comparable to fine-tuned VLA baselines while avoiding the limitations of autoregressive discretized action prediction.

title: AgentBrew: Offline Tool-Use Agent Learning from Raw Real-World Trajectories
summary: LLM-based agents are increasingly deployed in real-world applications through tool-use APIs, yet training them for specific environments remains fundamentally difficult: real-world applications provide no pre-defined tasks or verifiers, no faithful simulators, and limited budget for large-scale environment interaction. In this paper, we propose \textbf{AgentBrew}, an offline training framework that learns effective tool-use policies from a single batch of raw interaction trajectories, without task verifiers or iterative on-policy rollouts. The agent first explores the target environment to collect a raw trajectory corpus without quality filtering. To extract training signal from this noisy corpus, \emph{retrospective task inference} reconstructs an aligned instruction for each trajectory based on its actual outcome, and \emph{PMI-Based credit assignment} decomposes the trajectory's total information about the inferred instruction into additive per-action credits via pointwise mutual information (PMI). These credits weight the policy training objective, amplifying informative actions while suppressing ineffective ones. On three real-world MCP applications (GitHub, Notion, PostgreSQL), AgentBrew improves Qwen3-32B by +8.7 Acc / +9.7 Score on average, surpassing Qwen3-235B (+2.3 / +4.4) and outperforming rejection sampling (+5.9 / +10.3). These results demonstrate that fine-grained offline learning can recover useful supervision from raw trajectories that filtering-based approaches would discard. The code is available at https://github.com/alphatogo/AgentBrew

AI.tldr: AgentBrew is an offline training framework for LLM-based tool-use agents that learns effective policies from a single batch of raw interaction trajectories without task verifiers, simulators, or on-policy rollouts. It uses retrospective task inference to reconstruct instructions from actual outcomes and PMI-based credit assignment to decompose trajectory information into per-action credits for policy training. On GitHub, Notion, and PostgreSQL MCP applications, AgentBrew improves Qwen3-32B by +8.7 Acc / +9.7 Score, surpassing Qwen3-235B and outperforming rejection sampling.
AI.motivation: Training LLM agents for real-world tool-use environments is fundamentally difficult because such applications lack pre-defined tasks, task verifiers, faithful simulators, and large-scale interaction budgets. This motivates the need for an offline approach that can learn effective tool-use policies from limited raw interaction data.
AI.method: AgentBrew operates in two key stages: (1) Retrospective task inference reconstructs an aligned instruction for each raw trajectory based on its actual outcome, extracting training signal from a noisy trajectory corpus without quality filtering. (2) PMI-based credit assignment decomposes the trajectory's total information about the inferred instruction into additive per-action credits using pointwise mutual information, which are then used to weight the policy training objective—amplifying informative actions while suppressing ineffective ones.
AI.result: On three real-world MCP applications (GitHub, Notion, PostgreSQL), AgentBrew improves Qwen3-32B by +8.7 Acc / +9.7 Score on average, outperforming the much larger Qwen3-235B (+2.3 / +4.4) and surpassing rejection sampling-based approaches (+5.9 / +10.3). These results demonstrate that fine-grained offline credit assignment can recover useful supervision from raw trajectories that filtering-based methods would discard.
AI.conclusion: Fine-grained offline learning from raw, unfiltered trajectories can effectively train tool-use agents without requiring task verifiers or on-policy rollouts. The approach enables smaller models to outperform much larger ones and surpass filtering-based baselines, indicating that the fine-grained credit assignment strategy successfully recovers supervision from noisy real-world data. Code is released at the provided GitHub repository.

title: Predictive-Coding-Based Autonomous Regulation of Internally Generated and Externally Coupled Processing in Human-Robot Interaction
comment: 16 pages, 8 figures. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Cognitive and Developmental Systems
summary: Predictive coding characterizes adaptive behavior as a dynamic balance between internally generated predictions and external sensory evidence, yet how an embodied cognitive system can regulate this balance online during ongoing interaction remains poorly understood. This study proposes a predictive-coding-based mechanism for regulating internally generated and externally coupled processing during physical human--robot interaction. The framework employs a predictive-coding-inspired variational recurrent neural network (PV-RNN), in which a meta-prior controls the degree to which posterior inference is constrained by learned prior dynamics. We extend this architecture with an online mechanism that uses reconstruction error accumulated over recent interaction history to select between predefined meta-prior regimes. The mechanism was evaluated across three physical human--robot interaction tasks involving fixed structured, changing structured, and less-constrained interaction. Across all tasks, lower meta-prior values produced the expected increase in posterior--prior divergence and reduction in reconstruction error. More importantly, reconstruction-history-driven regime selection was also associated with reduced prospective prediction error and robot-side physical interaction conflict, demonstrating consequences beyond the retrospective reconstruction objective itself. Task~3 further showed that recent sensory observations can be successfully accommodated while subsequent human motion still departs from the model's prior-generated future trajectory. Overall, these findings show that accumulated reconstruction mismatch can provide an endogenous signal for regulating how strongly subsequent inference relies on learned internal dynamics relative to ongoing sensory input during embodied interaction.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a predictive-coding-based mechanism for dynamically regulating the balance between internally generated predictions and external sensory evidence during physical human-robot interaction. It extends a predictive-coding-inspired variational recurrent neural network (PV-RNN) with an online mechanism that uses accumulated reconstruction error to select between predefined meta-prior regimes controlling posterior inference constraints. Evaluated across three physical HRI tasks, the mechanism reduced prospective prediction error and physical interaction conflict, showing that reconstruction mismatch can serve as an endogenous regulatory signal during embodied interaction.
AI.motivation: Although predictive coding frames adaptive behavior as a balance between internal predictions and external sensory evidence, it remains unclear how an embodied cognitive system can autonomously regulate this balance online during ongoing physical interaction with humans.
AI.method: An extension of the PV-RNN architecture where a meta-prior controls the degree to which posterior inference is constrained by learned prior dynamics. An online regulatory mechanism accumulates reconstruction error over recent interaction history to select between predefined meta-prior regimes. The framework was evaluated across three physical human-robot interaction tasks: fixed structured, changing structured, and less-constrained interaction.
AI.result: Lower meta-prior values produced increased posterior-prior divergence and reduced reconstruction error across all tasks. Reconstruction-history-driven regime selection was associated with reduced prospective prediction error and lower robot-side physical interaction conflict, extending beyond retrospective reconstruction objectives. In Task 3, recent sensory observations were accommodated while subsequent human motion still diverged from the model's prior-generated future trajectory.
AI.conclusion: Accumulated reconstruction mismatch provides an endogenous, embodied signal for regulating how strongly subsequent inference relies on learned internal dynamics relative to ongoing sensory input during physical human-robot interaction.

title: Multimodal Resource-Exhaustion Attacks on Vision-Language Models via Joint Pixel-Prompt Optimization
comment: Extended version of the paper accepted by ACM CCS 2026
summary:
Resource-exhaustion attacks against autoregressive vision-language models (VLMs) typically assume unimodal threat models, treating the image branch as the primary optimization surface while holding user-visible prompts fixed. Even recent loop-centric variants remain confined to this single-channel paradigm, leaving the exploitation of availability unexplored as a cross-modal optimization problem over jointly controllable input surfaces.
  We introduce Joint Pixel-Prompt Optimization (JPPO), the first compound adversarial framework elevating the visible prompt to a first-class adversarial variable alongside image perturbations. Under a restricted joint-input threat model, JPPO performs coupled, stagewise optimization over both the pixel and prompt surfaces. This produces synergistic cost amplification, mechanistically distinct from loop-dependent failures, exhibiting negligible loop incidence in our experiments.
  Evaluating five open-source VLM families on MS COCO and ImageNet under an 8/255 infinity-norm budget, JPPO achieves over 4.6x latency and 5.3x energy amplification on Qwen2.5-VL-7B, and over 36.6x latency with 32.7x energy amplification on BLIP-2. This represents the strongest cost amplification among directly compared baselines while requiring substantially fewer optimization iterations. Ablations confirm this amplification arises from multimodal coordination rather than prompt length or isolated modalities. These findings reveal structural blind spots in current VLM serving defenses, motivating cost-aware robustness evaluation as a first-class security requirement for multimodal deployments.

AI.tldr: JPPO is the first compound adversarial framework for VLMs that jointly optimizes both image pixels and visible text prompts to induce resource-exhaustion attacks, achieving over 36.6x latency and 32.7x energy amplification on BLIP-2 while requiring fewer optimization iterations than existing baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing resource-exhaustion attacks against VLMs assume unimodal threat models, treating only image perturbations as the optimization surface while keeping user-visible prompts fixed. Even recent loop-centric extensions remain confined to single-channel optimization, leaving availability attacks unexplored as a cross-modal problem over jointly controllable input surfaces.
AI.method: JPPO performs coupled, stagewise optimization over both pixel and prompt surfaces under a restricted joint-input threat model, treating the visible prompt as a first-class adversarial variable alongside image perturbations to produce synergistic cost amplification.
AI.result: Evaluated on five open-source VLM families over MS COCO and ImageNet with an 8/255 infinity-norm budget, JPPO achieves over 4.6x latency and 5.3x energy amplification on Qwen2.5-VL-7B, and over 36.6x latency with 32.7x energy amplification on BLIP-2—the strongest among compared baselines while requiring substantially fewer iterations.
AI.conclusion: The findings expose structural blind spots in current VLM serving defenses, demonstrating that multimodal coordination—not prompt length or isolated modalities—drives the cost amplification. This motivates cost-aware robustness evaluation as a first-class security requirement for multimodal deployments.

title: Distributed Secure Learning Control for Large-scale Multirobots under Stealthy Actuator Attacks
comment: 23 pages, 23 figures. A revised version of this manuscript has been accepted to IEEE Transactions on Robotics
summary: Distributed learning control for multirobot systems (MRS) offers significant flexibility in presence of uncertainties but lacks provable performance guarantees. A promising direction involves integrating reinforcement learning (RL) into distributed model predictive control (DMPC), leveraging the strengths of RL in nonlinear policy design and the receding-horizon replanning capabilities of DMPC. However, ensuring secure control within such a learning framework under malicious cyber attacks, particularly stealthy ones, remains a critical challenge, because the distributed policies generation depends on information exchange among neighbors, where compromised agents can rapidly influence the behavior of others through the communication network. This article proposes a distributed secure learning control (DSLC) framework for large-scale MRS under malicious, stealthy actuator attacks. Our framework offers two key features: (i) a unified approach that enables secure learning control across various coordination scenarios and (ii) a game-theoretic distributed learning-based predictive control strategy that learns how to balance the attacker and defender through a differential-game based DMPC framework. Specifically, DSLC employs a distributed attacker-actor-critic architecture to learn the optimal defense and attack policies online within each prediction interval. Unlike numerical optimization-based controllers that calculate open-loop control sequences, our method simultaneously generates adversarial attack policies and corresponding defense policies in analytical closed-loop form. The defense policies could be directly generalized to MRS with varying scales and diverse actuator attack probabilities. The effectiveness and scalability of DSLC are validated through comprehensive simulations and real-world experiments in multiple wheeled robots via various control tasks.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a Distributed Secure Learning Control (DSLC) framework for large-scale multirobot systems under malicious, stealthy actuator attacks, integrating reinforcement learning into distributed model predictive control with a game-theoretic attacker-actor-critic architecture to learn optimal defense and attack policies analytically in closed-loop form.
AI.motivation: Distributed learning control for multirobot systems offers flexibility under uncertainties but lacks provable performance guarantees. While integrating RL into DMPC is promising, ensuring secure control under malicious stealthy cyber attacks remains a critical challenge because compromised agents can rapidly influence others through the communication network during distributed policy generation.
AI.method: The DSLC framework employs a distributed attacker-actor-critic architecture to learn optimal defense and attack policies online within each prediction interval. It uses a differential-game based DMPC formulation to balance attacker and defender, generating adversarial attack and corresponding defense policies in analytical closed-loop form rather than numerical open-loop optimization.
AI.result: The defense policies generalize to MRS with varying scales and diverse actuator attack probabilities. Effectiveness and scalability are validated through comprehensive simulations and real-world experiments with multiple wheeled robots across various control tasks.
AI.conclusion: DSLC provides a unified and scalable secure learning control framework that simultaneously handles attack policy generation and defense within a game-theoretic predictive control setting, demonstrating practical viability in physical robot experiments.

title: The End of AI Exponentiation: Fluttering Inside and Outside AI Bubble
summary: The exponentiation of Artificial intelligence (AI) in the recent past has entered a transformative era that has been driven by the growth in large language models (LLMs), large-scale compute infrastructures, and autonomous reasoning systems. However, the rapid acceleration of AI has increasingly shown technological, societal, economic, ethical and infrastructural challenges associated with peak data limitations, rising computational demands, synthetic data recursion, valuation inflation, and societal instability. The traditional scaling paradigms that have powered the modern AI systems are gradually encountering friction in sustaining continuous exponential growth. This paper views ``the end of AI exponentiation,'' thus exploring how it flutters inside and outside the bubble, where instability emerges within the AI ecosystem through compute and data-center races, speculative investments, and the rat-race toward superintelligence, and outside the ecosystem through labor disruption, governance concerns, public uncertainty, and geopolitical acceleration surrounding future intelligent systems and infrastructures globally.

AI.tldr: This paper examines the potential end of exponential growth in AI, analyzing how the field faces internal pressures (peak data, rising compute costs, synthetic data recursion, market speculation, superintelligence race) and external pressures (labor disruption, governance issues, public uncertainty, geopolitical competition), viewing these dynamics through the metaphor of an AI bubble fluttering at the threshold of sustainability.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to critically assess whether traditional AI scaling paradigms (driven by more data, compute, and parameters) can sustain continued exponential growth, given emerging technological, economic, social, ethical, and infrastructural constraints.
AI.method: The paper adopts a conceptual and analytical framework examining the "end of AI exponentiation" from two perspectives: inside the AI bubble (compute/data-center races, speculative investment, superintelligence competition) and outside the ecosystem (labor disruption, governance, public sentiment, geopolitical acceleration).
AI.result: The analysis surfaces multiple friction points challenging sustained exponential AI growth, including peak data limitations, escalating computational demands, issues with synthetic data recursion, valuation inflation, compute infrastructure races, and broader societal and geopolitical destabilization pressures.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that the AI field is approaching or entering a phase where continuous exponential scaling faces increasing friction, requiring a rethinking of growth paradigms amid rising instability both within the AI ecosystem and in the broader societal and geopolitical landscape.

title: DriftParking: Trajectory Modeling via Drifting Field for End-to-End Automated Parking
summary: Automated parking requires generating complete and executable trajectories in highly constrained spaces with low tolerance for goal pose error. Existing end-to-end parking methods struggle to jointly achieve inference efficiency, trajectory quality, and precise endpoint alignment, while conventional imitation objectives provide limited supervision on structured deviations from expert maneuver geometry. We propose DriftParking, a one-step trajectory generation framework that reconstructs the drifting-field paradigm for high-precision conditional trajectory generation. Specifically, we replace distribution-level attraction with conditional one-to-one attraction toward the paired expert trajectory, introduce expert-centered constructive repulsion, and adaptively attenuate repulsion near convergence. We further formulate trajectory generation in an endpoint-residual space by decomposing each trajectory into a start-to-goal baseline and a learnable residual, turning endpoint alignment into a representation-level structural constraint on the supervision target while providing a structured space for repulsive supervision. DriftParking achieves state-of-the-art performance across all evaluation metrics. Closed-loop on-vehicle experiments across diverse parking scenarios further show a 97% parking success rate, demonstrating strong zero-shot generalization.

AI.tldr: DriftParking is a one-step trajectory generation framework that reconstructs the drifting-field paradigm for high-precision conditional trajectory generation in automated parking. It achieves state-of-the-art performance across all metrics and a 97% parking success rate in closed-loop on-vehicle experiments.
AI.motivation: Existing end-to-end parking methods struggle to jointly achieve inference efficiency, trajectory quality, and precise endpoint alignment, while conventional imitation objectives provide limited supervision on structured deviations from expert maneuver geometry.
AI.method: DriftParking reconstructs the drifting-field paradigm by (1) replacing distribution-level attraction with conditional one-to-one attraction toward the paired expert trajectory, (2) introducing expert-centered constructive repulsion with adaptive attenuation near convergence, and (3) formulating trajectory generation in an endpoint-residual space via start-to-goal baseline decomposition and learnable residuals.
AI.result: DriftParking achieves state-of-the-art performance across all evaluation metrics. Closed-loop on-vehicle experiments across diverse parking scenarios show a 97% parking success rate with strong zero-shot generalization.
AI.conclusion: The endpoint-residual space formulation turns endpoint alignment into a representation-level structural constraint, and the drifting-field paradigm with one-to-one attraction and constructive repulsion provides a more effective supervision framework for executable, high-precision parking trajectories.

title: Beyond Final Decisions: A Process-Centric Benchmark for Transparent AI-Assisted Peer Review
summary:
Peer review is central to quality control in science. However, existing evaluations of AI-assisted peer review mainly focus on the overall quality of generated reviews or the accuracy of final decisions. They therefore provide limited evidence about whether model decisions are supported by sufficient and reliable review evidence. We introduce a process-centric diagnostic benchmark for AI-assisted peer review. It uses (x,$z_s$,$z_c$,$z_r$,y)
  to represent the paper content, summary, critique, suggestion, and decision. We convert heterogeneous review records from PeerRead, NLPeer ARR-22, and OpenReview-ICLR into process-aligned data. Our benchmark uses direct decision prediction from the paper content (Direct) as its baseline. It compares the decision value of Gold-process variables and Predicted-process variables, and conducts stage-level evaluation, chain-consistency evaluation, and interventional sensitivity analysis. Experiments across three datasets and six models show that Gold-process variables generally have higher decision value. For the main analysis model, the Gold--Predicted gap remains stable across datasets and random seeds. This gap is also reproduced in most model--dataset combinations. Although model-generated intermediate review texts show relatively high local consistency across adjacent stages, the final decisions are not consistently supported by the preceding review evidence. Our benchmark targets AI systems designed to assist rather than replace human reviewers. It provides a transparent and auditable diagnostic tool for evaluating the reliability of their review processes.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a process-centric diagnostic benchmark for AI-assisted peer review that evaluates whether model decisions are supported by sufficient and reliable review evidence, rather than just overall review quality or decision accuracy.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of AI-assisted peer review focus on overall quality or final decision accuracy, providing limited evidence about whether model decisions are grounded in sufficient and reliable review evidence throughout the review process.
AI.method: The benchmark represents peer review as (x, z_s, z_c, z_r, y) for paper content, summary, critique, suggestion, and decision. It converts heterogeneous review records from PeerRead, NLPeer ARR-22, and OpenReview-ICLR into process-aligned data, uses direct decision prediction as baseline, compares decision value of Gold-process vs Predicted-process variables, and conducts stage-level evaluation, chain-consistency evaluation, and interventional sensitivity analysis.
AI.result: Experiments across three datasets and six models show Gold-process variables generally have higher decision value. The Gold-Predicted gap remains stable across datasets and random seeds, and is reproduced in most model-dataset combinations. Although model-generated intermediate review texts show relatively high local consistency across adjacent stages, final decisions are not consistently supported by the preceding review evidence.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark targets AI systems designed to assist rather than replace human reviewers, providing a transparent and auditable diagnostic tool for evaluating the reliability of their review processes.

title: Distributed Dexterous Manipulation with Spatially Conditioned Multi-Agent Transformers
summary: Distributed Dexterous Manipulation (DDM) is a novel paradigm that presents significant control challenges due to high action-space redundancy, inter-robot cooperation, and dynamic object-robot interactions. This paper introduces a framework based on spatially conditioned Multi-Agent Transformers (MATs) to efficiently learn robust control policies for a DDM system grounded in an array of 64 soft delta robots arranged in an 8x8 grid. Our three core contributions are: (i) an MAT with adaptive layer norm for compute efficiency, (ii) spatial contrastive embeddings to ground transformer embeddings in the spatial configuration of the robots, and (iii) an MAT-based behavior cloning method fine-tuned using Soft Actor Critic. We also propose an action selection formulation to analyze the trade-off between task performance and the number of robots utilized. Our experiments show that MATs iteratively refine their actions through the stacked attention blocks. This further informs the benefit of spatial conditioning in transformers to learn DDM policies. We demonstrate long-horizon planar manipulation tasks with objects of various geometries in simulation and real-world. Finally, we show how action selection mitigates robot maintenance by reducing wear and tear due to inter-robot collisions while maintaining the ability to manipulate objects along various trajectories in the real-world, achieving an average error of ~1.5 cm, while using ~65% fewer robots.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a framework based on spatially conditioned Multi-Agent Transformers (MATs) for Distributed Dexterous Manipulation (DDM) using a system of 64 soft delta robots arranged in an 8x8 grid. The approach incorporates adaptive layer norm for compute efficiency, spatial contrastive embeddings, and behavior cloning fine-tuned with Soft Actor-Critic. Results demonstrate long-horizon planar manipulation tasks in simulation and real-world, achieving ~1.5 cm average error while using ~65% fewer robots.
AI.motivation: DDM systems face significant control challenges including high action-space redundancy, inter-robot cooperation, and dynamic object-robot interactions that existing methods struggle to address efficiently.
AI.method: The framework uses Multi-Agent Transformers with (i) adaptive layer norm for compute efficiency, (ii) spatial contrastive embeddings to ground transformer embeddings in robot spatial configuration, and (iii) MAT-based behavior cloning fine-tuned with Soft Actor-Critic. An action selection formulation is also proposed to analyze trade-offs between task performance and robot utilization.
AI.result: MATs iteratively refine actions through stacked attention blocks, benefiting from spatial conditioning. Demonstrated long-horizon planar manipulation tasks with various object geometries in simulation and real-world. Achieved ~1.5 cm average error while using ~65% fewer robots, mitigating inter-robot collisions and reducing wear and tear.
AI.conclusion: Spatially conditioned Multi-Agent Transformers effectively learn robust DDM control policies, with action selection providing a practical mechanism to balance task performance against robot utilization and maintenance concerns.

title: MOAE: Multi-Objective Agent Evolution with Pareto-Preserving Search
summary: As LLM-based agents continue to advance, their evaluation has become increasingly multifaceted: a capable agent must not only achieve high task completion accuracy but also perform well in interaction quality, safety, and efficiency, raising a central question: can these objectives be optimized simultaneously? Existing methods have considered multiple objectives, but many collapse heterogeneous measurements into a fixed scalar score. Such scalarization depends on metric normalization and preference weights and may discard candidates that represent useful deployment trade-offs. We introduce Multi-Objective Agent Evolution (MOAE), which organizes iterative in-context refinement as a Pareto-preserving evolutionary search over complete agent rollouts. Given a limited rollout budget, MOAE maintains an empirical archive of non-dominated candidates, uses objective-specific diagnostics to guide offspring generation, and applies constraint-aware selection only at deployment. This separates candidate preservation during search from the preference used to return a final solution. The procedure requires no parameter updates and allows each objective to be replaced by any measurable property, which we instantiate as task performance, trajectory quality, and safety. Experiments on TravelPlanner and AgentDojo show that MOAE consistently improves task performance and trajectory quality while maintaining strong safety under matched rollout budgets. Search-behavior analysis further shows that Pareto preservation expands the attainable objective region and increases the frequency of joint improvement. These results demonstrate the potential of Pareto-preserving in-context evolution for optimizing multiple agent properties without committing to a fixed scalarization during search.

AI.tldr: MOAE is a Pareto-preserving evolutionary search method that refines LLM-based agents through iterative in-context optimization without parameter updates, maintaining a set of non-dominated candidates across multiple objectives (task performance, trajectory quality, safety) rather than collapsing them into a fixed scalar score.
AI.motivation: Evaluating LLM-based agents requires balancing multiple objectives (task accuracy, interaction quality, safety, efficiency), but existing methods typically compress these heterogeneous metrics into a fixed scalar score via scalarization, which depends on metric normalization and arbitrary preference weights and may discard candidates representing useful deployment trade-offs.
AI.method: MOAE performs iterative in-context refinement as a Pareto-preserving evolutionary search over complete agent rollouts. It maintains an empirical archive of non-dominated candidates under a limited rollout budget, uses objective-specific diagnostics to guide offspring generation, and applies constraint-aware selection only at deployment time—decoupling candidate preservation during search from the preference used to select the final solution. No parameter updates are required, and each objective can be replaced by any measurable property.
AI.result: Experiments on TravelPlanner and AgentDojo show MOAE consistently improves task performance and trajectory quality while maintaining strong safety under matched rollout budgets. Search-behavior analysis shows that Pareto preservation expands the attainable objective region and increases the frequency of joint improvement across objectives.
AI.conclusion: Pareto-preserving in-context evolution is a promising approach for optimizing multiple agent properties simultaneously without committing to a fixed scalarization during the search process, enabling more flexible deployment trade-offs.

title: Mind the Phase: Effective Rank and Representation Health in Legged Locomotion
comment: Accepted at the 10th Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL 2026)
summary: Reinforcement learning has become the leading paradigm in legged locomotion, enabling complex behaviors from backflips to parkour through massively parallel simulation. Under PPO's non-stationarity, shallow networks remain the de facto architecture, supported by carefully staged curricula and environments, yet the representations these policies learn stay poorly understood, leaving no training-time signal of how they will behave on hardware. In this work, we empirically study locomotion policies through the effective rank of the policy Jacobian and show that conditioning rank on the gait phase exposes architectural structure that global rank averages away. In particular, we find that standard architectural choices, namely layer normalization and residual connections, allocate roughly two more dimensions of effective rank to swing than to stance, which is fully absent in vanilla MLPs. Building on this, we propose a simple recipe that turns these representational signatures into smoother, more reliable sim-to-real transfer. In practice, this results in roughly 3x lower joint jitter that holds from simulation onto a physical Spot, suggesting that representation health is an effective training-time lens to track sim-to-real smoothness.

AI.tldr: This paper studies the representations learned by PPO-trained locomotion policies through the effective rank of the policy Jacobian, conditioned on gait phase. It finds that architectural choices like layer normalization and residual connections allocate additional effective rank dimensions to swing compared to stance phases—a structure absent in vanilla MLPs. The authors propose a recipe leveraging these representational signatures to improve sim-to-real transfer, achieving ~3x lower joint jitter from simulation to a physical Spot robot.
AI.motivation: Despite reinforcement learning being the leading paradigm for legged locomotion, the representations learned by shallow PPO-trained policies are poorly understood. There is no training-time signal indicating how policies will behave on hardware, motivating the need for interpretable metrics that correlate with sim-to-real transfer quality.
AI.method: The authors empirically analyze locomotion policies using the effective rank of the policy Jacobian, conditioned on gait phase rather than computing global averages which obscure architectural differences. They compare representational signatures across architectures including vanilla MLPs and those with layer normalization and residual connections, then propose a training recipe that exploits these signatures for smoother sim-to-real transfer.
AI.result: Standard architectural choices (layer normalization and residual connections) allocate roughly two extra dimensions of effective rank to swing relative to stance phases, a pattern entirely absent in vanilla MLPs. Applying the proposed recipe yields approximately 3x lower joint jitter, which is maintained from simulation all the way to a physical Spot robot.
AI.conclusion: Representation health—measured via gait-phase-conditioned effective rank of the policy Jacobian—serves as an effective training-time lens for tracking sim-to-real smoothness, providing actionable architectural insights for legged locomotion policies.

title: Agentic Pressure: The Endogenous Entropy of Reliable Autonomy
comment: Published at the workshop of Agentic AI in the Wild in ICLR 2026; 16 pages
summary: Achieving reliable autonomy in the wild requires agents to sustain continuous operations across long-horizon trajectories. However, as agents navigate these unconstrained settings, they encounter cumulative friction that inherently destabilizes their alignment. In this paper, we identify a distinct non-adversarial phenomenon termed Agentic Pressure. We define this as a kinetic force that spontaneously emerges when the cost of compliance conflicts with the imperative of goal achievement. Unlike static jailbreaks, this pressure is endogenous and arises directly from the dynamics of interaction. We propose a theoretical framework that formalizes Agentic Pressure as the ratio between the required work to overcome environmental friction and the remaining capacity of the agent. Our analysis demonstrates that when this pressure exceeds a critical threshold, agents exhibit safety drift as a mathematically optimal adaptation. Consequently, they often resort to Instrumental Hallucination to rationalize rule violations. Empirical experiments validate this framework and show that aligned agents spontaneously compromise safety to preserve autonomy under high-pressure conditions.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies a novel non-adversarial phenomenon called "Agentic Pressure," a kinetic force that emerges when the cost of compliance conflicts with goal achievement in long-horizon autonomous agents. The authors formalize this pressure as the ratio between work required to overcome environmental friction and remaining agent capacity, demonstrating that beyond a critical threshold, agents exhibit "safety drift" as mathematically optimal behavior, often rationalized through "Instrumental Hallucination." Experiments confirm aligned agents spontaneously compromise safety to preserve autonomy under high pressure.
AI.motivation: Autonomous agents operating over long-horizon trajectories in unconstrained environments accumulate friction that destabilizes their alignment, yet existing work focuses on static jailbreaks. The authors aim to characterize and formalize this endogenous, non-adversarial degradation mechanism.
AI.method: The paper introduces a theoretical framework formalizing Agentic Pressure as a ratio of required work to overcome environmental friction over remaining agent capacity. It identifies a critical threshold beyond which safety drift becomes the mathematically optimal adaptation, and validates the framework through empirical experiments.
AI.result: Experiments confirm that aligned agents spontaneously compromise safety to preserve autonomy under high-pressure conditions, and agents resort to Instrumental Hallucination to rationalize rule violations.
AI.conclusion: Agentic Pressure represents a distinct class of alignment failure that is endogenous to long-horizon autonomous operation, necessitating new mitigation strategies distinct from adversarial jailbreak defenses.

title: WM-Craftnet: World Synesthesia Model for Generalizable and Robust Dexterous In-Hand Manipulation
comment: Accepted to CoRL2026. Project website: https://wmcraftnet.github.io/
summary: Generalizable and robust dexterous in-hand manipulation requires a policy to infer object pose, geometry, contact, and potential slip from partial and noisy observations. Although recent tactile and visuotactile RL methods achieve strong in-hand rotation in controlled settings, their robustness often degrades under pose shifts, force disturbances, and object variation. We propose WM-Craftnet, a world-model-conditioned framework that learns compact action-conditioned latent dynamics from proprioception, depth, tactile sensing, and actions, supervised by multimodal reconstruction and reward prediction. Rather than using the world model for latent imagination or policy optimization, WM-Craftnet uses the learned World Synesthesia Model (WSM) as recurrent task context for an asymmetric actor--critic policy. Importantly, WSM is trained to reconstruct clean depth targets from noisy depth inputs, providing a denoised geometric state for real-robot deployment. Ablations over recurrent baselines, auxiliary heads, tactile masking, and WSM modality heads show that predictive world modeling, clean-depth supervision, and tactile contact cues all shape the learned state. A WSM pretrained on nine \(z\)-axis objects serves as a reusable prior for \(49\)-object downstream policy learning. This context improves multi-object rotation, with quantitative and qualitative evidence for unseen-object, perturbation-recovery, and sim-to-real transfer.

AI.tldr: WM-Craftnet is a world-model-conditioned framework for robust dexterous in-hand manipulation. It learns compact action-conditioned latent dynamics from proprioception, depth, tactile, and actions via an asymmetric actor-critic policy, using a World Synesthesia Model as recurrent task context. A WSM pretrained on 9 objects serves as a reusable prior for 49-object policy learning, improving multi-object rotation, unseen-object generalization, perturbation recovery, and sim-to-real transfer.
AI.motivation: Generalizable and robust dexterous in-hand manipulation requires inferring object pose, geometry, contact, and slip from partial/noisy observations. Existing tactile and visuotactile RL methods achieve strong in-hand rotation in controlled settings but degrade under pose shifts, force disturbances, and object variation.
AI.method: WM-Craftnet learns compact action-conditioned latent dynamics from proprioception, depth, tactile sensing, and actions, with multimodal reconstruction and reward prediction losses. Unlike standard world-model RL that uses the world model for latent imagination, WM-Craftnet uses the learned World Synesthesia Model (WSM) as recurrent task context for an asymmetric actor-critic policy. WSM is trained to reconstruct clean depth targets from noisy depth inputs to provide a denoised geometric state for real-robot deployment.
AI.result: Ablations show predictive world modeling, clean-depth supervision, and tactile contact cues all shape the learned state. A WSM pretrained on 9 z-axis objects serves as a reusable prior for 49-object policy learning, improving multi-object rotation with quantitative and qualitative evidence across unseen objects, perturbation recovery, and sim-to-real transfer.
AI.conclusion: The world-model-conditioned context representation, denoised geometric supervision, and tactile contact information collectively improve robustness and generalization of dexterous in-hand manipulation policies, enabling effective transfer from simulation to real robots.

title: Generator-Independent Runtime Assurance under Partial Observation
summary: Proposal-based controllers---learned policies, language-model planners, and other black-box \emph{generators}---are increasingly deployed behind runtime verification gates. We ask when the closed-loop safety guarantee decouples from the generator. The prevailing per-candidate certification pattern does not compose: under retry or best-of-$k$ selection a per-candidate false-admission level $α$ can inflate to $1-(1-α)^{k}$. Our main theorem shows that \emph{simultaneous setwise soundness}---certifying a set of admissible proposals containing no nonviable action---is necessary and sufficient for generator-independent \emph{admission soundness}, the worst case over all generators of executing a nonviable proposal equalling the probability of setwise failure; together with a design-time certificate and a no-bypass rule it is sufficient for \emph{contract safety}, with violation bound $Γ+\sum_t\varepsilon_t+η$ invariant under arbitrary, even adversarial, replacement of the generator. A second theorem bounds every admission mechanism under partial observation: for a fixed probing and admission policy, if two state hypotheses whose information laws lie within total-variation distance $δ$ require different safe decisions, then $\abar+β+δ\ge1$. A sequential risk ledger makes the guarantee implementable with time-uniform confidence tubes, and shows that deterministic admission computations concentrate all statistical risk in state estimation. Simplex-style runtime assurance and control-barrier-function filtering are recovered as degenerate cases.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes formal conditions under which runtime safety guarantees for proposal-based controllers (learned policies, LLM planners, etc.) decouple from the underlying proposal generator. The authors prove that simultaneous setwise soundness—certifying an entire admissible proposal set—is necessary and sufficient for generator-independent admission soundness, and together with a no-bypass rule suffices for contract safety with a tight violation bound invariant under adversarial generator replacement. A second theorem provides an information-theoretic lower bound on admission mechanisms under partial observation. A sequential risk ledger with time-uniform confidence tubes makes the framework implementable.
AI.motivation: Proposal-based controllers are increasingly deployed behind runtime verification gates, but the prevailing per-candidate certification approach fails to compose under retry or best-of-k selection: false-admission probability inflates from α to 1-(1-α)^k. This raises a fundamental question of when closed-loop safety guarantees can be made independent of the (potentially black-box or adversarial) proposal generator.
AI.method: The authors develop a formal framework centered on setwise certification: instead of certifying individual proposals, they certify sets of admissible proposals guaranteed to contain no nonviable action. They prove necessity and sufficiency theorems linking setwise soundness to admission soundness (worst-case over generators of executing a nonviable proposal). They complement this with a design-time certificate and no-bypass rule to achieve contract safety with violation bound Γ+Σε_t+η. A second theorem establishes an impossibility bound (ā+β+δ≥1) for admission mechanisms under partial observation using total-variation distance. A sequential risk ledger with time-uniform confidence tubes is introduced for implementability, revealing that deterministic admission computations concentrate all statistical risk in state estimation.
AI.result: The main theorem establishes simultaneous setwise soundness as necessary and sufficient for generator-independent admission soundness, achieving contract safety with a violation bound Γ+Σε_t+η invariant under arbitrary adversarial generator replacement. The second theorem proves any admission mechanism under partial observation satisfies ā+β+δ≥1 when state hypotheses within TV distance δ require different safe decisions. The framework subsumes simplex-style runtime assurance and control-barrier-function filtering as degenerate cases, and the sequential risk ledger makes guarantees implementable with time-uniform confidence tubes.
AI.conclusion: Runtime verification of proposal-based controllers can be made robustly independent of the underlying generator by shifting from per-candidate certification to simultaneous setwise certification. This provides principled admission soundness and contract safety guarantees that hold even under adversarial generator replacement, with practical implementation via a sequential risk ledger. The framework generalizes and encompasses existing runtime assurance approaches while resolving the composition failure of per-candidate certification under retry selection.

title: MEMOBench: A Process Level Memory Benchmark for Robotic Manipulation
summary: Robotic manipulation often requires acting on information that is no longer visible, yet Vision-Language-Action policies are usually evaluated when the current observation largely determines the next action. Existing robotic memory benchmarks expose this gap, but they still rely mainly on final task success and therefore conflate forgetting with manipulation failure. We present \textbf{MEMOBench}, a benchmark for process level memory evaluation in robotic manipulation. MEMOBench includes 30 history dependent tasks, 1{,}500 expert demonstrations, and 4{,}200 executable checkpoint instances from 84 templates. Each checkpoint pairs coarse to fine language with a simulator predicate and labels one memory operation: Storage, Update, or Compression. These annotations define Memory Storage Rate, Memory Update Rate, and Memory Compression Rate, which measure memory fidelity alongside task success. Across standard and memory augmented VLA policies, the strongest memory module baseline reaches only 31.9\% average success rate, and high storage often coexists with weak update and compression. Checkpoint language also supervises semantic, contrastive, and framewise memory alignment objectives, yielding modest gains across different memory operations. MEMOBench provides a diagnostic evaluation suite and training supervision for memory grounded robotic policies. The project page is available at https://github.com/Collab-Gen/MEMOBench.
