AI.tldr: MEMOBench is a benchmark for process-level memory evaluation in robotic manipulation, containing 30 history-dependent tasks, 1,500 expert demonstrations, and 4,200 executable checkpoint instances from 84 templates. It introduces three memory-specific metrics (Storage, Update, Compression rates) that measure memory fidelity alongside task success, revealing that even the strongest memory-augmented VLA baseline only achieves 31.9% average success with substantial gaps between storage, update, and compression capabilities.
AI.motivation: Robotic manipulation often requires acting on information no longer visible, yet VLA policies are typically evaluated under conditions where current observation largely determines the next action. Existing robotic memory benchmarks rely mainly on final task success, conflating forgetting with manipulation failure and failing to provide process-level diagnostics about where and how memory fails.
AI.method: MEMOBench constructs 30 history-dependent tasks with 1,500 expert demonstrations and 4,200 executable checkpoint instances from 84 templates. Each checkpoint pairs coarse-to-fine language with a simulator predicate and labels one of three memory operations: Storage, Update, or Compression. The benchmark defines three rates (Memory Storage Rate, Memory Update Rate, Memory Compression Rate) to measure memory fidelity independently of task success. It also uses checkpoint language to supervise semantic, contrastive, and framewise memory alignment objectives for training.
AI.result: Across standard and memory-augmented VLA policies, the strongest memory module baseline reaches only 31.9% average success rate. High storage capability often coexists with weak update and compression performance. Checkpoint-language-supervised memory alignment objectives yield only modest gains across different memory operations.
AI.conclusion: MEMOBench provides a diagnostic evaluation suite and training supervision for memory-grounded robotic policies, offering process-level metrics that decouple memory fidelity from task success and revealing persistent gaps in update and compression operations that current VLA policies fail to close.

title: DAREBench: Deployment-Aware and Reliable Evaluation of Models as Agents
summary: As large language models evolve from question-answering systems into general-purpose agents, evaluation must move beyond static answer correctness to assess multimodal perception, multi-step execution, tool use, and artifact delivery. However, existing benchmarks are often tied to specific task types, execution environments, or scoring protocols, limiting their comparability, interpretability, and reliability for deployment decisions. We introduce DAREBench (Deployment-Aware and Reliable Evaluation of Models as Agents), a benchmark designed to capture workload variation and support reliable agent evaluation. Built on a shared OpenClaw execution environment, DAREBench organizes 233 tasks selected and adapted from 22 source benchmarks into a $2\times3$ workload matrix defined by input modality and execution form, and evaluates them under a unified contract-based protocol with evidence-based score auditing. We evaluate 23 commercial API models and 12 locally deployed open-weight models over 7,587 model--task runs, reporting accuracy and token consumption alongside reference costs for API models. Results show that no single model dominates all workload groups, text and multimodal tasks exhibit distinct accuracy--cost trade-offs, and local open-weight models are competitive in several groups but still trail frontier commercial models overall. These findings suggest that agent deployment and model selection should consider workload profiles, deployment mode, and accuracy--cost trade-offs rather than rely on a single aggregate score.

AI.tldr: DAREBench is a deployment-aware agent evaluation benchmark built on a shared OpenClaw execution environment, organizing 233 tasks from 22 source benchmarks into a 2×3 workload matrix (input modality × execution form) with unified contract-based scoring and evidence-based audit. Evaluations of 23 commercial API models and 12 local open-weight models across 7,587 runs reveal no single dominant model, distinct accuracy–cost trade-offs between text and multimodal tasks, and competitive but trailing performance of local models.
AI.motivation: Existing agent benchmarks are tied to specific task types, environments, or scoring protocols, limiting comparability, interpretability, and reliability for deployment decisions. As LLMs evolve into general-purpose agents, evaluation must go beyond static answer correctness to cover multimodal perception, multi-step execution, tool use, and artifact delivery.
AI.method: DAREBench constructs a 2×3 workload matrix defined by input modality and execution form from 233 tasks selected/adapted from 22 source benchmarks, runs on a shared OpenClaw execution environment, and evaluates under a unified contract-based protocol with evidence-based score auditing.
AI.result: Evaluated 23 commercial API models and 12 local open-weight models over 7,587 model–task runs, reporting accuracy, token consumption, and reference costs. No single model dominates all workload groups; text and multimodal tasks show distinct accuracy–cost trade-offs; local open-weight models are competitive in several groups but trail frontier commercial models overall.
AI.conclusion: Agent deployment and model selection should consider workload profiles, deployment mode, and accuracy–cost trade-offs rather than relying on a single aggregate score.

title: Large Discrete Policy: Advancing Explicit Behavior Modeling with Stochastic Iterative Scoring
summary: Behavior policies are often formulated as continuous generative models, whose iterative denoising processes are expressive but difficult to interpret and prone to producing implausible actions. We propose the Large Discrete Policy (LDiP), a fully discrete behavior modeling framework that selects actions from a large vocabulary of physically plausible candidates. Rather than perturbing actions, LDiP improves expressivity through stochastic iterative scoring: it progressively re-scores and prunes candidates with score-space stochasticity, enabling fine-grained ranking and exploration among plausible actions while preserving an explicit decision process. Across end-to-end planning, closed-loop driving, robotic manipulation, and vision-language-action settings, LDiP consistently outperforms strong discrete and continuous baselines in autonomous driving, and exceeds or matches continuous generative policies in robotic manipulation. These results show that discrete policies, when equipped with effective scoring mechanisms, offer an expressive, plausible, and interpretable alternative for behavior modeling. Project website: https://zhenxinli.net/LargeDiscretePolicy/.

AI.tldr: LDiP is a fully discrete behavior modeling framework that selects actions from a large vocabulary of physically plausible candidates via stochastic iterative scoring and pruning, outperforming discrete and continuous baselines in autonomous driving and matching/exceeding continuous policies in robotic manipulation.
AI.motivation: Continuous generative behavior policies, while expressive, suffer from opaque iterative denoising processes and can produce implausible actions, motivating a need for more interpretable, plausible alternatives.
AI.method: LDiP formulates behavior policies as fully discrete models, then improves expressivity through stochastic iterative scoring—progressively re-scoring and pruning candidate actions with score-space stochasticity for fine-grained ranking and exploration while keeping the decision process explicit.
AI.result: Across end-to-end planning, closed-loop driving, robotic manipulation, and vision-language-action settings, LDiP consistently outperforms strong discrete and continuous baselines in autonomous driving, and exceeds or matches continuous generative policies in robotic manipulation.
AI.conclusion: Discrete policies equipped with effective scoring mechanisms offer an expressive, plausible, and interpretable alternative for behavior modeling.

title: Explaining AI Agents Through Execution Traces
summary: AI Agents are increasingly deployed in real-world settings, where they interact with external tools and make sequential decisions with limited human oversight. This creates a pressing need for reliable and auditable explanations of what an agent did and why. However, traditional Explainable AI (XAI) methods fall short of providing the process-level transparency required for such interactive, multi-step systems, motivating a paradigm shift toward approaches specifically designed for AI Agents. To address this gap, we present a post-hoc XAI framework that transforms a lengthy agent's execution trace into a structured report and a faithful natural-language explanation explicitly grounded in its observable behavior. Because it relies solely on execution traces, the framework applies across different agent architectures, environments, and tasks. Human and automated evaluations across multiple benchmarks and architectures show that our framework produces high-quality, trace-faithful explanations while reliably identifying unsupported claims, unjustified actions, and evidence gaps, outperforming naive LLM-generated explanations.

AI.tldr: A post-hoc Explainable AI framework that converts AI agent execution traces into structured, faithful natural-language explanations, applicable across architectures and environments, outperforming naive LLM-generated explanations in identifying unsupported claims and evidence gaps.
AI.motivation: Traditional XAI methods are inadequate for interactive, multi-step AI agents that make sequential decisions with limited human oversight, creating a need for process-level transparency and auditable explanations of agent behavior.
AI.method: The framework transforms a lengthy agent execution trace into a structured report and a faithful natural-language explanation that is explicitly grounded in the agent's observable behavior, relying solely on execution traces to ensure cross-architecture, environment, and task applicability.
AI.result: Human and automated evaluations across multiple benchmarks and architectures show the framework produces high-quality, trace-faithful explanations and reliably identifies unsupported claims, unjustified actions, and evidence gaps, outperforming naive LLM-generated explanations.
AI.conclusion: Execution-trace-grounded post-hoc explanations offer a viable paradigm for trustworthy and auditable AI agent reasoning, filling the gap left by traditional XAI approaches.

title: Human-Aware Target Tracking and Navigation: Fusing Kinematic State Estimation with Structural Map Constraints
comment: Submitted to Australian Conference on Robotics and Automation
summary: Autonomous mobile robots performing person-following tasks often suffer from temporary occlusions and sensor track loss in dynamic environments. This research presents an end-to-end autonomous navigation stack that addresses target occlusion through map-informed spatial reasoning. The proposed system features a multi-modal perception pipeline, fusing deep learning-based visual tracking with 2-dimensional LiDAR point clustering to maintain high-fidelity tracking of a tagged person. A continuous state estimator integrates this perception data with wheel odometry and IMU sensors for stable localization. When the active track is lost due to occlusion, the system activates a map-based recovery framework. Leveraging a predefined topological map, the system executes a graph-based search to propagate the target's last known trajectory along structurally defined walking lanes, adhering to left-hand regional conventions. By generating a discrete set of feasible future trajectories, the robot reasons about potential structural trajectory changes, such as continuing a heading or turning at an intersection. This map-informed prediction is fed directly to the local obstacle avoidance planner, enabling the robot to continue following its target safely and predictably until the person is visually reacquired. Real-world evaluations in dense multi-person environments demonstrate the system's robustness, achieving a 71.4\% target reacquisition success rate during major occlusion events lasting up to 7 seconds.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an end-to-end autonomous navigation stack for mobile robots performing person-following tasks, addressing the challenge of temporary target occlusion and sensor track loss. The system fuses deep learning visual tracking with 2D LiDAR clustering for multi-modal perception, and when track is lost, employs a map-based recovery framework using topological graph search to predict feasible future trajectories along walking lanes. Real-world tests achieved a 71.4% target reacquisition rate during occlusions lasting up to 7 seconds.
AI.motivation: Autonomous mobile robots performing person-following tasks frequently experience performance degradation due to temporary occlusions and sensor track loss in dynamic environments, necessitating a robust solution that maintains target following continuity despite visual interruptions.
AI.method: The system comprises: (1) a multi-modal perception pipeline fusing deep-learning visual tracking with 2D LiDAR point clustering for high-fidelity tagged-person tracking; (2) a continuous state estimator integrating perception data with wheel odometry and IMU for stable localization; (3) a map-informed recovery mechanism triggered upon track loss, which uses a predefined topological map and graph-based search to propagate the target's last known trajectory along walking lanes (adhering to left-hand conventions); and (4) generation of discrete feasible future trajectories that account for structural changes (e.g., continuing straight or turning at intersections), fed directly to a local obstacle avoidance planner until visual reacquisition.
AI.result: Real-world evaluations in dense multi-person environments demonstrated robust performance, achieving a 71.4% target reacquisition success rate during major occlusion events lasting up to 7 seconds.
AI.conclusion: The proposed map-informed spatial reasoning approach effectively enables autonomous mobile robots to maintain safe and predictable person-following behavior through occlusion events, significantly mitigating the risks of permanent target loss in dynamic environments.

title: Generating Instance Generators in PDDL Planning
summary: PDDL, the de-facto standard language in the AI Planning community, is designed to specify planning domains: sets of instances that share the same predicates and action schemas. Yet it does not provide any means to specify the actual instance set, i.e., legality constraints on initial states and goal conditions, as well as possibly domain subset constraints specifying an instance subset we are interested in. One consequence of this is that instance generation has always been ad-hoc, with manually written domain- and subset-specific instance generators. Recent work has started to address this, through reasoning and learning methods that however suffer from scalability limitations. Here we introduce an alternative approach, leveraging LLMs to generate instance-generation programs, with built-in soundness guarantees through prescribed checks. We show that these automatically generated instance generators return large numbers of sound and diverse instances efficiently.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a novel approach using Large Language Models (LLMs) to automatically generate instance-generation programs for PDDL planning domains, addressing the lack of standardized means to specify legal instance sets. The generated programs include built-in soundness guarantees through prescribed checks, producing large numbers of sound and diverse planning instances efficiently.
AI.motivation: PDDL lacks mechanisms to formally specify legal instance sets (initial states, goal conditions, domain subset constraints). This makes instance generation ad-hoc, requiring manually written, domain-specific generators. Prior automated approaches using reasoning and learning suffer from scalability limitations.
AI.method: The paper leverages LLMs to generate instance-generation programs. These programs incorporate built-in soundness guarantees through prescribed verification checks, ensuring that generated instances satisfy legality constraints.
AI.result: The automatically generated instance generators produce large numbers of sound and diverse instances efficiently, overcoming the scalability issues of prior reasoning/learning-based approaches.
AI.conclusion: LLM-based generation of instance-generation programs is an effective and scalable alternative to manual generator writing and prior automated methods, with built-in soundness verification ensuring legal instances.

title: RoboDreamer: Anticipatory Humanoid Locomotion with Predictive State-Space Models
summary: Humanoid locomotion requires control policies that remain stable under imperfect sensing while exploiting temporal context for consistent motion. We present RoboDreamer, a two-stage teacher--student framework that combines next-observation consistency with randomized continuous temporal masking. A teacher is first trained on clean observations, and a student is then distilled under masked recent observations, encouraging the policy to infer missing current information from history. At inference, the same masking interface is reused for implicit closed-loop action refinement and optional multi-step action chunking. Mamba is used as the temporal backbone, while matched ablations show that masking/distillation provides a substantial part of the gain and Mamba contributes additional tracking improvements with real-time latency. Experiments in IsaacLab, MuJoCo, and on a Unitree G1 demonstrate robust motion tracking under observation masking and successful real-world deployment.

AI.tldr: RoboDreamer is a two-stage teacher-student framework for humanoid locomotion that combines next-observation consistency with randomized continuous temporal masking, using Mamba as a temporal backbone to enable robust motion tracking under imperfect sensing. It achieves real-time latency and successful deployment on a Unitree G1 robot.
AI.motivation: Humanoid locomotion control policies must remain stable under imperfect sensing (e.g., missing or noisy observations) while exploiting temporal context to produce consistent motion. Existing approaches lack robustness to observation masking and do not fully leverage history to infer current state.
AI.method: A two-stage teacher-student framework: (1) a teacher policy is trained on clean observations; (2) a student is distilled under randomized continuous temporal masking of recent observations, forcing it to infer missing current information from history. The same masking interface is reused at inference for implicit closed-loop action refinement and optional multi-step action chunking. Mamba serves as the temporal backbone for efficient sequence modeling.
AI.result: Matched ablations show that masking/distillation provides substantial performance gains, with Mamba contributing additional tracking improvements at real-time latency. Experiments in IsaacLab, MuJoCo, and on a Unitree G1 demonstrate robust motion tracking under observation masking and successful real-world deployment.
AI.conclusion: RoboDreamer demonstrates that combining next-observation consistency with randomized continuous temporal masking enables humanoid policies that are robust to imperfect sensing while maintaining real-time performance, validated both in simulation and on a real humanoid robot.

title: LayerRoute: Action-Conditioned Mixture-of-Layers Routing for Vision-Language-Action Policies
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies leverage pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) to guide action generation for robot control. VLMs provide hierarchical visual-semantic representations that evolve across layers, from local visual geometry to abstract, language-aligned semantics; different manipulation tasks may therefore require different mixtures of layer representations. Meanwhile, the action module maintains intermediate representations that evolve throughout action computation and may provide useful information for subsequent decisions. However, existing VLA interfaces offer limited flexibility in representation access: VLM information is exposed through fixed layer assignments for each action layer, while intermediate action states are only propagated implicitly through residual streams without explicit reuse. We introduce LayerRoute, an action-conditioned representation routing interface that enables adaptive access to VLM layers and action representations. The Layer Mixture Router dynamically forms mixtures of cached VLM representations, while Action-State Reread reuses earlier action representations. Across diverse simulation and real-world benchmarks, LayerRoute consistently improves StarVLA-$π$ and $π_{0.5}$, achieving up to 7.2 gains on LIBERO Long with only 0.31% / 3.87% additional parameters. Ablation studies validate the benefit of action-conditioned layer routing, while routing analyses reveal structured allocation patterns across action layers and task settings.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces LayerRoute, an action-conditioned representation routing interface for VLA policies that enables adaptive access to VLM layers and action representations, improving manipulation performance.
AI.motivation: Existing VLA interfaces offer limited flexibility in representation access: VLM information is exposed through fixed layer assignments for each action layer, and intermediate action states are only propagated implicitly through residual streams without explicit reuse. Different manipulation tasks require different mixtures of layer representations (from local visual geometry to abstract semantics).
AI.method: LayerRoute consists of two components: (1) Layer Mixture Router that dynamically forms mixtures of cached VLM representations conditioned on the action state, and (2) Action-State Reread that explicitly reuses earlier action representations.
AI.result: LayerRoute consistently improves StarVLA-pi and pi_0.5 across diverse simulation and real-world benchmarks, achieving up to 7.2 gains on LIBERO Long with only 0.31%/3.87% additional parameters. Ablation studies validate the benefit of action-conditioned layer routing; routing analyses reveal structured allocation patterns.
AI.conclusion: LayerRoute provides a parameter-efficient, adaptive routing interface that improves VLA policy performance by enabling dynamic, action-conditioned access to both VLM layer representations and intermediate action states.

title: Eventually Optimal and Scalable Multi-Agent Planning for Block Cave Mining
summary: Automation in underground mining has the potential to significantly enhance safety, operational efficiency, and sustainability. However, effectively coordinating fleets of autonomous vehicles in dynamic mine environments introduces substantial challenges in both optimization and motion planning. To address these challenges, we introduce and formalize the \emph{Block Cave Mining (BCM)} problem, which focuses on computing a transport plan that maximizes ore throughput while satisfying draw ratio constraints. To solve this problem, we propose SAMM, an eventually optimal anytime solver that jointly integrates task assignment, scheduling, and path planning via a mixed-integer linear programming formulation. To improve scalability, we also introduce SAMMS, a variant of SAMM that trades optimality guarantees for efficiency by decomposing the problem into shorter planning subcycles. Experimental evaluations using realistic industrial mine scenarios demonstrate that SAMMS achieves near-optimal throughput and scales effectively to larger fleets and mine layouts.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces and formalizes the Block Cave Mining (BCM) problem for coordinating autonomous vehicle fleets in underground mines, and proposes two solvers: SAMM, an anytime optimal solver using mixed-integer linear programming for joint task assignment, scheduling, and path planning; and SAMMS, a scalable variant that decomposes planning into subcycles. Experiments show SAMMS achieves near-optimal throughput with improved scalability.
AI.motivation: Automation in underground mining promises improved safety, efficiency, and sustainability, but coordinating fleets of autonomous vehicles in dynamic mine environments poses significant challenges in both optimization and motion planning. There is a need for a formal problem framework and solver that can maximize ore throughput while respecting draw ratio constraints.
AI.method: The paper formalizes the Block Cave Mining (BCM) problem as computing a transport plan maximizing ore throughput under draw ratio constraints. It proposes SAMM, an eventually optimal anytime solver that jointly integrates task assignment, scheduling, and path planning via a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) formulation. A scalable variant, SAMMS, is introduced that trades optimality guarantees for efficiency by decomposing the problem into shorter planning subcycles.
AI.result: Experimental evaluations using realistic industrial mine scenarios show that SAMMS achieves near-optimal throughput while scaling effectively to larger fleets and more extensive mine layouts compared to the optimal SAMM solver.
AI.conclusion: The proposed SAMMS approach demonstrates that near-optimal performance can be maintained with substantially improved scalability, making it practical for real-world industrial underground mining applications involving autonomous vehicle fleets.

title: SAP: State-Guided Data Synthesis with Argument Provenance for Multi-Turn Tool Use
summary: High-quality multi-turn tool-use data is essential for training agentic models, yet existing data synthesis methods often underrepresent the argument-level dependencies that are critical to long-horizon tool use. As a result, even when a model selects the correct tool, task execution may still fail because the model fills tool arguments with fabricated, stale, or weakly grounded values. To address this problem, we propose \textbf{State-Guided Data Synthesis with Argument Provenance (SAP)}. SAP combines state guidance, tool-argument provenance constraints, and turn-level validation to efficiently construct tool-use trajectories with long-range dependencies and high accuracy. Using data generated by SAP, we build SAP-4B, which is highly competitive even when compared with much larger models across multiple benchmarks. Source code, synthesized data, and trained weights are available at https://github.com/Zichen1024/SAP.

AI.tldr: SAP is a State-Guided Data Synthesis method with Argument Provenance that generates high-quality multi-turn tool-use trajectories by enforcing state guidance, tool-argument provenance constraints, and turn-level validation, yielding a competitive 4B agentic model that rivals much larger models.
AI.motivation: Existing data synthesis methods for multi-turn tool-use data underrepresent argument-level dependencies critical to long-horizon tool use, causing models to fail at task execution even when selecting the correct tool due to fabricated, stale, or weakly grounded argument values.
AI.method: SAP combines three components: (1) state guidance to track execution context across turns, (2) tool-argument provenance constraints to ensure arguments are grounded in real state rather than hallucinated, and (3) turn-level validation to ensure trajectory accuracy. The synthesized data is used to train SAP-4B, a 4B-parameter model.
AI.result: SAP-4B, trained on SAP-generated data, is highly competitive across multiple benchmarks even when compared against much larger models.
AI.conclusion: State-guided synthesis with argument provenance constraints effectively addresses the argument-dependency gap in tool-use data generation, producing high-performing agentic models at a compact scale.

title: From LLM-Generated Specifications to Learned Quadruped Locomotion
summary: Quadruped robot locomotion policies are often trained using reinforcement learning, which in turn relies heavily on hand-crafted reward functions. Designing reward functions requires substantial manual engineering, and it is often unclear which local rewards will induce the desired global behavior. Shaped rewards from formal specifications in languages like Signal Temporal Logic (STL) can make rewards more interpretable, but writing STL specifications itself still requires domain expertise. We study whether large language models (LLMs) can fill this gap by generating Parametric Signal Temporal Logic (PSTL) specifications that are subsequently used for policy learning. Given a natural language locomotion objective and a constrained specification grammar, GPT-5.5 and Qwen 3.6 independently propose STL templates for command tracking, safety, and gait structure. We instantiate the parameters of the generated PSTL templates using expert trajectories and retain only specifications that are consistent with demonstrated expert behavior. The resulting specifications are then transformed into smooth, finite-history reward functions and used to train a quadruped locomotion policy with Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) in MuJoCo XLA (MJX). We evaluate both \emph{gait-aware} and \emph{gait-agnostic} settings. The former specifies walking-trot, trot, and bound regimes, while the latter allows contact patterns to emerge from the task objective. We compare against hand-engineered rewards, Text2Reward-style LLM-generated reward code, and an expert-switching oracle. Gait-aware Qwen 3.6 specifications achieved 100\% survival and command success across all tested speeds (0.3--2.1 m/s) and matched the target gait at high speeds, whereas Text2Reward achieved 0\% for both metrics at $\geq 1.9$ m/s. Videos: https://stl-locomotion.github.io/

AI.tldr: The paper investigates whether LLMs can generate Parametric Signal Temporal Logic (PSTL) specifications from natural language locomotion objectives, which are then used to create interpretable reward functions for training quadruped robot locomotion policies via PPO. Generated specifications are validated against expert trajectories, and the resulting policy outperforms hand-engineered rewards and Text2Reward baselines in gait-aware and gait-agnostic settings.
AI.motivation: Reinforcement learning for quadruped locomotion relies on hand-crafted reward functions, which require significant manual engineering and often have unclear mappings between local rewards and global behavior. While formal specifications like STL can make rewards more interpretable, writing them still requires domain expertise. The paper explores whether LLMs can bridge the gap by generating formal specifications automatically from natural language objectives.
AI.method: The approach uses LLMs (GPT-5.5 and Qwen 3.6) to independently propose STL templates covering command tracking, safety, and gait structure, given a natural language objective and a constrained specification grammar. Parameters of the PSTL templates are instantiated using expert trajectories, retaining only specifications consistent with expert demonstrations. These specifications are converted into smooth, finite-history reward functions and used to train policies with PPO in MuJoCo XLA (MJX), evaluated in both gait-aware (walking-trot, trot, bound) and gait-agnostic settings.
AI.result: Gait-aware Qwen 3.6 specifications achieved 100% survival and command success at all tested speeds (0.3-2.1 m/s) and matched the target gait at high speeds. In contrast, Text2Reward achieved 0% for both metrics at speeds >= 1.9 m/s, demonstrating the advantage of the STL-based reward approach.
AI.conclusion: LLM-generated PSTL specifications offer a viable, interpretable alternative to hand-crafted and LLM-code-based reward functions for quadruped locomotion, yielding superior robustness and gait fidelity, especially at higher speeds. The approach reduces domain expertise requirements while maintaining specification consistency with expert behavior.

title: CWF: A Collaborative Writing Framework for Personalized and Reliable Popular Science Writing
summary: We introduce Personalized and Reliable Popular Science Writing, a novel task that requires adapting scientific explanations to audiences with different cognitive levels while preserving factual accuracy. However, improving personalization often introduces simplifications that increase the risk of hallucination and factual distortion. To address these challenges, we first construct a dataset of 39,134 entries and a reader-centric Personalized Science Communication Benchmark (PSCB) that jointly evaluates audience adaptation and factual accuracy. To reduce data and computational requirements while improving generalization across domains and audiences, we introduce DA-MoE, which explicitly decouples audience adaptation from domain knowledge through separate modeling. To enable robust verification and revision in evidence-scarce scenarios, a multi-agent fact-checking mechanism that augments limited evidence with role-specific agent debate and propagates confidence over a graph is proposed. Experiments on PSCB show that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance. Our code is open-sourced at https://github.com/DPInnovationWorks/CWF.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Personalized and Reliable Popular Science Writing, a task that adapts scientific explanations to different audience cognitive levels while preserving accuracy. The authors construct a 39,134-entry dataset and a Personalized Science Communication Benchmark (PSCB), propose DA-MoE to decouple audience adaptation from domain knowledge, and develop a multi-agent fact-checking mechanism with confidence propagation for evidence-scarce scenarios. The approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on PSCB.
AI.motivation: Popular science writing must balance personalization (adapting to audiences with different cognitive levels) with factual reliability. Improving personalization risks introducing simplifications that lead to hallucinations and factual distortions. Prior approaches struggle to jointly optimize both dimensions.
AI.method: The paper proposes: (1) constructing a 39,134-entry dataset and a reader-centric benchmark (PSCB) evaluating both audience adaptation and factual accuracy; (2) DA-MoE, a Mixture-of-Experts model that decouples audience adaptation from domain knowledge via separate modeling to improve generalization while reducing data/computational needs; (3) a multi-agent fact-checking mechanism that augments limited evidence through role-specific agent debate and propagates confidence over a graph for verification and revision.
AI.result: Experiments on PSCB demonstrate state-of-the-art performance across audience adaptation and factual accuracy metrics.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a benchmark, dataset, and framework for jointly achieving personalization and reliability in popular science writing, with open-sourced code for reproducibility.

title: MAC-I$^2$: Learned Metrics-Aware Covariance for Robust Visual-Inertial Fusion in Initialization and Calibration
summary: Visual-Inertial (VI) fusion is fundamental to accurate and robust state estimation, where camera and IMU measurements are combined according to their respective uncertainties. Existing methods, however, fuse the two modalities with predefined uncertainties, regardless of how reliable each is in the local context, and thus often struggle under challenging environments involving illumination changes, dynamic objects, and textureless regions. In this paper, we present MAC-I$^2$, which achieves robust VI fusion through learned metric-aware covariance for both modalities, so that vision and IMU compete on their own merits rather than relying on predefined uncertainties. Here, metrics-aware means that each predicted covariance faithfully reflects the actual magnitude of the corresponding measurement noise. On the visual side, we propagate learned feature-matching uncertainties into pose covariances for the fusion. On the inertial side, motivated by the observation that integration error accumulates sharply at the early stage and grows slowly afterward, we design a learned IMU model with a learnable initial covariance, and propose a dedicated fine-tuning strategy on a held-out training subset to enable the metrics-aware covariance on unseen sequences. As a showcase, we build a VI initialization and calibration system, since accurate and robust initialization and calibration are the prerequisite for any reliable VI system. Experiments on EuRoC, and VBR show that MAC-I$^2$ substantially outperforms existing methods: it achieves a 99.9% initialization success rate on EuRoC, reducing gravity and velocity errors by about 60% and 42% over the strongest baseline, and maintains 80% success rate on challenging VBR sequences where baseline methods such as VINS-Mono drop below 10%.

AI.tldr: MAC-I² is a visual-inertial fusion framework that learns metric-aware covariances for both camera and IMU measurements, replacing predefined uncertainties with context-dependent ones, achieving significantly higher initialization success rates and lower estimation errors on challenging datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing VI fusion methods use predefined, fixed uncertainties for camera and IMU measurements regardless of local reliability, leading to poor performance in challenging environments such as illumination changes, dynamic objects, and textureless regions where the actual measurement quality varies unpredictably.
AI.method: MAC-I² learns metric-aware covariances for both modalities. For vision, learned feature-matching uncertainties are propagated into pose covariances. For IMU, a learned model with a learnable initial covariance captures the observation that integration error accumulates sharply early then grows slowly. A dedicated fine-tuning strategy on a held-out subset enables metric-aware covariance generalization to unseen sequences. The system is demonstrated on VI initialization and calibration.
AI.result: On EuRoC, MAC-I² achieves 99.9% initialization success rate with gravity and velocity errors reduced by ~60% and ~42% over the strongest baseline. On challenging VBR sequences, it maintains 80% success rate where VINS-Mono drops below 10%.
AI.conclusion: Learning metric-aware covariance for both vision and IMU modalities allows them to compete on their own merits, substantially improving robustness and accuracy of VI state estimation initialization and calibration across diverse and challenging environments.

title: Substrate-Portable Execution for Production LLM Workflows
summary: Production LLM agents execute tool-calling loops, retrieval chains, and compositional workflows in multiple modes, yet execution semantics are often coupled to one runtime. We encountered this portability problem in Rufus, a conversational AI assistant with a large tool catalog that serves millions of Amazon customers. Rufus supports real-time serving, asynchronous background tasks, and high-volume batch workloads such as evaluation and content pregeneration. Each mode has distinct service-level objectives and typically uses a separate runtime. Reusing streaming orchestration makes asynchronous and batch workloads blocking and prevents use of batch inference APIs, which offer a 50 percent discount at published prices. We present a binding-adaptive agent execution platform that separates workflow definition from execution substrate. Developers define a workflow once as a typed dataflow graph. The platform compiles the graph to in-process streaming for real-time serving, durable AWS SWF orchestration for asynchronous execution, or distributed Apache Flink stream processing for batch inference. No workflow code changes are required. LLM inference is represented as a suspendable graph node whose behavior depends on the substrate: streaming delivery online, durable retry asynchronously, and batched submission offline. We validated dozens of production agent configurations across five orchestration patterns: single-inference RAG, iterative ReAct, compositional PreAct, conditional routing, and multi-agent deep research. Across all three bindings, we found no detectable difference in output quality. Batch execution reduced per-query inference cost in line with published batch API pricing while operating alongside the streaming path at production scale.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a binding-adaptive agent execution platform that decouples workflow definitions from execution substrates, allowing production LLM agents to run across real-time streaming, asynchronous durable orchestration, and distributed batch processing runtimes without code changes. Validated on the Rufus conversational AI assistant serving millions of Amazon customers.
AI.motivation: Production LLM agents need to execute across multiple modes (real-time serving, asynchronous tasks, batch workloads), each with distinct service-level objectives, yet execution semantics are typically coupled to a single runtime. This portability problem forces mode-specific code and prevents leveraging cost-efficient batch inference APIs.
AI.method: Developers define a workflow once as a typed dataflow graph. The platform compiles this graph to three execution substrates: in-process streaming for real-time serving, durable AWS SWF orchestration for asynchronous execution, and distributed Apache Flink stream processing for batch inference. LLM inference is modeled as a suspendable graph node whose behavior adapts per substrate (streaming delivery, durable retry, batched submission). No workflow code changes are required across bindings.
AI.result: Validated dozens of production agent configurations across five orchestration patterns: single-inference RAG, iterative ReAct, compositional PreAct, conditional routing, and multi-agent deep research. Across all three execution bindings, no detectable difference in output quality was observed. Batch execution reduced per-query inference cost in line with published batch API pricing (50% discount), while operating alongside the streaming path at production scale.
AI.conclusion: Workflow definition can be cleanly separated from execution substrate in production LLM agent systems. Binding-adaptive compilation enables mode-appropriate execution without portability overhead or quality degradation, and unlocks significant cost savings via batch inference APIs.

title: Beyond Task Success: Stage-Wise Reliability of World Model Planning under Sensing Degradation
summary: In world model planning, sensing inputs pass through an encoder and predictor before affecting planner decisions, so final task success alone cannot reveal where sensing disturbances attenuate or persist in the pipeline. We apply 10 visual and temporal sensing degradations to a world model planner and track their effects across representation, future prediction, planner preference, and physical outcome using paired evaluation on the same 50 tasks. The relative impact of degradations was not preserved across stages: large representation shifts could attenuate downstream, while smaller initial shifts could persist to the outcome, and internal-response ordering did not directly match physical-outcome ordering. Temporal degradations also showed distinct patterns: even with similar overall changes in observation history, responses differed substantially with the location of corrupted information and the planner's actual exposure. This non-uniform stage-wise response was also observed in secondary evaluations with another manipulation task and a different world model. Stage-wise diagnosis can therefore identify where sensing disturbances attenuate or persist and help prioritize subsequent model verification and sensing mitigation.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically applies 10 visual and temporal sensing degradations to a world model planner and tracks their effects across four stages: representation, future prediction, planner preference, and physical outcome, revealing that degradation impact is not preserved across pipeline stages.
AI.motivation: In world model planning, sensing inputs pass through an encoder and predictor before reaching the planner, so final task success alone cannot reveal where sensing disturbances attenuate or persist in the pipeline. A stage-wise diagnosis is needed to understand degradation propagation.
AI.method: Applied 10 visual and temporal sensing degradations to a world model planner and tracked their effects across representation, future prediction, planner preference, and physical outcome using paired evaluation on the same 50 tasks. Secondary evaluations were also conducted with a manipulation task and a different world model.
AI.result: The relative impact of degradations was not preserved across stages: large representation shifts could attenuate downstream, while smaller initial shifts could persist to the outcome, and internal-response ordering did not match physical-outcome ordering. Temporal degradations showed distinct patterns based on the location of corrupted information and the planner's actual exposure.
AI.conclusion: Stage-wise diagnosis can identify where sensing disturbances attenuate or persist in the world model planning pipeline and help prioritize subsequent model verification and sensing mitigation efforts.

title: IIns-VAE+: A Robust Transfer Learning Framework for Environmental Identification in Wireless Sensing
summary: Environmental identification in wireless sensing is essential for 6G integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) systems to achieve reliable situational awareness. However, deep learning (DL) models for this task often fail to generalize under domain shift across diverse environments. While the Inter-Instance Variational Auto-encoder (IIns-VAE) learns features of rich representation, its neural classifier remains vulnerable to these distribution changes. In this paper, we propose IIns-VAE+, a hybrid model that combines the IIns-VAE framework with Minimax Risk Classifiers (MRC) to improve adaptability in transfer learning scenarios. We use real-world datasets to evaluate our framework across three transfer learning scenarios, including general to specific room environments, high to low label resolutions, and mixed to specific environments. The experimental results indicate that IIns-VAE+ significantly outperforms baselines, demonstrating its critical value in building adaptable and robust perceptive networks in future 6G systems.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes IIns-VAE+, a hybrid model combining Inter-Instance Variational Auto-encoder (IIns-VAE) with Minimax Risk Classifiers (MRC) to improve domain-shift generalization for environmental identification in 6G ISAC wireless sensing systems. Evaluated on real-world datasets across three transfer learning scenarios, it significantly outperforms baselines in adaptability and robustness.
AI.motivation: Deep learning models for environmental identification in wireless sensing fail to generalize under domain shift across diverse environments. While IIns-VAE learns rich feature representations, its neural classifier remains vulnerable to distribution changes, limiting reliability for 6G ISAC systems.
AI.method: IIns-VAE+ hybridizes the IIns-VAE feature extraction framework with Minimax Risk Classifiers (MRC) to enhance robustness and adaptability in transfer learning scenarios. The model is evaluated on real-world datasets across three transfer scenarios: general-to-specific room environments, high-to-low label resolutions, and mixed-to-specific environments.
AI.result: Experimental results demonstrate that IIns-VAE+ significantly outperforms baseline methods across all three transfer learning scenarios, confirming its effectiveness for building adaptable and robust perceptive networks in future 6G systems.
AI.conclusion: IIns-VAE+ proves to be a critical approach for improving domain adaptation and reliability in environmental identification for 6G ISAC systems, offering a viable path toward transfer learning robustness under distribution shift.

title: EquiGQNet: Fast Grasp Quality Evaluation via Shared Equivariant Point Cloud Encoding
comment: 8 pages, 6 figures, 4 tables. Submitted to IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RA-L)
summary: Planning six-degree-of-freedom (6-DoF) grasps for unseen objects in cluttered tabletop scenes from a single-view depth image requires accurate and efficient evaluation of diverse grasp candidates. Existing early-fusion methods capture local object geometry relative to each grasp candidate but repeatedly encode the scene, whereas late-fusion methods reuse a shared scene representation but may lose this grasp-relative local geometry. We propose EquiGQNet, an efficient 6-DoF grasp quality evaluator that combines the strengths of both approaches. For grasp orientation, EquiGQNet replaces the early-fusion operation of rotating and re-encoding the point cloud for each grasp candidate with an SO(3)-equivariant encode-once-then-rotate scheme, yielding grasp-aligned geometric features from a shared scene encoding. For grasp translation, Mid-level Action Fusion (MAF) injects the grasp position into intermediate features before global aggregation, retaining local geometry relative to each candidate. We evaluate EquiGQNet in two grasp planning pipelines: Cross-Entropy Method (CEM)-based continuous grasp search and candidate ranking with a pretrained generative planner. In simulation, EquiGQNet achieves grasping performance comparable to the early-fusion baseline and substantially outperforms late fusion on objects with complex geometry and limited graspable regions, while reducing CEM planning time from 3.31s to 0.48s, a 6.9x speedup over early fusion. In real-world household-object decluttering, EquiGQNet achieves a 95.2% grasp success rate and 230 picks per hour, versus 153 and 170 for early- and late-fusion baselines. Code is available at https://equigqnet.github.io/.

AI.tldr: EquiGQNet is an efficient 6-DoF grasp quality evaluator that combines early-fusion and late-fusion strengths via SO(3)-equivariant encode-once-then-rotate for grasp orientation and Mid-level Action Fusion (MAF) for grasp translation, achieving performance comparable to early-fusion baselines with a 6.9x speedup in planning and high real-world grasp success.
AI.motivation: Existing grasp quality evaluators face a trade-off: early-fusion methods capture grasp-relative local geometry but repeatedly re-encode the scene for each candidate (computationally wasteful), while late-fusion methods reuse scene representations but lose grasp-relative local geometric detail. The paper aims to combine both strengths efficiently.
AI.method: EquiGQNet uses an SO(3)-equivariant encode-once-then-rotate scheme for grasp orientation, replacing the early-fusion rotate-and-re-encode operation to derive grasp-aligned geometric features from a shared scene encoding. For grasp translation, Mid-level Action Fusion (MAF) injects grasp position into intermediate features before global aggregation, preserving local geometry relative to each grasp candidate.
AI.result: In simulation, EquiGQNet matches early-fusion grasping performance and significantly outperforms late-fusion on complex-geometry objects, while cutting CEM planning time from 3.31s to 0.48s (6.9x speedup). In real-world household decluttering, it achieves 95.2% grasp success rate and 230 picks/hour versus 153 and 170 for early- and late-fusion baselines.
AI.conclusion: EquiGQNet demonstrates that it is possible to retain grasp-relative local geometry without per-candidate scene re-encoding, delivering both high grasp accuracy and significant computational efficiency for 6-DoF grasp planning from single-view depth images.

title: MVFA: A Multi-View Text-Guided Multimodal Fusion LLM Adapter for Sentiment Analysis and Emotion Recognition
summary: Multimodal sentiment analysis and emotion recognition in conversations demand effective modeling of heterogeneous interactions across textual, acoustic, and visual modalities. Although large language models (LLMs) offer powerful language understanding, adapting them to multimodal affective computing remains challenging: full-model fine-tuning is computationally prohibitive, while many existing lightweight adapters fail to preserve rich textual cues during cross-modal fusion. To address these limitations, we propose the multi-view text-guided multimodal fusion adapter (MVFA), a parameter-efficient framework that augments frozen LLMs with strong multimodal reasoning capability. MVFA first constructs complementary text views via max pooling, mean pooling, and attention pooling; these views then guide cross-modal interactions with audio and visual features. The fused multimodal representations are subsequently compressed into a compact set of learnable pseudo-tokens through an Enhanced Q-Former Fusion Module. Using ChatGLM3-6B-base as the primary backbone, we further validate MVFA on LLaMA2-7B and Qwen3-8B to examine its portability across multiple frozen LLM backbones. MVFA is evaluated on three challenging datasets: CH-SIMS V2.0, MELD, and CHERMA. Experimental results demonstrate that MVFA achieves state-of-the-art performance on key metrics while updating only a small fraction of parameters. Specifically, it attains 84.62\% Acc2 and 84.59\% F1 on CH-SIMS V2.0, 67.36\% Acc and 66.03\% WF1 on MELD, and 74.66\% Acc on CHERMA. These findings establish multi-view text-guided fusion as an effective and scalable paradigm for parameter-efficient multimodal LLM adaptation in affective computing. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/Overwhelm1208/MVFA.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes MVFA (multi-view text-guided multimodal fusion adapter), a parameter-efficient framework that augments frozen large language models for multimodal sentiment analysis and emotion recognition. It constructs complementary text views via different pooling strategies to guide cross-modal fusion with audio and visual features, then compresses representations into learnable pseudo-tokens via an Enhanced Q-Former Fusion Module. Evaluated on CH-SIMS V2.0, MELD, and CHERMA datasets, MVFA achieves state-of-the-art results while updating only a small fraction of parameters across multiple frozen LLM backbones.
AI.motivation: Adapting large language models to multimodal affective computing faces two key challenges: full-model fine-tuning is computationally prohibitive, and existing lightweight adapters fail to preserve rich textual cues during cross-modal fusion. The authors aim to bridge this gap with a parameter-efficient approach that maintains strong multimodal reasoning while keeping most of the LLM frozen.
AI.method: MVFA first creates complementary text views using max pooling, mean pooling, and attention pooling. These views guide cross-modal interactions with audio and visual features. The fused multimodal representations are then compressed into a compact set of learnable pseudo-tokens via an Enhanced Q-Former Fusion Module. The framework is validated on ChatGLM3-6B-base as the primary backbone, with additional portability tests on LLaMA2-7B and Qwen3-8B.
AI.result: MVFA achieves state-of-the-art results on three challenging datasets while updating only a small fraction of parameters: 84.62% Acc2 and 84.59% F1 on CH-SIMS V2.0, 67.36% Acc and 66.03% WF1 on MELD, and 74.66% Acc on CHERMA. The method demonstrates portability across ChatGLM3-6B-base, LLaMA2-7B, and Qwen3-8B backbones.
AI.conclusion: Multi-view text-guided fusion is established as an effective and scalable paradigm for parameter-efficient multimodal LLM adaptation in affective computing. The code is made publicly available for reproducibility and further research.

title: State-of-the-Art in Learning-by-Demonstration with Passive Observation for Industrial Assembly Automation
summary: Learning-by-Demonstration (LbD) enables intuitive robot programming by capturing expert skills, which is crucial for agility in high-mix, low- volume manufacturing. This systematic literature review analyzes passive LbD for industrial assembly processes, focusing on the perception architecture and the generalization of the perceived demonstration. We specifically investigate one-shot approaches where only a single demonstration is required. The review evaluates how systems adapt to new assemblies using this limited data. We identify a shift towards object-centric perception, allowing learned primitives to be transferred to new product variants with minimal training.

AI.tldr: A systematic literature review of passive one-shot Learning-by-Demonstration for industrial assembly, analyzing perception architectures and generalization capabilities from single demonstrations.
AI.motivation: LbD enables intuitive robot programming for high-mix, low-volume manufacturing, but there is a need to systematically understand how passive LbD systems perceive demonstrations and generalize from limited (single-demonstration) data across new product variants.
AI.method: A systematic literature review approach focused on passive LbD for industrial assembly, specifically examining one-shot learning scenarios, perception architectures, and how systems generalize demonstrated skills to new assemblies.
AI.result: The review identifies a paradigm shift toward object-centric perception that enables learned primitives to transfer to new product variants with minimal retraining.
AI.conclusion: Object-centric perception is emerging as the key enabler for generalizable one-shot LbD in industrial assembly, allowing skills learned from single demonstrations to be adapted to novel assemblies efficiently.

title: Customer Relationship Intelligence: Integrating CRM and MDM for Enhanced Customer Engagement
comment: Preprint submitted to 16th IEEE ICCCNT 2025. 8 pages, 12 tables
summary: This study examines how Customer Relationship Management (CRM), Master Data Management (MDM), and Customer Knowledge Management (CKM) jointly constitute a Customer Relationship Intelligence (CRI) framework for enhanced Customer Engagement (CE). A cross-sectional survey of 100 participants across retail, healthcare, IT, and telecommunications sectors was analysed using Spearman rho correlation and ordinal logistic regression (IBM SPSS). Bivariate correlations were weak and non-significant (r<0.19, p>0.06). Regression identified CRM (beta=0.717, p=0.002) and CKM (beta=0.581, p=0.009) as significant positive predictors of CE; MDM showed a positive but non-significant direct effect (beta=0.346, p=0.071). The model explained 20.5% of CE variance (Nagelkerke R^2=0.205). Parallel mediation analysis (Hayes PROCESS Model 4, 5,000 bootstrap samples) found no significant indirect effects of MDM on CE via CRM (IE=0.021, 95% BC CI [-0.072, 0.121]) or CKM (IE=0.032, 95% BC CI [-0.061, 0.126]); Hypothesis H4 was not supported. CRM and CKM emerge as the principal drivers of CE within the CRI framework, while MDM functions as a foundational data quality enabler whose strategic value is realised through its enabling effect on CRM execution and knowledge management. Findings should be treated as exploratory given the sample size and cross-sectional design. Future research should replicate with larger sector-specific samples and longitudinal designs, particularly in regulated BFSI contexts where MDM architecture is shaped by data governance mandates.

AI.tldr: This study investigates how CRM, Master Data Management (MDM), and Customer Knowledge Management (CKM) jointly form a Customer Relationship Intelligence (CRI) framework to enhance Customer Engagement (CE). Analysis of 100 cross-sector survey responses shows CRM and CKM are significant direct predictors of CE, while MDM has a non-significant direct effect and no significant mediating pathway. MDM is positioned as a foundational data-quality enabler rather than a direct driver of engagement.
AI.motivation: To understand how CRM, MDM, and CKM integrate into a unified Customer Relationship Intelligence framework and to identify which components most directly drive Customer Engagement across diverse industry sectors.
AI.method: Cross-sectional survey of 100 participants from retail, healthcare, IT, and telecommunications. Analyses included Spearman rho correlations, ordinal logistic regression (IBM SPSS), and parallel mediation analysis using Hayes PROCESS Model 4 with 5,000 bootstrap samples.
AI.result: CRM (beta=0.717, p=0.002) and CKM (beta=0.581, p=0.009) significantly predicted CE. MDM's direct effect was positive but not significant (beta=0.346, p=0.071). Model explained 20.5% of CE variance (Nagelkerke R²=0.205). No significant indirect effects of MDM via CRM or CKM; mediation hypothesis (H4) unsupported. Bivariate correlations were weak and non-significant.
AI.conclusion: CRM and CKM are the principal drivers of Customer Engagement within the CRI framework. MDM acts as a foundational data-quality enabler whose value is realized through facilitating CRM execution and knowledge management. Findings are exploratory due to sample size and cross-sectional design; replication with larger sector-specific samples and longitudinal designs is recommended, particularly in regulated BFSI contexts.

title: Phase-and-First-Arrival VLM Feedback for Sparse-Reward Reinforcement Learning in Surgical Manipulation
comment: 8 pages, 8 figures. Submitted to IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RA-L). Project page: https://surgphase.verloge.space
summary: Sparse outcome feedback limits what robots can learn from unsuccessful attempts at complex manipulation. Failed multi-stage surgical attempts can contain grasps, lifts, or transfers worth reusing. In sparse-reward reinforcement learning, terminal rewards collapse such attempts to the same outcome, while scalar vision-language model (VLM) ratings reveal neither what progress merits credit nor when it occurred. We introduce phase-and-first-arrival feedback: one VLM query per recorded episode identifies the furthest visually verified task phase and when that phase is first reached, allowing the learner to reuse partial behavior and localize credit. We instantiate it in SurgPhaseBench, a phase-structured suite spanning rigid and deformable tasks, and evaluate it in simulation and hardware. Across five simulated tasks, our method reaches 75.2% mean success, compared with 52.1% for a reward based on Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP) using the same visual input; the advantage persists when only the feedback representation changes. On hardware, the same record supports autonomous block picking and slip recovery. Together, these results show that trajectory-level visual supervision can preserve partial progress while providing the temporal credit needed for sparse-reward control.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces phase-and-first-arrival feedback for sparse-reward robot learning, where a single VLM query per episode identifies the furthest visually verified task phase and when it was first reached, enabling credit assignment and partial behavior reuse. Evaluated on SurgPhaseBench (five simulated + hardware tasks), it achieves 75.2% mean success versus 52.1% for CLIP-based reward.
AI.motivation: Sparse outcome feedback limits learning in multi-stage manipulation because terminal-only rewards collapse all failed attempts to the same outcome, and scalar VLM ratings fail to convey what progress deserves credit or when it occurred. This is especially problematic for surgical tasks where partial grasps, lifts, or transfers in failed attempts are worth reusing.
AI.method: The paper proposes phase-and-first-arrival feedback: one VLM query per recorded episode determines (1) the furthest visually verified task phase achieved and (2) the timestep at which that phase was first reached. This trajectory-level supervision allows the learner to reuse partial behavior and localize temporal credit. The method is instantiated in SurgPhaseBench, a phase-structured benchmark suite covering rigid and deformable manipulation tasks.
AI.result: Across five simulated tasks, the method achieves 75.2% mean success versus 52.1% for a CLIP-based reward using the same visual input. The advantage persists when only the feedback representation is changed. On hardware, the same approach supports autonomous block picking and slip recovery.
AI.conclusion: Trajectory-level visual supervision can preserve partial progress information while supplying the temporal credit signal required for sparse-reward control, demonstrating that richer feedback representations extracted from VLM queries can significantly improve multi-stage manipulation learning.

title: SCIRIGOR:Evaluating Open-Ended Scientific Analysis Beyond Final Scores
summary:
Scientific coding agents produce interdependent code, results, figures, and claims, yet evaluating final
  outputs alone does not establish whether their conclusions are scientifically supported. We formulate
  evidence-grounded multimodal scientific analysis, requiring agents to produce executable analyses and claims
  supported by results and visualizations from the same run. We introduce SciRIGOR, an evaluation framework and
  benchmark comprising 100 cases from scientific articles across six domains and 17 subfields. The framework
  reconstructs typed evidence graphs, separates artifact fidelity from relational validity, and scores complete
  claim-support paths while localizing the earliest unsupported relation. Source-grounded alternative paths
  accommodate scientifically equivalent analyses and visualizations. We evaluate 11 agent/model configurations.
  On full-benchmark runs, claims agree with faithful and unfaithful results at nearly identical rates (91.8%
  versus 91.0%). Yet no system exceeds 62.6% on the soft evidence-chain score or 18.0% strict whole-chain
  success. These findings show that internal coherence does not establish scientific correctness: evaluation
  must verify support along the complete data-to-claim path.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SciRIGOR, an evaluation framework and benchmark with 100 scientific cases across six domains for assessing evidence-grounded multimodal scientific analysis by coding agents. It finds that while claims agree with faithful and unfaithful results at nearly identical rates (~91%), no system exceeds 62.6% on soft evidence-chain scoring or 18.0% strict whole-chain success, demonstrating internal coherence does not establish scientific correctness.
AI.motivation: Scientific coding agents generate interdependent code, results, figures, and claims, but evaluating only final outputs fails to determine whether their conclusions are scientifically supported by the evidence they produce.
AI.method: The framework reconstructs typed evidence graphs, separates artifact fidelity from relational validity, and scores complete claim-support paths while localizing the earliest unsupported relation. Source-grounded alternative paths accommodate scientifically equivalent analyses and visualizations. The benchmark comprises 100 cases from scientific articles across six domains and 17 subfields. Eleven agent/model configurations were evaluated.
AI.result: Claims agree with faithful and unfaithful results at nearly identical rates (91.8% versus 91.0%). No system exceeds 62.6% on the soft evidence-chain score or 18.0% strict whole-chain success, showing that internal coherence alone does not indicate scientific validity.
AI.conclusion: Evaluation of scientific coding agents must verify support along the complete data-to-claim path rather than relying on internal coherence, as current agent systems can produce internally consistent yet scientifically unsupported conclusions.

title: Generalizable 6D Pose Estimation of Textureless Objects with Planar-based Gaussian Splatting
comment: 7 pages, 5 figures. Accepted by the IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS 2026)
summary: Estimating the 6D pose of textureless objects without prior CAD models remains a critical challenge due to the lack of appearance features. While recent generalizable approaches alleviate the dependence on object-specific models, their performance on low-texture objects is often limited by insufficient geometric constraints in the underlying representations. In this work, we propose PG-Pose, a geometry-aware framework combining Planar-based Gaussian Splatting (PGS) reconstruction and Geometry-driven pose optimization. In the offline representation extraction stage, three distinct representations of the object are extracted from multi-view reference RGB images with known poses. PG-Pose reconstructs a 3D Gaussian representation and renders high-fidelity depth maps to generate 3D point clouds through back projection. In the online pose inference stage, the initial pose of the input image is estimated by 2D-3D correspondence matching between the input image and the reconstructed 3D point clouds, followed by a PGS-Refiner for iterative pose optimization. Evaluations on the OnePose-LowTexture datasets, PG-Pose achieves an average accuracy of 94.2% ADD(S)@0.1d, with a 2.1% improvement average accuracy compared with the state-of-the-art (SOTA) GS-based approach. To further demonstrate the effectiveness of PG-Pose for industrial robots in grasping tasks, we deploy it on a dual-arm industrial robot and successfully realize the grasping task on an unseen object.

AI.tldr: PG-Pose is a geometry-aware framework for estimating the 6D pose of textureless objects without CAD models, combining Planar-based Gaussian Splatting reconstruction and geometry-driven pose optimization. It achieves 94.2% ADD(S)@0.1d accuracy on the OnePose-LowTexture dataset, outperforming the SOTA GS-based method by 2.1%, and is validated on an industrial dual-arm robot for real-world grasping.
AI.motivation: Estimating the 6D pose of textureless objects without prior CAD models is challenging due to the lack of appearance features. Existing generalizable approaches perform poorly on low-texture objects because their underlying representations lack sufficient geometric constraints.
AI.method: PG-Pose uses a two-stage pipeline: (1) Offline reconstruction extracts three representations from multi-view RGB images, reconstructing a 3D Gaussian representation and rendering high-fidelity depth maps to generate 3D point clouds via back projection. (2) Online inference estimates the initial pose via 2D-3D correspondence matching between the input image and reconstructed point clouds, followed by a PGS-Refiner for iterative pose optimization.
AI.result: On the OnePose-LowTexture dataset, PG-Pose achieves an average accuracy of 94.2% ADD(S)@0.1d, a 2.1% improvement over the SOTA GS-based approach. It also successfully performs grasping tasks on unseen objects when deployed on a dual-arm industrial robot.
AI.conclusion: The Planar-based Gaussian Splatting representation with geometry-driven optimization effectively addresses the geometric constraint deficiency in textureless object pose estimation, and the framework generalizes to real-world industrial robotic grasping scenarios.

title: Predicting Wind Turbine Power Using Machine Learning and Weather Forecasts
summary: Offshore wind turbines are widely used to generate renewable energy, but their maintenance can result in decreased efficiency due to forced shutdowns. Accurate wind turbine power predictions can identify periods of low power that would be ideal for scheduling maintenance. However, the effects of data volume, feature selection, and data preprocessing on the performance of such power prediction models have not been thoroughly studied. Besides, current models have limited transferability between different wind turbines. Therefore, this study developed a baseline Linear Regression for performance comparison with a more complex Artificial Neural Network model to predict the power output of a wind turbine, using weather conditions only to enhance applicability. A range of data preprocessing techniques were studied, and models were trained on one month and one year of data to determine the effects of data preprocessing and volume on model performance. Feature selection was explored using a Random Forest Regressor. The best results from the different models showed that the Artificial Neural Network models provided the highest accuracy, with an R2 score of 0.98 and a low Mean Absolute Error of 194, when compared with the baseline model (R2 score of 0.94 and Mean Absolute Error of 441). The model performance is comparable to the range of results in past studies, with the advantage that the proposed method leverages a separate weather dataset from a nearby weather station, enabling future applications for similar wind turbines in different locations. The Artificial Neural Network model was then used to identify 4-h periods of low power predictions over 2 months (simulating application for future periods), providing power output savings of approximately 2000 kW for each maintenance event.

AI.tldr: This study compares a baseline Linear Regression model with an Artificial Neural Network (ANN) for predicting offshore wind turbine power output using only weather data, achieving an R2 of 0.98 and MAE of 194 with the ANN. The model enables scheduling maintenance during predicted low-power periods, saving approximately 2000 kW per event.
AI.motivation: Offshore wind turbine maintenance causes forced shutdowns that reduce efficiency. Accurate power predictions could identify optimal low-power periods for maintenance scheduling, but previous work has under-explored the effects of data volume, feature selection, and preprocessing on prediction model performance, and existing models have limited transferability between turbines.
AI.method: A baseline Linear Regression model was compared with an Artificial Neural Network for predicting wind turbine power output using weather conditions only. Various data preprocessing techniques were tested, models were trained on one-month and one-year datasets to assess the effect of data volume and preprocessing, and feature selection was performed using a Random Forest Regressor.
AI.result: The ANN achieved the highest accuracy with an R2 score of 0.98 and a Mean Absolute Error of 194, outperforming the baseline Linear Regression (R2 of 0.94, MAE of 441). The model identified 4-hour low-power prediction periods over 2 months, providing approximately 2000 kW power output savings per maintenance event.
AI.conclusion: The proposed ANN approach performs comparably to prior studies while offering enhanced transferability by leveraging a separate weather dataset from a nearby station, making it applicable to similar wind turbines at different locations for maintenance scheduling.

title: Singularity-Free Guiding Vector Fields on SO(3) with Designer-Specified Progression Behavior
summary: This paper develops a singularity-free guiding vector field (SF-GVF) for path following on the special orthogonal group SO(3). First, we lift the Euclidean SF-GVF construction to SO(3), integrating the augmented-state approach with the intrinsic Lie-group geometry and obtaining a closed-form geometric guidance law whose integral curves converge to a designer-specified attitude path. The field is defined on a dense open subset of SO(3), excluding only the measure-zero antipodal set - a manifestation of the topological obstruction to continuous global stabilization on SO(3). The construction requires no per-step optimization and produces a control input intrinsically in so(3) as body angular rates. Second, we formalize the progression behavior along the path as a designer-supplied function ν(ξ), promoting the parametric speed from an implicitly resolved degree of freedom to a first-class design specification. In contrast to the Euclidean condition v = 0, which excludes vehicles with minimum-speed constraints, the corresponding condition ω= 0 on SO(3) is physically admissible for most platforms with active attitude control, making the progression behavior a design freedom structurally available on SO(3) but absent in the Euclidean setting. The framework's structural results are established under a bi-invariant Riemannian metric and hold uniformly across choices of path, progression, and Lyapunov gain. The framework is illustrated in simulation on self-intersecting paths under both constant and point-convergence progression behaviors.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a singularity-free guiding vector field (SF-GVF) for path following on the special orthogonal group SO(3), integrating an augmented-state approach with Lie-group intrinsic geometry to achieve closed-form attitude guidance laws. The framework formalizes parametric speed along the path as a designer-specified progression function, eliminating the need for per-step optimization and providing structural convergence results under bi-invariant Riemannian metrics.
AI.motivation: To address the challenge of attitude path following on SO(3), which involves inherent topological obstructions to continuous global stabilization, and to overcome limitations of Euclidean path-following frameworks (e.g., minimum-speed constraints) by exploiting the unique geometric structure of SO(3).
AI.method: The method lifts the Euclidean SF-GVF construction to SO(3) by merging an augmented-state approach with intrinsic Lie-group geometry, yielding a closed-form geometric guidance law. The field is defined on a dense open subset of SO(3) excluding a measure-zero antipodal set. Parametric progression is formalized as a designer-supplied function ν(ξ), and structural results are proven under a bi-invariant Riemannian metric, with control inputs generated intrinsically in so(3).
AI.result: The framework produces integral curves that converge to designer-specified attitude paths without requiring per-step optimization. Simulations demonstrate effectiveness on self-intersecting paths under both constant and point-convergence progression behaviors.
AI.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that progression behavior is a design freedom structurally available on SO(3) (absent in the Euclidean setting, where ω=0 is physically admissible), and the constructed SF-GVF converges uniformly across varying path choices, progression functions, and Lyapunov gains.

title: AutoKD: Autonomous Knowledge Discovery
summary: Scientific discovery in data-rich domains is currently constrained by human bandwidth: the growth in the volume and complexity of real-world data far outpaces the rate at which researchers can read, reason, and synthesize. Recent LLM-based multi-agent systems have begun to automate portions of the research cycle, but they target hypothesis generation in settings where validation cannot itself be automated, and each run is one-shot, with no mechanism for findings to accumulate or steer subsequent inquiry. This paper introduces AutoKD, a multi-agent framework for autonomous knowledge discovery that is both computational and cumulative, allowing validated findings to persist and inform subsequent inquiry. Six coordinated LLM agents collaborate in an open-ended discovery loop, where accepted findings are stored in a persistent insight graph that serves as both long-term memory and an exploration-steering mechanism. We evaluate AutoKD on three diverse datasets from two perspectives: Open-ended Quality against published findings, and Conditioned Quality via literature-derived queries.
