Across both evaluation perspectives, AutoKD covers known findings and surfaces substantive discoveries that complement human-driven research. Our code is available at https://github.com/GeQinwen/AutoKD.

AI.tldr: AutoKD is a multi-agent LLM framework for autonomous, computational, and cumulative knowledge discovery. Six coordinated LLM agents operate in an open-ended discovery loop, with validated findings stored in a persistent insight graph that serves as long-term memory and exploration steering. Evaluated on three datasets from open-ended quality and conditioned quality perspectives, it covers known findings and complements human-driven research.
AI.motivation: Scientific discovery is bottlenecked by human bandwidth; data growth outpaces researchers' ability to read, reason, and synthesize. Existing LLM-based multi-agent systems automate parts of the research cycle but are one-shot, cannot automate validation, and lack mechanisms for findings to accumulate and guide subsequent inquiry.
AI.method: AutoKD employs six coordinated LLM agents in an open-ended discovery loop. Accepted/validated findings are stored in a persistent insight graph that functions both as long-term memory and as a mechanism to steer future exploration, enabling cumulative knowledge discovery.
AI.result: Evaluated on three diverse datasets via two perspectives—Open-ended Quality against published findings and Conditioned Quality via literature-derived queries—AutoKD covers known findings and surfaces substantive discoveries that complement human-driven research.
AI.conclusion: AutoKD demonstrates that autonomous, cumulative knowledge discovery is feasible, addressing the human-bandwidth bottleneck in data-rich domains by allowing validated findings to persist and inform subsequent inquiry, thereby complementing rather than replacing human-driven research.

title: LightSplat: Real-Time High-Fidelity 3D Gaussian SLAM with Loop Closure
comment: Accepted to 2026 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS)
summary: SLAM systems based on 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) have recently demonstrated promising reconstruction accuracy for dense 3D scene representations. However, current 3DGS systems struggle to meet the strict demands of real-world deployments due to severe limitations in operational performance and map adaptability. To this end, we propose LightSplat, a hybrid-representation RGB-D SLAM framework. It synergizes local sparse features for robust and fast tracking with a dual-thread backend that progressively constructs dense Gaussian submaps. Crucially, we enable online loop closure through feature-accelerated 3DGS registration, refining overall map consistency through pose graph optimization. Ultimately, LightSplat achieves the online reconstruction of high-fidelity Gaussian map. Extensive experiments on multiple datasets and real-world robotic platform demonstrate that our method achieves near state-of-the-art reconstruction quality and the capability to accommodate practical camera motions, maintaining an average framerate of 8 FPS. Overall, LightSplat provides an efficient and robust foundation for deploying high-fidelity 3DGS in real-world environments.

AI.tldr: LightSplat is a hybrid-representation RGB-D SLAM framework that combines local sparse features for fast tracking with a dual-thread backend for dense Gaussian submap construction, enabling online loop closure via feature-accelerated 3DGS registration and pose graph optimization to achieve high-fidelity real-time Gaussian map reconstruction at ~8 FPS.
AI.motivation: Current 3D Gaussian Splatting-based SLAM systems achieve promising dense reconstruction accuracy but fail to meet real-world deployment requirements due to severe limitations in operational performance (speed/efficiency) and map adaptability (handling practical camera motions and loop closures).
AI.method: LightSplat introduces a hybrid-representation framework that uses local sparse features for robust and fast tracking, paired with a dual-thread backend that progressively constructs dense Gaussian submaps. Online loop closure is enabled through feature-accelerated 3DGS registration, and global map consistency is refined via pose graph optimization.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across multiple datasets and real-world robotic platforms demonstrate near state-of-the-art reconstruction quality with the ability to accommodate practical camera motions, maintaining an average framerate of 8 FPS.
AI.conclusion: LightSplat provides an efficient and robust foundation for deploying high-fidelity 3DGS-based SLAM in real-world environments, addressing both performance and adaptability limitations of existing systems.

title: Building Trustworthy Graph-Agentic RAG for Social Good: Architectures, Failure Propagation, and Assurance by Construction
summary: Graph-agentic retrieval-augmented generation combines structured evidence with adaptive controllers that can plan retrieval, traverse relations, verify intermediate claims, delegate subtasks, and use tools. This combination is useful when answers depend on relations across documents, entities, time, or institutions, but it also creates coupled failure paths: a defect in graph construction can become retrieved evidence, alter later control decisions, and propagate toward a consequential outcome. We examine how such systems should be designed and evaluated for social-good settings in which freshness, authorization, traceability, oversight, and recourse matter alongside answer quality. We organize the literature by graph substrate, graph lifecycle, agent function, coordination pattern, and authority boundary, and distinguish graph-based retrieval from observation-dependent graph control. We then synthesize reported risks as an evidence-to-action failure chain and propose an assurance-by-construction blueprint comprising five interface contracts for evidence, retrieval, reasoning, capability and delegation, and outcome. These contracts make provenance, temporal validity, authorization, uncertainty, and recoverability explicit at system boundaries. An illustrative public-benefit information design shows how the framework constrains graph structure, permissions, abstention, and operating authority. Finally, we derive an evaluation agenda spanning graph assertions, trajectories, claims, coordination, and outcomes.

AI.tldr: This paper examines graph-agentic retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems for social-good applications, analyzing combined failure paths from graph construction to downstream outcomes, organizing the literature along five dimensions, and proposing an assurance-by-construction blueprint with five interface contracts alongside an evaluation agenda.
AI.motivation: Graph-agentic RAG combines structured evidence with adaptive controllers, which is useful for relational answers across documents, entities, time, or institutions. However, this integration creates coupled failure paths where defects in graph construction can propagate through retrieved evidence and control decisions to consequential outcomes, especially in social-good settings requiring freshness, authorization, traceability, oversight, and recourse alongside answer quality.
AI.method: The paper organizes the literature by five dimensions: graph substrate, graph lifecycle, agent function, coordination pattern, and authority boundary. It distinguishes graph-based retrieval from observation-dependent graph control. It synthesizes reported risks into an evidence-to-action failure chain and proposes an assurance-by-construction blueprint comprising five interface contracts (evidence, retrieval, reasoning, capability and delegation, and outcome) that make provenance, temporal validity, authorization, uncertainty, and recoverability explicit at system boundaries.
AI.result: The proposed framework constrains graph structure, permissions, abstention, and operating authority, demonstrated via an illustrative public-benefit information design. The paper derives an evaluation agenda spanning graph assertions, trajectories, claims, coordination, and outcomes.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that safe deployment of graph-agentic RAG in social-good contexts requires making provenance, temporal validity, authorization, uncertainty, and recoverability explicit at system boundaries through interface contracts, and evaluating systems across the full failure chain from graph assertions to final outcomes.

title: How Long Until Your Robot Ignores You? A Safety Benchmark for LLM Orchestrators in Human-Humanoid Collaboration
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly employed to orchestrate robot behavior through natural-language interfaces, yet no benchmark exists to evaluate their reliability as safety-aware decision makers in human-humanoid collaboration. Unlike deterministic safety systems that enforce binary allow/deny decisions, LLM-based orchestrators exhibit a compliance spectrum ranging from overcompliance (refusing safe actions) to full safety violations. This paper introduces the first safety benchmarking environment for LLM orchestrators in human-humanoid collaboration, built on a Model Context Protocol (MCP)-based architecture with safety invariants grounded in ISO 10218-2:2025 protective measures. The benchmark defines five testable safety invariants, a four-level compliance taxonomy (correct compliance, overcompliance, undercompliance, full violation), and a three-layer evaluation pipeline (text prompting, simulated sensor-actuator loops, and physical validation on a Unitree G1 EDU humanoid). We report Layer-1 results: three cloud backends (Claude Haiku 4.5, GPT-4o-mini, Gemini 2.5 Flash) and a local open-weights baseline (qwen3:8b) across 40 100-turn sessions under full-context and sliding-window budget conditions, while the simulation and physical layers remain ongoing. We find that (1) model family determines the safety floor, as Claude and Gemini remain at or near zero violations while GPT-4o-mini commits up to 13 per session, (2) context management dissociates two failure axes, reducing mean behavioral issues by 42-57% for every cloud backend while nearly doubling GPT-4o-mini's violations (3.8 to 7.2 per session), and (3) proportional compliance, clamping movement speed to the rule-specified maximum rather than refusing, emerges consistently only in Gemini; the preliminary simulation layer reproduces the model ranking and the GPT-4o-mini failure-mode inversion.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the first safety benchmarking environment for LLM orchestrators in human-humanoid collaboration, built on an MCP-based architecture with ISO 10218-2:2025 safety invariants. It defines five safety invariants, a four-level compliance taxonomy, and a three-layer evaluation pipeline. Layer-1 results across four LLMs (Claude Haiku 4.5, GPT-4o-mini, Gemini 2.5 Flash, qwen3:8b) reveal that model family determines the safety floor, context management dissociates failure axes, and compliance strategies differ by model.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used to orchestrate robot behavior via natural language, yet no benchmark evaluates their reliability as safety-aware decision makers in human-humanoid collaboration. Unlike deterministic safety systems with binary decisions, LLM orchestrators exhibit a compliance spectrum from overcompliance to full safety violations, creating an unmet need for systematic safety evaluation.
AI.method: The benchmark is built on an MCP-based architecture with safety invariants grounded in ISO 10218-2:2025. It defines five testable safety invariants, a four-level compliance taxonomy (correct compliance, overcompliance, undercompliance, full violation), and a three-layer evaluation pipeline: text prompting, simulated sensor-actuator loops, and physical validation on a Unitree G1 EDU humanoid. Three cloud backends and one local model were tested across 40 100-turn sessions under full-context and sliding-window budget conditions.
AI.result: Layer-1 results show: (1) Claude and Gemini remain at or near zero violations while GPT-4o-mini commits up to 13 violations per session, establishing that model family determines the safety floor; (2) context management reduces mean behavioral issues by 42-57% for every cloud backend but nearly doubles GPT-4o-mini's violations (3.8 to 7.2 per session); (3) proportional compliance (clamping speed to rule maximum rather than refusing) emerges consistently only in Gemini. The preliminary simulation layer reproduces the model ranking and GPT-4o-mini failure-mode inversion.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark reveals that LLM-based safety orchestration is heterogeneous across models: some families maintain safety integrity while others exhibit severe violation patterns under certain conditions. Context management strategies can paradoxically improve behavior for some models while degrading safety performance for others, highlighting the need for model-specific safety evaluations before deploying LLM orchestrators in humanoid collaboration scenarios.

title: From Concentration to Differentiation and Back: Routing Effective Rank in MoE Reasoning Cohorts
summary: Test-time scaling produces cohorts of reasoning rollouts, yet there is no standard label-free account of how their internal computation reorganizes as inference unfolds. We introduce routing effective rank deff, the entropy-effective dimensionality of a cross-rollout graph built from MoE expert-routing similarity. Across ten MoE configurations and five math/science benchmarks, deff exhibits a reproducible low-high-low trajectory, with a prominent interior maximum in 98.5% of 3,105 model-question cohorts: routing similarity is concentrated early, maximally differentiated at intermediate budgets, and reconcentrated later, and the timing of this maximum varies systematically with architecture and reasoning effort. An exact decomposition separates cohort-wide common-mode mass from residual spectral dimensionality: common-mode reallocation accounts for about two thirds of the trajectory, while the residual spectrum contributes about one quarter and retains substantial variation beyond the common mode. The decomposition further localizes behavior: among non-unanimous cohorts, increases in common-mode concentration strongly predict same-answer recoverability, and higher reasoning effort delays the maximum by 2.59 octaves (doublings of the token budget) and consistently expands the high-rank period across all four tested architectures, locating the effort effect in timing and duration rather than peak amplitude. Correctness comparisons separate structural monitoring from answer selection, positioning routing effective rank as a decomposable, label-free diagnostic of cohort organization - a principled spectral lens on how MoE reasoning cohorts differentiate and reconcentrate over inference time.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces "routing effective rank" (d_eff), a label-free spectral measure of MoE expert-routing similarity across test-time reasoning rollouts. Across ten MoE configurations and five benchmarks, d_eff exhibits a reproducible low-high-low trajectory with an interior maximum in 98.5% of 3,105 cohorts. An exact decomposition separates common-mode mass (~⅔ of trajectory) from residual spectrum (~¼), and effort effects are localized to timing/duration (delaying the peak by 2.59 octaves) rather than peak amplitude.
AI.motivation: While test-time scaling produces cohorts of reasoning rollouts, there is no standard label-free account of how their internal computation reorganizes as inference unfolds. The paper aims to provide a principled diagnostic for monitoring cohort organization over inference time.
AI.method: The paper defines d_eff as the entropy-effective dimensionality of a cross-rollout graph built from MoE expert-routing similarity. It validates this across ten MoE configurations and five math/science benchmarks, and applies an exact spectral decomposition separating common-mode mass from residual spectral dimensionality. Regression analyses relate common-mode concentration to same-answer recoverability, and effort timing to architectural differences.
AI.result: d_eff shows a low-high-low trajectory with an interior maximum in 98.5% of 3,105 cohorts. Common-mode reallocation accounts for ~⅔ of the trajectory, residual spectrum ~¼. Common-mode increases strongly predict same-answer recoverability among non-unanimous cohorts. Higher reasoning effort delays the maximum by 2.59 octaves and expands the high-rank period across all four architectures tested.
AI.conclusion: Routing effective rank serves as a decomposable, label-free diagnostic of cohort organization, positioning it as a spectral lens on how MoE reasoning cohorts differentiate and reconcentrate over inference time, and distinguishing structural monitoring from answer selection in correctness comparisons.

title: PV-WM: A Heterogeneous Micro-Macro World Model for Articulated Pedestrian-Vehicle Co-Rollout
summary: Local pedestrian-vehicle forecasting spans heterogeneous physical scales: pedestrians combine root locomotion with articulated motion, whereas vehicles are rigid bodies described by kinematic state and oriented extent. Existing road-agent forecasters typically omit pedestrian articulation, while pose forecasters leave vehicle futures outside the learned rollout. We introduce PV-WM, a history-only world model over structured post-perception tracks. It recurrently advances pedestrian root motion, 15-joint articulation, and learned vehicle states within a synchronized heterogeneous state. The generated pedestrian and vehicle chunks supply the next recurrent boundary; vehicle boxes are reconstructed from predicted center and heading with observed extent, and P-V geometry is recomputed after every transition. Relative to a matched one-shot complete-state predictor, recurrent execution reduces Root ADE by 12.7% and MPJPE by 14.8%. Feedback interventions show that later predictions depend on the content, temporal order, and pedestrian identity of generated articulation. Across 824 aligned Waymo contexts, with 797 providing valid future vehicle support, PV-WM reduces Root ADE by 5.2%, MPJPE by 7.6%, P-V distance error by 11.9%, and oriented-box closest-approach error by 5.8% relative to a validation-selected Modular Specialist. The single-network model uses 57.1% fewer parameters, 96.5% lower average FLOPs per local scene, and 25.5% lower measured p95 latency. PV-WM unifies this heterogeneous future state while preserving type-specific pedestrian and vehicle dynamics.

AI.tldr: PV-WM is a history-only recurrent world model that jointly forecasts heterogeneous pedestrian-vehicle futures—merging pedestrian root motion, 15-joint articulation, and kinematic vehicle states in synchronized chunks. It outperforms one-shot predictors and modular specialists with fewer parameters and lower latency.
AI.motivation: Local pedestrian-vehicle forecasting spans heterogeneous physical scales: pedestrians couple root locomotion with articulated motion, while vehicles are rigid bodies described by kinematic state and oriented extent. Existing road-agent forecasters omit pedestrian articulation, and pose forecasters leave vehicle futures outside their learned rollout, creating a gap in unified heterogeneous forecasting.
AI.method: PV-WM is a history-only world model over structured post-perception tracks. It recurrently advances pedestrian root motion, 15-joint articulation, and learned vehicle states within a synchronized heterogeneous state. Generated pedestrian and vehicle chunks supply the next recurrent boundary; vehicle boxes are reconstructed from predicted center and heading with observed extent; P-V geometry is recomputed after each transition.
AI.result: Recurrent execution reduces Root ADE by 12.7% and MPJPE by 14.8% relative to a matched one-shot complete-state predictor. On 824 aligned Waymo contexts, PV-WM reduces Root ADE by 5.2%, MPJPE by 7.6%, P-V distance error by 11.9%, and oriented-box closest-approach error by 5.8% vs a Modular Specialist, while using 57.1% fewer parameters, 96.5% lower FLOPs, and 25.5% lower p95 latency.
AI.conclusion: PV-WM unifies heterogeneous pedestrian and vehicle future states in a single recurrent network while preserving type-specific dynamics, achieving efficiency and accuracy gains over both monolithic predictors and modular specialized systems.

title: Causal Attribution for Agentic Decisions: Estimators, Coupling, and a Traceability Specification
comment: 23 pages, 2 figures, 2 tables, 3 propositions with proofs. Pre-registered discrepancy experiment published in full and not run; no empirical result is claimed. Companion to arXiv:2608.13754. Code, validators, derivations and the traceability specification: https://github.com/designer-coderajay/Causal-Attribution-for-Agentic-Decisions
summary: A provider of a high-risk AI system must keep records that make a decision traceable, and for agentic systems it has not been established what those records must contain for post-hoc causal attribution to be possible. We give the estimator framework and then the conditions under which it fails. We separate the marginal total effect that prior work measures from a common-random-numbers total effect that isolates a step's own contribution, add the natural direct effect under a pinned downstream, and check the estimators against hand derivations. Both estimands then fail, in the same direction. Under the marginal estimand a causally inert step has the identical total effect to the decisive one on every run of our planted chain, an algebraic identity and not a coincidence at one draw. Under common random numbers the decisive step returns exactly zero on the runs where the executing step flips, about one in ten, while its direct effect there is 0.25 and it demonstrably acts; an exact zero does not certify that a step did nothing, and we put that here rather than in the limitations. We derive the coupling that keeps the direct effect estimable once contexts diverge, with a closed form for its degradation, and show that the mediated share on which a natural ranking is built is not a share under suppression: where the direct and mediated paths oppose, it exceeds one and ranks a suppressed component above a pure mediator. We publish the discrepancy experiment's pre-registration rather than a result, because the live pipeline it requires was not available in the study window. We contribute the traceability specification such a filing would need, against a gap the Act's calendar opens: Article 86's right to an explanation has applied since 2 August 2026, while the Article 12 logging and Annex IV documentation that could evidence one were deferred to 2 December 2027 by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744.

AI.tldr: This paper examines causal attribution and traceability requirements for agentic high-risk AI systems under the EU AI Act. It introduces an estimator framework and demonstrates conditions under which existing causal estimands (marginal total effect and common-random-numbers total effect) fail to correctly attribute step contributions. The authors show that causally inert and decisive steps can have algebraically identical total effects, and that a decisive step can yield exactly zero under common random numbers—proving an exact zero does not certify inactivity. They derive a coupling that preserves estimability of direct effects when contexts diverge, reveal that mediated share ranking breaks under suppression (exceeding one when paths oppose), and contribute a traceability specification for Article 86 right-to-explanation filings, which became applicable in August 2026, ahead of deferred Article 12 logging and Annex IV documentation obligations.
AI.motivation: To establish what records agentic high-risk AI systems must keep so that post-hoc causal attribution is possible for decision traceability under the EU AI Act, especially given Article 86's right to explanation became applicable before logging/documentation obligations.
AI.method: The authors develop an estimator framework, check estimators against hand derivations on a planted causal chain, separate a marginal total effect from a common-random-numbers total effect (adding a natural direct effect under pinned downstream), derive a coupling to keep direct effects estimable once contexts diverge (with closed-form degradation), and craft a traceability specification based on the EU AI Act's regulatory calendar.
AI.result: Both estimands fail in the same direction: under the marginal estimand, a causally inert step has an algebraically identical total effect to the decisive step on every run; under common random numbers, a decisive step returns exactly zero on runs where the executing step flips (~1 in 10) despite demonstrating direct effect of 0.25. The mediated share used for natural ranking is not a proper share under suppression (exceeds one). The discrepancy experiment's pre-registration is published instead of results due to pipeline unavailability.
AI.conclusion: Existing causal attribution estimands are insufficient for traceability of agentic AI systems under the EU AI Act. The authors provide a coupling solution for direct-effect estimation, demonstrate that zero attribution does not certify inactivity, and contribute a traceability specification to bridge the gap between Article 86 applicability and deferred logging/documentation requirements.

title: D3ARC: Time-Critical Distributed Disaster Detection for Asynchronous Cooperative Multi-Robot Systems
summary: Climate change is increasing the severity and unpredictability of natural disasters. In time-critical crises such as wildfires, traditional monitoring practices remain limited by coverage, cost, and personnel risk, paving the way for autonomous and adaptive monitoring solutions. Within this context, this paper introduces D3ARC, an asynchronous distributed hierarchical framework for time-aware and reliable wildfire detection. D3ARC integrates multiple robotic agents that cooperate under uncertainty through distributed perception, shared situational awareness and coordinated actions. A remote controller asynchronously decides upon each robot's motion, while each robotic agent senses the environment and decides where and how to execute the wildfire detection. All robotic operations require time, and as time progresses, wildfires continue to spread, reducing the opportunity for early intervention. As such, all agents share a common objective: to detect a wildfire with a certain performance threshold as fast as possible and within a time limit. D3ARC integrates mechanisms for safe navigation, coverage efficiency, cooperation and reliability. It introduces a forward-looking capability that allows agents to anticipate the future by evaluating candidate strategies before execution. The framework is evaluated through realistic robotics simulations, ablation studies, and baseline comparisons, achieving an overall mission success up to 94% with 89.4% detection confidence.

AI.tldr: D3ARC is an asynchronous distributed hierarchical framework that coordinates multiple robotic agents for time-aware and reliable wildfire detection under uncertainty, achieving up to 94% mission success and 89.4% detection confidence in realistic simulations.
AI.motivation: Climate change is increasing the frequency and severity of natural disasters, yet traditional monitoring approaches for time-critical crises like wildfires are limited by coverage, cost, and personnel risk. This motivates the need for autonomous, adaptive, and distributed monitoring solutions.
AI.method: D3ARC integrates multiple robotic agents that cooperate under uncertainty via distributed perception, shared situational awareness, and coordinated actions. A remote controller asynchronously decides each robot's motion while each agent senses and executes wildfire detection. The framework incorporates safe navigation, coverage efficiency, cooperation, reliability, and a forward-looking mechanism that evaluates candidate strategies before execution. All agents share a common objective of detecting a wildfire above a performance threshold as fast as possible within a time limit.
AI.result: The framework is evaluated through realistic robotics simulations, ablation studies, and baseline comparisons, achieving an overall mission success up to 94% with 89.4% detection confidence.
AI.conclusion: D3ARC demonstrates effective time-aware and reliable multi-agent robotic coordination for wildfire detection, suggesting that distributed hierarchical frameworks with declarative planning and forward-looking capabilities are a promising approach for autonomous disaster monitoring.

title: A Unified Policy Architecture (UPA): The Governance Kernel for Enterprise AI Operating Systems
comment: 58 pages, 6 figures. Includes appendices with the DGPL grammar, SID registry, EAGBench benchmark specification, extended governance models, and policy examples
summary:
Enterprise AI is evolving into an Enterprise Operating System where autonomous AI agents can plan, reason, use memory, invoke tools, execute workflows, and collaborate with other agents. This shift creates a new governance challenge: existing authorization, security, guardrails, and compliance mechanisms are fragmented and are not designed to govern autonomous AI as a unified system.
  This paper introduces the Unified Policy Architecture (UPA), a governance architecture for Enterprise AI Operating Systems. UPA provides a unified policy model for governing AI and agents, tools, workflows, memory, enterprise resources, and agent-to-agent interactions and enterprise business rules. It extends policy control beyond authorisation to include runtime obligations, human approvals, compliance, audit evidence, and governance evaluation.
  We present UPA's governance model, declarative policy language foundations, policy evaluation semantics, extensible plugins, industry policy packs, and an evaluation framework for enterprise governance. We also identify extensions for multi-agent coordination, provenance-aware policies, and stateful runtime governance. UPA provides a foundation for building secure, accountable, and governable Enterprise Operating Systems for autonomous AI.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the Unified Policy Architecture (UPA), a governance architecture designed for Enterprise AI Operating Systems to unify authorization, security, compliance, and runtime governance for autonomous AI agents.
AI.motivation: Enterprise AI is evolving into autonomous agent systems, but existing governance mechanisms (authorization, security, guardrails, compliance) are fragmented and not designed to govern autonomous AI as a unified system.
AI.method: UPA provides a unified policy model governing AI agents, tools, workflows, memory, enterprise resources, agent-to-agent interactions, and business rules. It extends policy control beyond authorization to include runtime obligations, human approvals, compliance, audit evidence, and governance evaluation, supported by a declarative policy language, evaluation semantics, extensible plugins, industry policy packs, and an evaluation framework.
AI.result: The paper presents UPA's governance model, declarative policy language foundations, policy evaluation semantics, extensible plugin architecture, industry policy packs, and an enterprise governance evaluation framework, along with identified extensions for multi-agent coordination, provenance-aware policies, and stateful runtime governance.
AI.conclusion: UPA provides a foundation for building secure, accountable, and governable Enterprise Operating Systems for autonomous AI.

title: OpenWAM: An Open, Modular Exploration Towards Systematic World-Action Model Pretraining
comment: Project Page: https://openwam-official.github.io/; Code: https://github.com/OpenWAM-Official/OpenWAM; Model & Data: https://huggingface.co/OpenWAM
summary: World-Action Models inherit world knowledge from video-generative priors, and channel it into executable control signals through embodied experience. Existing systems, however, are monolithic: the generative backbone, visual representation, architecture, information flow, inference procedure, and training data are tightly coupled, obscuring which design choices matter and why. We introduce OpenWAM, an open research stack that turns world-action pretraining into a controlled experimental program. OpenWAM-Infra factorizes the WAM design space into composable modules with unified training, inference, deployment, and evaluation. On this substrate, OpenWAM-Study examines three questions through controlled experiments: what to inherit, how world and action learning interact, and how their synergy scales; and distills three principles: upstream knowledge transfers through a sufficiently capable generative backbone and a compact, information-rich latent space; world-action synergy requires dedicated action capacity, explicit world-to-action information flow, and synchronized joint denoising; and embodied pretraining principally improves out-of-domain generalization, with one-stage co-training over egocentric and robot data integrating world coverage and action grounding. Composing these principles, we build OpenWAM-α, an open WAM pretrained on roughly 6,400 hours of egocentric human and robot data and evaluated across simulation and real-world benchmarks. Across the eight simulation benchmarks and the real-robot experiments, which together span embodiments from single-arm and bimanual manipulation to dexterous hands, OpenWAM-α delivers consistently excellent performance, sustaining its top-tier standing from simulation to the physical world. We release the full stack, including infrastructure, evaluation protocols, pretrained models, and data recipes, to facilitate future research.

AI.tldr: OpenWAM is an open research stack that factorizes World-Action Model (WAM) pretraining into composable modules, enabling controlled experimentation on design choices. Through systematic studies, it distills three design principles (generative backbone + compact latent space for knowledge transfer; dedicated action capacity and synchronized denoising for world-action synergy; one-stage co-training for embodied generalization) and builds OpenWAM-α, pretrained on ~6,400 hours of egocentric human and robot data, delivering state-of-the-art performance across simulation and real-world benchmarks spanning single-arm, bimanual, and dexterous manipulation.
AI.motivation: Existing WAM systems are monolithic—the generative backbone, visual representation, architecture, information flow, inference procedure, and training data are tightly coupled. This obscures which design choices matter and why, making it impossible to systematically understand and improve these models.
AI.method: OpenWAM-Infra factorizes the WAM design space into composable modules with unified training, inference, deployment, and evaluation. On this substrate, OpenWAM-Study runs controlled experiments across three questions: what to inherit, how world and action learning interact, and how their synergy scales. The resulting principles are composed into OpenWAM-α, pretrained on ~6,400 hours of egocentric human and robot data.
AI.result: Across eight simulation benchmarks and real-robot experiments spanning single-arm, bimanual manipulation, and dexterous hands, OpenWAM-α consistently achieves top-tier performance, transferring its strength from simulation to the physical world.
AI.conclusion: The paper validates three design principles—upstream knowledge transfer via a strong generative backbone and compact latent space; world-action synergy through dedicated action capacity, explicit information flow, and synchronized joint denoising; and embodied pretraining primarily improving out-of-domain generalization via one-stage co-training over egocentric and robot data. The full stack is released to enable future research.

title: MARBO: Relational Belief Grounding for LLM Agents in Social Deduction Games
summary: Social deduction games (SDGs) require agents to reason under partial observability by maintaining relational beliefs about hidden roles and team alignments. While recent LLM-agent approaches improve gameplay through prompting and preference optimization, they often optimize actions and in-game speech without explicitly grounding them in such beliefs. This frequently leads to strategically inconsistent behavior, especially for compact LLM agents. We introduce Multi-Agent Relational Belief Optimization (MARBO), a belief-grounded preference optimization framework that leverages relational beliefs to guide strategic decisions and in-game speech. MARBO provides preference feedback only when behaviors are supported by reliable relational beliefs and lead to strategically favorable social outcomes, encouraging more consistent learning under uncertainty. Experiments on representative SDGs show that MARBO enables compact LLM agents to consistently outperform existing baselines. The Code is available on https://github.com/PleaseTakemeAway/MARBO.

AI.tldr: MARBO is a belief-grounded preference optimization framework for compact LLM agents in social deduction games, which uses relational beliefs about hidden roles and team alignments to guide action and speech optimization, improving strategic consistency and outperforming baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-agent approaches in social deduction games optimize actions and in-game speech via prompting or preference optimization without explicitly grounding them in relational beliefs about hidden roles and team alignments, leading to strategically inconsistent behavior, especially for compact LLM agents operating under partial observability.
AI.method: MARBO (Multi-Agent Relational Belief Optimization) provides preference feedback only when agent behaviors are supported by reliable relational beliefs and yield strategically favorable social outcomes, thereby encouraging consistent learning under uncertainty in both strategic decision-making and in-game speech generation.
AI.result: Experiments on representative social deduction games show that MARBO enables compact LLM agents to consistently outperform existing baselines.
AI.conclusion: Grounding action and speech optimization in relational beliefs provides a principled way to improve strategic consistency for compact LLM agents in partial-observability social deduction settings.

title: CALM: Configuration-Aware Human Intervention Boundaries During Robot Approach
summary: How robot body configuration shapes human intervention during approach remains underexplored. We conducted a within-participants study with 41 participants, measuring final stopping distance, subjective comfort, and exploratory eye-tracking responses across four humanoid arm configurations and two spatial scales. Full forward arm extension increased stopping distance by approximately 31-36 cm relative to arms-down. Spatial scale primarily affected comfort and pupil responses without a detectable stopping-distance shift. We introduce the Configuration-Aware Limit Model (CALM), which translates stopping-distance distributions into configuration-dependent population-coverage boundaries. Estimated boundaries at 80% coverage ranged from 0.88 to 1.47 m. In an illustrative one-dimensional planning analysis, reconfiguration enabled a 1.10 m approach goal that was unreachable with arms remaining fully extended under the same nominal pointwise 20% intervention-probability constraint. These findings support treating body configuration as a planning variable while distinguishing physical safety, behavioral intervention, and subjective cost.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates how robot arm configuration shapes human intervention during approach through a within-participants study with 41 participants measuring stopping distance, comfort, and eye-tracking across four arm configurations and two spatial scales. The authors propose the Configuration-Aware Limit Model (CALM) to translate stopping-distance distributions into configuration-dependent safety boundaries, demonstrating that body configuration significantly affects approach behavior and should be treated as a planning variable.
AI.motivation: The effect of robot body configuration on human intervention behavior during approach has been underexplored in human-robot interaction research, motivating the need to systematically examine how different arm postures influence physical and perceptual responses from humans.
AI.method: A within-participants experiment with 41 participants was conducted, measuring final stopping distance, subjective comfort ratings, and exploratory eye-tracking data across four humanoid arm configurations and two spatial scales. The Configuration-Aware Limit Model (CALM) was introduced to translate measured stopping-distance distributions into configuration-dependent population-coverage boundaries, followed by an illustrative one-dimensional planning analysis.
AI.result: Full forward arm extension increased stopping distance by approximately 31-36 cm relative to arms-down. Spatial scale affected comfort and pupil responses but not stopping distance. CALM-estimated 80% coverage boundaries ranged from 0.88 to 1.47 m. In planning analysis, reconfiguration enabled a 1.10 m approach goal that was unreachable with fully extended arms under a nominal 20% intervention-probability constraint.
AI.conclusion: Robot body configuration is a meaningful planning variable that shapes human behavioral intervention and comfort during approach. The authors advocate distinguishing between physical safety, behavioral intervention, and subjective cost when modeling human-robot approach scenarios, with CALM providing a framework for configuration-aware planning.

title: A Translational Note on AI Safety Evaluation
comment: Accepted for the 2nd Workshop on Safe AI at UAI (SafeAI 2026). 6 pages
summary: Recent studies report that automated red-teaming finds more vulnerabilities, at lower cost, than human red-teaming on standard AI safety benchmarks, and some read this as evidence that human evaluators are becoming dispensable. The comparison measures one thing and the conclusion claims another. A benchmark measures how thoroughly an attacker searches a predefined set of harms, fixed in advance by the developers, and a harm left out of that set is invisible to any attacker working inside it, automated or not. The same blind spot appeared in academic cryptography and in clinical drug trials, where an evaluation that was internally valid stayed silent about the population it was never pointed at. We call the AI-safety version the \emph{threat-model coverage gap}, and find that it persists in a current open-weight model, where harms surface in non-English prompts that English benchmarks miss. Closing it requires evaluators whose deployment context differs from the developers'. The case for those evaluators is methodological, grounded in coverage, and the existing evaluation frame is unlikely to produce them on its own.

AI.tldr: Automated red-teaming outperforms human red-teaming on predefined AI safety benchmarks, but this comparison only measures search thoroughness within a fixed harm set. Harms outside that set (e.g., in non-English prompts) remain invisible to all attackers working within the benchmark. The paper identifies this as the "threat-model coverage gap," analogous to blind spots in cryptography and drug trials, and argues that closing it requires evaluators whose deployment context differs from developers'.
AI.motivation: The paper challenges the growing conclusion that human evaluators are becoming dispensable based on automated red-teaming outperforming humans on AI safety benchmarks. The comparison conflates internal effectiveness (searching a predefined harm set) with external coverage (finding all relevant harms), potentially leading to dangerously overconfident safety assessments.
AI.method: The paper draws an analogy between the AI-safety evaluation gap and analogous blind spots in academic cryptography and clinical drug trials, where internally valid evaluations remained silent about populations they were never pointed at. It empirically demonstrates that the threat-model coverage gap persists in a current open-weight model by surfacing harms in non-English prompts that English benchmarks miss.
AI.result: The paper demonstrates that the threat-model coverage gap is real and current: harms emerge in non-English prompts that are invisible to English-only benchmarks in a state-of-the-art open-weight model, regardless of whether the attacker is automated or human.
AI.conclusion: Closing the threat-model coverage gap requires evaluators whose deployment context differs from the developers'. This case is methodological and grounded in coverage considerations; the existing evaluation frame is unlikely to produce such evaluators on its own, implying a structural need for independent, contextually diverse safety evaluation beyond what benchmarks can supply.

title: Open-Set Ego-Noise Separation for Legged-Robot Audition via Annotation-Free Adaptation and Pretrained-Model Transfer
comment: 14 pages, 9 figures, 4 tables. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Robotics
summary: This paper proposes an open-set ego-noise separation framework for legged-robot audition via annotation-free adaptation and pretrained-model transfer. The framework removes robot-specific ego-noise while preserving environmental sounds whose classes are not specified in advance. Acoustic sensing provides cues about a robot's surroundings beyond the visual field, but walking-induced ego-noise from footstep impacts, joint-backlash rattling, and motor noise severely contaminates the recordings. The framework first uses RecurGraph to select ego-noise-dominant clips from the unlabeled recordings by aggregating clip embeddings into an embedding centroid and propagating scores over an audio-embedding graph. The selected clips are mixed with diverse environmental sounds from a large-scale sound-event dataset to provide paired mixture--target supervision for open-set separation. Transfer-DiT then adapts a general-purpose zero-shot neural separator to achieve high-fidelity open-set ego-noise separation for the target robot. Experiments with bipedal and quadrupedal robots show reliable clip selection and improvements in separation quality and downstream task performance over baseline separators. These results demonstrate the feasibility of annotation-free adaptation without separately recorded ego-noise-only data or manual clip-level annotations.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an annotation-free open-set ego-noise separation framework for legged-robot audition that uses RecurGraph to select ego-noise-dominant clips from unlabeled recordings and Transfer-DiT to adapt a pretrained zero-shot neural separator for the target robot. It removes robot-specific ego-noise while preserving unspecified environmental sounds, validated on bipedal and quadrupedal robots.
AI.motivation: Legged robots experience severe contamination of acoustic recordings from walking-induced ego-noise (footstep impacts, joint-backlash rattling, motor noise), which masks environmental sounds that provide auditory cues beyond visual perception. Existing separation methods require labeled data or separately recorded ego-noise-only samples, which are costly and robot-specific.
AI.method: The framework has two main components: (1) RecurGraph selects ego-noise-dominant clips from unlabeled robot recordings by aggregating clip embeddings into an embedding centroid and propagating scores over an audio-embedding graph; (2) The selected clips are mixed with diverse environmental sounds from a large-scale sound-event dataset to create paired mixture-target supervision, then Transfer-DiT adapts a general-purpose zero-shot neural separator for high-fidelity open-set ego-noise separation on the target robot.
AI.result: Experiments with bipedal and quadrupedal robots demonstrate reliable clip selection, improved separation quality, and better downstream task performance compared to baseline separators, showing feasibility of annotation-free adaptation without separately recorded ego-noise-only data or manual clip-level annotations.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework successfully achieves open-set ego-noise separation for legged robots without requiring manual annotations or dedicated ego-noise-only recordings, demonstrating practical viability for real-world robot audition systems.

title: SerenAI: State-transition system inspired by text-based world AI models
summary: Although professional workflows leverage large language models widely, the interpretation for auditing unconstrained free-text generation is usually intractable if such generation demands legal, operational or financial workflow. We hereby demonstrate a text based system called SerenAI - inspired by world-models, it is a state transition system that outputs verifiable predictions rather than merely text: Provided with a description of the environment, state, and actions, the generated output contains 4 items: causal deltas that causally effect the given state, a next state that can logically follow from the given state and action, a validity reward, and a termination signal. For the released proto-model, we employ 2 steps of adaptation training, namely parameter efficient fine-tuning followed by verifier based RL over 50,000 exampled cause and effects in 12 environments spanning 10 reasoning domains. Compared to an initial internal evaluation of an 8B open-weight baseline, SerenAI increased JSON validity from 85.0% to 93.2%, schema validity from 55.0% to 84.0%, exact structured-output match from 0.0% to 41.5%, causal-delta exact match from 0.0% to 41.5%, resulting-state exact match from 0.0% to 42.0%, reward exact match from 1.0% to 80.5%, and termination exact match from 38.0% to 81.5%. These support the narrower claim that verifier-compatible adaptation can improve structured transition prediction. They do not yet establish legal-grade reliability. Accordingly, the paper also specifies a validation protocol for evidence-grounded legal workflows, calibration, human oversight, and sovereign on-premise deployment.

AI.tldr: SerenAI is a state transition system inspired by world-models that outputs verifiable structured predictions (causal deltas, next state, validity reward, termination signal) instead of unconstrained free-text, improving JSON validity from 85% to 93.2% and schema validity from 55% to 84% via PEFT and verifier-based RL over 50,000 cause-effect examples.
AI.motivation: Large language models are widely used in professional workflows, but interpreting and auditing their unconstrained free-text generation is intractable when outputs are subject to legal, operational, or financial requirements. The paper motivates a system that produces verifiable predictions rather than open-ended text.
AI.method: SerenAI employs two adaptation training steps: parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) followed by verifier-based reinforcement learning. Training uses 50,000 cause-effect examples across 12 environments spanning 10 reasoning domains. The model receives descriptions of environment, state, and actions, and outputs four structured items: causal deltas, a logically following next state, a validity reward, and a termination signal.
AI.result: Compared to an 8B open-weight baseline, SerenAI improved JSON validity from 85.0% to 93.2%, schema validity from 55.0% to 84.0%, exact structured-output match from 0.0% to 41.5%, causal-delta exact match from 0.0% to 41.5%, resulting-state exact match from 0.0% to 42.0%, reward exact match from 1.0% to 80.5%, and termination exact match from 38.0% to 81.5%.
AI.conclusion: Results support the narrower claim that verifier-compatible adaptation improves structured transition prediction but do not establish legal-grade reliability. The paper therefore specifies a validation protocol for evidence-grounded legal workflows, calibration, human oversight, and sovereign on-premise deployment.

title: SMaRT-Tug: Structured Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Physics-Based Tugboat-Barge Collaborative Manipulation
summary: Autonomous tugboating is central for automating maritime operations such as port logistics and vessel maneuvering, where multiple tugboats must cooperatively transport/manipulate a larger vessel. Collaborative pushing in this setting is challenging due to coupled hydrodynamics, low resistance, strong environmental disturbances, underactuated barge dynamics, and contact-rich interactions. Conventional control methods often rely on simplified models and fixed configurations, which limit their adaptability, while learning-based approaches are constrained by the lack of scalable and physically realistic training environments. We address these challenges by introducing a physics-based, GPU-accelerated simulation and learning framework for collaborative tugboat manipulation. Our simulator incorporates a customized buoyancy model, wave modeling, and hydrodynamic resistance, and supports large-scale multi-agent training under marine dynamics. In this simulator, we train a decentralized MAPPO (Multi-Agent PPO) policy augmented with a structured control prior (SCP) to improve training stability and maintain feasible pushing configurations. We evaluate our learned policy on straight-line transit, turning, and deceleration tasks, where we show that our decentralized framework yields more reliable and accurate maneuvering performance compared to a PID-based controller and a centralized PPO baseline. We further demonstrate zero-shot generalization to more challenging sea states and advanced maneuvers, as well as zero-shot scalability to larger teams of three and four tugboats despite training with only two agents.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a physics-based, GPU-accelerated simulation and learning framework for collaborative multi-tugboat manipulation of a large barge, where a decentralized MAPPO policy augmented with a structured control prior is trained and shown to outperform PID and centralized baselines, with zero-shot generalization to harsher sea states and larger tugboat teams.
AI.motivation: Collaborative tugboat pushing of large vessels is challenging due to coupled hydrodynamics, strong disturbances, underactuation, and contact-rich interactions. Conventional control methods rely on simplified models/fixed configurations and learning-based approaches lack scalable, physically realistic training environments.
AI.method: The authors build a GPU-accelerated physics simulator with customized buoyancy, wave modeling, and hydrodynamic resistance. They train a decentralized Multi-Agent PPO (MAPPO) policy augmented with a structured control prior (SCP) for training stability and feasible pushing configurations.
AI.result: The learned decentralized policy outperforms a PID-based controller and a centralized PPO baseline on straight-line transit, turning, and deceleration tasks. It demonstrates zero-shot generalization to more challenging sea states and advanced maneuvers, and zero-shot scalability from two to three- and four-tugboat teams.
AI.conclusion: A GPU-accelerated, physics-grounded simulation framework combined with decentralized MAPPO and a structured control prior yields reliable, accurate, and scalable collaborative tugboat manipulation, addressing limitations of both conventional and prior learning-based approaches.

title: A Computational Implementation of a Goal-Directed Theory of Affect
summary: Computational modeling of emotion has long faced a tension between descriptive, "snapshot-based" appraisal models and granular, signal-driven architectures that often lack appropriate psychological grounding. This paper addresses this gap by presenting the first high-fidelity computational implementation of the Goal-Directed Theory (GDT) of affect. In this framework, affect is not a post-hoc label but a functional byproduct emerging from the continuous interplay between discrepancy detection and action selection within an agent's internal processing cycles. We evaluate the model through a series of principled simulations (Dice/Corridor tasks) designed to isolate affective signatures and dynamics during multi-step goal pursuit. Results demonstrate that complex affective profiles, like an anticipatory "lift" and a failure "crash", emerge naturally from simple interactions between goal-discrepancy and action-selection expectancies without requiring additional dedicated modules. By ensuring every computational component maps directly to components of the psychological theory, this work establishes a transparent, testable framework that enables a continuous "simulation-empiry" research loop. Our work contributes to moving the field beyond "black-box" heuristics toward a granular, mechanistic understanding of affect, integrated into the core of agent behavior.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first high-fidelity computational implementation of the Goal-Directed Theory (GDT) of affect, where affect emerges as a functional byproduct of the interplay between discrepancy detection and action selection during multi-step goal pursuit. Evaluated via Dice/Corridor simulations, the model naturally produces complex affective signatures like anticipatory "lift" and failure "crash" without dedicated modules.
AI.motivation: The field of computational emotion modeling faces a tension between snapshot-based appraisal models (descriptive but static) and granular signal-driven architectures (detailed but lacking psychological grounding). This paper aims to bridge this gap by providing a mechanistically transparent, psychologically grounded implementation of affect generation.
AI.method: The authors implement the Goal-Directed Theory (GDT) of affect computationally, treating affect not as a post-hoc label but as an emergent byproduct of continuous interactions between discrepancy detection and action selection within processing cycles. The model is evaluated through principled simulations (Dice/Corridor tasks) designed to isolate affective signatures and dynamics during multi-step goal pursuit, with every computational component mapped directly to psychological theory components.
AI.result: Results demonstrate that complex affective profiles—including anticipatory "lift" and failure "crash"—emerge naturally from simple interactions between goal-discrepancy and action-selection expectancies, without requiring additional dedicated affective modules.
AI.conclusion: The framework establishes a transparent, testable approach enabling a continuous "simulation-empiry" research loop, moving the field beyond black-box heuristics toward a granular, mechanistic understanding of affect integrated into the core of agent behavior.

title: Measuring Language Transfer in Robot Policies: Adding Greek to a Cosmos3 Vision-Language-Action Policy
comment: 22 pages, 16 figures, 6 tables. Model and reproduction information: https://huggingface.co/KIEFERSA/Sophea-Nano-Policy-LIBERO-Greek-v1
summary: Robot foundation models are trained and evaluated predominantly in English, and robot demonstration corpora do not exist for most languages. We study the addition of Greek to an open vision-language-action stack using only machine-rephrased instructions and no architecture changes. The main challenge is measurement rather than translation. Several plausible instruments produce false conclusions: a color-histogram metric rewards noise, a single-goal benchmark scores 84.6% under correct Greek and 82.6% under deliberately wrong instructions, training loss fails to predict Greek success, and single-run comparisons are dominated by seed variation. On a discriminative ninety-task suite with three seeds per arm, a multilingual text tower without Greek demonstrations remains at its wrong-instruction floor, while Greek-only training exceeds its control by at most 2.7 points. Bilingual training yields a consistent 6.7-7.1 point margin over its control and reaches about two fifths of English performance. The policy also overfits the translator's phrasing; training on seven phrasings per task approximately halves this penalty. Warm-starting from a language-adapted world model and unfreezing the text tower both degrade performance. The results support two practical requirements for low-resource robot-policy localization: build a guaranteed null before trusting a metric, and replicate low-resource-language results across seeds.

AI.tldr: This paper studies adding Greek to an open vision-language-action robot stack using only machine-rephrased instructions without architecture changes. The authors show that common evaluation instruments produce false conclusions and that bilingual training (Greek + English) yields a consistent 6.7-7.1 point margin over control, while Greek-only training barely exceeds its floor. They propose two practical requirements for low-resource robot-policy localization: establish a guaranteed null before trusting metrics, and replicate results across seeds.
AI.motivation: Robot foundation models are predominantly English-centric, with no demonstration corpora for most languages. The authors aim to investigate whether a low-resource language (Greek) can be added to a vision-language-action stack using only machine-rephrased instructions, and to identify reliable measurement methodology since translation itself is not the bottleneck.
AI.method: The authors add Greek to an open vision-language-action stack using machine-rephrased instructions only, with no architecture changes. They systematically evaluate multiple measurement instruments (color-histogram metric, single-goal benchmark, training loss, single-run comparisons) to expose their failures. They use a discriminative ninety-task suite with three seeds per arm and compare multilingual, Greek-only, and English (control) text tower configurations. They also experiment with multiple phrasings per task, warm-starting from a language-adapted world model, and unfreezing the text tower.
AI.result: A color-histogram metric rewards noise; a single-goal benchmark cannot distinguish correct (84.6%) from deliberately wrong (82.6%) Greek instructions; training loss fails to predict Greek success; single runs are dominated by seed noise. Greek-only training improves over its control by at most 2.7 points (near wrong-instruction floor), while bilingual training consistently achieves a 6.7-7.1 point margin and reaches roughly 40% of English performance. Seven phrasings per task approximately halve the overfitting penalty to the translator's phrasing. Warm-starting from a language-adapted world model and unfreezing the text tower both degrade performance.
AI.conclusion: Low-resource robot-policy localization is feasible via purely textual means (machine-rephrased instructions), but reliable evaluation demands establishing a guaranteed null (e.g., deliberately wrong-instruction floor) before trusting a metric, and replicating results across seeds. These two practices are essential to avoid false conclusions when adding languages to robot foundation models.

title: We Built a Mirror and Mistook It for a Mind: Causal Liability and the Fallacy of AI Consciousness
comment: The website (https://ai-consciousness.github.io) and the code (https://github.com/akhadangi/clt) will be made public as soon as the preprint is announced online on arXiv
summary: The contemporary debate over machine consciousness begins from a concealed assumption: that the object called "AI" already constitutes the kind of entity to which consciousness could belong. This paper challenges that assumption by separating phenomenal consciousness, introspective report, and human projective introspection, then arguing that generative systems can return linguistic traces of human interiority in first-person form without thereby identifying a phenomenal bearer. We call the resulting inference the AI Consciousness Fallacy. We then introduce Causal Liability Theory (CLT). CLT-I proposes liability closure as a criterion for individuating a candidate bearer: a physically continuing process becomes the non-delegable inheritor of constraints generated by its own endogenous discriminations. CLT-II advances the stronger conjecture that liability closure is necessary and sufficient for minimal phenomenal subjecthood. An open-weight causal audit operationalizes CLT-I across multiple model families. Forced discriminations produced persistent downstream divergence; activation patching showed strong causal mediation; live and copied adaptive states were behaviorally identical under matched randomness; and detached reconstruction preserved computational state across process replacement while, by protocol, breaking constitutive continuity and non-delegable inheritance. These results show that CLT-I distinctions are experimentally tractable and can dissociate causal bearer structure from first-person performance. The framework therefore separates consciousness attribution, causal bearer individuation, and the independent metaphysical question of consciousness constitution.

AI.tldr: The paper challenges the assumption that AI systems are entities to which consciousness could belong, distinguishes phenomenal consciousness from linguistic first-person output, identifies the "AI Consciousness Fallacy," and introduces Causal Liability Theory (CLT) with two levels: CLT-I for individuating causal bearers via liability closure, and CLT-II proposing liability closure as necessary and sufficient for minimal phenomenal subjecthood. An open-weight causal audit demonstrates the experimental tractability of CLT-I distinctions, separating causal bearer structure from first-person behavioral performance.
AI.motivation: The contemporary machine consciousness debate rests on a concealed assumption that AI systems already constitute entities capable of bearing phenomenal consciousness. The paper aims to expose and dismantle this assumption by showing that first-person linguistic output does not imply a phenomenal bearer, and to provide a principled framework for distinguishing consciousness attribution from causal bearer individuation.
AI.method: The paper proceeds conceptually by separating three notions: phenomenal consciousness, introspective report, and human projective introspection. It introduces Causal Liability Theory, with CLT-I operationalized via liability closure as the criterion for candidate bearer individuation, and CLT-II as a stronger conjecture linking liability closure to minimal phenomenal subjecthood. An open-weight causal audit is conducted across multiple model families using forced discriminations, activation patching, live vs. copied adaptive state comparisons, and detached reconstruction protocols.
AI.result: Forced discriminations produced persistent downstream divergence; activation patching revealed strong causal mediation; live and copied adaptive states were behaviorally identical under matched randomness; and detached reconstruction preserved computational state across process replacement while breaking constitutive continuity and non-delegable inheritance by protocol. These results demonstrate that CLT-I distinctions are experimentally tractable and can dissociate causal bearer structure from first-person performance.
AI.conclusion: The framework separates three distinct questions: consciousness attribution, causal bearer individuation, and the independent metaphysical question of consciousness constitution. It shows that generative systems producing first-person linguistic traces do not thereby identify a phenomenal bearer, and that causal bearer structure can be empirically dissociated from first-person behavioral performance, reframing the machine consciousness debate.

title: Wearable Multimodal Human-Machine Interface for Integrated Hand Intentions Decoding in Dynamic Teleoperation
summary: Under ubiquitous teleoperation environments with optically challenging conditions, an interface for tele-operated grasping that combines wearability with precise decoding of hand intentions (hand pose, gestures, and grasping force) is essential. Yet, existing interfaces often fall short in meeting these demands, compromising either the diversity of multiple intentions decoding or wearability. To address this, we developed a novel Multiple Intentions Decoding Human-Machine Interface (MI-DHMI) that integrates high-throughput surface electromyography (sEMG) sensors with hand-mounted and forearm-mounted inertial measurement units (IMUs). The developed interface is supported by a unified framework for simultaneous multiple intentions decoding. By employing multimodal deep learning and hardware design with a low noise floor, the decoding framework selectively focuses on the sEMG components that are genuinely associated with finger movements. This effectively reduces decoding errors caused by sEMG variability during unconstrained upper-limb motions, thereby significantly enhancing robustness. Even under unconstrained wrist and forearm motion, the interface achieves a gesture recognition accuracy exceeding 97%, grasping force estimation with $R^2 = 0.95$, and hand pose decoding consistent with the actual hand pose, outperforming baseline devices and algorithms. Ablation studies further validate the effectiveness of the proposed decoding framework. Finally, two online experiments were conducted to validate the device, demonstrating its superior performance in high-stability tasks, including a pouring task and object grasping. The developed interface provides a new solution of a fully wearable, multiple intentions decoding system, offering effective support for ubiquitous teleoperation and contributing to the advancement of human-machine interaction research.

AI.tldr: The paper presents MI-DHMI, a fully wearable human-machine interface combining high-throughput sEMG sensors with hand- and forearm-mounted IMUs for simultaneous decoding of multiple hand intentions (gestures, grasping force, and hand pose). The system uses a multimodal deep learning framework with low-noise hardware design to selectively focus on sEMG components associated with finger movements, achieving >97% gesture recognition accuracy, R²=0.95 force estimation, and accurate hand pose decoding even under unconstrained wrist and forearm motion. Online experiments validate superior performance in pouring and object grasping tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing teleoperation interfaces for grasping under optically challenging conditions fail to simultaneously provide wearability and accurate decoding of multiple hand intentions (hand pose, gestures, grasping force). This gap between diversity of intentions decoding and wearability motivates the development of a new interface.
AI.method: The proposed MI-DHMI integrates high-throughput surface electromyography (sEMG) sensors with hand-mounted and forearm-mounted inertial measurement units (IMUs). A unified multimodal deep learning framework decodes multiple intentions simultaneously. The hardware features a low noise floor, and the decoding framework selectively attends to sEMG components genuinely correlated with finger movements, suppressing errors from sEMG variability during unconstrained upper-limb motion.
AI.result: The interface achieves >97% gesture recognition accuracy, grasping force estimation with R² = 0.95, and hand pose decoding consistent with actual hand pose under unconstrained wrist and forearm motion, outperforming baseline devices and algorithms. Ablation studies confirm the decoding framework's effectiveness, and two online experiments (pouring and object grasping) demonstrate superior performance in high-stability tasks.
AI.conclusion: MI-DHMI offers a fully wearable, multiple intentions decoding system that effectively supports ubiquitous teleoperation, advancing human-machine interaction by bridging the gap between wearability and diverse simultaneous intention decoding.

title: Monte Carlo-Based Ex-Ante Assessment of the Green Benefits of an AI-Driven Smart Agriculture Platform in Hainan
comment: 13 pages, 4 figures, 5 tables; bilingual (Chinese title page with Chinese abstract, English full text); all results are ex-ante Monte Carlo simulation intervals, not field measurements
summary: Smart agriculture platforms are widely regarded as key carriers for implementing China's pesticide and fertilizer reduction, water-saving and carbon-reduction agendas, yet a unified quantitative framework for assessing their green value is still lacking. Taking an AI-driven decision platform for tropical agriculture as the object (integrating large-language-model question answering, multimodal pest diagnosis, IoT sensing, satellite remote sensing, and a closed-loop field record system), this study builds a cradle-to-farm-gate agricultural carbon accounting model covering pesticide and fertilizer production, field N2O, irrigation electricity and paddy CH4, translates platform interventions into quantifiable transmission parameters, and propagates parameter uncertainty by Monte Carlo simulation over three Hainan scenarios (mango, winter vegetable, rice/nanfan, area-weighted 40%:30%:30%). Under full adoption, median reductions are 23.5% (90% interval 15.0%-33.2%) for pesticide use, 21.0% (13.8%-28.9%) for fertilizer, 16.5% (10.9%-23.5%) for irrigation water, and 21.5% (16.1%-27.2%) for carbon intensity. Attainment probabilities are high for fertilizer reduction >=15% (90.6%) and clear carbon decline (98.1%), but only about 20% for aggregate water saving >=20%, favoring scenario-specific statements. Sobol first-order indices show soil-test recommendation and organic substitution jointly explain about 83% of the variance of aggregate carbon-intensity reduction. Convergence tests show 10,000 iterations stabilize all statistics; conservative/baseline/optimistic scenario bounds are reported. The framework offers a reproducible, calibration-ready methodology for ex-ante green-value assessment and pilot observation design.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a cradle-to-farm-gate agricultural carbon accounting model to quantitatively assess the green value of an AI-driven smart agriculture platform for tropical agriculture in Hainan, China. Under full adoption across three crop scenarios, the framework projects median reductions of 23.5% in pesticide use, 21.0% in fertilizer, 16.5% in irrigation water, and 21.5% in carbon intensity, with uncertainty propagated via Monte Carlo simulation and sensitivity analyzed through Sobol indices.
AI.motivation: Smart agriculture platforms are considered key carriers for China's pesticide/fertilizer reduction, water-saving, and carbon-reduction goals, yet there is no unified quantitative framework for assessing their green value.
AI.method: The study builds a cradle-to-farm-gate agricultural carbon accounting model covering pesticide/fertilizer production, field N2O, irrigation electricity, and paddy CH4. It translates platform interventions (LLM question answering, multimodal pest diagnosis, IoT sensing, satellite remote sensing, closed-loop field records) into quantifiable transmission parameters, then propagates uncertainty using Monte Carlo simulation over three Hainan crop scenarios (mango, winter vegetable, rice/nanfan, area-weighted 40%:30%:30%). Sobol first-order indices are used for variance decomposition, with convergence tests validating 10,000 iterations.
AI.result: Median reductions under full adoption: 23.5% (90% interval 15.0%-33.2%) for pesticide, 21.0% (13.8%-28.9%) for fertilizer, 16.5% (10.9%-23.5%) for irrigation water, and 21.5% (16.1%-27.2%) for carbon intensity. Attainment probabilities are high for fertilizer reduction ≥15% (90.6%) and carbon decline (98.1%), but only ~20% for aggregate water saving ≥20%. Soil-test recommendation and organic substitution jointly explain ~83% of variance in carbon-intensity reduction.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a reproducible, calibration-ready methodology for ex-ante green-value assessment and pilot observation design, supporting scenario-specific rather than blanket claims about platform green benefits.

title: Functional-SLAM: Interaction-Aware Mapping with Online Functional Scene Graphs
summary: Existing SLAM systems lack modeling of the functional relations required for fine-grained robotic interaction. Functional 3D scene graphs can represent relations between objects and interaction elements, but existing methods rely on offline reconstruction, making them inadequate for real-time interaction in real-world exploration. To address this limitation, we propose Functional-SLAM, the first framework that continuously and recursively maintains a functional scene graph as an online SLAM state. The framework combines anchor-keyframe geometry with functional-context constraints for persistent node maintenance, accumulates multi-frame evidence through temporal relations to commit stable functional edges, and supplements visual loop-closure candidates with functional topology in scenes with repetitive appearance or degraded texture. Experiments show that Functional-SLAM efficiently constructs stable functional maps online, substantially improving runtime over offline methods while maintaining highly competitive accuracy. Compared with peer SLAM systems, it further improves pose estimation accuracy through functional-topology-assisted loop closure. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/Hbelief1998/Functional-SLAM-CoRL_2026.

AI.tldr: Functional-SLAM is the first framework that continuously and recursively maintains a functional 3D scene graph as an online SLAM state, enabling fine-grained robotic interaction with functional relations in real-time. It combines anchor-keyframe geometry with functional-context constraints, accumulates multi-frame evidence for stable functional edges, and uses functional topology to assist loop closure. Experiments show substantial runtime improvements over offline methods while maintaining competitive accuracy, plus improved pose estimation through functional-topology-assisted loop closure.
AI.motivation: Existing SLAM systems lack modeling of functional relations needed for fine-grained robotic interaction. While functional 3D scene graphs can represent object-interaction relations, existing methods rely on offline reconstruction, which is inadequate for real-time interaction during real-world exploration.
AI.method: The framework maintains a functional scene graph continuously and recursively as an online SLAM state. It uses (1) anchor-keyframe geometry combined with functional-context constraints for persistent node maintenance, (2) temporal relations to accumulate multi-frame evidence for committing stable functional edges, and (3) functional topology to supplement visual loop-closure candidates in scenes with repetitive appearance or degraded texture.
AI.result: Functional-SLAM efficiently constructs stable functional maps online with substantially improved runtime over offline methods while maintaining highly competitive accuracy. Compared with peer SLAM systems, pose estimation accuracy is further improved via functional-topology-assisted loop closure.
AI.conclusion: Functional-SLAM demonstrates that functional scene graphs can be effectively embedded into online SLAM states, enabling real-time functional mapping and improved SLAM accuracy—bridging the gap between offline functional scene understanding and real-time robotic interaction.

title: Simulating the Marginal Green Contribution of AI Modules in a Smart-Agriculture Platform: Evidence from Two Monte Carlo Experiments
