comment: 10 pages, 5 figures, 5 tables; bilingual (Chinese title page with Chinese abstract, English full text); companion to platform-level green-value assessment; all results are ex-ante Monte Carlo simulation intervals, not field measurements
summary: Smart agriculture platforms usually bundle AI diagnosis, IoT sensing and decision push into a single package, so the green benefit attributable to each component remains unclear and resource-allocation decisions lack quantitative evidence. Building on a previous platform-level Monte Carlo assessment, this paper makes the components explicit and runs two controlled simulation experiments. Experiment 1 follows the chain from AI capability to farmer behavior to agrochemical input reduction, modeling pesticide/fertilizer reduction as avoidable blind-application share times prescription effectiveness times decision-touch coverage times adoption rate, and compares an experienced-extension mode with the AI mode: the probability of reaching 20% pesticide reduction is essentially zero in the extension mode but 20.7% at baseline, up to 49% with diagnosis accuracy 0.95 and adoption 0.85 under AI; the probability of 15% fertilizer reduction rises from near zero to 52.0%. Experiment 2 compares current practice (P0), IoT engineering retrofit (P1), and P1 plus AI irrigation scheduling (P2): median aggregate water saving rises from 7.8% (P0) to 11.0% (P1) and 16.0% (P2), with AI adding 5.0 percentage points beyond engineering; paddy CH4 reduction reaches 30.5% under AI scheduling versus 19.8% under manual operation, and the rice irrigation-methane subsystem carbon intensity declines 27.9%. Sensitivity analyses of both experiments consistently indicate that the primary bottleneck for meeting green targets is farmer adoption rather than algorithm accuracy, and that AI data fusion is robust to soil-moisture sensing errors. This work provides a reproducible simulation framework for component-level green-value evaluation and promotion-strategy optimization of smart agriculture platforms.

AI.tldr: This paper decomposes a smart agriculture platform into explicit components (AI diagnosis, IoT sensing, decision push) and uses two controlled Monte Carlo simulation experiments to quantify the green benefit attributable to each. Experiment 1 shows AI substantially outperforms experienced-extension for pesticide/fertilizer reduction (reaching 49% probability of 20% pesticide reduction at high accuracy/adoption), while Experiment 2 isolates IoT engineering retrofit from AI scheduling for water saving (7.8%→11.0%→16.0%) and methane reduction (30.5% under AI vs 19.8% manual). Sensitivity analyses show farmer adoption, not algorithm accuracy, is the binding constraint, and AI is robust to sensing errors.
AI.motivation: Smart agriculture platforms bundle AI diagnosis, IoT sensing, and decision push into one package, obscuring the individual green contribution of each component and leaving resource-allocation decisions without quantitative evidence.
AI.method: Extends a previous platform-level Monte Carlo assessment by making components explicit and running two controlled simulation experiments. Experiment 1 models pesticide/fertilizer reduction as avoidable blind-application share × prescription effectiveness × decision-touch coverage × adoption rate, comparing experienced-extension vs AI modes. Experiment 2 compares current practice (P0), IoT engineering retrofit (P1), and P1 plus AI irrigation scheduling (P2) for water saving and methane/carbon metrics, with sensitivity analyses on adoption, accuracy, and sensing errors.
AI.result: Experiment 1: probability of 20% pesticide reduction is ~0 under extension but up to 49% under AI (diagnosis accuracy 0.95, adoption 0.85); probability of 15% fertilizer reduction rises from near zero to 52.0%. Experiment 2: median aggregate water saving rises from 7.8% (P0) to 11.0% (P1) to 16.0% (P2), AI adds 5.0 pp beyond engineering; paddy CH4 reduction 30.5% under AI vs 19.8% under manual; rice irrigation-methane carbon intensity declines 27.9%. Sensitivity shows farmer adoption is the primary bottleneck, and AI data fusion is robust to soil-moisture sensing errors.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a reproducible simulation framework for component-level green-value evaluation and promotion-strategy optimization of smart agriculture platforms, enabling quantitative, evidence-based resource allocation across platform components.

title: CosmoH2G: A Hand-to-Gripper Transfer Dataset and Baseline Method for Object Manipulation with Complex Spatial Movements
summary: Transferring human hand demonstrations to robotic grippers has recently emerged as a cost-effective solution for robot learning. However, existing methods are largely confined to simple, planar tasks and fail to handle complex spatial movements (e.g., intricate trajectories involving rotations or flips) that are essential for robot manipulation. Motivated by this gap, we adopt an implicit, data-driven approach guided by fine-grained hand-pose motions. To this end, we introduce a scalable acquisition pipeline to collect hand-gripper paired demonstrations, governed by a rigorous protocol that prioritizes motion complexity and leverages a handheld gripper for seamless action mimicry. This yields a large-scale paired dataset comprising 6,189 episodes across 1,254 unique objects, exhibiting significantly higher spatial complexity than existing benchmarks. However, learning such complex mappings remains challenging. We observe that naive end-to-end generation of full gripper pose sequences is insufficient, as minor trajectory deviations compound rapidly under intricate dynamics. To address this, we propose a two-stage framework: Stage I predicts sparse gripper keyframes (initial and terminal) to simplify the mapping objective, while Stage II generates the full continuous action sequence conditioned on these keyframes. Furthermore, to mitigate cumulative drift, we keep the gripper's orientation being learned while post-optimizing its translation based on the grasping heuristic and kinematic consistency. In both simulation and real-robot experiments, our framework enables stable and precise hand-to-gripper transfer of complex spatial manipulations, significantly outperforming traditional baselines. Project page: https://cosmoh2g.github.io.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a scalable pipeline for collecting hand-gripper paired demonstrations and a two-stage framework for transferring complex spatial hand manipulations to robotic grippers, outperforming baselines in simulation and real-world experiments.
AI.motivation: Existing hand-to-gripper transfer methods are limited to simple, planar tasks and fail to handle complex spatial movements involving rotations and flips, which are essential for robot manipulation.
AI.method: A scalable acquisition pipeline collects 6,189 paired hand-gripper demonstration episodes across 1,254 objects using a handheld gripper and a protocol prioritizing motion complexity. Learning uses a two-stage framework: Stage I predicts sparse gripper keyframes (initial/terminal), and Stage II generates full continuous action sequences conditioned on these keyframes. Orientation is learned while translation is post-optimized to mitigate cumulative drift using grasping heuristics and kinematic consistency.
AI.result: The proposed framework demonstrates stable and precise hand-to-gripper transfer of complex spatial manipulations in both simulation and real-robot experiments, significantly outperforming traditional baselines on a benchmark with higher spatial complexity than existing datasets.
AI.conclusion: A two-stage keyframe-conditioned framework combined with a motion-complexity-prioritized data collection pipeline enables reliable transfer of intricate spatial hand demonstrations to robotic grippers, addressing a key limitation of prior planar-only approaches.

title: Reason Through the Latent! Making Latent Visual Reasoning Necessary
summary: Latent visual reasoning aims to perform multimodal reasoning through hidden-state computation rather than explicit textual chains of thought. However, visual information being present in a latent state does not imply that the model actually relies on that state when producing its answer, especially when alternative image-conditioned paths remain available. We introduce \textbf{C}ausal \textbf{V}isual \textbf{R}ecurrent \textbf{R}easoning (CVRR), which preserves pretrained visual competence while making recurrent computation the required image-conditioned path to prediction. CVRR initializes recurrence from the question hidden state after the pretrained vision-language model has incorporated the image, then repeatedly updates this state while re-reading the same fixed visual evidence. Before decoding, visual states and the original multimodal KV cache are removed so that only the final recurrent state carries image-conditioned information to the answer. Across the $V^*$, MMVP, BLINK, and MME-RealWorld-Lite benchmarks, CVRR retains strong performance under this strict interface, while compatible latent reasoners fail to recover comparable visual competence even when retrained under the same constraint. Causal interventions further show that predictions remain sensitive to recurrent content when the question is held fixed, and that persistent visual evidence causally revises the recurrent trajectory. These results distinguish latent informativeness from latent computation that is actually used for prediction.

AI.tldr: Introduces Causal Visual Recurrent Reasoning (CVRR), a method that makes recurrent computation the sole image-conditioned pathway to prediction in latent visual reasoning, ensuring the model actually relies on recurrent visual states rather than alternative image-conditioned paths. CVRR achieves strong performance across four benchmarks while compatible latent reasoners fail under the same constraint.
AI.motivation: Latent visual reasoning computes through hidden states rather than explicit textual chains of thought, but visual information present in a latent state does not guarantee the model actually uses it for prediction—alternative image-conditioned paths may remain available, conflating latent informativeness with latent computation actually used.
AI.method: CVRR initializes recurrence from the question hidden state after a pretrained vision-language model has incorporated the image, then repeatedly updates this state while re-reading the same fixed visual evidence. Before decoding, visual states and the original multimodal KV cache are removed so that only the final recurrent state carries image-conditioned information to the answer, making recurrent computation the required image-conditioned path.
AI.result: Across V*, MMVP, BLINK, and MME-RealWorld-Lite benchmarks, CVRR retains strong performance under the strict interface, while compatible latent reasoners fail to recover comparable visual competence even when retrained under the same constraint. Causal interventions show predictions remain sensitive to recurrent content with a fixed question, and persistent visual evidence causally revises the recurrent trajectory.
AI.conclusion: The work distinguishes latent informativeness from latent computation that is actually used for prediction, demonstrating that CVRR's architecture ensures causal reliance on recurrent visual states while preserving pretrained visual competence.

title: Generation of Vectorized Maps Beyond Vehicle View
summary: Autonomous driving relies on High Definition (HD) maps for safe navigation. Traditional HD maps construction is costly in hardware, data and human resources, which together with its update limitations hinders scalability. Recent works have proposed online alternatives for HD vectorized mapping from onboard sensors. However, sensor field of view is limited, and the range of the reconstructed maps ahead of the vehicle is insufficient for safe planning. This paper aims to address this limitation by proposing the novel beyond-view vectorized map generation problem: given vectorized maps of the area sensed by the vehicle (in-view), to generate plausible map continuations. To experimentally assess its feasibility, we propose BeyondFormer, which, to the best of out knowledge, is the first work designed towards beyond-view map generation. Given the novelty of the problem, we generate the first dataset specifically designed for it and evaluate the proposed approach. The results demonstrate consistent performance across diverse scenarios, establishing learning-based methods as a promising direction for map forecasting in autonomous driving. Beyond demonstrating the feasibility of the task, we provide an extensive discussion of the method's limitations and identify key future research directions for scaling it to more complex driving conditions. Code is available at https://git-autopia.car.upm-csic.es/beyondformer.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the novel beyond-view vectorized map generation problem for autonomous driving, proposing BeyondFormer—the first learning-based method to generate plausible map continuations beyond the sensor field of view from in-view vectorized maps—along with a new dataset, experimental validation, and discussion of limitations and future directions.
AI.motivation: Traditional HD map construction is costly in hardware, data, and human resources and suffers from scalability and update limitations. Online vectorized mapping from onboard sensors offers an alternative, but the reconstructed map range is limited by the sensor field of view, which is insufficient for safe planning.
AI.method: The authors formalize the beyond-view vectorized map generation problem: given vectorized maps of the sensed (in-view) area, generate plausible continuations of the map. They propose BeyondFormer, the first approach designed for this task, and create a dedicated dataset to evaluate it.
AI.result: BeyondFormer demonstrates consistent performance across diverse scenarios, showing that learning-based methods are a promising direction for map forecasting in autonomous driving. The feasibility of the beyond-view map generation task is established experimentally.
AI.conclusion: Beyond-view map generation is feasible with learning-based approaches like BeyondFormer, but the method has limitations that must be addressed to scale to more complex driving conditions. Several key future research directions are identified for advancing this task.

title: Improving Proficiency and Efficiency of Android GUI Agents via Self-Generating Tool Actions
summary: Android agents using a hybrid action space that combines GUI actions and tool actions (e.g., accessing application data via APIs) remain largely underexplored, mainly due to the excessive effort required to create tools. To address this gap, we introduce DroidTool, a framework for augmenting the agents with self-generated tools, which are realized as Python functions operating on application states (e.g., a database). To create tools with minimal human labor, DroidTool employs an agentic workflow featuring stages: proposal, implementation, test generation and execution, and repair. Notably, when testing the created tools for verification, it constructs relational tests across relevant tools for natural preparation of appropriate test preconditions and improved test coverage, rather than testing each tool separately. The GUI agents augmented with the generated tools achieved approximately 4.47%p higher performance with approximately 20.05% fewer interactions than the GUI-only agents, averaged across representative benchmarks: AndroidWorld, B-MoCA, and MobileSafetyBench.

AI.tldr: DroidTool is a framework that automatically generates Python-function tools operating on application states (e.g., databases) for Android agents using a hybrid action space combining GUI and tool actions. It employs an agentic workflow (proposal, implementation, test generation/execution, repair) with relational tests across tools, achieving ~4.47% higher performance with ~20.05% fewer interactions than GUI-only agents on AndroidWorld, B-MoCA, and MobileSafetyBench.
AI.motivation: Hybrid action spaces combining GUI and tool actions (e.g., API access) for Android agents remain underexplored because creating tools requires excessive manual effort. DroidTool addresses this by enabling self-generated tools with minimal human labor.
AI.method: DroidTool comprises an agentic workflow with stages: (1) proposal, (2) implementation, (3) test generation and execution, and (4) repair. Tools are realized as Python functions operating on application states (e.g., a database). For verification, it constructs relational tests across relevant tools to naturally prepare test preconditions and improve test coverage, rather than testing each tool in isolation.
AI.result: GUI agents augmented with DroidTool-generated tools achieved approximately 4.47 percentage points higher performance with approximately 20.05% fewer interactions than GUI-only agents, averaged across AndroidWorld, B-MoCA, and MobileSafetyBench.
AI.conclusion: Self-generated tools via an automated agentic workflow can effectively augment Android GUI agents, improving task performance while reducing interaction costs, demonstrating the viability of hybrid action spaces without excessive manual tool creation.

title: P$^2$Calib: Utilizing Pattern Priors for LiDAR-Camera Extrinsic Calibration
summary: Target-based LiDAR-camera extrinsic calibration is a prerequisite for multi-sensor fusion in robotics. However, in the widely adopted four-hole pipeline, calibration accuracy is bottlenecked by LiDAR-side hole-center extraction, which suffers from sparse angular coverage and mixed-pixel corruption. This paper presents P$^2$Calib, which exploits pattern priors, geometric constraints specified by the CAD model of the target board, to improve calibration accuracy. First, we incorporate the known hole radius as a fitting constraint to prevent center estimates from degrading under sparse angular coverage. Building on the improved hole estimates, we further enforce the rigid rectangular layout of the four holes as a global consistency constraint to correct residual errors across holes. Both priors are integrated into an interactive calibration tool that provides a complete extrinsic calibration pipeline. Experiments on simulated and real datasets show that P$^2$Calib lowers the joint registration residual by 90\% and 82\% and the held-out reprojection error by 96\% and 77\% over the baseline. Code, https://github.com/JokerJohn/P2Calib.git, and data will be released to facilitate future research.

AI.tldr: P²Calib is a LiDAR-camera extrinsic calibration method that leverages CAD-model pattern priors of a four-hole target board to overcome the accuracy bottleneck caused by sparse angular coverage and mixed-pixel corruption in LiDAR-side hole-center extraction, achieving 90%/82% lower joint registration residual and 96%/77% lower held-out reprojection error on simulated/real datasets.
AI.motivation: In the four-hole LiDAR-camera calibration pipeline, calibration accuracy is bottlenecked by LiDAR-side hole-center extraction, which degrades under sparse angular coverage and mixed-pixel corruption. Improving extrinsic calibration accuracy requires addressing this fundamental limitation.
AI.method: P²Calib exploits two pattern priors derived from the CAD model of the target board: (1) the known hole radius is used as a fitting constraint to prevent center estimation degradation under sparse angular coverage; (2) the rigid rectangular layout of the four holes is enforced as a global consistency constraint to correct residual errors across holes. Both priors are integrated into an interactive calibration tool providing a complete extrinsic calibration pipeline.
AI.result: Experiments on simulated and real datasets demonstrate that P²Calib reduces the joint registration residual by 90% and 82%, and the held-out reprojection error by 96% and 77%, respectively, over the baseline.
AI.conclusion: P²Calib demonstrates that exploiting CAD-derived geometric priors of the target board can substantially improve LiDAR-camera extrinsic calibration accuracy, and the authors plan to release code and data to support future research.

title: Unsound Search with Policy and Value Networks in Legends of Code and Magic
comment: 6 pages, 3 figures, 1 table. Also available as a Zenodo preprint, doi:10.5281/zenodo.22547763
summary: Decision-time search in perfect and imperfect information games with enumerable belief states are effective methods for game AI. Collectible card games are imperfect information games with large belief states. Legends of Code and Magic is a collectible card game competition where the belief states are $2^{101}$. The Legends of Code and Magic (LoCM) champion, ByteRL, plays with no search. Other works claim sound enumeration-based search is unusable in the genre due to the number of belief states. We measured three previously defined properties that predict where theoretically unsound perfect information Monte Carlo's defects are cheap and found LoCM sits in the favorable region. Starting with imitation learning of the runner-up policy, NeteaseOPD, we created a policy and value feed-forward network. Our agent searches over worlds sampled from a prior over the opponent's deck built from the runner-up's drafts. Using our strictest configuration in the battle phase we beat ByteRL with a win percentage of 51.35% 95% CI [50.37, 52.33], over 10,000 pre-registered games using the LoCM official referee and time limit. Search is not a minor factor on the matchup between our agent and ByteRL. Without search this agent scores 26.8% and adding search adds +24.6 points. Unsound search in imperfect information games could be exploitable. We replicate a published best-response attack against ByteRL. We then apply the same attack protocol to two search configurations of our agent, and each one resists it better than ByteRL at every iteration. In LoCM unsound search gives us a stronger and more resilient agent.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates that unsound (imperfect-information-Monte-Carlo style) decision-time search can be effectively applied to Legends of Code and Magic (LoCM), a collectible card game with huge belief states ($2^{101}$). By combining imitation learning from the runner-up policy with search over sampled worlds, the authors build an agent that beats the champion ByteRL (51.35% win rate with strict search config) while also being more robust to best-response attacks than ByteRL.
AI.motivation: Collectible card games have enormous belief states making exact search intractable, and prior work argued sound enumeration-based search is unusable in this genre. The champion agent ByteRL uses no search. The authors aim to show that theoretically unsound perfect-information Monte Carlo search can nevertheless be effective and practical in such games when placed in the right region of game-dependent properties.
AI.method: The authors measure three previously defined game properties that predict when unsound perfect-information Monte Carlo search defects are cheap, and find LoCM sits in a favorable region. They train a policy and value feed-forward network via imitation learning from the runner-up agent NeteaseOPD. The agent performs decision-time search over worlds sampled from a prior over the opponent's deck, constructed from the runner-up's drafts. They evaluate the strictest search configuration against ByteRL under the official referee with pre-registered games, and also run best-response attacks against both ByteRL and their search-based agents.
AI.result: The search-enabled agent beats ByteRL with a 51.35% win rate (95% CI [50.37, 52.33]) over 10,000 pre-registered games. Without search the agent scores only 26.8%; adding search adds +24.6 points, showing search is a significant factor. Against best-response attacks, both search configurations of the new agent resist better than ByteRL at every iteration.
AI.conclusion: Unsound search is viable and advantageous in imperfect-information collectible card games like LoCM, contradicting prior claims that such search is unusable in the genre. It yields both a stronger and more resilient agent, though the authors caution that unsound search could be exploitable in general imperfect-information settings.

title: PhysReal: Learning Real-World Deformable Object Physics via Hybrid Constitutive Modeling
summary: Learning physically plausible dynamics from visual observations is essential for interactive world models and embodied agents. However, modeling real-world deformable objects remains challenging because their dynamics often arise from complex, spatially heterogeneous material responses. To address this challenge, we propose PhysReal, a video-driven framework for learning and simulating the underlying physics of real deformable objects. PhysReal integrates a spatially varying hybrid expert-neural constitutive model with a differentiable MPM simulator and 3DGS renderer. Analytical expert models provide interpretable physical priors, while neural constitutive residuals capture material responses beyond predefined formulations. Spatially distributed patches parameterize the constitutive field, enabling a continuous representation of local material variations. To organize the identification of this model from sparse visual observations, we adopt a progressive curriculum that sequentially optimizes global material properties, spatially varying local parameters, and neural constitutive residuals, together with complementary motion and mask supervision. Extensive experiments on diverse deformable-object interactions demonstrate that PhysReal achieves superior performance in dynamic reconstruction and future-state prediction, while showing strong potential for downstream robotic applications.

AI.tldr: PhysReal is a video-driven framework that learns and simulates physically plausible dynamics of real deformable objects by integrating a spatially varying hybrid expert-neural constitutive model with a differentiable MPM simulator and 3DGS renderer, using a progressive curriculum for parameter identification from sparse visual observations.
AI.motivation: Modeling real-world deformable objects is challenging because their dynamics arise from complex, spatially heterogeneous material responses, which are difficult to capture with existing approaches. Learning physically plausible dynamics from visual observations is essential for interactive world models and embodied agents.
AI.method: PhysReal integrates a spatially varying hybrid expert-neural constitutive model with a differentiable MPM (Material Point Method) simulator and 3DGS (3D Gaussian Splatting) renderer. Analytical expert models provide interpretable physical priors while neural constitutive residuals capture material responses beyond predefined formulations. Spatially distributed patches parameterize the constitutive field for continuous local material variation representation. A progressive curriculum sequentially optimizes global material properties, spatially varying local parameters, and neural constitutive residuals with complementary motion and mask supervision.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on diverse deformable-object interactions show PhysReal achieves superior performance in dynamic reconstruction and future-state prediction, with strong potential for downstream robotic applications.
AI.conclusion: PhysReal demonstrates that combining physically interpretable expert priors with neural residuals and spatially varying constitutive parameterization within a differentiable simulation-rendering pipeline enables accurate and generalizable learning of real deformable object physics from video.

title: Formation of structural attractors in neuromorphic systems
summary: This paper examines the theory of Invariant Structural Learning (ISL), which proposes a non-optimization approach to concept formation. Learning is interpreted as convergence to structural attractors in a hypergraph space, rather than as the minimization of a global loss function. The paper presents the ISL model, including its mathematical formalization, computational verification, and a hypothetical neurobiological interpretation. The mathematical section introduces the formal apparatus of the structural reduction process and proves its finite convergence, the existence and uniqueness of class structural attractors, and the self-organization of attractor maps. The computational section demonstrates the feasibility of the proposed approach on classical image recognition tasks, utilizing the proposed learning mechanism without backpropagation and with extremely small training datasets. Finally, the neurobiological section formulates hypotheses regarding the possible implementation of structural attractors in dendritic trees, neural coding as a projection of internal attractor dynamics, and the development of neural architectures supporting the proposed learning concept. These hypotheses are discussed in the context of modern experimental data in the fields of dendritic computations, synaptic plasticity, and the structural organization of neural circuits. The proposed neurobiological mechanisms are presented as testable hypotheses rather than established biological facts. The results demonstrate the mathematical consistency and computational feasibility of the proposed model, while the neurobiological hypotheses outline potential directions for its experimental verification.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Invariant Structural Learning (ISL), a non-optimization framework for concept formation based on convergence to structural attractors in hypergraph space, and demonstrates its mathematical consistency, computational feasibility on image recognition tasks without backpropagation using minimal training data, and proposes testable neurobiological hypotheses for its implementation in dendritic trees and neural circuits.
AI.motivation: The paper challenges the dominant paradigm of learning as loss-function minimization (e.g., backpropagation-based deep learning), proposing an alternative conceptualization where learning emerges from structural dynamics converging to attractors in a hypergraph space—potentially more aligned with biological neural computation.
AI.method: The ISL model is formalized through: (1) mathematical proofs of finite convergence of structural reduction, existence/uniqueness of class structural attractors, and self-organization of attractor maps; (2) computational experiments on classical image recognition tasks using the ISL mechanism without backpropagation and with extremely small training datasets; (3) speculative neurobiological hypotheses linking structural attractors to dendritic tree computations, neural coding as projections of internal attractor dynamics, and neural architecture development, evaluated against modern experimental data.
AI.result: The paper establishes mathematical consistency of the ISL framework through formal proofs, demonstrates computational feasibility on image recognition tasks with a non-backpropagation learning mechanism requiring minimal training data, and outlines neurobiological hypotheses that are consistent with (though not confirmed by) current experimental findings in dendritic computation, synaptic plasticity, and neural circuit organization.
AI.conclusion: ISL offers a mathematically sound and computationally viable alternative to optimization-based learning, with the neurobiological hypotheses providing clearly articulated, testable predictions for future experimental validation rather than claims of established biological mechanisms.

title: Zero-Shot Sim-to-Real Contact-Rich Assembly via Proprioception-Anchored Cross-Modal Pretraining
summary: Contact-rich assembly remains challenging because it requires submillimeter spatial accuracy and reliable interpretation of forces during sustained contact. Although simulation-based reinforcement learning offers a scalable training paradigm, discrepancies in visual observations, contact dynamics, and force/torque (F/T) measurements often limit policy transfer. We observe that proprioception is comparatively consistent across domains because calibrated joint positions and consistently computed joint velocities align closely between simulation and hardware. Based on this observation, we present PACE (Proprioception-Anchored Cross-Modal Encoder), which supervises temporal visual and F/T representations by predicting proprioceptive state transitions. Static domain-specific factors, including lighting, texture, and sensor bias, contain little information about joint motion; the proposed objective therefore encourages the encoder to suppress these factors while retaining task-relevant motion cues. Policies trained on frozen PACE features are deployed on hardware without real-world fine-tuning or object-pose tracking. Across four contact-rich assembly tasks, PACE attains an average real-world success rate of 93.3\% and only a 2.7-percentage-point sim-to-real drop, meanwhile remaining robust to perturbations that substantially degrade pose-based and learned-fusion baselines.

AI.tldr: PACE is a proprioception-anchored cross-modal encoder that supervises temporal visual and F/T representations by predicting proprioceptive state transitions, enabling effective zero-shot sim-to-real transfer for contact-rich assembly tasks by suppressing domain-specific factors while retaining task-relevant motion cues. It achieves 93.3% average real-world success across four assembly tasks with only a 2.7-percentage-point sim-to-real drop.
AI.motivation: Contact-rich assembly requires submillimeter accuracy and reliable force interpretation during sustained contact. While simulation-based RL offers scalable training, discrepancies in visual observations, contact dynamics, and F/T measurements limit policy transfer. However, proprioception is comparatively consistent across simulation and hardware, suggesting it can serve as a stable anchor.
AI.method: PACE supervises temporal visual and F/T representations by predicting proprioceptive state transitions. The training objective encourages the encoder to suppress static domain-specific factors (lighting, texture, sensor bias) that carry little information about joint motion, while retaining task-relevant motion cues. Policies are trained on frozen PACE features and deployed without fine-tuning or object-pose tracking.
AI.result: Across four contact-rich assembly tasks, PACE achieves an average real-world success rate of 93.3% with only a 2.7-percentage-point sim-to-real gap, while remaining robust to perturbations that substantially degrade pose-based and learned-fusion baselines.
AI.conclusion: Anchoring cross-modal representation learning to proprioceptive state transitions provides an effective mechanism for domain-invariant feature extraction, enabling strong zero-shot transfer of contact-rich assembly policies from simulation to real hardware.

title: NormViz: A Benchmark and Framework for Grounding Multimodal Reasoning in Global Cultures
comment: Accepted to Conference on Language Modeling (COLM) 2026. 37 pages, 23 figures
summary: AI systems are used worldwide, but they struggle to serve the needs of culturally diverse populations. Prior work on cultural understanding evaluates AI systems on text-only settings or on visual artifact recognition (e.g. foods, clothing). The ability to reason about visually observable behaviors through local social norms, which we call visual norm understanding, remains unexamined. We introduce NormViz-Bench, a high quality, human-validated benchmark of 3,268 contrastive image pairs (6,536 images) spanning 16 countries. Each pair varies only in the culturally relevant behavior (e.g., objects, attributes, spatial relations, and actions) that alters how each image is interpreted. Each image is labeled as conforming to, violating, or irrelevant to local social norms, and pair-level evaluation requires both images to be correctly classified, thereby preventing reliance on superficial visual shortcuts. Even the strongest VLMs, Gemini 3.0 Flash and Qwen2.5 VL 7B, succeed on only 26.6% and 21.6% of pairs, struggling most with identifying violating and culturally benign visual behaviors. Towards bridging this, we introduce NormViz-Train, a training dataset of 64k images paired with explanations. Though absolute performance remains low (<30%), finetuning on NormViz-Train improves pair accuracy relatively by up to 125% and 36% Qwen3-VL 4B and 8B respectively, showing a path forward to teach models to connect visual perception to cultural significance. Together, NormViz-Bench and NormViz-Train establish visual norm understanding as a challenging and consequential frontier for multimodal AI.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces NormViz-Bench, a human-validated benchmark of 3,268 contrastive image pairs (6,536 images) across 16 countries for evaluating visual norm understanding—the ability to reason about culturally appropriate behaviors through images. State-of-the-art VLMs achieve only 21.6-26.6% pair accuracy. The authors also release NormViz-Train (64k images with explanations), which improves pair accuracy relatively by up to 125% after finetuning, establishing this task as a challenging frontier for multimodal AI.
AI.motivation: Existing cultural understanding benchmarks evaluate AI on text-only settings or visual artifact recognition (e.g., foods, clothing), but fail to examine whether AI can reason about visually observable behaviors through local social norms—a capability termed visual norm understanding. This gap matters because AI systems deployed globally need to serve culturally diverse populations appropriately.
AI.method: The authors construct NormViz-Bench, a human-validated benchmark with 3,268 contrastive image pairs spanning 16 countries, where each pair differs only in culturally relevant behaviors (objects, attributes, spatial relations, actions) that change interpretation. Images are labeled as conforming to, violating, or irrelevant to local norms. Pair-level evaluation requires both images to be correctly classified to prevent superficial shortcut reliance. They also build NormViz-Train, a 64k-image training dataset with explanations, and finetune VLM models on it.
AI.result: Strongest VLMs (Gemini 3.0 Flash and Qwen2.5 VL 7B) succeed on only 26.6% and 21.6% of pairs respectively, struggling most with identifying violating and culturally benign visual behaviors. Finetuning on NormViz-Train improves pair accuracy relatively by up to 125% (Qwen3-VL 4B) and 36% (Qwen3-VL 8B), though absolute performance remains below 30%.
AI.conclusion: Visual norm understanding is a challenging and consequential frontier for multimodal AI, and while finetuning on NormViz-Train demonstrates a promising path to connect visual perception with cultural significance, current models still perform far below adequate levels, highlighting substantial room for future progress.

title: Anti-Gravity Walking by a Flying Humanoid Robot via Thrust-Rate Input Whole-Body Model Predictive Control
summary: Flying humanoids are expected to perform tasks in diverse environments, while their existing locomotion is mainly limited to aerial flight and ground walking. The capability to move in complex three-dimensional space can greatly expand their application range. For such walking motion on ceilings and similar anti-gravity environments, whole-body MPC is effective. However, the discontinuous changes in dynamic structure accompanying contact switching during walking can induce thrust spikes, resulting in control instability. Therefore, in this work, we propose and implement a real-time whole-body MPC framework for anti-gravity bipedal walking. First, we formulate whole-body MPC using the time derivative of thrust, namely thrust-rate, as the control input. This formulation guarantees continuity of the thrust trajectory during contact switching while preserving the sparse structure of the optimal control problem for fast computation. Second, we address the lack of natural support forces in anti-gravity environments. We introduce lower bounds on the foot-normal component of the contact force, and smoothly transfer them during the doublesupport phase. Finally, we implement the proposed framework and demonstrate anti-gravity walking by a flying humanoid through simulation and a hardware experiment. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first demonstration of multi-contact whole-body MPC for a transformable aerial robot and walking by a flying humanoid beyond the ground.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a real-time whole-body MPC framework for anti-gravity bipedal walking of flying humanoids (e.g., on ceilings), using thrust-rate as the control input to ensure thrust continuity during contact switching, and introducing lower bounds on foot-normal contact forces with smooth transitions during double support to address the lack of natural support in anti-gravity environments. The framework is validated via simulation and hardware experiments, marking the first demonstration of multi-contact whole-body MPC for transformable aerial robots walking beyond the ground.
AI.motivation: Flying humanoids are limited to aerial flight and ground walking, and cannot navigate complex 3D environments such as ceilings. Whole-body MPC is effective for anti-gravity walking but suffers from thrust spikes and control instability due to discontinuous dynamic structure changes during contact switching. Additionally, anti-gravity environments lack natural support forces, which must be addressed for stable walking.
AI.method: 1) Formulate whole-body MPC with thrust-rate (time derivative of thrust) as the control input, ensuring thrust trajectory continuity during contact switching while preserving sparse optimal control structure for real-time computation. 2) Introduce lower bounds on the foot-normal component of contact forces to compensate for the lack of natural support in anti-gravity environments, with smooth force transfer during the double-support phase. 3) Implement the framework on a flying humanoid and validate via simulation and hardware experiments.
AI.result: The proposed framework was successfully implemented and demonstrated anti-gravity walking by a flying humanoid in both simulation and hardware experiments. This is the first demonstration of multi-contact whole-body MPC for a transformable aerial robot and walking by a flying humanoid beyond ground-level environments.
AI.conclusion: Using thrust-rate as a control input in whole-body MPC effectively eliminates thrust spikes during contact switching, and the introduction of contact force lower bounds enables stable anti-gravity walking. The work opens new possibilities for flying humanoids to expand locomotion beyond ground and aerial modes to arbitrary 3D surfaces.

title: Learning transferable human physiology from two million hours of sleep with SleepFM-2
summary: Sleep provides a nightly window into health by capturing coordinated activity across the brain, heart, muscles and respiratory system. We introduce SleepFM-2, a sleep foundation model developed and evaluated on 282,511 polysomnography recordings from 26 cohorts, including 235,865 used for pretraining. These data span more than two million hours of multimodal physiology. Compared with SleepFM, SleepFM-2 improves disease prediction and sleep scoring, supports arousal, limb movement and respiratory event detection, and transfers to wearable sensing and subjective sleep phenotypes. A model combining its PSG representation with age, sex and BMI met a prespecified discrimination and significance criterion for 215 subsequently recorded EHR phenotypes in two held-out cohorts, including one health system unseen during pretraining. For 155 phenotypes, the PSG representation added reproducible information beyond demographics. SleepFM-2 also outperformed a 480-feature baseline derived from the same recordings. Its disease scores revealed a reproducible principal component associated with reduced sigma-band spatial coupling and increased hypnodensity entropy. The frozen encoder performed within the observed range of expert scorers for sleep events and transferred to wakeful EEG, headband and in-ear EEG, wrist PPG and wrist accelerometry. It improved sleep staging across six accelerometry cohorts and achieved disease-prediction performance in UK Biobank similar to models pretrained directly on accelerometry. Finally, SleepFM-2 captured aspects of subjective sleep not recovered by conventional PSG summaries, particularly reports of the recorded night. These results show that multimodal sleep physiology can provide a transferable representation of human health across diseases, clinical tasks, sensors and subjective experience.

AI.tldr: SleepFM-2 is a sleep foundation model pretrained on 282,511 polysomnography recordings (235,865 for pretraining) spanning over two million hours of multimodal physiology across 26 cohorts. It improves disease prediction and sleep scoring over SleepFM, supports event detection (arousals, limb movements, respiratory events), transfers to wearable sensors and subjective sleep phenotypes, and combines PSG representations with demographics to meet prespecified discrimination criteria for 215 EHR phenotypes in held-out cohorts.
AI.motivation: Sleep provides a rich, nightly window into health through coordinated activity across brain, heart, muscles, and respiratory systems, yet previous models (e.g., SleepFM) lacked scale and generalizability. The authors aim to build a large-scale sleep foundation model that transfers across clinical tasks, sensors, and diverse health phenotypes to provide a unified representation of human health from sleep physiology.
AI.method: SleepFM-2 is pretrained on 282,511 polysomnography recordings from 26 cohorts (235,865 used for pretraining) totaling over two million hours of multimodal physiology. It performs disease prediction, sleep scoring, event detection (arousals, limb movements, respiratory events), and transfer to wearable sensing (wakeful EEG, headband/in-ear EEG, wrist PPG, wrist accelerometry) and subjective sleep phenotypes. Evaluations include held-out phenotype discrimination against prespecified criteria, comparison to a 480-feature baseline, and UK Biobank accelerometry transfer.
AI.result: A combined PSG representation with age, sex, and BMI met prespecified discrimination/significance criteria for 215 EHR phenotypes in two held-out cohorts (including an unseen health system). For 155 phenotypes, the PSG representation added reproducible information beyond demographics. The model outperformed a 480-feature baseline, revealed a reproducible principal component tied to reduced sigma-band spatial coupling and increased hypnodensity entropy, performed within expert scoring range on sleep events, improved sleep staging across six accelerometry cohorts, achieved UK Biobank disease prediction comparable to models pretrained directly on accelerometry, and captured aspects of subjective sleep (especially night-of-recording reports) beyond conventional PSG summaries.
AI.conclusion: Multimodal sleep physiology can provide a transferable representation of human health across diseases, clinical tasks, sensors, and subjective experience, demonstrating that foundation models trained on large-scale polysomnography can generalize broadly beyond their pretraining scope.

title: ICI-VLA: In-Context Imitation with Spatiotemporally Aligned Demonstrations for Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies are commonly adapted to new manipulation settings through additional gradient updates, which limits rapid deployment when task-specific data or compute is scarce. We present ICI-VLA, a training and retrieval framework that equips a text-action VLM with few-shot test-time adaptation through in-context demonstrations. Unlike mainstream VLA designs based on action-specific multimodal fusion, ICI-VLA retains the native text-generation interface. ICI-VLA updates its parameters only during offline training; at inference, the policy remains fixed and conditions action generation on retrieved micro-demonstrations. The framework decomposes long trajectories into short, semantically labeled examples and trains an RD-Encoder with positives mined by Dynamic Time Warping (DTW), aligning the retrieved context with the phase and geometry of the current subtask. We further introduce Target Action Masking, a context-corruption objective designed to reduce direct action copying and increase reliance on the current observation. ICI-VLA reaches average success rates of 97.7% on LIBERO and 60.4% on RoboTwin 2.0, exceeding the highest reported baseline average on RoboTwin 2.0 by 19.3 percentage points. It also achieves 83.2% across four physical tasks. These results indicate that a fixed VLA policy can benefit from conditioning on spatiotemporally aligned demonstrations at test time.

AI.tldr: ICI-VLA is a training and retrieval framework that equips a text-action VLM with few-shot test-time adaptation through in-context demonstrations, retaining the native text-generation interface. It decomposes long trajectories into short semantically labeled examples, uses DTW-based positive mining for retrieval encoding, and introduces Target Action Masking to prevent direct action copying. It achieves 97.7% success on LIBERO, 60.4% on RoboTwin 2.0 (+19.3 pp over the best baseline), and 83.2% across four physical tasks, demonstrating that a fixed VLA policy can benefit from spatiotemporally aligned demonstrations at test time.
AI.motivation: Standard VLA policies require additional gradient updates to adapt to new manipulation settings, which limits rapid deployment when task-specific data or compute is scarce. The paper seeks to enable few-shot adaptation without parameter updates at inference time.
AI.method: ICI-VLA (1) retains the native text-generation interface of a VLM rather than using action-specific multimodal fusion; (2) only updates parameters during offline training while the policy stays fixed at inference; (3) decomposes long trajectories into short, semantically labeled examples; (4) trains an RD-Encoder with positives mined via Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) to align retrieved context with the phase and geometry of the current subtask; (5) introduces Target Action Masking, a context-corruption objective that reduces direct action copying and increases reliance on current observations.
AI.result: ICI-VLA achieves average success rates of 97.7% on LIBERO and 60.4% on RoboTwin 2.0, surpassing the best reported baseline average on RoboTwin 2.0 by 19.3 percentage points, and 83.2% across four physical tasks.
AI.conclusion: A fixed VLA policy that remains unchanged at inference can effectively benefit from conditioning on spatiotemporally aligned in-context demonstrations at test time, enabling rapid few-shot adaptation without additional gradient updates.

title: A visual large language foundational model for medical image recognition using clinician-oriented social media
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities across diverse domains, showing considerable potential in medicine. However, their application in medical settings remains limited by the scarcity of visual question answering (VQA) datasets that capture clinical reasoning and explicit image-text alignment. Here, we leverage de-identified medical images and expert commentaries shared on clinician-oriented social media. By combining an advanced LLM with clinician-in-the-loop verification, we established a rigorous pipeline to construct ThoughtMed-1M, a long-form medical VQA dataset containing over one million VQA pairs and designed to capture structured clinical logic and medical image-text alignment. To demonstrate its utility, we developed a FOundational LLM Trained on ThoughtMed-1M (FOLTMed). FOLTMed achieved state-of-the-art performance across 42 medical VQA benchmark datasets, with a macro accuracy of 85.4%, and generated more clinically coherent responses on the ThoughtMed-1M test set. It outperformed state-of-the-art models by 3--5% across factuality and similarity metrics, highlighting a scalable paradigm for advancing research on clinically grounded multimodal LLMs.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ThoughtMed-1M, a large-scale long-form medical VQA dataset with over one million question-answer pairs built from de-identified medical images and expert clinician commentary through a pipeline combining advanced LLMs and clinician-in-the-loop verification. The authors also present FOLTMed, a foundational multimodal LLM trained on this dataset, which achieves state-of-the-art results across 42 medical VQA benchmarks with 85.4% macro accuracy.
AI.motivation: The application of LLMs in medical settings is limited by the scarcity of visual question answering datasets that capture clinical reasoning and explicit image-text alignment, which are necessary for clinically grounded multimodal understanding.
AI.method: The authors construct ThoughtMed-1M by leveraging de-identified medical images and expert commentaries from clinician-oriented social media, using an advanced LLM combined with clinician-in-the-loop verification in a rigorous pipeline. They then train FOLTMed, a foundational multimodal LLM, on this dataset.
AI.result: FOLTMed achieved state-of-the-art performance on 42 medical VQA benchmark datasets with a macro accuracy of 85.4%, and outperformed state-of-the-art models by 3-5% across factuality and similarity metrics on the ThoughtMed-1M test set while generating more clinically coherent responses.
AI.conclusion: The work highlights a scalable paradigm for advancing research on clinically grounded multimodal LLMs, demonstrating that combining expert knowledge curation with LLM-generated data can produce high-quality medical VQA resources.

title: Dex-X: Learning Visual-Tactile Dexterous Manipulation From Human Videos with Simulated Interaction
summary:
Human videos are an abundant source of dexterous manipulation behaviors, but they lack tactile information that is crucial for contact-rich interaction. This raises a fundamental question: can robots learn deployable visual-tactile dexterous manipulation policies from human video demonstrations without robot-side data collection?
  We present DEX-X, a framework for learning visual-tactile dexterous manipulation from human videos through simulation. Our key insight is that simulation can serve as a tactile completion engine. Given monocular human demonstrations, DEX-X reconstructs hand-object interactions in simulation, where physically grounded contact dynamics provide tactile supervision unavailable in the original videos. Leveraging this recovered tactile information, we train visual-tactile dexterous manipulation policies and distill them into deployable policies operating on point-cloud observations and tactile sensing.
  We demonstrate zero-shot sim-to-real transfer on a dexterous hand-arm platform across diverse grasping and contact-rich tool-use tasks. The teacher policy achieves 65.9% average success across six task categories in simulation, while the distilled visual-tactile policy achieves 93% success on real-world cube picking and 53% on the challenging table-cleaning task. Zero-shot generalization to unseen object geometries is also observed on object-picking tasks.
  Our results suggest that simulated interaction is a key bridge between human videos and deployable dexterous manipulation policies, providing the missing physical supervision needed for scalable robot skill learning from Internet-scale human video data.

AI.tldr: DEX-X is a framework that learns deployable visual-tactile dexterous manipulation policies from human videos by using simulation as a tactile completion engine. It reconstructs hand-object interactions in simulation to recover physically grounded tactile supervision absent in the original videos, then trains and distills policies that operate on point-cloud and tactile observations, achieving zero-shot sim-to-real transfer on grasping and tool-use tasks.
AI.motivation: Human videos provide abundant dexterous manipulation demonstrations but lack tactile information essential for contact-rich interactions. The authors aim to answer whether robots can learn deployable visual-tactile policies from human video demonstrations without requiring robot-side data collection, addressing the scalability bottleneck in robot skill learning.
AI.method: DEX-X reconstructs hand-object interactions in simulation from monocular human videos. Simulation provides physically grounded contact dynamics that serve as tactile supervision. A visual-tactile teacher policy is trained using this recovered tactile information, then distilled into deployable policies operating on point-cloud observations and tactile sensing, enabling zero-shot sim-to-real transfer.
AI.result: The teacher policy achieves 65.9% average success across six task categories in simulation. The distilled visual-tactile policy achieves 93% success on real-world cube picking and 53% on a challenging table-cleaning task. Zero-shot generalization to unseen object geometries was also observed on object-picking tasks.
AI.conclusion: Simulated interaction serves as a key bridge between human video demonstrations and deployable dexterous manipulation policies, providing the missing physical supervision needed for scalable robot skill learning from Internet-scale human video data.

title: When and Why LLM Causal Priors Help: Closed-Loop Prior Selection for Amortized Causal Inference
summary: Causal effect estimation asks how an outcome would change under an intervention, and medicine, economics, and public policy all treat it as a foundational task. Prior-data fitted networks (PFNs) amortize the task: a model trained on large numbers of programmatically generated synthetic causal tasks reads a new problem's observational data into context and returns an interventional-effect estimate in a single forward pass. The capability of such models is largely determined by the synthetic training prior, which is currently designed by hand, a bottleneck acknowledged by both Do-PFN and CausalPFN. Large language models (LLMs) can now ``draw'' plausible causal graphs for a given domain, suggesting that LLM-distilled graphs could serve as prior material. Whether injecting such graphs helps at all, where any gain comes from, and when injection helps. Practice has so far relied on manual trial and error. We propose a \emph{closed-loop prior selection framework} that casts prior injection as a budget-constrained optimization over a candidate prior pool. Candidates undergo cheap post-training and are scored by a composite metric dominated by real-domain generalization; the winner then receives full training and paired statistical validation. On a 7.34M-parameter Do-PFN, the framework's winner attains a formally significant $2.75\times$ gain on the primary evaluation domain, and its error falls below that of the uninjected official base. Generalization on an adjacent monitoring domain improves significantly, and no monitored capability degrades. Mechanism experiments show that the gain depends on the semantic content of the distilled graph rather than its structural diversity alone does not produce it (directional evidence). With this framework and this regularity in hand, the use of LLM causal priors stops being manual trial and error and becomes an empirically verifiable selection problem.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a closed-loop prior selection framework for causal effect estimation with Prior-data Fitted Networks (PFNs). Rather than manually designing synthetic training priors or blindly injecting LLM-distilled causal graphs, the framework casts prior injection as a budget-constrained optimization over a candidate prior pool, where candidates undergo cheap post-training, are scored by a composite metric dominated by real-domain generalization, and the winner receives full training and statistical validation. On a 7.34M-parameter Do-PFN, the framework achieves a statistically significant 2.75x gain on the primary evaluation domain with no capability degradation, and mechanism experiments reveal the gain stems from semantic content of the distilled graph rather than structural diversity alone.
AI.motivation: Causal effect estimation is foundational across medicine, economics, and public policy. PFNs amortize this task but their capability is determined by synthetic training priors that are currently designed by hand—a recognized bottleneck by both Do-PFN and CausalPFN. While LLMs can generate plausible causal graphs that could serve as prior material, whether such injection helps, where gains come from, and when to inject has relied on manual trial and error rather than a principled framework.
AI.method: The authors propose a closed-loop prior selection framework that treats prior injection as a budget-constrained optimization over a candidate prior pool. Candidates are generated (e.g., LLM-distilled causal graphs), undergo cheap post-training, and are scored by a composite metric dominated by real-domain generalization. The winning candidate receives full training followed by paired statistical validation. Mechanism experiments are conducted to isolate whether gains come from semantic content of graphs or merely structural diversity.
AI.result: On a 7.34M-parameter Do-PFN, the framework's selected candidate attains a formally significant 2.75x gain on the primary evaluation domain, with error below that of the uninjected official base. Generalization on an adjacent monitoring domain improves significantly with no monitored capability degrading. Mechanism experiments provide directional evidence that the gain depends on the semantic content of the distilled graph rather than structural diversity alone.
AI.conclusion: With the proposed closed-loop selection framework and the discovered regularity that semantic content (not structural diversity) drives gains, the use of LLM causal priors shifts from manual trial-and-error to an empirically verifiable, budget-constrained selection problem that can be systematically optimized and statistically validated.

title: ComVLA: Communication-Aware Split Inference for VLA Models in 6G-Connected Robotics
summary: Connected robotics is an emerging 6G application where mobile robots follow natural-language instructions to manipulate physical objects. The Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models that enable this are too large to run on the robot; a common trend is to offload inference to the cloud. The wireless link, however, limits how much sensing data the edge can transmit per control step. Two recent lines address this constraint: semantic communication codecs compress sensor data but require channel-specific retraining, and VLA token pruners select tokens from image but ignore the channel. Our insight is that the dense semantic information contained in the language already indicates which visual tokens matter. We propose ComVLA, a framework that uses this language guidance to adapt the VLA token budget to the channel capacity. Transmitting 32 tokens instead of 512 on the LIBERO benchmark, ComVLA cuts inference compute by 74% and inference latency by 22% versus the original OpenVLA-OFT baseline, at a cost of 1.5 pp in average task success (95.4% vs. 96.9%), and it stays within the capacity budget under Rayleigh and Rician fading. These results demonstrate that co-designing VLA inference and wireless communication is a practical direction for 6G-connected robotics.

AI.tldr: ComVLA is a framework for 6G-connected robotics that uses language guidance to adapt Vision-Language-Action (VLA) token budgets to wireless channel capacity, reducing transmitted tokens from 512 to 32 on the LIBERO benchmark, cutting inference compute by 74% and latency by 22% with only a 1.5 percentage-point drop in task success (95.4% vs. 96.9%), while staying within capacity under Rayleigh and Rician fading.
AI.motivation: VLA models are too large to run on robots and require cloud offloading, but wireless links limit sensing data transmission per control step. Existing approaches either require channel-specific retraining (semantic codecs) or ignore channel conditions entirely (token pruners). The paper identifies that language instructions themselves contain semantic cues about which visual tokens matter, enabling a tighter co-design of VLA inference and wireless communication for 6G robotics.
AI.method: ComVLA leverages the dense semantic information in natural-language instructions to guide visual token selection for transmission. It dynamically adapts the visual token budget to the available wireless channel capacity, transmitting only the most task-relevant tokens (32 instead of 512) from the robot to the cloud-based VLA model.
AI.result: On the LIBERO benchmark, ComVLA reduces inference compute by 74% and inference latency by 22% versus the OpenVLA-OFT baseline while maintaining 95.4% average task success (vs. 96.9% baseline). It operates within capacity constraints under both Rayleigh and Rician fading channel models.
AI.conclusion: Co-designing VLA inference with wireless communication is a practical and effective direction for 6G-connected robotics, as demonstrated by ComVLA's ability to maintain high task performance while dramatically reducing communication overhead and inference cost.

title: iBrain: A Unified Foundation Model Reading the Brain from Surface to Spikes
summary: Invasive neural recordings provide high-fidelity measurements of brain activity, with signals such as intracranial EEG (iEEG) and intracortical spiking activity capturing neural dynamics at different spatial and temporal scales. Yet existing neural foundation models have largely been developed independently for different invasive recording paradigms, leaving joint pretraining across heterogeneous invasive signals underexplored. In this work, we introduce iBrain, a unified foundation model that jointly learns from iEEG and spiking activity. iBrain employs signal-specific encoders to accommodate their distinct signal characteristics and a shared spatiotemporal Transformer backbone to model dependencies across recording channels and time. We pretrain iBrain on over 7,000 hours of heterogeneous neural recordings using masked signal reconstruction and channel-view alignment, promoting contextual modeling of neural dynamics and robustness across different channels. iBrain consistently outperforms single-signal pretraining baselines and achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple benchmarks. Further experiments demonstrate that iBrain exhibits transferability and data efficiency across diverse recording settings. These results highlight the potential of joint pretraining on heterogeneous invasive neural recordings to support scalable neural modeling and transferable representations across recording settings and downstream tasks.

AI.tldr: iBrain is a unified foundation model that jointly pretrains on heterogeneous invasive neural recordings—intracranial EEG (iEEG) and intracortical spiking activity—using signal-specific encoders and a shared spatiotemporal Transformer backbone, achieving state-of-the-art performance across multiple benchmarks with demonstrated transferability and data efficiency.
AI.motivation: Existing neural foundation models are developed independently for different invasive recording paradigms (iEEG vs. spiking activity), leaving joint pretraining across heterogeneous invasive signals unexplored, despite these signals capturing complementary neural dynamics at different spatial and temporal scales.
AI.method: iBrain uses signal-specific encoders to handle distinct signal characteristics of iEEG and spiking activity, combined with a shared spatiotemporal Transformer backbone to model dependencies across recording channels and time. Pretraining is performed on over 7,000 hours of heterogeneous neural recordings using two objectives: masked signal reconstruction and channel-view alignment.
AI.result: iBrain consistently outperforms single-signal pretraining baselines and achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple benchmarks. Experiments further demonstrate transferability and data efficiency across diverse recording settings.
AI.conclusion: Joint pretraining on heterogeneous invasive neural recordings can support scalable neural modeling and produce transferable representations across different recording settings and downstream tasks, highlighting a promising direction for unified neural foundation models.

title: Scene Graph-Driven Haptic Feedback for Safety Enhancement in Robotic Ophthalmic Surgery via Physically Simulated iOCT
comment: 7 pages, 9 figures, 2 tables. Accepted at the 2026 IEEE RAS/EMBS 11th International Conference on Biomedical Robotics and Biomechatronicsnics (BioRob 2026)
summary: Robotic ophthalmic surgery offers high precision but introduces a "sensory gap" by decoupling the surgeon from their instrument, resulting in a loss of tactile feedback. This paper presents a novel haptic feedback system for subretinal injection tasks leveraging Scene Graphs (SG). The system bridges the sensory gap by analyzing a physically simulated intraoperative Optical Coherence Tomography (iOCT) feed to construct a real-time surgical SG. The SG serves as a semantic abstraction layer for the surgical scene, which is then utilized by a deterministic, rule-based engine to generate state-dependent haptic feedback on a robotic input device. The system was evaluated in a user study (N=16) using an anthropomorphic head phantom and a custom-built surgical robot. Results demonstrate that the SG-driven haptic feedback improved surgical precision, reducing needle alignment error by 14% (p = 0.044) and improving System Usability Scale (SUS) scores by 8% (p = 0.015), while maintaining comparable task completion times. A needle trajectory analysis revealed the emergence of a safer "Align-then-Approach" strategy, in which our haptic negative reinforcement prompted users to fine-tune the tool's trajectory before approaching the retinal target. This work suggests that SGs can effectively serve as the direct computational foundation for real-time, safety-enhancing context-aware haptic feedback in robotic microsurgery.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a haptic feedback system for robotic subretinal injection that uses Scene Graphs constructed from intraoperative OCT feeds to bridge the sensory gap surgeons experience when decoupled from their instruments. A user study (N=16) showed the system reduced needle alignment error by 14% and improved SUS scores by 8% while maintaining task completion times, and revealed a safer "Align-then-Approach" surgical strategy.
AI.motivation: Robotic ophthalmic surgery provides high precision but creates a "sensory gap" by removing tactile feedback from the surgeon-instrument loop, which is critical for delicate procedures like subretinal injection.
AI.method: The system analyzes a physically simulated intraoperative OCT feed to construct a real-time surgical Scene Graph, which serves as a semantic abstraction layer. A deterministic rule-based engine then uses this SG to generate state-dependent haptic feedback on a robotic input device. The system was evaluated with 16 users on an anthropomorphic head phantom with a custom surgical robot.
AI.result: SG-driven haptic feedback reduced needle alignment error by 14% (p=0.044) and improved System Usability Scale scores by 8% (p=0.015), with comparable task completion times. Needle trajectory analysis revealed an emergent "Align-then-Approach" strategy where haptic negative reinforcement prompted users to fine-tune tool trajectory before approaching the retinal target.
AI.conclusion: Scene Graphs can effectively serve as the direct computational foundation for real-time, safety-enhancing context-aware haptic feedback in robotic microsurgery.

title: SSP-DMGTimeNet: Physics-Constrained Learning for Spatiotemporal Trajectory Prediction of Vehicle Platoons
summary: Existing car-following prediction methods mainly optimize trajectory accuracy, while rarely considering whether predicted disturbances propagate realistically along a vehicle platoon. This limitation may lead to accurate but string-unstable predictions. We propose SSP-DMGTimeNet, a physics-constrained learning framework for spatiotemporal trajectory prediction of vehicle platoons. The model combines multi-scale temporal representations with cross-vehicle interaction features to capture complex and time-varying platoon dynamics. A propagation-delay-aware causal attention mechanism explicitly models upstream-to-downstream disturbance propagation by learning response delays between adjacent vehicles and accumulating them along the platoon. In addition, time- and frequency-domain string-stability losses relieve disturbance amplification across both adjacent vehicles and arbitrary sub-platoons during training. Experiments on HighD show that SSP-DMGTimeNet achieves an unstable-window rate of 0.65\% for five-vehicle platoons and a maximum head-to-tail amplification of 0.898 on the ground-truth excitation subset, while maintaining competitive trajectory prediction performance. In zero-shot evaluation on NGSIM US-101 and I-80, the model achieves velocity MAEs of 1.316~m/s and 1.252~m/s, with unstable-window rates of 3.90\% and 4.10\%, respectively. These results demonstrate that incorporating platoon-level physical constraints can effectively balance trajectory prediction accuracy and disturbance propagation stability.

AI.tldr: SSP-DMGTimeNet is a physics-constrained deep learning framework for spatiotemporal car-following trajectory prediction that jointly optimizes trajectory accuracy and string-stability of disturbance propagation along vehicle platoons, using multi-scale temporal representations, cross-vehicle interaction features, a propagation-delay-aware causal attention mechanism, and time/frequency-domain string-stability losses.
AI.motivation: Existing car-following prediction methods focus solely on trajectory accuracy and ignore whether predicted disturbances propagate realistically along a vehicle platoon. This can yield predictions that are accurate but string-unstable (i.e., disturbances amplify rather than attenuate along the platoon), which is physically unrealistic and unsafe for downstream applications.
AI.method: The model, SSP-DMGTimeNet, combines multi-scale temporal representations with cross-vehicle interaction features to model complex, time-varying platoon dynamics. A propagation-delay-aware causal attention mechanism explicitly learns response delays between adjacent vehicles and accumulates them along the platoon to model upstream-to-downstream disturbance propagation. Training incorporates time-domain and frequency-domain string-stability losses to suppress disturbance amplification across adjacent vehicles and arbitrary sub-platoons.
AI.result: On HighD, SSP-DMGTimeNet achieves an unstable-window rate of 0.65% for five-vehicle platoons and a maximum head-to-tail amplification of 0.898 on the ground-truth excitation subset, while maintaining competitive trajectory prediction accuracy. In zero-shot transfer to NGSIM US-101 and I-80, it achieves velocity MAEs of 1.316 m/s and 1.252 m/s with unstable-window rates of 3.90% and 4.10%, respectively.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating platoon-level physical constraints (string stability) into the learning objective can effectively balance trajectory prediction accuracy and disturbance propagation stability, producing physically realistic yet accurate platoon trajectory predictions with good generalization to unseen datasets.

title: M3-Tele: A Unified Multimodal Teleoperational Framework for Compliant Whole-Body Mobile Manipulation
summary: Executing contact-rich tasks efficiently requires the seamless integration of whole-body coordination and physical compliance regulation. However, existing teleoperation and data-collection frameworks often overlook the joint consideration of multimodal perception and coordinated whole-body operation. This limitation can reduce the efficiency and quality of demonstration collection, thereby affecting the effectiveness of downstream policy learning. In this work, we present \textbf{M3-Tele}: A Unified \underline{M}ultimodal \underline{Tele}operational Framework for Compliant Whole-Body \underline{M}obile \underline{M}anipulation, enabling stable physical interaction and capturing aligned visual, tactile, force, and proprioceptive observations during task execution. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed framework significantly improves contact-rich teleoperation performance. The proposed controller reduces the force tracking error from 4.132~N to 0.346~N, the contact loss from 2.46 to 0.02 events per trial and the tactile deformation error by 65\%. User studies across four mobile manipulation tasks also verify the reliability and usability of the proposed system. Furthermore, Diffusion Policy experiments highlight the value of joint tactile and force sensing.

AI.tldr: M3-Tele is a unified multimodal teleoperational framework for compliant whole-body mobile manipulation that integrates visual, tactile, force, and proprioceptive feedback, significantly improving contact-rich teleoperation performance and enabling better downstream policy learning.
AI.motivation: Existing teleoperation and data-collection frameworks often neglect the joint consideration of multimodal perception and coordinated whole-body operation, which reduces the efficiency and quality of demonstration collection and limits downstream policy learning effectiveness in contact-rich tasks.
AI.method: The framework unifies multimodal teleoperation for compliant whole-body mobile manipulation, integrating coordinated whole-body control with physical compliance regulation while capturing aligned visual, tactile, force, and proprioceptive observations during task execution.
AI.result: The proposed controller reduces force tracking error from 4.132 N to 0.346 N, contact loss from 2.46 to 0.02 events per trial, and tactile deformation error by 65%. User studies across four mobile manipulation tasks confirm system reliability and usability, while Diffusion Policy experiments demonstrate the value of joint tactile and force sensing.
AI.conclusion: M3-Tele demonstrates that a unified multimodal framework for compliant whole-body teleoperation substantially improves contact-rich manipulation performance and enhances downstream policy learning through richer multimodal demonstration data.

title: RedKnot-MLA: Multi-Head Offline-Online Reuse for DeepSeek-V4 Long-Context Serving
summary: Multi-head latent attention (MLA) exposes many logical query heads through one packed latent KV stream. This representation is memory efficient, but it removes the physical per-head cache boundary assumed by conventional head-wise reuse. We present our system, a DeepSeek-V4 realization of RedKnot's head-aware reuse principle. Each immutable document is processed offline at canonical position zero; certified Local-head contributions are retained as MLA-Off. At serving time, query-side RoPE relocation restores the document's request position, a small Global-head set and protected Local token rows are recomputed as MLA-Online, and the two paths are merged before a single shared output projection. The packed MLA latent is never split.
