DeepSeek-V4-Flash uses 37 reusable layers and a 56/8 Local/Global partition, giving a 75.29% analytic logical head-row ceiling; the Pro-0813 profile uses 55 layers and 112/16 heads, giving 78.89%. Frozen Flash operating points show hot-artifact TTFT speedups of 2.02-3.84x. At 256K, the archived three-dataset study reports an aggregate F1 change of +3.24 percentage points, an EM change of +4.16 points, and a 78.7-79.5% analytic major-operator arithmetic saving, while one dataset decreases by 2.81 F1 points. A separate author-reported 256K hot-artifact QPS measurement is approximately 2.0x; because its raw concurrency trace is not included in this bundle, we mark it as preliminary rather than archived evidence. We describe the factorization, position repair, token-row closure, sparse-MoE support, TP8 integration, and the measurement boundaries needed to interpret these results.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a DeepSeek-V4 system implementing RedKnot's head-aware reuse principle for MLA (multi-head latent attention). By processing immutable documents offline at canonical position zero, retaining certified Local-head contributions (MLA-Off), and recomputing a small Global-head set plus protected Local token rows at serving time (MLA-Online), the system achieves head-aware KV reuse without ever splitting the packed MLA latent. Reported benefits include 2.02-3.84x TTFT speedups on frozen Flash operating points, high analytic logical head-row ceilings (75-79%), and archived 256K evaluation gains of +3.24/+4.16 F1/EM points with ~79% major-operator arithmetic savings, though one dataset degrades by 2.81 F1 points and one QPS measurement is marked preliminary.
AI.motivation: MLA packs many logical query heads into one latent KV stream for memory efficiency, but this removes the physical per-head cache boundary that conventional head-wise KV reuse depends on. The goal is to enable effective cache reuse and precomputation for MLA under a streaming/chat KV-cache setting despite the absence of separable per-head caches.
AI.method: The system realizes RedKnot's head-aware reuse for MLA without splitting the packed latent. Offline, each immutable document is processed at canonical position zero, retaining certified Local-head contributions (MLA-Off). At serving time, query-side RoPE relocation restores the document's request position, a small set of Global heads and protected Local token rows are recomputed (MLA-Online), and the two paths are merged before one shared output projection. The work details factorization, position repair, token-row closure, sparse-MoE support, TP8 integration, and measurement boundaries. Two profiles are given: DeepSeek-V4-Flash (37 reusable layers, 56/8 Local/Global) and Pro-0813 (55 layers, 112/16).
AI.result: DeepSeek-V4-Flash achieves a 75.29% analytic logical head-row ceiling; the Pro-0813 profile reaches 78.89%. Frozen Flash operating points show hot-artifact TTFT speedups of 2.02-3.84x. The archived three-dataset study at 256K reports aggregate F1 change of +3.24 points, EM change of +4.16 points, and 78.7-79.5% analytic major-operator arithmetic savings, though one dataset decreases by 2.81 F1 points. A separate author-reported 256K hot-artifact QPS measurement (~2.0x) is marked preliminary because raw concurrency traces are absent.
AI.conclusion: Head-aware reuse can be effectively applied to MLA by splitting work into offline (MLA-Off) and online (MLA-Online) paths with RoPE-based position repair, achieving significant TTFT latency speedups and arithmetic savings at long context. The packed MLA latent is never split, preserving its memory-efficiency advantages. Results should be interpreted with clear measurement boundaries: not all datasets improve, one detail set regresses by 2.81 F1, and the QPS figure is only preliminary without concurrency traces.

title: Conditional Timed Partial Orders: An Expressive and Interpretable Framework for Robot Task Specification and Planning
summary: Timed Partial Orders (TPOs), originally proposed for workflows, provide an interpretable framework for robot task specification with planning algorithms based on mixed-integer linear programming (MILP). However, TPOs are limited in expressivity, capturing only partial-order events with simple timing constraints. In this paper, we introduce Conditional TPOs (cTPOs), which extend TPOs with richer relative-timing constraints and conditional event activations based on environmental conditions. We show that planning for cTPOs also reduces to an MILP problem; however, the added expressivity results in significantly larger MILPs that can become computationally intractable. To address this challenge, we propose a decomposition algorithm that partitions a cTPO into smaller sub-TPOs, yielding a sequence of smaller MILP problems. We prove that this decomposition is complete and preserves plan optimality while improving the interpretability of complex tasks. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of cTPOs as a task specification framework and the efficiency of our decomposition approach, achieving up to four orders of magnitude speedup over the monolithic MILP.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Conditional Timed Partial Orders (cTPOs), an extension of TPOs that adds richer relative-timing constraints and conditional event activations based on environmental conditions for robot task specification. Planning for cTPOs reduces to MILP, but the added expressivity creates computationally intractable problems; the authors propose a decomposition algorithm that partitions cTPOs into smaller sub-TPOs, yielding a sequence of smaller MILPs that is provably complete, preserves optimality, and improves interpretability. Experiments show up to four orders of magnitude speedup over the monolithic MILP approach.
AI.motivation: Timed Partial Orders (TPOs) provide an interpretable framework for robot task specification with MILP-based planning, but their expressivity is limited to partial-order events with simple timing constraints. There is a need for a richer task specification language that can capture conditional activations based on environmental conditions and more complex relative-timing relationships, while remaining computationally tractable for planning.
AI.method: The authors extend TPOs to Conditional TPOs (cTPOs) with richer relative-timing constraints and environment-conditioned event activations. They show planning for cTPOs reduces to MILP. To address computational intractability of large MILPs, they propose a decomposition algorithm that partitions a cTPO into smaller sub-TPOs, solving a sequence of smaller MILP problems instead of one monolithic one. They prove the decomposition is complete and preserves plan optimality.
AI.result: Experimental results demonstrate that cTPOs are an effective task specification framework, and the decomposition approach achieves up to four orders of magnitude speedup over the monolithic MILP formulation, while also improving interpretability of complex tasks.
AI.conclusion: cTPOs significantly expand the expressivity of TPOs for robot task specification while maintaining a formal planning framework via MILP. The proposed decomposition method makes cTPO planning scalable and practical, with provable completeness and optimality guarantees alongside large computational speedups.

title: Beyond One-Shot Expansion: Contrastive Evidence Exploration for Multi-Hop Retrieval
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) critically depends on retrieving the evidence necessary for effective reasoning. However, this remains particularly challenging in multi-hop question answering (QA), where supporting passages are often linked through intermediate entities and relations that must be progressively uncovered. Existing retrieval approaches typically rely on a single retrieval intent or one-shot query expansion, limiting their ability to adapt to newly retrieved evidence and potentially introducing noisy or redundant retrieval signals. To address these limitations, we propose a training-free multi-hop retrieval framework that integrates evidence-conditioned exploration, passage-specific contrastive refinement, and coverage-aware final ranking. During offline indexing, the framework constructs passage-specific contrastive facets that characterize each passage relative to its semantically similar neighbors, providing fine-grained signals to distinguish closely related candidates. At inference time, the framework iteratively retrieves evidence, generates probes targeting unresolved information needs, refines candidate relevance using the contrastive facets, and selects a complementary set of passages that collectively cover diverse evidence-seeking intents. Experiments on MuSiQue, HotpotQA, and 2WikiMultihopQA demonstrate consistent improvements in retrieval quality and downstream QA performance over baselines.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a training-free multi-hop retrieval framework for RAG that integrates evidence-conditioned exploration, passage-specific contrastive refinement, and coverage-aware final ranking to improve multi-hop question answering.
AI.motivation: Multi-hop QA retrieval is challenging because supporting passages are connected through intermediate entities/relations. Existing approaches rely on a single retrieval intent or one-shot query expansion, which limits adaptability to newly retrieved evidence and can introduce noisy or redundant signals.
AI.method: The framework has three key components: (1) offline indexing that constructs passage-specific contrastive facets characterizing each passage against semantically similar neighbors; (2) iterative inference-time retrieval that generates probes targeting unresolved information needs; (3) passage-specific contrastive refinement of candidate relevance and coverage-aware final ranking that selects complementary passages collectively covering diverse evidence-seeking intents.
AI.result: Experiments on MuSiQue, HotpotQA, and 2WikiMultihopQA show consistent improvements in retrieval quality and downstream QA performance over baselines.
AI.conclusion: The proposed training-free framework effectively addresses limitations of existing multi-hop retrieval methods by providing fine-grained contrastive signals and adaptive, coverage-aware retrieval, leading to better retrieval and QA performance across multiple benchmark datasets.

title: A Multimodal Label Forecasting Method for Aperiodic Visuo-Motor Time Series
summary: Deep learning models have been increasingly applied to Time Series Forecasting (TSF) in recent years. Transformer-based and MLP-based models have both been used effectively on many real-world TSF regression benchmarks, and there is ongoing debate as to which family of methods is best. While these benchmarks have drawn much attention, it is also worth noting that many current datasets and methods assume approximate periodicity in the time series. In this work, we focus on a new TSF task without periodicity: anticipating falls during humanoid locomotion, on the basis of egocentric vision and proprioception. When the locomotion trajectories are sufficiently diverse, periodicity is violated. We contribute two new benchmark datasets (one from simulation, one from real hardware), showing that periodicity is violated and recent deep TSF methods struggle on these benchmarks. We also propose a novel deep learning architecture that exploits both endogenous and exogenous variables and a training process that rigorously enforces i.i.d sampling of training examples. Our results show statistically significant improvement over prior art in multiple experimental conditions, by 12.73% or more on the real data and 10.40% or more on the simulation data. Code and datasets will be available upon acceptance.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a new Time Series Forecasting task without periodicity—anticipating falls during humanoid locomotion using egocentric vision and proprioception—along with two new benchmark datasets (simulation and real hardware). The authors show that recent deep TSF methods struggle on these non-periodic benchmarks and propose a novel deep learning architecture exploiting both endogenous and exogenous variables with a training process that enforces i.i.d. sampling, achieving statistically significant improvements over prior art (12.73%+ on real data, 10.40%+ on simulation).
AI.motivation: Current deep TSF benchmarks and methods largely assume approximate periodicity in time series, which limits their applicability to real-world tasks where trajectories are diverse and non-periodic—such as anticipating falls during humanoid locomotion. There is also an ongoing debate between Transformer-based and MLP-based methods without clear resolution on non-periodic tasks.
AI.method: The authors contribute two new benchmark datasets (one simulation, one real hardware) for fall anticipation during humanoid locomotion based on egocentric vision and proprioception. They propose a novel deep learning architecture that leverages both endogenous and exogenous variables, and introduce a training process that rigorously enforces i.i.d. sampling of training examples to address the non-periodic nature of the data.
AI.result: Recent deep TSF methods struggle on these non-periodic benchmarks. The proposed architecture achieves statistically significant improvements over prior art across multiple experimental conditions: 12.73% or more improvement on real data and 10.40% or more on simulation data.
AI.conclusion: Non-periodic TSF is an underexplored but important problem class; the new benchmarks expose limitations of existing deep TSF models and the proposed approach demonstrates clear gains. Code and datasets will be made available upon acceptance.

title: VST: Verifiable Structured Transport for Auditable Agent-to-Agent Alpha Discovery
summary: Agent-to-agent (A2A) alpha discovery is slowed by repeated feedback cycles between mining and evaluation agents, whose hand-offs, in contemporary LLM multi-agent systems, are free-form natural-language messages that carry no stable contract and cannot be replayed. We first restructure this communication as a structured agent-to-agent protocol of \emph{typed, causally addressable, unicast records}, so that the committed stream forms a causal trajectory. On that trajectory a single predictor with four typed heads forecasts the accumulated guidance the two miners would receive several cycles ahead; a transactional verify--leap controller then commits a multi-cycle speculative outcome only when it passes a four-level gate, and otherwise rolls back to the exact prior state. Structure is the enabling contribution, and its value is not accuracy. A controlled ablation shows an equal-information free-text channel reaches the same predictor hit rate. What typing provides is a state that can be schema-checked, replayed deterministically, and prevented by construction from leaking a forecast to an evaluator: auditability by construction, not an empirically stress-tested guarantee. On a CSI~1000 out-of-sample holdout, our single run is the only one among eight methods (seven baselines and ours) to hold a positive median annualized return and Sharpe at the factor level, though the median return \emph{in excess} of the benchmark stays negative for every method including ours; its development-selected top-20 portfolios reach a $0.71$ median holdout Sharpe, selected on a split inside the optimization horizon. We report these single-run results descriptively, gross of costs, and are explicit about their limits throughout; in particular we do not isolate the effect of the leap machinery from the inherited search substrate, which we leave to future work.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes restructuring agent-to-agent (A2A) communication in LLM-based trading/alpha-discovery systems from free-form natural language into a structured protocol of typed, causally addressable, unicast records. This forms a causal trajectory that enables a four-headed predictor and a transactional verify–leap controller for speculative multi-cycle commitment with rollback. The key contribution is auditability by construction (schema-checkable, replayable, leak-proof), not predictive accuracy—an ablation shows typing does not improve hit rate over free text. On a CSI 1000 out-of-sample holdout, the method is the only one of eight to achieve positive median annualized return and factor-level Sharpe, though excess return over benchmark remains negative for all; top-20 portfolios reach 0.71 median holdout Sharpe. Results are single-run, gross of costs, reported descriptively with explicit limitations.
AI.motivation: A2A alpha discovery is slowed by repeated feedback cycles between mining and evaluation agents; their hand-offs are free-form natural-language messages with no stable contract and cannot be replayed, limiting reproducibility, auditability, and rollback capability.
AI.method: Restructure A2A communication as a protocol of typed, causally addressable, unicast records forming a causal trajectory. On this trajectory, a single predictor with four typed heads forecasts future accumulated guidance; a transactional verify–leap controller commits a multi-cycle speculative outcome only when it passes a four-level gate, otherwise rolling back to the exact prior state.
AI.result: On a CSI 1000 out-of-sample holdout, the single run is the only one among eight methods to hold positive median annualized return and Sharpe at the factor level; top-20 portfolios reach 0.71 median holdout Sharpe. However, median excess return over benchmark is negative for all methods. A controlled ablation showed typing does not improve predictor hit rate over equal-information free-text.
AI.conclusion: The value of typing/structuring is not predictive accuracy but auditability by construction—states that are schema-checkable, deterministically replayable, and structurally prevented from leaking forecasts to evaluators. Results are reported descriptively, gross of costs, with acknowledged limits; isolating the leap machinery's effect from the search substrate is left to future work.

title: SPOT: Spatial Perception-Oriented Long-Horizon Humanoid Teleoperation
summary: High-quality demonstration data is becoming a central bottleneck for training general-purpose humanoid robots. While recent humanoid teleoperation systems have made substantial progress in retargeting human motion to robot motion, long-horizon loco-manipulation requires another capability: operators must maintain task-relevant spatial awareness over time, e.g., object locations, surrounding environments, the robot's pose. We call the extent of this awareness the operator's perceptual horizon. However, existing methods often shorten this: narrow views miss peripheral events, robot-mounted cameras become unstable during locomotion, and coupled head-view control makes looking around interfere with robot motion. We present SPOT, a Spatial Perception-Oriented VR Teleoperation system for collecting long-horizon humanoid demonstration data by providing extended perceptual horizon. SPOT combines a robot-mounted binocular fisheye camera, a wide-field stereoscopic display, viewpoint-decoupled free-looking, and visual stabilization to provide a robot-centric view that is wide, stable, and actively inspectable. Unlike conventional egocentric interfaces, SPOT decouples visual exploration from robot actuation: the egocentric stereo observation is rendered on a virtual hemisphere around the operator, so natural head rotations change where the operator looks within the wide-field view rather than commanding the robot head, camera, or torso. We evaluate SPOT on perception-critical humanoid data-collection tasks spanning drop recovery, peripheral retrieval, large-workspace bimanual manipulation, fine alignment, and dynamic interaction. SPOT improves efficiency, accuracy, and recovery speed, demonstrating its effectiveness for user-friendly and scalable long-horizon humanoid data collection.

AI.tldr: SPOT is a VR teleoperation system that extends the operator's perceptual horizon for long-horizon humanoid data collection by combining a robot-mounted binocular fisheye camera, wide-field stereoscopic display, viewpoint-decoupled free-looking, and visual stabilization, decoupling visual exploration from robot actuation.
AI.motivation: High-quality demonstration data is a central bottleneck for training general-purpose humanoid robots. Long-horizon loco-manipulation tasks require operators to maintain task-relevant spatial awareness over time, but existing teleoperation systems suffer from limited perceptual horizons due to narrow views, unstable robot-mounted cameras during locomotion, and coupled head-view control that interferes with robot motion.
AI.method: SPOT provides an extended perceptual horizon through four key components: (1) a robot-mounted binocular fisheye camera for wide field-of-view capture, (2) a wide-field stereoscopic display, (3) viewpoint-decoupled free-looking where head rotations change what the operator sees within the wide-field view rather than commanding robot actuation, and (4) visual stabilization. The egocentric stereo observation is rendered on a virtual hemisphere around the operator, enabling natural head exploration without affecting robot motion.
AI.result: SPOT was evaluated on perception-critical humanoid data-collection tasks including drop recovery, peripheral retrieval, large-workspace bimanual manipulation, fine alignment, and dynamic interaction. Results show improved efficiency, accuracy, and recovery speed compared to conventional approaches.
AI.conclusion: SPOT demonstrates that decoupling perceptual exploration from robot actuation with wide, stable, and actively inspectable views provides a user-friendly and scalable solution for collecting high-quality long-horizon humanoid demonstration data.

title: A Hierarchical Consistency Framework for Auditing Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is commonly evaluated by whether the final answer is correct. That test is insufficient: an answer can match its reference while the context that produced it contains a direct contradiction, leaving the contested evidence invisible to answer-only review and retrieval relevance scores. This paper presents the Hierarchical Consistency Framework (HCF), a post-hoc, model-agnostic audit of three distinct levels of a RAG process: the knowledge corpus, the final retrieved context, and the generated answer. HCF represents corpus conflicts as source-linked atomic facts, thereby identifying the documents responsible, and returns each Answer Consistency Score (ACS) with an explanation of supporting and contradictory contextual statements. We evaluate HCF on several controlled corpora spanning five domains and 100 query-corpus instances. A human evaluator compares every generated response with its supplied ground-truth response. The results show that the three diagnostic levels can dissociate: the corpus with the highest mean retrieval similarity has the lowest mean ACS, while a structurally degraded corpus performs worse at corpus level but better at answer level. Most importantly, HCF identifies contradictory retrieved evidence in several cases where the answer still matches the ground truth. HCF does not certify factual truth; it makes the evidence supporting and challenging an answer inspectable and attributable.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Hierarchical Consistency Framework (HCF), a post-hoc, model-agnostic audit tool for RAG systems that evaluates three levels—the knowledge corpus, retrieved context, and generated answer—exposing contradictions that answer-only evaluations miss. HCF decomposes corpus conflicts into source-linked atomic facts and produces Answer Consistency Scores (ACS) with explanatory evidence. Evaluated across five domains and 100 query-corpus instances, HCF reveals that diagnostic levels can dissociate and identifies contradictory retrieved evidence even when answers match ground truth.
AI.motivation: Standard RAG evaluation—checking whether the final answer is correct—is insufficient because an answer can match its reference while the context producing it contains direct contradictions. This leaves contested evidence invisible to answer-only review and retrieval relevance scoring, motivating a need for deeper, multi-level auditing of the RAG pipeline.
AI.method: HCF audits three distinct RAG levels post-hoc: (1) the knowledge corpus, (2) the final retrieved context, and (3) the generated answer. It represents corpus conflicts as source-linked atomic facts to identify responsible documents and computes the Answer Consistency Score (ACS) alongside explanations of supporting and contradictory contextual statements. Evaluation was conducted on controlled corpora spanning five domains and 100 query-corpus instances, with a human evaluator comparing generated responses against ground-truth responses.
AI.result: The three diagnostic levels dissociate: the corpus with the highest mean retrieval similarity had the lowest mean ACS, while a structurally degraded corpus performed worse at the corpus level yet better at the answer level. Critically, HCF identified contradictory retrieved evidence in several cases where the answer still matched the ground truth.
AI.conclusion: HCF does not certify factual truth; instead, it makes the evidence supporting and challenging an answer inspectable and attributable, offering a more transparent and diagnostic evaluation of RAG systems than answer-only correctness checks.

title: mjorbit: A Simulation Framework for Space Robotics
summary: This paper presents a general framework for simulating multi-body space robots with contact. We bring efficient, large-scale robot simulation to in-space servicing, assembly, and manufacturing applications. First, we perform an empirical trade study of methods for coupling orbit propagation with existing robotics simulation frameworks. Next, we present mjorbit, a general, flexible, and performant framework built on the MuJoCo engine widely used in robotics, to which we add key spacecraft dynamics, actuators, and sensors. We provide a low-latency C++ CPU backend and a high-throughput GPU backend behind a simple Python API. We demonstrate mjorbit by solving several realistic on-orbit case studies with both model-predictive control and reinforcement learning. Open-source code and examples are available at: https://johnzhang3.github.io/mjorbit/

AI.tldr: This paper introduces mjorbit, a general framework for simulating multi-body space robots with contact in on-orbit servicing, assembly, and manufacturing scenarios. Built on the MuJoCo robotics engine with added spacecraft dynamics, actuators, and sensors, it offers both low-latency C++ CPU and high-throughput GPU backends behind a Python API. It is validated through realistic case studies using model-predictive control and reinforcement learning.
AI.motivation: To bring efficient, large-scale robot simulation capabilities to in-space servicing, assembly, and manufacturing applications, which currently lack a general and performant simulation framework for multi-body space robots with contact dynamics.
AI.method: The authors perform an empirical trade study of methods coupling orbit propagation with existing robotics simulation frameworks. They then build mjorbit on the MuJoCo engine, augmenting it with spacecraft dynamics, actuators, and sensors, and provide both C++ CPU and GPU backends behind a Python API.
AI.result: mjorbit is demonstrated on multiple realistic on-orbit case studies using model-predictive control and reinforcement learning, showing its flexibility, generality, and performance. The open-source code and examples are released.
AI.conclusion: mjorbit provides an effective, general, and performant open-source framework for large-scale simulation of multi-body space robots with contact, enabling robotics-centric methods to be applied to on-orbit applications.

title: Risk Is Not Review Value: Wrong-Answer Exposure Under Bounded Review Budgets
summary: LLM assistants often produce more answers than humans can review before users see them. Most evaluations ask whether an answer is wrong, unsupported, or low-confidence. Bounded review budgets instead ask which answers should be checked first under a fixed review budget. Risk alone is not enough: a high-risk answer may be hard to repair, while a moderately risky answer may be directly correctable from available evidence. For generated-answer evaluation, we model review prioritization as exposure reduction, where review value combines estimated wrongness, intervention affordance, impact, and cost. We evaluate review queues with Wrong-Answer Exposure Ratio (WAER), the fraction of wrong answers left unreviewed, and post-repair residual exposure (PRRE), the fraction still exposed after deterministic benchmark-supported repairs. PRRE uses repairability rules that do not numerically reuse the affordance scores used for ranking. On a 720-item TAT-QA/SciFact stress benchmark, review-value ranking keeps answer-level WAER nearly unchanged at 20% budget (0.605 vs. 0.600) but lowers PRRE from 0.881 to 0.716. These results show that trustworthy LLM evaluation should measure not only error detection, but also how limited review capacity reduces exposed wrong answers.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes that LLM evaluation under limited review budgets should prioritize which answers to check based not just on risk of wrongness, but on exposure reduction—combining wrongness, intervention affordance, impact, and cost. The authors introduce WAER and PRRE metrics, showing that review-value ranking significantly reduces post-repair residual exposure (0.881 to 0.716) while keeping wrong-answer exposure nearly unchanged.
AI.motivation: LLM assistants generate more answers than human reviewers can check, yet current evaluation frameworks focus on detecting wrong/unsupported/low-confidence answers rather than optimally allocating limited review capacity. Risk alone is insufficient because high-risk answers may be hard to repair while moderately risky ones may be easily correctable from evidence.
AI.method: The paper frames review prioritization as an exposure reduction problem, where review value is a composite of estimated wrongness, intervention affordance (repairability), impact, and cost. Two new metrics are proposed: Wrong-Answer Exposure Ratio (WAER) measures the fraction of wrong answers left unreviewed at a given budget, while Post-Repair Residual Exposure (PRRE) measures exposure after deterministic benchmark-supported repairs. PRRE uses repairability rules independent of the affordance scores used for ranking.
AI.result: On a 720-item TAT-QA/SciFact stress benchmark at 20% review budget, review-value ranking maintains answer-level WAER nearly unchanged (0.605 vs. 0.600 baseline) but reduces PRRE substantially from 0.881 to 0.716.
AI.conclusion: Trustworthy LLM evaluation must account not only for error detection but also for how limited human review capacity can best reduce the total number of wrong answers exposed to users.

title: DISEIL: Demonstration Distillation for Sample-Efficient Imitation Learning
summary: A robot that can be taught a new task from a handful of demonstrations has to work out for itself what it still cannot do, and then ask for exactly that. Interactive imitation learning takes a step in that direction by letting a policy practice on its own and calling an expert when it goes wrong. Existing methods decide when to interrupt the learner. A further 2 decisions are left to whichever episode happened to trigger the interruption: which failure to correct, and where the demonstration should start. This paper is a first attempt at making both of them deliberately. DISEIL (Demonstration dIstillation for Sample-Efficient Imitation Learning) marks each failed episode at the step where the policy first becomes unreliable, represents that moment with a geometric descriptor, and groups the failures into recurring failure modes. A vision-language model and a language model read the selected mode and write a request for the next demonstration, and a store of task constraints checks that the request can be carried out before any expert time is spent. No model produces a robot action. Across 5 simulated tasks under state and image observations, changing only what the expert is asked for gives the highest mean held-out success rate in all 10 settings, with a tie in 1, and the margin is widest at the smallest budget we tested. The scope is narrow: a single round of practice at a time, in simulation, with experts that are mostly scripted. The longer-term aim is a learner that also tracks what its demonstration set already covers, and that asks a human teacher for the missing behavior in proportion to the effort each request costs them.

AI.tldr: DISEIL is an interactive imitation learning method that makes two previously arbitrary decisions deliberate: which failure mode to correct and where the expert demonstration should start. It identifies failure modes via geometric descriptors of unreliable policy steps, uses vision-language and language models to formulate expert requests, and validates requests against task constraints.
AI.motivation: Interactive imitation learning lets a policy practice on its own and query an expert when it fails, but existing methods only decide when to interrupt the learner. Two crucial decisions—which failure to correct and where the demonstration should start—are left to chance, depending on whichever episode triggered the interruption. This paper addresses this gap by making these decisions deliberate.
AI.method: DISEIL marks each failed episode at the step where the policy first becomes unreliable, represents that moment with a geometric descriptor, and groups failures into recurring failure modes. A vision-language model (VLM) and a language model (LM) read the selected failure mode and generate a request for the next demonstration, while a store of task constraints verifies the request is executable before any expert time is spent. Notably, no model produces robot actions directly.
AI.result: Across 5 simulated tasks under both state and image observations, changing only what the expert is asked for achieves the highest mean held-out success rate in all 10 settings (with a tie in 1), with the widest margin at the smallest demonstration budget tested.
AI.conclusion: The approach demonstrates that deliberately choosing what to ask the expert significantly improves sample efficiency in interactive imitation learning. The scope is acknowledged as narrow—single rounds of practice, simulation only, mostly scripted experts. The long-term aim is a learner that tracks what its demonstration set already covers and requests missing behavior from human teachers in proportion to user effort cost.

title: Beyond Sparse Rewards: A New Benchmark and Structure-Aware Graph Alignment for Micro-Drama Understanding
summary: Micro-dramas, characterized by ultra-short durations and hyper-dense storylines, pose unique challenges for video understanding that conventional benchmarks fail to address. To bridge this gap, we introduce M-Drama, the first large-scale bilingual benchmark for micro-drama comprehension, featuring over 35K instances across 9,138 clips. Furthermore, while reinforcement learning can enhance VLMs on complex narratives, existing reward metrics often suffer from sparse and superficial signals, failing to capture intricate character identities and temporal structures. We propose SAGA (Structure-Aware Graph Alignment), a novel graph-matching reward function that models narratives as heterogeneous graphs. SAGA computes dense, rigorous rewards via decoupled semantic triplet and structural temporal matching. Extensive experiments on Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct demonstrate that SAGA outperforms existing baselines, delivering substantial improvements in open-ended accuracy and summary quality, while maintaining competitive out-of-domain generalization. Code is available at https://github.com/qyx1121/MDrama_SAGA.

AI.tldr: Introduces M-Drama, the first large-scale bilingual benchmark for micro-drama comprehension with over 35K instances across 9,138 clips, and proposes SAGA (Structure-Aware Graph Alignment), a graph-matching reward function for reinforcement learning that models narratives as heterogeneous graphs with decoupled semantic triplet and structural temporal matching, demonstrating improvements over baselines on Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct.
AI.motivation: Micro-dramas with ultra-short durations and hyper-dense storylines pose unique video understanding challenges not addressed by conventional benchmarks. Additionally, existing RL reward metrics for VLMs on complex narratives suffer from sparse and superficial signals that fail to capture intricate character identities and temporal structures.
AI.method: Constructs M-Drama, a first-of-its-kind large-scale bilingual micro-drama benchmark (35K+ instances, 9,138 clips). Proposes SAGA, a structure-aware graph alignment reward function that models narrative structure as heterogeneous graphs and computes dense, rigorous rewards via decoupled semantic triplet matching and structural temporal matching.
AI.result: Experiments on Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct show SAGA outperforms existing baselines, yielding substantial improvements in open-ended accuracy and summary quality while maintaining competitive out-of-domain generalization.
AI.conclusion: SAGA provides a more effective reward mechanism for reinforcement learning on complex micro-drama narratives, and M-Drama serves as a valuable benchmark for advancing micro-drama video comprehension.

title: OmniNav: Robust Long-Horizon Target Navigation in Dynamic Environments
summary: Long-horizon target navigation requires a robot to sustain task execution across evolving observations, decisions, and physical interactions. This requires three coupled capabilities: maintaining valid scene memory, revising target beliefs under partial observability, and selecting interaction-feasible navigation endpoints. However, the state underlying each capability is only conditionally valid: scene representations become stale when objects move or disappear, unsuccessful searches alter beliefs over target locations, and geometrically convenient endpoints may still be infeasible for manipulation. To address these challenges, we present OmniNav, which formulates long-horizon navigation as continual inference over a factorized task state posterior coupling scene validity, target belief, and interaction feasibility. For representation, OmniNav incrementally constructs an updatable 3D object scene memory, preventing stale scene evidence from propagating to subsequent decisions. For exploration, it introduces an evidence-aware Bayesian belief-revision mechanism that derives dependency-aware region priors from semantic context, incorporates unsuccessful searches as negative evidence, and updates them for posterior-guided frontier selection. For interaction, OmniNav incorporates manipulation reachability and collision constraints into navigation-endpoint selection and propagates execution feedback through hierarchical closed-loop recovery. Extensive experiments demonstrate that OmniNav achieves the highest success rates among the compared methods on semantic ObjectNav and fine-grained instance navigation benchmarks, remains robust to target relocation, and improves real-world pick-and-place success from 53.3% to 71.7% over an adapted open-loop baseline. The project page of OmniNav is available at https://omni-nav.github.io/.

AI.tldr: OmniNav is a framework for long-horizon target navigation that jointly models scene validity, target belief, and interaction feasibility as a factorized posterior, enabling robust semantic and instance navigation under partial observability, changing environments, and manipulation constraints.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon target navigation requires three coupled capabilities—maintaining valid scene memory, revising target beliefs under partial observability, and selecting interaction-feasible navigation endpoints—yet the underlying state for each is only conditionally valid. Scene representations become stale when objects move or disappear, unsuccessful searches alter beliefs, and geometrically convenient endpoints may be infeasible for manipulation. These challenges have not been jointly addressed.
AI.method: OmniNav formulates long-horizon navigation as continual inference over a factorized task-state posterior that couples scene validity, target belief, and interaction feasibility. It (1) incrementally builds an updatable 3D object scene memory to prevent stale evidence propagation, (2) employs an evidence-aware Bayesian belief-revision mechanism that derives dependency-aware region priors from semantic context, treats unsuccessful searches as negative evidence, and uses the posterior for frontier selection, and (3) integrates manipulation reachability and collision constraints into navigation-endpoint selection with hierarchical closed-loop recovery from execution feedback.
AI.result: OmniNav achieves the highest success rates among compared methods on semantic ObjectNav and fine-grained instance navigation benchmarks, remains robust to target relocation, and improves real-world pick-and-place success from 53.3% to 71.7% over an adapted open-loop baseline.
AI.conclusion: By jointly reasoning over scene validity, target beliefs, and interaction feasibility, OmniNav provides a robust and general framework for long-horizon navigation that outperforms prior methods in simulation and demonstrates significant gains in real-world manipulation-constrained navigation tasks.

title: EEG-Driven Decoding Framework for Passenger Hazard Perception in Highly Automated Vehicles
comment: 31 pages, 8 figures, 13 tables, including appendices. Accepted for publication in Automotive Innovation. Yingkai Yang and Ashton Yu Xuan Tan contributed equally. Corresponding author: Hong Wang. Data: https://doi.org/10.21227/jw72-m261 ; Code: https://github.com/SOTIF-AVLab/EEG2023
summary: Reliable risk assessment remains a central challenge for Autonomous Vehicles (AVs). Despite advances in automation, passenger cognition provides a non-intrusive auxiliary signal that improves both objective and perceived safety without requiring active human intervention. We introduce an Electroencephalogram (EEG)-based Brain-Computer Interface (BCI) that decodes passenger neural responses for both Risk Prediction (RP) and Danger Identification (DI), explicitly modeling humans as passengers to match real-world AV use. To achieve this, we propose the Passenger Cognitive Model (PCM), Risk-aware Sequential Labeling (RSL), and the Passenger EEG Decoding Strategy (PEDS), which integrates a 3D Convolutional Recurrent Neural Network (3D-CRNN) model for joint EEG decoding. Experimental results show that 3D-CRNN achieves a Balanced Accuracy (BA) of $95.3\% \pm 2.7\%$ in RP and improves single-subject DI from $80.9\% \pm 3.9\%$ to $85.0\% \pm 3.2\%$ with RSL. Event-wise analyses further show that 3D-CRNN consistently outperforms other models across different event types in RP and DI. In generalization experiments, 3D-CRNN achieves $77.0\% \pm 5.3\%$ BA in cross-session DI and $77.4\% \pm 1.1\%$ BA on seen subjects in cross-subject evaluation, while maintaining a $64.9\% \pm 8.5\%$ BA on unseen subjects, demonstrating promising generalizability and transferability across both intra-subject and inter-subject variability. These findings establish an Electroencephalogram (EEG) decoding framework for AV passenger hazard perception and suggest that passenger cognitive signals can provide auxiliary supervision for future AV decision-making and Safety of the Intended Functionality (SOTIF) support.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces an EEG-based Brain-Computer Interface (BCI) framework for Autonomous Vehicles (AVs) that decodes passenger neural responses for Risk Prediction (RP) and Danger Identification (DI). It proposes the Passenger Cognitive Model (PCM), Risk-aware Sequential Labeling (RSL), and a 3D Convolutional Recurrent Neural Network (3D-CRNN) for joint EEG decoding, achieving up to 95.3% balanced accuracy in risk prediction and demonstrating cross-session and cross-subject generalizability.
AI.motivation: Reliable risk assessment remains a central challenge for AVs. Passenger cognitive signals, captured via EEG, provide a non-intrusive auxiliary signal to improve both objective and perceived safety without requiring active human intervention—motivating the development of a passenger-centric EEG decoding framework for real-world AV scenarios.
AI.method: The authors propose: (1) Passenger Cognitive Model (PCM), which explicitly models humans as passengers to match real AV use; (2) Risk-aware Sequential Labeling (RSL), a labeling strategy for sequential EEG data; (3) Passenger EEG Decoding Strategy (PEDS), integrating a 3D Convolutional Recurrent Neural Network (3D-CRNN) for joint RP and DI decoding.
AI.result: 3D-CRNN achieves 95.3% ± 2.7% balanced accuracy (BA) in RP, improves single-subject DI from 80.9% ± 3.9% to 85.0% ± 3.2% with RSL, achieves 77.0% ± 5.3% BA in cross-session DI and 77.4% ± 1.1% BA on seen subjects in cross-subject evaluation, with 64.9% ± 8.5% BA on unseen subjects.
AI.conclusion: The findings establish an EEG decoding framework for AV passenger hazard perception and suggest passenger cognitive signals can provide auxiliary supervision for future AV decision-making and Safety of the Intended Functionality (SOTIF) support.

title: Dual-Layer Semantic-Spatial Belief Mapping for Aerial Object Goal Navigation
comment: Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Multimedia
summary: Aerial Object Goal Navigation (ObjectNav) requires an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) to locate a described target in an unknown outdoor environment using onboard visual observations. Vision-language models (VLMs) can interpret open-ended target descriptions and visual observations, but their frame-level outputs are often noisy, sparse, and spatially transient. We propose AeroBelief, a dual-layer semantic-spatial belief mapping framework that transforms transient VLM observations into persistent spatial guidance. It separates broad contextual plausibility from target-specific evidence: an intuition layer accumulates scene-level semantic cues for exploration, while an evidence layer preserves qualified target-specific observations for approach and confirmation. Evidence-gated fusion combines the two layers into spatial belief hotspots. We further introduce object-conditioned visual reasoning with conservative evidence qualification to improve observation reliability before spatial accumulation. In parallel, egocentric regional guidance converts quadtree coverage into UAV-centered, yaw-aligned directional proposals and stabilizes them through temporal commitment. Its regional scoring is independent of semantic belief values, maintaining exploration pressure and reducing repeated low-gain search. Experiments on the UAV-ON benchmark show that AeroBelief achieves the best reported overall SR, OSR, and SPL among the compared methods, reaching 21.61%, 35.57%, and 10.62, respectively. These results support the effectiveness of persistent semantic-spatial belief, conservative evidence qualification, and temporally stable regional guidance for aerial ObjectNav.

AI.tldr: AeroBelief is a dual-layer semantic-spatial belief mapping framework for aerial Object Goal Navigation (ObjectNav) that transforms transient VLM observations into persistent spatial guidance. It uses an intuition layer for scene-level exploration, an evidence layer for target-specific approach, evidence-gated fusion for belief hotspots, conservative evidence qualification for reliability, and egocentric regional guidance for stable directional proposals. It achieves state-of-the-art results on the UAV-ON benchmark (SR 21.61%, OSR 35.57%, SPL 10.62).
AI.motivation: VLMs can interpret open-ended target descriptions for aerial ObjectNav but produce noisy, sparse, and spatially transient frame-level outputs that cannot provide reliable persistent guidance for UAV navigation in unknown outdoor environments.
AI.method: AeroBelief proposes a dual-layer semantic-spatial belief mapping framework comprising: (1) an intuition layer accumulating scene-level semantic cues for exploration and an evidence layer preserving qualified target-specific observations; (2) evidence-gated fusion to combine layers into spatial belief hotspots; (3) object-conditioned visual reasoning with conservative evidence qualification to improve observation reliability; and (4) egocentric regional guidance that converts quadtree coverage into UAV-centered, yaw-aligned directional proposals with temporal commitment, with regional scoring independent of semantic belief values to maintain exploration pressure.
AI.result: On the UAV-ON benchmark, AeroBelief achieves the best reported overall Success Rate (SR) of 21.61%, OSR of 35.57%, and SPL of 10.62 among all compared methods.
AI.conclusion: Persistent semantic-spatial belief mapping, conservative evidence qualification, and temporally stable regional guidance are effective strategies for improving aerial ObjectNav performance, as demonstrated by state-of-the-art results on the UAV-ON benchmark.

title: Encoded Early, Used Late: Where Transformers Begin to Act on an Inferred Partner's Expertise
comment: Published at the Scientific Understanding of Foundation Models (Sci-FM) Workshop at COLM 2026
summary: A transformer can make an attribute linearly decodable in its residual stream at a depth where that attribute does not yet influence the output. This gap between where information is readable and where it is used has been shown for attributes stated directly in the input. We ask whether it also holds for an attribute the model must infer gradually over a conversation, namely how expert its dialogue partner is. Using ExpertCollab, a corpus of multi-turn research-planning dialogues between model-played personas at four expertise levels, we find that partner expertise is most decodable in the early layers and falls to near chance before the midpoint of the network. Counterfactual patching shows that injecting the expertise difference at the layer of peak decodability barely changes a fixed late-layer readout, whereas the same difference injected past the midpoint propagates almost completely, a separation of more than an order of magnitude. A content-matched random control and a probe-free diagnostic place the transition at the same early layer, and a statically specified control attribute stays decodable throughout. An inferred relational attribute is therefore represented well before it becomes causally active, which bounds where any attempt to read out or steer partner-conditioned behavior must intervene. We use one model on a synthetic corpus as an initial demonstration.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether an inferred relational attribute (dialogue partner expertise) becomes linearly decodable in the residual stream before it causally influences model output. Using ExpertCollab, a corpus of multi-turn research-planning dialogues, the authors find that partner expertise is most decodable in early layers and drops to near chance by the network midpoint. Counterfactual patching reveals a large gap: injecting expertise differences at peak-decodability layers barely changes readouts, while injections past the midpoint propagate almost completely—a >10x separation. Control experiments (content-matched random and statically specified attributes) confirm this transition is specific to inferred relational attributes.
AI.motivation: Prior work showed that attributes stated directly in the input become readable in the residual stream before they influence output. The authors ask whether this decodability-before-causality gap also holds for attributes that must be inferred gradually over a conversation—specifically, the expertise level of a dialogue partner, which is not directly stated but must be learned through interaction.
AI.method: The authors construct ExpertCollab, a synthetic corpus of multi-turn research-planning dialogues generated by model-played personas at four expertise levels. They train linear probes to decode partner expertise from residual stream activations across layers. They use counterfactual patching to intervene at specific layers and measure causal impact on a fixed late-layer readout. Controls include content-matched random attributes and a statically specified control attribute, plus a probe-free diagnostic.
AI.result: Partner expertise is most decodable in early layers and falls to near chance before the network midpoint. Injecting the expertise difference at the peak-decodability layer produces almost no change in a late-layer readout, whereas injection past the midpoint propagates almost completely—a separation exceeding an order of magnitude. Content-matched and probe-free controls place the transition at the same early layer, while a statically specified control attribute remains decodable throughout all layers.
AI.conclusion: An inferred relational attribute is represented in the residual stream well before it becomes causally active. This decodability-before-causality gap establishes a boundary for where any attempt to read out or steer partner-conditioned behavior must intervene. The authors note this is an initial demonstration using one model on a synthetic corpus.

title: Monkey See, Can Monkey Do? A Benchmark for Evaluating Robot Skill Learning by Observation
comment: 31 pages, 8 tables, 11 figures. In Proceedings of CoRL 2026
summary: Learning from Observation (LfO) is a fundamental robotic capability that replicates how humans and animals socially learn from each other. Beyond its biological parallels, this modality provides a practical solution for data scaling in sample-inefficient and data-starved domains like robotics. Recent work has demonstrated promising results in learning manipulation skills from human videos, yet progress in this area remains difficult to assess. Existing methods vary widely in assumptions, hardware choices, and environment setups making it difficult to draw meaningful comparisons and identify advances in the field. To address these challenges, we introduce RoboReel: a unified benchmark for evaluating models that learn policies from human videos. RoboReel consists of bundled real-world human demonstration videos, simulated robot trajectories, and evaluation environments on ten manipulation tasks. We develop four test suites to evaluate the models' performance on multiple axes, including the robustness to visual distractors and the ability to complete long-horizon tasks. Our benchmark covers learning-from-observation models from different categories, and studies the effectiveness of multiple representation choices in our benchmark evaluation that covers over seven state-of-the-art algorithms (including our VLA based variants) in the field of LfO. Finally, we present an analysis of the different types of algorithms showing that long-horizon tasks and tasks with low tolerances are still challenging for current models. Webpage: https://roboreel.github.io

AI.tldr: RoboReel is a unified benchmark for evaluating robot learning-from-observation (LfO) models that learn manipulation policies from human demonstration videos. It includes ten manipulation tasks, bundled real-world human videos, simulated robot trajectories, and evaluation environments, with four test suites assessing robustness to distractors and long-horizon task performance across seven state-of-the-art algorithms.
AI.motivation: Progress in learning manipulation skills from human videos is difficult to assess because existing methods vary widely in assumptions, hardware choices, and environment setups, making meaningful comparisons and identification of advances challenging.
AI.method: RoboReel provides a unified benchmark comprising ten manipulation tasks with bundled human demonstration videos, simulated robot trajectories, and evaluation environments. It includes four test suites measuring performance across multiple axes such as robustness to visual distractors and long-horizon task completion. The benchmark evaluates multiple categories of LfO models, covering seven state-of-the-art algorithms including VLA-based variants and studies the effectiveness of different representation choices.
AI.result: The analysis across different algorithm types reveals that long-horizon tasks and tasks with low tolerances remain challenging for current LfO models, highlighting persisting limitations in the state of the art.
AI.conclusion: RoboReel serves as a standardized benchmark to facilitate meaningful comparisons and track advances in LfO from human videos; however, current models still struggle with long-horizon tasks and those requiring high precision/low tolerance.

title: An Auditable Symbolic-RAG-Generative AI Architecture for Goal-Oriented Conversation Orchestration
comment: 14 pages, 3 figures, 6 tables, Appendices with complete experiments
summary: Goal-oriented conversational systems must answer factual questions, understand visitor-provided information, and advance business objectives without becoming rigid questionnaires. This paper proposes a Symbolic-RAG-Generative architecture centered on the Goal-oriented Retrieval-Augmented Conversation Engine (GRACE). An instruction-constrained Business Goal Compiler transforms business intent into an immutable objective set, normalized priority vector, canonical questions, and initial state vector. At runtime, GRACE receives the complete conversation history, latest visitor message, current state, and grounded answer generated by a separate RAG component. It updates completion only from visitor-authored evidence and selects one contextually modulated follow-up. The core policy maximizes expected business progress subject to a minimum visitor-utility constraint. We formalize the state, monotonic transitions, source separation, question modulation, and constrained policy; present the reference architecture; and define an evaluation comprising 24 English real-estate and 10 Spanish professional-cleaning conversations, totaling 119 protocol-defined visitor turns. Across both domains, GRACE achieves 84.9% exact state-transition accuracy, 91.6% evidence precision, 89.6% evidence recall, 100% monotonicity, and 94.1% terminal-state accuracy. The evaluation establishes compelling symbolic-state performance across standard, multi-goal, RAG-detour, validation, refusal, and robustness scenarios.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes GRACE, a Goal-oriented Retrieval-Augmented Conversation Engine with a Symbolic-RAG-Generative architecture, for goal-oriented conversational systems. GRACE transforms business intent into immutable objectives and selects contextually modulated follow-ups by maximizing expected business progress under a minimum visitor-utility constraint. Evaluated on 24 English real-estate and 10 Spanish professional-cleaning conversations, it achieves 84.9% exact state-transition accuracy, 91.6% evidence precision, 89.6% evidence recall, 100% monotonicity, and 94.1% terminal-state accuracy across standard, multi-goal, RAG-detour, validation, refusal, and robustness scenarios.
AI.motivation: Goal-oriented conversational systems must balance answering factual questions, understanding visitor-provided information, and advancing business objectives without becoming rigid or questionnaire-like. Existing approaches struggle to maintain this balance, motivating a structured architecture that separates symbolic goal tracking from retrieval-augmented generation.
AI.method: GRACE uses an instruction-constrained Business Goal Compiler to convert business intent into an immutable objective set, normalized priority vector, canonical questions, and initial state vector. At runtime, GRACE processes the complete conversation history, latest visitor message, current state, and grounded RAG-generated answer. It updates completion only from visitor-authored evidence and selects contextually modulated follow-ups. The core policy maximizes expected business progress subject to a minimum visitor-utility constraint. The paper formalizes the state, monotonic transitions, source separation, question modulation, and constrained policy.
AI.result: Across 24 English real-estate and 10 Spanish professional-cleaning conversations totaling 119 protocol-defined visitor turns, GRACE achieves 84.9% exact state-transition accuracy, 91.6% evidence precision, 89.6% evidence recall, 100% monotonicity, and 94.1% terminal-state accuracy across six scenario types.
AI.conclusion: The evaluation demonstrates that GRACE provides compelling symbolic-state performance across standard, multi-goal, RAG-detour, validation, refusal, and robustness scenarios, establishing the effectiveness of the Symbolic-RAG-Generative architecture for goal-oriented conversational systems.

title: TacClip: a clip-on sensor measures dynamic contact forces without covering the fingerpads
summary: TacClip is a minimally encumbering wearable device for recording fingertip deformation caused by contact forces and vibrations. It can be combined with vision- or glove-based hand tracking systems that leave the fingertips uncovered and provides a measure of dynamic contact interactions, while leaving the finger pads exposed so that the user retains natural sensitivity to texture, friction, temperature, and fine surface features. The signal is produced by a Fiber Bragg Grating (FBG) embedded on a small plastic clip mounted over the fingernail. Optionally, for use with vision-based tracking, additional FBGs on polyimide strips can complement camera-based pose estimation. In finger pressing tests, TacClip estimates the force magnitude with typical errors below $0.5~\mathrm{N}$ over a $0$--$8~\mathrm{N}$ range. In tests of cloth handling and tape edge finding, we show that it captures the vibrations and dynamic events generated during exploratory sliding. With no electronics, TacClip can also be used submerged in water, while preserving bare finger contact.

AI.tldr: TacClip is a minimally encumbering wearable fingertip deformation sensor using a Fiber Bragg Grating mounted on a nail clip that records contact forces and vibrations while leaving the finger pad exposed. It estimates forces with errors below 0.5 N over a 0–8 N range and works underwater.
AI.motivation: To provide a wearable tactile sensing solution that records dynamic contact interactions at the fingertip without interfering with natural touch sensitivity, and that can complement vision- or glove-based tracking systems which leave fingertips uncovered.
AI.method: An FBG is embedded in a small plastic clip mounted over the fingernail to measure nail deformation induced by fingertip contact forces. Optional polyimide strips with additional FBGs complement vision-based pose estimation. The device is fully passive with no electronics.
AI.result: Force magnitude estimation errors below 0.5 N over a 0–8 N range in pressing tests. Captures vibrations and dynamic events during cloth handling and tape edge finding. Functions submerged in water due to the absence of electronics.
AI.conclusion: TacClip offers a wearable, unobtrusive, and waterproof solution for capturing dynamic fingertip contact interactions while preserving bare-pad tactile sensitivity, suitable for integration with hand tracking systems.

title: PhysMAS: Physics-Grounded Multi-Agent Synthesis of Compositional 4D Gaussians
summary: Efficient, fully automatic, and physically plausible 4D Gaussian synthesis is an important goal for dynamic scene generation. Recent physics-based methods couple 3D Gaussians with the Material Point Method (MPM) to generate physically driven motion, but extending this paradigm to heterogeneous multi-part objects and interacting multi-object scenes remains challenging. Object-level physical assignment collapses distinct parts into a single material state, while one-shot predictions from large language models, vision-language models, or agents neither reliably bind different materials to identified parts nor verify that the resulting MPM configuration is executable. Score Distillation Sampling (SDS)-based parameter optimization, meanwhile, requires repeated per-scene score evaluations and gradient backpropagation, incurring lengthy optimization and potentially yielding suboptimal or unstable solutions. We therefore present PhysMAS, a physics-grounded multi-agent framework. From a motion prompt and four scene views, an Object-Part Scene Agent establishes persistent identities and calls a Material Reasoning Agent for part-wise profiles. It invokes solver-aware skills to bind these identities and profiles to per-particle MPM fields and execute all objects in a shared domain; the framework then screens candidate forward-simulation results. This supports heterogeneous multi-part and interacting multi-object scenes without per-scene diffusion-score backpropagation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that, compared with recent physics-based 4D Gaussian baselines that rely on SDS, PhysMAS achieves better semantic alignment and perceived physical plausibility while requiring less runtime.

AI.tldr: PhysMAS is a physics-grounded multi-agent framework for efficient, fully automatic, and physically plausible 4D Gaussian synthesis. It uses an Object-Part Scene Agent to establish persistent object identities, a Material Reasoning Agent for part-wise material profiles, and solver-aware skills to bind these to per-particle MPM fields, enabling heterogeneous multi-part and multi-object scenes without per-scene diffusion-score backpropagation, achieving better semantic alignment and physical plausibility than SDS-based baselines at lower runtime.
AI.motivation: Efficient, fully automatic, and physically plausible 4D Gaussian synthesis remains challenging. Existing physics-based methods (3D Gaussians + MPM) fail on heterogeneous multi-part objects and interacting multi-object scenes because object-level physical assignment collapses distinct parts into a single material state, and one-shot LLM/VLM/agent predictions neither reliably bind materials to parts nor verify MPM executability. SDS-based optimization requires repeated per-scene score evaluations and gradient backpropagation, yielding lengthy optimization and potentially suboptimal or unstable solutions.
AI.method: PhysMAS introduces a physics-grounded multi-agent framework. From a motion prompt and four scene views, an Object-Part Scene Agent establishes persistent identities for parts and invokes a Material Reasoning Agent to generate part-wise material profiles. Solver-aware skills are then used to bind these identities and profiles to per-particle MPM fields and execute all objects within a shared simulation domain. The framework subsequently screens candidate forward-simulation results, avoiding per-scene diffusion-score backpropagation entirely.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show that compared to recent physics-based 4D Gaussian baselines relying on SDS, PhysMAS achieves better semantic alignment and perceived physical plausibility while requiring less runtime.
AI.conclusion: PhysMAS demonstrates that decomposing physical assignment and material reasoning across specialized agents, combined with solver-aware skill execution and forward-simulation screening, can replace SDS-based optimization for producing physically plausible dynamic scenes, offering a more efficient and scalable paradigm for 4D Gaussian synthesis.

title: Bridging Language and Physics: Automated Design of Continuum Robots with Large Language Models
comment: The first three authors contributed equally to this work
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have recently emerged as a promising tool for automating robot design from high-level specifications, yet they remain ineffective for robots operating under complex physical interactions. This limitation stems from the gap between language-based reasoning and the physical consequences of embodiment, often resulting in designs with low physical validity. In this work, we propose a multi-layered framework, AID-SR, that establishes a closed loop by translating simulator-observed physical states into structured feedback for the LLM designer. Combined with semantic critique, human feedback, and iterative refinement, the framework promotes the generation of physically feasible and functionally meaningful robot designs. We evaluate our approach on tendon-driven continuum robots across a benchmark of 14 tasks spanning reaching, grasping, locomotion, and manipulation. The proposed framework achieves 96.2% rate for passing the simulation feasibility check and by applying a common reinforcement learning training, 26.7% robots can successfully fulfill the corresponding task. We then fabricate three designed robots of AID-SR that successfully complete the task in real-world. These extensive experiments across simulation and real-world environments demonstrate and break the wall of utilizing the LLMs for automated design of continuum robots. The source code and experimental resources are publicly available at https://github.com/UNITES-Lab/AID-SR.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces AID-SR, a multi-layered framework that establishes a closed loop between simulator-observed physical states and LLM-based robot design feedback. It achieves 96.2% simulation feasibility and 26.7% task success across 14 tasks for tendon-driven continuum robots, with three designs validated in the real world.
AI.motivation: LLMs show promise for automating robot design from high-level specifications but struggle with robots operating under complex physical interactions due to a gap between language-based reasoning and physical consequences of embodiment, producing designs with low physical validity.
AI.method: The approach, AID-SR, is a multi-layered framework that closes the loop by translating simulator-observed physical states into structured feedback for the LLM designer. It integrates semantic critique, human feedback, and iterative refinement to promote physically feasible and functionally meaningful robot generation.
AI.result: On a benchmark of 14 tasks (reaching, grasping, locomotion, manipulation) for tendon-driven continuum robots, AID-SR achieves a 96.2% simulation feasibility check pass rate and 26.7% task success after reinforcement learning training. Three designed robots were fabricated and successfully completed tasks in the real world.
AI.conclusion: Extensive simulation and real-world experiments demonstrate that AID-SR breaks the wall for using LLMs in automated design of continuum robots, showing that structured physical feedback enables physically feasible and functionally meaningful robot designs.

title: EmoMed: An Emotionally-Aware Agent for Multimodal Medical Support with Real-Time Information Retrieval
summary: We present EmoMed - a multimodal medical consultation agent that adapts its responses based on users' emotional states while maintaining clinical accuracy. The system processes text and medical images, detects affect indicators (anxiety, confusion, urgency) from user input, and adjusts response tone, structure, and detail level accordingly. To ensure factual reliability, the agent grounds clinical information through a dual retrieval mechanism: web-based fact-checking and an API-connected, continuously updated medical knowledge base. We evaluate our approach across seven state-of-the-art language models (GPT-4/5, Qwen3, Llama 4, Gemini 2.5, Grok4, Claude3) using comprehensive metrics including LLM-as-judge assessments, MedQA style accuracy tests, BERT Score, safety/helpfulness ratings, and multimodal medical benchmarks. The results demonstrate that emotionally adaptive responses consistently outperform neutral baseline across evaluation dimensions, without compromising clinical accuracy. A controlled user study validated these findings, with participants reporting improved perceived empathy and communication clarity, while maintaining trust in factual accuracy. Source code: https://github.com/NasonovIvan/EmoMed-Agent

AI.tldr: EmoMed is a multimodal medical consultation agent that dynamically adapts its responses to users' emotional states (anxiety, confusion, urgency) while preserving clinical accuracy through a dual retrieval grounding mechanism combining web fact-checking and an API-connected medical knowledge base.
AI.motivation: Traditional medical AI agents prioritize clinical accuracy but often neglect emotional context, leading to responses that may be technically correct yet fail to address user anxiety, confusion, or urgency—factors critical for effective patient communication and trust.
AI.method: EmoMed processes text and medical images, detects affect indicators from user input, and adjusts response tone, structure, and detail. Clinical reliability is ensured via a dual retrieval mechanism: web-based fact-checking plus an API-connected, continuously updated medical knowledge base. Evaluated across seven LLMs (GPT-4/5, Qwen3, Llama 4, Gemini 2.5, Grok4, Claude3) using LLM-as-judge, MedQA accuracy tests, BERT Score, safety/helpfulness ratings, and multimodal medical benchmarks, with a controlled user study.
AI.result: Emotionally adaptive responses consistently outperformed neutral baselines across all evaluation dimensions without compromising clinical accuracy. User study participants reported improved perceived empathy and communication clarity while maintaining trust in factual accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Emotional adaptivity and clinical accuracy are not mutually exclusive; EmoMed demonstrates that affect-aware response generation can enhance communication quality while preserving medical reliability, suggesting emotion-adaptive design as a valuable direction for future medical AI systems.

title: 3DWay: Generalizing Robot Manipulation via 3D Consistent Waypoints
summary: Intermediate representations are key to bridging the modality gap between generalizable manipulation policies and large-scale pretrained vision-language models (VLMs). Among these, trajectory-based representations compactly represent motion-relevant cues, yet most existing approaches predict trajectories in 2D image space, resulting in intrinsic 3D ambiguity. Moreover, using 2D trajectories with depth still leaves the free-space waypoints ambiguous, limiting reliable 3D reasoning. To address this, we propose predicting 3D consistent waypoints (3DWay) from multi-view images. By reformulating 3D waypoints prediction as generating multi-view consistent 2D waypoints followed by geometric triangulation, we enable explicit 3D motion specification while preserving the strong priors of pretrained VLMs. The predicted waypoints can guide existing VLA models for better generalization or be directly executed on simple tasks. Extensive experiments show that 3DWay substantially improves 3D spatial grounding and vision-language reasoning, demonstrating strong potential for generalizable robot manipulation. Codes will be released at https://github.com/ziqin-h/3DWay.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes 3DWay, a method for predicting 3D consistent waypoints from multi-view images by reformulating 3D waypoint prediction as multi-view consistent 2D waypoint generation followed by geometric triangulation, enabling explicit 3D motion specification while preserving pretrained VLM priors for generalizable robot manipulation.
AI.motivation: Trajectory-based intermediate representations are key for bridging manipulation policies and VLMs, but existing approaches predict trajectories in 2D image space, leading to inherent 3D ambiguity. Even using 2D trajectories with depth leaves free-space waypoints ambiguous, limiting reliable 3D reasoning for robot manipulation.
AI.method: 3DWay predicts 3D consistent waypoints from multi-view images. It reformulates 3D waypoint prediction as generating multi-view consistent 2D waypoints followed by geometric triangulation, which enables explicit 3D motion specification while preserving the strong priors of pretrained VLMs. The predicted waypoints can guide existing VLA models or be directly executed on simple tasks.
AI.result: Extensive experiments demonstrate that 3DWay substantially improves 3D spatial grounding and vision-language reasoning, showing strong potential for generalizable robot manipulation.
AI.conclusion: 3DWay effectively addresses the 3D ambiguity in trajectory-based intermediate representations by leveraging multi-view consistency and geometric triangulation, offering a promising direction for grounding VLM-based manipulation policies in 3D space.

title: Agentic Algorithm Engineering: Improving Shared-Memory Exact Minimum Cuts
summary: The minimum cut problem for an undirected edge-weighted graph asks us to divide its set of nodes into two blocks while minimizing the weighted sum of the cut edges. Over the last years, we engineered a range of fast algorithms for this problem. Our fastest exact algorithm uses an inexact algorithm to obtain a better bound for the problem, reductions that depend on this bound, improved data structures and parallel contraction routines. It is available in the open-source package VieCut and, on real-world instances, outperformed the previously fastest solvers by a factor of up to 2.5 sequentially and up to 12.9 when run in parallel. We improve this algorithm using agentic algorithm engineering (AAE), a methodology that we introduce here, in which autonomous large language model agents run the algorithm engineering cycle on an existing code base: they form hypotheses about where running time is lost, implement them, benchmark the result on a fixed instance set and keep or discard the change. Even though we had already tuned our algorithm by hand extensively, the agent finds significant optimizations, in particular on the DIMACS core instances: factors of 1.28 (sequential) and 1.63 (32 threads) on real-world k-cores, and 6.26 and 127 on the DIMACS core instances.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an improved minimum cut algorithm built on top of the VieCut solver, using a novel methodology called agentic algorithm engineering (AAE) where autonomous LLM agents run the algorithm engineering cycle—hypothesize, implement, benchmark, and keep/discard changes—to find optimizations that outperform the previous hand-tuned solver by up to 12.9x on real-world instances and up to 127x on DIMACS core instances.
AI.motivation: The authors previously engineered fast exact minimum cut algorithms for undirected edge-weighted graphs, achieving state-of-the-art performance with their VieCut package. However, despite extensive manual tuning, they seek to further improve performance using a new methodology where AI agents can systematically explore optimization opportunities in the existing codebase, potentially finding improvements human engineers overlooked.
AI.method: The paper introduces agentic algorithm engineering (AAE), a methodology in which autonomous large language model agents execute the algorithm engineering cycle on the existing VieCut codebase. Agents form hypotheses about where running time is lost, implement potential optimizations, benchmark the results on a fixed instance set, and decide whether to keep or discard each change. The underlying algorithm combines an inexact algorithm for better bounds, bound-dependent reductions, improved data structures, and parallel contraction routines.
AI.result: The AAE-driven agents found significant optimizations beyond the already hand-tuned algorithm.
