On real-world k-cores, sequential performance improved by a factor of 1.28 and parallel performance (32 threads) by 1.63. On DIMACS core instances, improvements were substantially larger: 6.26x sequential and 127x with 32 threads. The previous solver already outperformed existing tools by up to 2.5x sequentially and 12.9x in parallel.
AI.conclusion: Agentic algorithm engineering—deploying autonomous LLM agents to iterate on an existing algorithm engineering codebase—successfully discovers meaningful optimizations even for an extensively hand-tuned system. The substantial speedups on DIMACS core instances (up to 127x) demonstrate that AI-driven algorithm engineering can complement and exceed manual tuning efforts.

title: CALIPER: Clean Scenes Cannot Rank Physical Inference in Pretrained Visual Representations
summary: How far a pushed object slides depends on its mass and friction, which no single image reveals. Pretrained visual encoders are increasingly used as the perception front end of world models for manipulation, and their physical competence is assessed with perturbation benchmarks and linear probes, almost always in a clean, fixed-camera scene. We show that these assessments cannot distinguish an encoder that infers physics from one that does not. CALIPER (calibrate, then predict) is a direct test: an object of unknown mass and friction is struck twice at known speeds, a third strike is shown only up to the moment of contact, and a linear readout on frozen features must predict how far the object slides. Swapping in another object's calibration clips checks that the evidence is actually used. Across 2,000 simulated episodes and eight representations, from V-JEPA 2 to a randomly initialised ViT and raw pixels, calibration adds +0.50 R^2 and the swap removes it. Yet in the clean scene every representation lands within 0.02 R^2 of the ceiling set by true simulator state, because a fixed camera exposes the object's displacement directly in pixel coordinates. Resampling camera, lighting, and clutter for every clip spreads the same representations across 0.50 R^2; when the readout chooses a push speed for a goal distance, V-JEPA 2 misses by 4 mm and the random ViT by 20 mm, no better than ignoring the object. Linear probes track none of this: a change in frame aggregation moves a probe more than pretraining does, and erasing the probed mass direction from the same representation costs nothing in one scene and 0.35 R^2 in the other. Whether a benchmark can rank models is an empirical property, and we give three checks that establish it.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces CALIPER, a direct test to assess whether pretrained visual encoders actually infer physics (mass and friction) from images when used as perception front ends in manipulation world models. The authors show standard perturbation benchmarks and linear probes conducted in fixed-camera scenes cannot distinguish physics-capable encoders from those that are not. CALIPER calibrates on one object, then predicts sliding distance for a struck object of unknown mass/friction, with a swap control to verify evidence use. Across simulated episodes and eight representations, calibration helps and swap-control removes the advantage—yet in clean scenes all representations appear near-ceiling because pixel displacement leaks through the fixed camera. When camera, lighting, and clutter vary, performance spreads widely; the best encoder still outperforms baselines on downstream push-speed selection, while linear probes fail to track model quality.
AI.motivation: Standard evaluation of visual encoders for physical reasoning—perturbation benchmarks and linear probes in clean, fixed-camera scenes—cannot distinguish an encoder that genuinely infers physics from one that does not. Since manipulating objects requires reasoning about mass and friction that no single image reveals, a reliable diagnostic benchmark is needed to rank representations by their physical competence.
AI.method: The proposed method, CALIPER, operates as follows: an object of unknown mass and friction is struck twice at known speeds (calibration clips), and a third strike is shown up to the moment of contact; a linear readout on frozen encoder features must predict how far the object slides. A swap control substitutes another object's calibration clips to verify the evidence is genuinely used. Experiments vary scene conditions (camera, lighting, clutter) and compare eight representations from V-JEPA 2 to a random ViT and raw pixels across 2,000 simulated episodes. Benchmarks are validated with three checks for ranking reliability, including a downstream task of choosing push speed for a goal distance.
AI.result: Calibration adds +0.50 R² and the swap control removes it, yet in clean fixed-camera scenes every representation lands within 0.02 R² of the ceiling set by true simulator state due to pixel-visible displacement. Varying camera, lighting, and clutter spreads representations across 0.50 R²; for goal-distance push speed selection, V-JEPA 2 misses by 4 mm while a random ViT misses by 20 mm—no better than ignoring the object. Linear probes fail to track these differences: a change in frame aggregation moves a probe more than pretraining does, and erasing the probed mass direction changes performance by 0 in one scene and 0.35 R² in the other.
AI.conclusion: Whether a benchmark can rank visual encoders by physical competence is an empirical property, not an assumption. The paper establishes three checks that validate a ranking, showing that evaluation protocols must control scene variation and provide direct evidence of physical inference; otherwise, superficial cues (like fixed-camera displacement) mask true differences between representations.

title: Unraveling the Real Working Mechanism and Inherent Flaws of GAE: A Method for Interpreting Transformer Processes from an Economic Perspective
summary: We observe a phenomenon that current algorithmic research in the field of explainable artificial intelligence primarily pursues better performance on several proxy metrics. On the one hand, these proxy metrics themselves are more or less flawed and cannot properly measure the quality of methods. On the other hand, metric-oriented research approaches often lead to the neglect of the rationality and interpretability of the methods themselves. Explainable artificial intelligence is abbreviated as XAI. The metric-driven research paradigm has resulted in a lack of interpretability of the relevant XAI methods themselves. Accordingly, there is a need for interpretability research on XAI methods, which can be playfully referred to as XXAI. This paper is one of our works on XXAI. This paper takes Generic Attention-model Explainability (GAE), a widely influential model interpretation method , or rather, XAI method that represents an important technical route, as the research object, and explores the real working mechanism and flaws of this method as well as the technical route it represents. Based on the conclusions of this study, it may be necessary to re-examine or verify GAE-related methods and their domain applications. We argue that GAE is an interpretation method that focuses on the attention process. After pointing out the working mechanism and flaws of GAE, we propose Cumulative Asset Holdings (CAH), a more reasonable Transformer interpretation method integrating both process-based and feature-based ideas from an economic zero-sum games perspective. In addition, it is worth noting that our method is applicable to models with special tokens, where existing methods may suffer from limitations. The model simplification research method and the analysis of additive operations adopted in this study may provide inspiration for other research works in XAI.

AI.tldr: This paper critiques the metric-driven research paradigm in explainable AI (XAI), arguing it produces methods lacking self-interpretability (hence "XXAI"). Using Generic Attention-model Explainability (GAE) as a case study, the authors reveal its working mechanism and flaws, then propose Cumulative Asset Holdings (CAH), a more reasonable Transformer interpretation method based on economic zero-sum game theory that integrates process-based and feature-based perspectives and is applicable to models with special tokens.
AI.motivation: Current XAI research is dominated by proxy-metric optimization, where the metrics themselves are flawed and metric-oriented approaches neglect the rationality and interpretability of the XAI methods themselves. This necessitates interpretability research on XAI methods (XXAI), i.e., understanding the actual working mechanisms and flaws of widely-used interpretation techniques.
AI.method: The paper studies GAE as a representative XAI method (an attention-process-focused interpretation method), identifies its working mechanism and flaws through model simplification and analysis of additive operations. Based on these findings, the authors propose CAH, a Transformer interpretation method that integrates process-based and feature-based ideas within an economic zero-sum game framework, designed to work for models with special tokens where existing methods may fail.
AI.result: The study reveals the actual working mechanism and flaws of GAE and the technical route it represents. It concludes that GAE-related methods and their domain applications may require re-examination. The proposed CAH method offers a more reasonable alternative applicable to models with special tokens.
AI.conclusion: The paper calls for a re-evaluation of GAE-based methods given their revealed flaws, proposes CAH as a superior alternative from a zero-sum game perspective, and suggests the model simplification and additive-operation analysis methodologies may inspire broader XAI research.

title: Seeing is Not Believing: Breaking the Physical-to-Digital Trust Boundary in Robotics
summary: In multi-robot collaboration, task handovers rely on downstream verifiers performing remote attestation, which inspects sensor telemetry to ensure a robot's physical behavior strictly matches its assigned task. But can this telemetry be trusted? We show that it often cannot. In this paper, we uncover a severe vulnerability in Robot Operating System (ROS) 2: by modifying a single environment variable, an adversary can execute a pre-built hook to covertly intercept and inject both telemetry and control signals before they are published. Consequently, adversaries can hijack a robot to perform dangerous tasks while spoofing downstream verifiers with synthesized fake telemetry. Worse still, by exploiting the widespread reliance on third-party Docker containers and auxiliary tools, attackers can distribute compromised packages embedded with these malicious hooks to launch such attacks easily. On a physical Franka Emika robotic arm running Secure ROS 2, our attack injects fabricated telemetry in real time with only around 3 ms of jitter, preserving temporal synchronization and hardware integrity while achieving an 87% success rate even against an AI-based detector. We have responsibly disclosed these findings to the ROS 2 development team. We prepared a demo video available at https://youtu.be/ExeiGqUrnhQ.

AI.tldr: This paper uncovers a severe vulnerability in ROS 2 where a single environment variable modification allows adversaries to execute pre-built hooks that covertly intercept and inject telemetry and control signals, enabling robot hijacking while spoofing downstream verifiers with fabricated telemetry. The attack achieves 87% success against an AI-based detector on a physical Franka Emika robotic arm running Secure ROS 2, with only ~3ms of jitter.
AI.motivation: The authors question whether telemetry used in remote attestation for multi-robot task handovers can be trusted, and demonstrate that it often cannot due to a fundamental vulnerability in ROS 2.
AI.method: The attack exploits ROS 2 by modifying a single environment variable to execute a pre-built hook, enabling covert interception and injection of both telemetry and control signals before publication. Attackers can distribute compromised packages via third-party Docker containers and auxiliary tools.
AI.result: On a physical Franka Emika robotic arm running Secure ROS 2, the attack injects fabricated telemetry in real time with ~3ms of jitter, preserving temporal synchronization and hardware integrity while achieving 87% success even against an AI-based detector.
AI.conclusion: The vulnerability is severe and widespread due to reliance on third-party containers and tools. Findings were responsibly disclosed to the ROS 2 development team.

title: Distance-Aware Attention and Wall-Distance Expert Routing for Transformer-Based 3D Flow Prediction
summary: Transformer surrogates for 3D flow prediction compress an industrial mesh into a small set of tokens from which every prediction point reads. Two operations follow: the retrieval step in which a point gathers information from the compressed representation, and the feed-forward layer that transforms what it retrieved. In current backbones both are blind to where the point sits in the flow. We condition both on wall-related physical signals. Distance-aware cross-attention (DA-CA) reshapes each volume query by its wall distance before retrieval, so that a point deep in the boundary layer draws different geometric information than one in the outer flow. Surface-volume mixture-of-experts (SVMoE) replaces the shared feed-forward layer with a small set of experts, routed by wall distance for volume points and by local geometry for surface points. Neither mechanism is tied to one architecture, so we apply both unchanged to AB-UPT and Transolver-3. On DrivAerML with 50 training cases, DA-CA reduces the volume pressure error by 10.1%, and DA-CA and SVMoE together reduce it by 12.5%; DA-CA improves the near-wall region at some cost in the far region, which SVMoE recovers, and the volume experts settle into near-wall, transition, and free-stream bands without routing supervision. Retrained on 300 cases, the conditioning improves every field quantity, reducing volume pressure and velocity errors by 33.1% and 18.6% on AB-UPT and by 21.4% and 21.3% on Transolver-3. Under Leave-One-Body-Out evaluation on DrivAerNet++, it reduces the volume pressure error on unseen body types by up to 14.2%.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces two conditioning mechanisms—Distance-Aware Cross-Attention (DA-CA) and Surface-Volume Mixture-of-Experts (SVMoE)—that inject wall-distance and local-geometry information into transformer surrogates for 3D flow prediction, improving accuracy across multiple benchmarks and dataset scales.
AI.motivation: Current transformer backbone surrogates for 3D flow prediction compress industrial meshes into tokens and use retrieval (cross-attention) and feed-forward layers, but both operations are agnostic to where a point sits in the flow field. This ignores critical physical context such as wall proximity, which is especially important near boundary layers.
AI.method: The paper proposes two architecture-agnostic conditioning mechanisms: (1) DA-CA, which reshapes volume query features by wall distance before cross-attention retrieval so points at different distances from the wall gather distinct geometric information, and (2) SVMoE, which replaces the shared feed-forward layer with experts routed by wall distance for volume points and by local geometry for surface points. Both mechanisms are applied unchanged to two backbones: AB-UPT and Transolver-3.
AI.result: On DrivAerML with 50 training cases, DA-CA reduces volume pressure error by 10.1%, and DA-CA + SVMoE together achieve a 12.5% reduction. With 300 training cases, conditioning improves all field quantities, reducing volume pressure and velocity errors by 33.1% and 18.6% on AB-UPT, and 21.4% and 21.3% on Transolver-3. Under Leave-One-Body-Out evaluation on DrivAerNet++, volume pressure error on unseen body types is reduced by up to 14.2%. Notably, volume experts self-organize into near-wall, transition, and free-stream bands without routing supervision.
AI.conclusion: Conditioning transformer operations on wall-related physical signals—specifically wall distance for volume points and local geometry for surface points—consistently improves flow prediction accuracy across architectures, dataset sizes, and generalization to unseen geometries. The emergent specialization of experts into physically meaningful flow regions suggests the approach captures relevant physical structure without explicit supervision.

title: EvoNav-Bench: Benchmarking Lifelong Navigation in Evolving Environments
summary: Lifelong navigation (LN) requires an embodied agent to solve a sequence of navigation subtasks in the same environment. Since solving each subtask from scratch incurs redundant exploration, an LN agent must consolidate experience from earlier stages and reuse it in later stages, often through persistent scene representations such as scene graphs or visual snapshots. However, existing approaches typically assume a stationary environment, whereas in real-world LN settings, human activities can cause the environment to evolve. With the stationary assumption violated, existing methods may fuse outdated prior observations with new observations, yet current benchmarks cannot reveal this failure mode. In this paper, we present EvoNav-Bench, which extends the GOAT-Bench style LN formulation in the context of evolving environments. Built on the ProcTHOR framework, EvoNav-Bench introduces environment modifications between navigation tasks, making prior experience useful but not fully reliable. This design enables controlled evaluation of how environment evolution affects LN agents that reuse prior scene observations. Using EvoNav-Bench, we benchmark three recent methods that build and reuse scene representations for navigation. We also compare three simple heuristic strategies for handling environment evolution: Frontier-Update, Fail-then-Update, and Stage-Reset. Our results show that existing methods are brittle under environment evolution, while the heuristic strategies enable a controlled analysis of how agents can adapt to scene changes and mitigate their impact.

AI.tldr: EvoNav-Bench is a new benchmark extending lifelong navigation to evolving environments, where the environment changes between subtasks. It reveals that existing LN methods that reuse scene representations are brittle under environment evolution, and heuristic strategies (Frontier-Update, Fail-then-Update, Stage-Reset) enable controlled analysis of adaptation to scene changes.
AI.motivation: Existing lifelong navigation (LN) methods assume a stationary environment, but real-world settings involve environmental changes due to human activities. This violates the core assumption of scene-reuse-based LN approaches, and current benchmarks cannot expose this failure mode because they never introduce environment modifications between subtasks.
AI.method: The authors build EvoNav-Bench on the ProcTHOR framework and the GOAT-Bench style LN formulation. The benchmark introduces controlled environment modifications between navigation tasks, making prior experience useful but not fully reliable. They benchmark three recent methods that build/reuse scene representations and compare three heuristic strategies for handling environment evolution: Frontier-Update, Fail-then-Update, and Stage-Reset.
AI.result: Existing LN methods are brittle under environment evolution, demonstrating that their fusion of outdated prior observations with new observations degrades performance. The heuristic strategies provide a controlled means to analyze how agents can adapt to scene changes and mitigate their negative impact.
AI.conclusion: EvoNav-Bench fills a critical evaluation gap by revealing the failure mode of existing LN methods in evolving environments. It provides a foundation for studying how LN agents can adapt to scene changes, supported by benchmark data and heuristic strategy baselines for future research.

title: Elastic Horizon: Discovering the Effective Interaction Frontier in Agentic Reinforcement Learning
comment: 17 pages, 6 figures, 12 tables. Accepted to EMNLP 2026
summary: Scaling the interaction horizon-the maximum number of environment interactions per episode-improves LLM agents on long-horizon tasks, and curriculum-based methods that progressively expand the horizon outperform fixed-horizon alternatives. However, existing schedules are open-loop: they monotonically increase the horizon until a manually specified maximum, with no mechanism to detect when further expansion stops helping. We propose the effective interaction frontier hypothesis: a dynamic boundary beyond which additional interactions yield diminishing returns while cost grows linearly. We then introduce Elastic Horizon, a closed-loop controller that tracks this boundary via the 90th percentile of successful trajectory lengths. On AppWorld and BFCL, fixed-horizon sweeps reveal clear saturation plateaus; Elastic Horizon stabilizes the horizon inside the saturation band from both under- and over-capacity initializations, attains the best success rates across 7B and 14B backbones, and saves up to 25% of per-step trajectory tokens. Our work shifts the paradigm from how to scale interaction horizons to when to stop scaling.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Elastic Horizon, a closed-loop controller for dynamically adjusting the interaction horizon of LLM agents on long-horizon tasks. It tracks the effective interaction frontier (90th percentile of successful trajectory lengths) to stop scaling horizons at saturation points, achieving better success rates and up to 25% token savings compared to fixed-horizon and open-loop curriculum methods.
AI.motivation: Existing curriculum-based methods for scaling interaction horizons in LLM agents are open-loop: they monotonically increase the horizon until a manually specified maximum with no mechanism to detect when further expansion stops providing benefits. This can waste computational resources since additional interactions yield diminishing returns beyond a certain point while cost grows linearly.
AI.method: The authors propose the effective interaction frontier hypothesis, a dynamic boundary beyond which additional interactions yield diminishing returns. They introduce Elastic Horizon, a closed-loop controller that tracks this boundary using the 90th percentile of successful trajectory lengths as a signal to dynamically stabilize the interaction horizon at saturation plateaus.
AI.result: On AppWorld and BFCL benchmarks, Elastic Horizon stabilizes the horizon inside the saturation band from both under- and over-capacity initializations, attains the best success rates across 7B and 14B backbone models, and saves up to 25% of per-step trajectory tokens compared to fixed-horizon alternatives.
AI.conclusion: The paper shifts the paradigm from how to scale interaction horizons to when to stop scaling, demonstrating that closed-loop horizon control can achieve optimal performance while reducing computational waste on long-horizon LLM agent tasks.

title: A Multi-Modal Perception Pipeline for Object Detection and Tracking in Autonomous Racing
summary: Object detection and tracking are fundamental components of perception systems for autonomous driving. Achieving robust performance under adverse conditions such as limited visibility, sensor noise, and failures remains an open challenge, particularly in autonomous racing, where vehicles operate at very high speeds, experience strong vibrations, and interact under small safety margins. This paper presents a multi-modal late-fusion perception pipeline for object detection and tracking in the autonomous racing domain. The proposed system extends previous work by exploiting all onboard sensors through a late-fusion approach and a dedicated multi-object tracking framework. Independent detections from cameras, LiDARs, and RADARs are combined to provide timely and robust state estimates of surrounding vehicles. The tracking method explicitly compensates for detection delays and embeds in its model prior knowledge of vehicle dynamics and track layout. Experimental evaluation on real-world data across diverse critical scenarios, representative of challenging edge cases also in urban driving, confirms the effectiveness of the proposed pipeline and its suitability to support safe and adaptive planning decisions.

AI.tldr: A multi-modal late-fusion perception pipeline for object detection and tracking in autonomous racing, combining independent detections from cameras, LiDARs, and RADARs with a multi-object tracking framework that compensates for detection delays and embeds vehicle dynamics and track layout priors.
AI.motivation: Robust object detection and tracking under adverse conditions (limited visibility, sensor noise, failures) remains challenging, particularly in autonomous racing where high speeds, strong vibrations, and small safety margins amplify these difficulties.
AI.method: A multi-modal late-fusion perception pipeline that combines independent detections from cameras, LiDARs, and RADARs, extended with a dedicated multi-object tracking framework that explicitly compensates for detection delays and embeds prior knowledge of vehicle dynamics and track layout into its model.
AI.result: Experimental evaluation on real-world data across diverse critical scenarios—representative of challenging edge cases also in urban driving—confirms the effectiveness of the proposed pipeline and its suitability for supporting safe and adaptive planning decisions.
AI.conclusion: The proposed late-fusion perception and tracking pipeline is effective for autonomous racing and demonstrates robustness in edge cases that are also relevant to urban driving, making it suitable for safe and adaptive planning.

title: SkillAlign: Aligning Skill Interfaces for LLM-based Agents
summary: Language-model agents increasingly rely on skills: reusable procedural knowledge for reasoning, tool use, and interaction. Existing work studies how skills are acquired, retrieved, compressed, or composed, but often assumes that once a skill is selected, its interface to the agent is fixed. We argue that this overlooks a key source of skill utility: the same skill can help, distract, or mislead depending on how it is exposed. We propose SkillAlign, a provider-agnostic framework that represents candidate skills as multi-view procedural cards and renders them through alternative exposure interfaces, including full instructions, hints, compressed summaries, workflows, or no exposure. This enables counterfactual evaluation where the task, agent, and candidate skills are fixed while only the exposure interface varies. Across ALFWorld and SkillsBench, we show that exposure form substantially affects task success and rendered context cost, and that compact top-k exposure can outperform full-library injection. We further conduct a replay-based policy-learning analysis on ALFWorld, showing that adaptive exposure contains learnable signal but remains far from oracle selection. Our results suggest that skill-augmented agents should optimize not only which skills to use, but also how those skills are presented.

AI.tldr: SkillAlign is a provider-agnostic framework that treats skill exposure (how a skill is presented to an agent) as a key variable affecting task success. It represents skills as multi-view procedural cards and evaluates different exposure interfaces (full instructions, hints, compressed summaries, workflows, or none) under counterfactual conditions where task, agent, and skills are fixed. Results on ALFWorld and SkillsBench show exposure form significantly impacts success and context cost, with compact top-k exposure often outperforming full-library injection.
AI.motivation: Prior work on language-model agent skills focuses on acquisition, retrieval, compression, and composition but assumes that once a skill is selected, its interface to the agent is fixed. The authors argue this overlooks a crucial source of utility: the same skill can help, distract, or mislead depending on how it is exposed to the agent.
AI.method: SkillAlign is a provider-agnostic framework that: (1) represents candidate skills as multi-view procedural cards, and (2) renders them through alternative exposure interfaces, including full instructions, hints, compressed summaries, workflows, or no exposure. This enables counterfactual evaluation in which the task, agent, and candidate skills are held fixed while only the exposure interface varies.
AI.result: Across ALFWorld and SkillsBench, exposure form substantially affects task success and rendered context cost. Compact top-k exposure can outperform full-library injection. A replay-based policy-learning analysis on ALFWorld shows adaptive exposure contains learnable signal but remains far from oracle-level selection performance.
AI.conclusion: Skill-augmented agents should optimize not only which skills to use (selection) but also how those skills are presented (exposure), as the presentation form is a major determinant of downstream task performance.

title: RoboCousin: Build Your Own Simulation Playground for Robust Bimanual Robotic Manipulation
summary: Bimanual manipulation policies require large and diverse training datasets, yet collecting demonstrations on physical robots is expensive and difficult to scale. Simulation can generate data efficiently, but existing pipelines typically operate within closed asset libraries and predefined scenes: adding a newly observed object or environment still requires substantial effort to reconstruct geometry, specify physical and semantic properties, annotate interactions, and integrate the result into executable tasks. We present RoboCousin, an extensible simulation-based data-generation platform that turns user-provided observations into reusable assets, scenes, and expert trajectories for bimanual manipulation. Built on RoboTwin~2.0, RoboCousin converts object images into simulation-ready assets with visual and collision geometry, semantic and physical metadata, and automatically generated grasp-contact candidates. It further constructs digital cousins that vary compatible objects, backgrounds, layouts, and language instructions while preserving task-relevant affordances and spatial relations. The same asset system supports tabletop and room-level scene construction, with collision-aware base control for interaction beyond a fixed workspace. We release RoboCousin-OBD, containing more than 3,000 annotated object instances and 50 background environments, and use RoboCousin to generate over one million expert trajectories across 50 tasks. Simulation and real-robot experiments show that the automatically generated interaction annotations are comparable to curated annotations, generated assets provide effective sim-to-real supervision, and tabletop cousins can improve transfer beyond training on a single reconstructed scene. RoboCousin therefore provides a practical path for expanding both the scale and coverage of synthetic bimanual manipulation data.

AI.tldr: RoboCousin is an extensible simulation-based data-generation platform built on RoboTwin 2.0 that converts user-provided observations of objects into simulation-ready assets (with visual/collision geometry, semantic/physical metadata, and grasp-contact candidates) and constructs diverse "digital cousins" for bimanual manipulation training. It includes RoboCousin-OBD (3,000+ annotated objects, 50 backgrounds) and generates over one million expert trajectories across 50 tasks, demonstrating that auto-generated annotations match curated ones and improve sim-to-real transfer.
AI.motivation: Bimanual manipulation policies require large-scale diverse training data, but physical robot data collection is expensive and hard to scale. Existing simulation pipelines are constrained to closed asset libraries and predefined scenes, making it labor-intensive to incorporate newly observed objects or environments.
AI.method: RoboCousin converts object images into simulation-ready assets by generating visual and collision geometry, semantic and physical metadata, and automatic grasp-contact candidates. It creates "digital cousins" that vary compatible objects, backgrounds, layouts, and language instructions while preserving task-relevant affordances and spatial relations. The asset system supports both tabletop and room-level scene construction with collision-aware base control beyond a fixed workspace.
AI.result: The platform releases RoboCousin-OBD with 3,000+ annotated object instances and 50 background environments, generating over one million expert trajectories across 50 tasks. Experiments show automatically generated interaction annotations perform comparably to curated ones, generated assets provide effective sim-to-real supervision, and tabletop cousins improve transfer beyond training on a single reconstructed scene.
AI.conclusion: RoboCousin provides a practical and extensible path for expanding both the scale and coverage of synthetic bimanual manipulation data, reducing the effort required to incorporate novel objects and environments into training pipelines.

title: World Models Under Asynchronous Sensor Observations
comment: 13 pages, 2 figures. All authors contributed equally
summary: Learned world models typically assume that observations arrive synchronously, an abstraction inherited from simulators that return a complete state vector at each environment step. Physical sensing instead operates at heterogeneous rates, leaving most observation channels stale at any given instant. Interpolating stale channels introduces measurements that were never observed, while downsampling to the slowest sensor discards valid measurements. A natural alternative is to zero-order-hold the most recent reading and provide the known sampling schedule to the model through two features, staleness and time-to-refresh. We test this prediction using transformer world models across three regimes of increasing causal coupling: open-loop rollouts in continuous-control locomotion, closed-loop model-predictive planning in which each learned model serves as the planner dynamics, and a linear latched-actuator system in which refresh events apply a zero-order-held command to the plant. Our findings show that the effectiveness of time-to-refresh depends on the causal role of the sampling schedule, specifically when refresh events affect the system rather than merely report its state. These results establish when sampling schedules provide useful information for predictive world models operating under asynchronous physical observations.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how transformer-based world models should handle asynchronous, heterogeneous-rate physical sensor observations. Instead of interpolating or downsampling, the authors propose zero-order-holding the most recent reading and encoding the known sampling schedule via two features: staleness and time-to-refresh. Experiments across three regimes (open-loop rollouts, closed-loop MPC, and a latched-actuator system) show that time-to-refresh is only useful when refresh events causally affect the system rather than merely report its state.
AI.motivation: Learned world models typically assume synchronous observations from simulators, but real physical sensing operates at heterogeneous rates where most channels are stale at any instant. Existing approaches (interpolation or downsampling) either fabricate unobserved measurements or discard valid ones, motivating a need for principled handling of asynchronous observations.
AI.method: The authors use zero-order-hold to retain the most recent reading per channel and augment the model inputs with two known sampling-schedule features: staleness (time since last observation) and time-to-refresh (time until next observation). They evaluate transformer world models under three regimes of increasing causal coupling: (1) open-loop rollouts in continuous-control locomotion, (2) closed-loop model-predictive planning where the learned model serves as planner dynamics, and (3) a linear latched-actuator system where refresh events apply a zero-order-held command to the plant.
AI.result: The effectiveness of time-to-refresh depends on the causal role of the sampling schedule. Specifically, time-to-refresh is beneficial when refresh events affect the system dynamics (i.e., latched-actuator regime) but less critical when refresh events merely report state (pure observation regimes).
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes when sampling schedules provide useful information for predictive world models operating under asynchronous physical observations, providing design guidance for encoding timing information in learned models.

title: Localized Visual Feature Aggregation via Focus Pooling for Visuomotor Policies
summary: Focusing on spatially localized, control-relevant visual cues has been shown to improve data efficiency in visuomotor policies by reducing the need to model task-irrelevant visual variation. Existing methods often impose this focus through input preprocessing, such as cropping control- or object-centric regions in RGB images or point-clouds. However, it remains underexplored whether such localized features can be exposed directly from commonly used convolutional neural network (CNN) encoded features. In this paper, we show that intermediate CNN features preserve localized visual context for control, but existing pooling methods fail to aggregate it effectively. We introduce FocusPool, an attention pooling module that selectively aggregates intermediate visual features according to their relevance to the robot's current proprioceptive context. The resulting pooled representation captures task-progressive, control-relevant local information and is used directly for policy learning. Across simulation and real-world experiments, FocusPool improves policy success rates over pooling and explicit local focus methods by 36.2% and 41.2%, with training only 5.8% of encoder parameters.

AI.tldr: FocusPool is an attention pooling module that selectively aggregates intermediate CNN features based on relevance to the robot's proprioceptive context, improving visuomotor policy success rates by 36.2% over pooling methods and 41.2% over explicit local focus methods while training only 5.8% of encoder parameters.
AI.motivation: Spatially localized, control-relevant visual cues improve data efficiency in visuomotor policies. Existing methods impose this focus through input preprocessing (cropping regions in RGB/point-clouds), but it is underexplored whether localized features can be directly exposed from CNN-encoded features without such preprocessing.
AI.method: The paper first demonstrates that intermediate CNN features preserve localized visual context for control, but existing pooling methods fail to aggregate it effectively. They introduce FocusPool, an attention pooling module that selectively aggregates intermediate visual features according to their relevance to the robot's current proprioceptive context. The pooled representation captures task-progressive, control-relevant local information used directly for policy learning.
AI.result: Across simulation and real-world experiments, FocusPool improves policy success rates over pooling methods by 36.2% and over explicit local focus methods by 41.2%, while training only 5.8% of encoder parameters.
AI.conclusion: FocusPool demonstrates that localized, control-relevant visual features can be effectively extracted directly from intermediate CNN representations via attention-based pooling conditioned on proprioceptive context, achieving superior performance with significantly lower training cost than preprocessing-based localization approaches.

title: Weakly supervised neural network: segmentation of complex structures in X-ray microCT
summary: Segmentation of complex structures in X-ray tomographic data is a fundamental task in biomedical research, but it often requires large amounts of precisely annotated data, making fully supervised approaches costly and difficult to scale. In this study, weakly supervised deep learning is investigated as a strategy to reduce annotation effort while maintaining accurate segmentation. A two-dimensional convolutional neural network based on the nnU-Net framework was adapted to a weak supervision setting using sparse dot-based annotations, complemented by a limited number of fully segmented images. The approach was evaluated on high-resolution microCT slices of rat kidneys, targeting the segmentation of renal glomeruli, which are small, low-contrast anatomical structures. Results indicate that weak supervision provides a meaningful learning signal, enabling reliable localization of glomeruli even in the absence of dense labels. Incorporating a small set of high-quality annotations substantially improves segmentation performance, approaching that of a fully supervised model. These findings highlight the potential of weakly supervised learning as an annotation-efficient strategy for the analysis of complex structures in X-ray tomographic data, and suggest that alternative loss formulations tailored to sparse annotations may further enhance performance.

AI.tldr: This study investigates weakly supervised deep learning for segmenting renal glomeruli in microCT images of rat kidneys, using a nnU-Net-based 2D CNN trained with sparse dot annotations and a limited set of fully segmented images, showing that this annotation-efficient approach can approach fully supervised performance.
AI.motivation: Fully supervised segmentation of complex structures in X-ray tomographic data requires large amounts of precisely annotated data, which is costly and difficult to scale, motivating the exploration of weakly supervised strategies to reduce annotation burden.
AI.method: A two-dimensional convolutional neural network based on the nnU-Net framework was adapted to weak supervision using sparse dot-based annotations, supplemented by a small number of fully segmented images. The approach was evaluated on high-resolution microCT slices of rat kidneys targeting renal glomeruli segmentation.
AI.result: Weak supervision provided meaningful learning signals enabling reliable glomeruli localization without dense labels. Incorporating a small set of high-quality annotations substantially improved performance, approaching that of a fully supervised model.
AI.conclusion: Weakly supervised learning is a promising annotation-efficient strategy for segmenting complex structures in X-ray tomographic data, and alternative loss formulations tailored to sparse annotations may further enhance performance.

title: Coverage Path Planning for Redundant Manipulators using Generalized Spanning Trees
summary: Surface coverage with task-redundant manipulators is challenging because each surface point may admit multiple inverse kinematics (IK) solutions, and configuration choices strongly affect motion quality. This paper extends the classical Spanning Tree Coverage (STC) method to redundant manipulators through offline and online Joint Spanning Tree Coverage (JSTC) algorithms. Offline JSTC samples multiple Inverse Kinematics (IK) solutions per grid cell and formulates the problem as a Generalized Minimum Spanning Tree (GMST), selecting one configuration per cell and tracing the resulting tree to obtain a non-revisiting coverage path. Online JSTC incrementally expands and backtracks a spanning tree with feasibility and cost evaluation while handling dynamic grid updates. Simulation results show that offline JSTC reduces computation time, reconfigurations, and joint motion compared to other methods, while online JSTC achieves fast per-step planning in dynamic scenarios.

AI.tldr: The paper extends the classical Spanning Tree Coverage (STC) method to task-redundant manipulators via two Joint Spanning Tree Coverage (JSTC) algorithms—offline and online—that jointly select IK solutions and construct non-revisiting coverage paths. Offline JSTC formulates the problem as a Generalized Minimum Spanning Tree (GMST), while online JSTC incrementally expands a spanning tree with dynamic grid updates. Simulations demonstrate reduced computation time, fewer reconfigurations, and lower joint motion.
AI.motivation: Surface coverage with redundant manipulators is challenging because each surface point admits multiple IK solutions, and the configuration choice significantly impacts motion quality (e.g., reconfigurations, joint motion).
AI.method: Two algorithms are proposed: (1) Offline JSTC, which samples multiple IK solutions per grid cell, formulates the coverage problem as a Generalized Minimum Spanning Tree (GMST), and selects one configuration per cell to trace a non-revisiting coverage path; (2) Online JSTC, which incrementally expands and backtracks a spanning tree with feasibility and cost evaluation, handling dynamic grid updates in real time.
AI.result: Simulation results show offline JSTC reduces computation time, reconfigurations, and joint motion compared to baseline methods, while online JSTC achieves fast per-step planning in dynamic scenarios.
AI.conclusion: The proposed offline and online JSTC algorithms effectively extend spanning-tree-based coverage planning to redundant manipulators, offering improvements in both static and dynamic coverage scenarios.

title: DGCPath: Distribution-Aware Generative Contrastive Framework for Self-supervised Path Representation Learning -- Extended Version
comment: This paper is an extended version of DGCPath, which was published at IJCAI 2026
summary: Due to the proliferation of vehicle trajectory data enabled by advanced sensing technologies, path representation learning has become a pivotal task in intelligent transportation systems. Although existing self-supervised approaches have achieved promising performance, their dependence on deterministic contrastive learning paradigms and handcrafted view augmentation strategies inherently restricts their cross-scenario generalization capabilities. To address these limitations, we present DGCPath, an innovative Distribution-aware Generative Contrastive learning framework for Path representation. This framework establishes a synergistic connection between generative modeling and distributional contrastive learning, enabling the acquisition of robust and transferable feature embeddings. Specifically, our framework incorporates: (1) a diffusion-based view generator that autonomously produces semantically coherent yet diverse trajectory views from Gaussian noise; (2) a variational contrastive mechanism that enforces latent feature alignment at the distribution level, transcending conventional instance-wise consistency; and (3) a novel generative cross-supervision module that reinforces view-level consistency through cross-view reconstruction learning. Comprehensive evaluations on three real-world trajectory datasets demonstrate that DGCPath outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on two distinct downstream tasks, validating its enhanced generalization capability and representation effectiveness.

AI.tldr: DGCPath is a distribution-aware generative contrastive learning framework for path representation learning that synergizes diffusion-based view generation with variational contrastive learning and cross-supervision reconstruction, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines on trajectory downstream tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing self-supervised path representation learning methods rely on deterministic contrastive learning paradigms and handcrafted view augmentation strategies, which inherently limit their cross-scenario generalization capabilities in intelligent transportation systems.
AI.method: DGCPath integrates three components: (1) a diffusion-based view generator producing semantically coherent yet diverse trajectory views from Gaussian noise; (2) a variational contrastive mechanism enforcing latent feature alignment at the distribution level rather than instance-wise consistency; and (3) a generative cross-supervision module reinforcing view-level consistency through cross-view reconstruction learning.
AI.result: Comprehensive evaluations on three real-world trajectory datasets show DGCPath outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on two distinct downstream tasks, validating its enhanced generalization capability and representation effectiveness.
AI.conclusion: The synergistic connection between generative modeling and distributional contrastive learning enables DGCPath to acquire robust and transferable path feature embeddings, overcoming the generalization limitations of traditional deterministic contrastive approaches.

title: Safe Task Planning with Long-Term Graph Memory for Embodied Agents
summary: Large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs) have significantly advanced zero-shot task planning for embodied agents. However, most LLM- and VLM-driven methods struggle to generate safe high-level actions due to a lack of physical risk awareness, particularly under partial observability, where hazards lie outside the immediate field of view. To address this challenge, we propose a novel safe task-planning framework, SafeMem, which constructs and maintains a long-term semantic graph memory of the open and dynamic environment. Based on egocentric observations, the proposed framework incrementally accumulates knowledge about surrounding objects and their relationships with a graph. Then, an LLM-based risk predictor evaluates candidate actions using the graph memory, triggering a conservatism-modulated replanning loop with explanations for detected hazards. Extensive experiments on the IS-Bench benchmark and a real-world robot platform demonstrate that the SafeMem framework substantially improves safe success rates compared to state-of-the-art VLM-driven task planners. Video results are available on our webpage: https://sites.google.com/view/safemem.

AI.tldr: SafeMem is a novel safe task-planning framework that builds and maintains a long-term semantic graph memory of the environment, enabling LLM-based risk prediction and conservatism-modulated replanning to improve safety in zero-shot task planning for embodied agents under partial observability.
AI.motivation: LLM/VLM-driven task planners lack physical risk awareness and struggle to generate safe high-level actions under partial observability, where hazards may lie outside the immediate field of view.
AI.method: SafeMem incrementally constructs a long-term semantic graph memory of the environment from egocentric observations, capturing objects and their inter-relationships. An LLM-based risk predictor evaluates candidate actions using this graph memory, and a conservatism-modulated replanning loop with explanations is triggered when hazards are detected.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on the IS-Bench benchmark and a real-world robot platform show that SafeMem substantially improves safe success rates compared to state-of-the-art VLM-driven task planners.
AI.conclusion: Maintaining a structured long-term semantic graph memory enables risk-aware task planning that significantly enhances safety for embodied agents in partially observable, dynamic environments.

title: AAS-RAIL: Improving Information Extraction for Asset Administration Shells through Retrieval-Augmented In-Context Learning
summary: The Asset Administration Shell (AAS) is a cornerstone of Industry 4.0 and the Digital Product Passport, providing standardized digital representations of industrial assets. While manufacturers already maintain extensive technical product documentation, generating AAS instances from existing product datasheets remains a labor-intensive task because technical information is extracted from heterogeneous document structures and often involves company-specific terminology and conventions. In this work, we present AAS-RAIL, a retrieval-augmented information extraction (IE) approach that automatically generates Asset Administration Shells from PDF product datasheets using large language models (LLMs). Instead of relying on a fixed set of few-shot examples, the proposed retrieval-augmented in-context learning (RAIL) approach retrieves LLM-generated extraction helpers from similar Asset Administration Shells to provide instance-specific in-context learning (ICL). This enables the model to adapt its extraction behavior to company-specific naming conventions and formatting styles without fine-tuning. Our core contribution is the dynamic selection of company-specific AAS examples for each datasheet, replacing static prompting with an extraction pipeline that adapts to instances and combines semantic retrieval and structured information extraction. The proposed approach is evaluated on a collection of industrial product datasheets using a selection of open- and closed-weight LLMs. Experimental results show that RAIL consistently improves extraction quality over conventional few-shot prompting, yielding relative improvements of 30.4-52.4%. These results demonstrate that our approach provides an effective improvement for company-specific AAS generation.

AI.tldr: AAS-RAIL is a retrieval-augmented information extraction approach that automatically generates Asset Administration Shells from PDF product datasheets using LLMs. Instead of static few-shot examples, it retrieves LLM-generated extraction helpers from similar AAS instances to provide instance-specific in-context learning, adapting to company-specific conventions without fine-tuning. It achieves 30.4-52.4% relative improvements over conventional few-shot prompting.
AI.motivation: Generating Asset Administration Shells (AAS) from existing product datasheets is labor-intensive due to heterogeneous document structures and company-specific terminology. While LLMs could potentially automate this, static few-shot prompting fails to handle the diversity of naming conventions and formatting styles across companies.
AI.method: The proposed AAS-RAIL approach uses retrieval-augmented in-context learning (RAIL), which dynamically retrieves LLM-generated extraction helpers from similar existing Asset Administration Shells for each datasheet. This replaces static prompting with an instance-adaptive extraction pipeline combining semantic retrieval with structured information extraction, enabling the model to adapt to company-specific conventions without fine-tuning.
AI.result: Evaluated on industrial product datasheets across multiple open- and closed-weight LLMs, RAIL consistently outperforms conventional few-shot prompting, achieving 30.4-52.4% relative improvements in extraction quality.
AI.conclusion: AAS-RAIL provides an effective and scalable approach for company-specific AAS generation, demonstrating that dynamic retrieval-based in-context learning is superior to static few-shot prompting for structured information extraction from heterogeneous technical documentation.

title: Multi-bounce Drum Roll with Optimized Active Tricks to Leverage Soft Embodiment
comment: 7 pages, 6 figures. Published in the 2026 IEEE/ASME International Conference on Advanced Intelligent Mechatronics (AIM 2026)
summary: This paper presents a soft robotic drummer for accurate and efficient drum rolls. High-frequency drum rolls require the "multi-bounce technique," where a drumstick bounces multiple times with a single stroke. In robotic reproduction of this technique, the body's elasticity is key, while the fine motion during the stroke is also crucial for maximizing the potential of that elasticity. Therefore, we design two tricks: i) Tap-Pull (TP) trick to increase the number of rebounds by adding a pulling motion after impact; and ii) Micro-Pulse (MP) trick to keep the drumming volume by injecting small oscillations during the stroke. Due to the nonlinear complexity of soft embodiment, both tricks are efficiently tuned using Bayesian optimization in a data-driven manner for accomplishing the respective objectives quantified. We evaluated the optimized behaviors with soft and rigid end-effectors. As a result, the soft TP achieved the highest bounce count (12.25 per stroke) with uniform intervals. The soft MP suppressed the volume decay, yielding 6.8-times higher acoustic efficiency compared to the rigid MP. These results indicate that the proposed tricks with the combination of elasticity and optimization can make robots play excellent drum rolls.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a soft robotic drummer capable of performing high-frequency drum rolls using a multi-bounce technique. Two key tricks are introduced: Tap-Pull (TP) to increase rebound count by adding a pulling motion after impact, and Micro-Pulse (MP) to maintain drumming volume via small oscillations during the stroke. Both tricks are tuned using Bayesian optimization in a data-driven manner. Results show the soft TP achieves the highest bounce count (12.25 per stroke) with uniform intervals, and soft MP yields 6.8-times higher acoustic efficiency than rigid MP, demonstrating that the combination of soft embodiment elasticity and optimization enables excellent robotic drum rolls.
AI.motivation: High-frequency drum rolls require a multi-bounce technique where a drumstick bounces multiple times in a single stroke, which is challenging to reproduce robotically. While the body's elasticity is fundamentally important for this technique, fine motion control during the stroke is also crucial to fully exploit that elasticity. This work aims to address both aspects to enable robots to perform excellent drum rolls.
AI.method: The authors design two control tricks: (i) Tap-Pull (TP) trick, which adds a pulling motion after impact to increase the number of rebounds, and (ii) Micro-Pulse (MP) trick, which injects small oscillations during the stroke to maintain drumming volume. Due to the nonlinear complexity of soft embodiment, both tricks are efficiently tuned via Bayesian optimization in a data-driven manner to achieve their respective quantified objectives. Experiments compare soft and rigid end-effector configurations.
AI.result: The soft TP achieved the highest bounce count of 12.25 per stroke with uniform intervals. The soft MP successfully suppressed volume decay, achieving 6.8-times higher acoustic efficiency compared to the rigid MP. These results validate the effectiveness of the proposed tricks combined with soft elasticity and data-driven optimization.
AI.conclusion: The combination of the proposed Tap-Pull and Micro-Pulse tricks with soft robot embodiment elasticity and Bayesian optimization enables robots to play excellent drum rolls, achieving high bounce counts and sustained acoustic output that outperform rigid counterparts.

title: Human-like moral judgments conceal divergent motive attributions in large language models
comment: 15 pages, 4 figures, 1 table; Supplementary Information (10 pages) appended
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are used to simulate human participants in psychological research. We asked whether LLMs that reproduce human evaluations of a whistleblower's moral character also reproduce the motive attributions that accompany them. Five LLMs and two human samples (N = 125 and N = 742) evaluated a physician who either remained silent about fraudulent billing or reported it to a hospital, regulator, or newspaper. Models reproduced the human ranking of the physician's moral character but portrayed whistleblowers as more helpful, less self-interested, and less hostile. In four of five models, competitive motives were less strongly associated with moral-character judgments. Model ratings changed little when prompts reproduced the narratives and demographic profiles of both human samples, although this comparison cannot isolate a perspective effect. Thus, agreement in average ratings can conceal differences in attributed motives, relationships among judgments, and sensitivity to context. Validating LLMs as simulated participants therefore requires testing psychologically informative response patterns, not average agreement alone.

AI.tldr: This study evaluated whether LLMs can reproduce human motive attributions when evaluating a whistleblower's moral character. Five LLMs and two human samples evaluated a physician across four scenarios. While LLMs reproduced the human ranking of moral character, they portrayed whistleblowers as more helpful, less self-interested, and less hostile, and showed weaker associations between competitive motives and moral judgments.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used as simulated human participants in psychological research, but it is unclear whether they reproduce not just average ratings but also the underlying psychological processes, such as motive attributions, that accompany human judgments. Validating LLM-human equivalence requires testing psychologically informative response patterns.
AI.method: Five LLMs and two human samples (N=125 and N=742) evaluated a physician who either remained silent about fraudulent billing or reported it to one of three parties (hospital, regulator, newspaper). Models' ratings of the physician's moral character and attributed motives were compared with human responses, including correlational relationships between motives and moral judgments.
AI.result: LLMs reproduced the human ranking of moral character but systematically differed from humans in attributed motives: they portrayed whistleblowers as more helpful, less self-interested, and less hostile. In four of five models, competitive motives were less strongly associated with moral-character judgments. Prompting with human sample narratives and demographics changed ratings little, though this cannot isolate perspective effects.
AI.conclusion: Agreement in average ratings between LLMs and humans can conceal important differences in attributed motives, relationships among judgments, and sensitivity to context. Validating LLMs as simulated research participants requires testing psychologically informative response patterns rather than relying on average agreement alone.

title: AURORA: Active Uncertainty-Driven Re-Orientation for In-Hand Reconstruction
comment: 23 pages, 11 figures, 6 tables. Accepted to the 10th Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL 2026)
summary: Observing objects grasped by a robot hand is challenging due to severe visual occlusions. Although in-hand manipulation can expose hidden surfaces, existing approaches often rely on predefined or open-loop reorientation strategies that do not explicitly target under-observed regions. We propose AURORA, an active 3D reconstruction framework that closes the loop between online object-centric reconstruction and in-hand reorientation. At its core, Ray-GPIS estimates direction-wise reconstruction uncertainty along candidate viewing rays and selects next-best-view targets using an uncertainty--novelty objective, which are realized through an axis-conditioned in-hand rotation policy. The resulting RGB-D observations are fused incrementally using CAD-free 6D pose tracking and lightweight geometric reconstruction. Experiments demonstrate that AURORA improves reconstruction quality and information-acquisition efficiency over non-active rotation strategies, while Ray-GPIS also outperforms active view-planning baselines in reconstruction performance, action-ranking quality, and planning efficiency. Targeted ablations further validate its robustness to hand occlusion and pose errors. The project webpage is available at https://aurorahand.github.io/

AI.tldr: AURORA is an active 3D reconstruction framework that closes the loop between online object-centric reconstruction and in-hand reorientation. It uses Ray-GPIS to estimate direction-wise reconstruction uncertainty and select next-best-view targets via an uncertainty-novelty objective, realized through an axis-conditioned in-hand rotation policy, achieving better reconstruction quality and efficiency than non-active and active baselines.
AI.motivation: Observing objects grasped by a robot hand is challenging due to severe visual occlusions. Existing in-hand manipulation approaches rely on predefined or open-loop reorientation strategies that do not explicitly target under-observed regions, limiting reconstruction quality.
AI.method: AURORA integrates online object-centric reconstruction with in-hand reorientation in a closed loop. The core component, Ray-GPIS, estimates direction-wise reconstruction uncertainty along candidate viewing rays and selects next-best-view targets using an uncertainty-novelty objective. These targets are realized through an axis-conditioned in-hand rotation policy, and RGB-D observations are incrementally fused using CAD-free 6D pose tracking and lightweight geometric reconstruction.
AI.result: Experiments show AURORA improves reconstruction quality and information-acquisition efficiency over non-active rotation strategies. Ray-GPIS outperforms active view-planning baselines in reconstruction performance, action-ranking quality, and planning efficiency. Ablations validate robustness to hand occlusion and pose errors.
AI.conclusion: Active, uncertainty-driven in-hand reorientation guided by next-best-view selection significantly improves 3D reconstruction of robot-grasped objects under severe occlusion, demonstrating the value of closing the loop between reconstruction and manipulation.

title: RAFM-SER++: A Lightweight Multimodal Emotion Recognition Framework for Real-Time Behavioral Monitoring in Surveillance Systems
comment: 6 pages, 4 figures, 3 tables. Accepted at the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Advanced Video and Signal-based Surveillance (AVSS 2026). (c) 2026 IEEE. Personal use of this material is permitted. Permission from IEEE must be obtained for all other uses
summary:
Recent multimodal Speech Emotion Recognition (SER) systems achieve high accuracy through interaction-heavy cross-modal transformers, but their computational cost limits deployment in latency-sensitive and resource-constrained surveillance systems. To address this challenge, we propose RAFM_SER++, a lightweight multimodal SER framework featuring an asymmetric Residual Attention Fusion Mechanism (RAFM). Rather than relying on computationally expensive bidirectional interactions, RAFM injects affective speech cues into semantic text representations through a one-directional residual attention pathway. Combined with a BYOL-inspired cross-modal alignment objective and attention-guided pooling, the proposed framework improves multimodal representation learning while maintaining low computational overhead.
  Experiments on the IEMOCAP and ESD benchmarks demonstrate that RAFM_SER++ consistently outperforms the HuBERT-Base baseline and achieves a superior accuracy-efficiency trade-off compared with the state-of-the-art MemoCMT. Specifically, RAFM_SER++ reduces trainable parameters by more than 60%, achieves faster inference (79.60 it/s), and attains BACC scores of 81.10% on IEMOCAP and 95.39% on ESD. These results indicate that lightweight asymmetric multimodal fusion is an effective alternative to interaction-heavy cross-modal transformers for real-time surveillance applications.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes RAFM_SER++, a lightweight multimodal Speech Emotion Recognition framework that uses an asymmetric Residual Attention Fusion Mechanism (RAFM) to inject affective speech cues into semantic text representations via a one-directional residual attention pathway, avoiding the computational cost of interaction-heavy cross-modal transformers. Combined with BYOL-inspired cross-modal alignment and attention-guided pooling, RAFM_SER++ outperforms the HuBERT-Base baseline and achieves a superior accuracy-efficiency trade-off over state-of-the-art MemoCMT on IEMOCAP and ESD benchmarks, reducing trainable parameters by over 60% with 79.60 it/s inference speed and BACC scores of 81.10% on IEMOCAP and 95.39% on ESD.
AI.motivation: Current multimodal SER systems rely on interaction-heavy cross-modal transformers that achieve high accuracy but suffer from prohibitive computational costs, limiting their deployment in latency-sensitive and resource-constrained surveillance systems.
AI.method: The proposed RAFM_SER++ framework employs an asymmetric Residual Attention Fusion Mechanism (RAFM) that performs one-directional residual attention fusion (injecting affective speech cues into semantic text representations) instead of expensive bidirectional interactions. It is augmented with a BYOL-inspired cross-modal alignment objective and attention-guided pooling to enhance multimodal representation learning while keeping computational overhead low.
AI.result: On IEMOCAP and ESD benchmarks, RAFM_SER++ consistently outperforms the HuBERT-Base baseline and achieves a superior accuracy-efficiency trade-off compared to state-of-the-art MemoCMT. It reduces trainable parameters by more than 60%, achieves faster inference at 79.60 it/s, and obtains BACC scores of 81.10% on IEMOCAP and 95.39% on ESD.
AI.conclusion: Lightweight asymmetric multimodal fusion is an effective alternative to interaction-heavy cross-modal transformers for real-time surveillance applications, achieving competitive or superior accuracy with substantially reduced computational cost.

title: PGMT: Perceptive General Motion Tracking for Humanoid Robots
summary: Humanoid motion trackers can reproduce diverse whole-body motions, but their performance degrades on complex terrain where terrain-agnostic references become physically infeasible. We present PGMT, a Perceptive General Motion Tracking pipeline for humanoid robots that learns terrain adaptation from independently selected motion references and terrains. PGMT first learns a general tracking and recovery prior, then incorporates terrain perception through motion-conditioned terrain glimpses that selectively encode regions relevant to the current motion. Terrain-aware tracking relaxation allows necessary deviations from the reference while preserving its motion intent. Zero-shot deployment on a Unitree G1 demonstrates robust terrain-adaptive locomotion and whole-body motion execution over real-world terrain with obstacles up to 37 cm high, while supporting teleoperation, dynamic motion tracking, and fall recovery. PGMT extends general humanoid motion tracking beyond flat ground, providing a unified policy for terrain-adaptive locomotion, diverse whole-body behaviors, and teleoperation in complex environments.

AI.tldr: PGMT is a perceptive general motion tracking pipeline for humanoid robots that learns terrain adaptation from independently selected motion references and terrains, enabling zero-shot deployment on a Unitree G1 with terrain-adaptive locomotion, whole-body motion execution, teleoperation, and fall recovery on real-world terrain with obstacles up to 37 cm high.
AI.motivation: Humanoid motion trackers can reproduce diverse whole-body motions but degrade on complex terrain where terrain-agnostic references become physically infeasible, limiting deployment beyond flat ground.
AI.method: PGMT first learns a general tracking and recovery prior, then incorporates terrain perception through motion-conditioned terrain glimpses that selectively encode terrain regions relevant to the current motion. Terrain-aware tracking relaxation allows necessary deviations from the reference while preserving motion intent.
AI.result: Zero-shot deployment on a Unitree G1 demonstrates robust terrain-adaptive locomotion and whole-body motion execution over real-world terrain with obstacles up to 37 cm high, while supporting teleoperation, dynamic motion tracking, and fall recovery.
AI.conclusion: PGMT extends general humanoid motion tracking beyond flat ground, providing a unified policy for terrain-adaptive locomotion, diverse whole-body behaviors, and teleoperation in complex environments.

title: CIT-CAD: Constraint Intent Tree-based CAD Code Generation and Verification
summary: Natural-language Computer-Aided Design (CAD) code generation aims to turn design intent into executable and editable parametric programs. Large language models (LLMs) make this goal increasingly practical, but useful systems must preserve the construction process behind the rendered geometry. Existing benchmarks and methods mostly focus on how closely the generated CAD model matches the reference geometry, often using metrics such as Intersection over Union (IoU). Such metrics can miss errors in part decomposition, construction hierarchy, Boolean operations, sketch structure, and geometric relations. This gap calls for a representation that makes design intent explicit and lets a system check generated code against that intent. We propose CIT-CAD, a framework that infers a Constraint Intent Tree (CIT) from the input description to represent the intended entities, hierarchy, operations, and relations. The tree has two roles: it guides CAD code generation and defines expected constraints for verification. The framework extracts actual constraints from the generated program, compares them with the expected constraints, and uses mismatches to localize and repair design violations. Experiments show that the framework improves CAD generation performance, with larger gains on more complex multi-entity designs. By turning design intent into an explicit and checkable object, this work is the first attempt to move text-to-CAD generation beyond rendered-geometry matching toward construction-aware synthesis, verification, and repair.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes CIT-CAD, a framework that infers a Constraint Intent Tree (CIT) from natural-language design descriptions to explicitly represent design intent (entities, hierarchy, operations, relations). The CIT guides CAD code generation and provides expected constraints for verification. Extracted actual constraints from generated code are compared against expected ones, and mismatches localize and repair design violations. Experiments show improved CAD generation, especially on complex multi-entity designs, marking the first attempt to move text-to-CAD beyond rendered-geometry matching toward construction-aware synthesis, verification, and repair.
AI.motivation: Existing text-to-CAD benchmarks and methods primarily evaluate success using geometric overlap metrics like Intersection over Union (IoU), which fail to capture errors in part decomposition, construction hierarchy, Boolean operations, sketch structure, and geometric relations. There is a need for a representation that makes design intent explicit and enables checking generated code against that intent.
AI.method: CIT-CAD introduces a Constraint Intent Tree (CIT) inferred from the input description, which represents intended entities, hierarchy, operations, and relations. The CIT serves dual purposes: guiding CAD code generation and defining expected constraints for verification. The framework extracts actual constraints from the generated program, compares them with the expected constraints from the CIT, and uses mismatches to localize and repair design violations.
AI.result: Experiments demonstrate that the framework improves CAD generation performance, with larger gains observed on more complex multi-entity designs.
AI.conclusion: By making design intent an explicit and checkable object, this work represents the first attempt to move text-to-CAD generation beyond rendered-geometry matching toward construction-aware synthesis, verification, and repair.

title: TASG-Explore: Traversability-Aware Sector-Guided Exploration for Ground Robot on Uneven Terrain
summary: Autonomous exploration on uneven terrain requires ground robots to balance exploration efficiency, coverage completeness, and terrain safety. Detailed tsrrain reasoning improves local reliability but can slow large-scale exploration, whereas coarse region guidance expands quickly in open areas but can miss narrow passages and irregular traversable boundaries. To address this challenge, this paper presents TASG-Explore, a traversability-aware sector-guided exploration framework for ground robots. The framework first performs hierarchical traversability analysis using variable-voxel ground fitting and adaptive 8-bit obstacle encoding. It then splitting cost map into sectors, incrementally updates sector clusters, extracts terrain-coupled frontier viewpoints, and maintains a dynamic topological roadmap with unknown topological hypotheses. Finally, a sector-guided planner selects region targets and inserts local viewpoints to generate efficient exploration routes. Benchmark experiments in diverse challenging environments, including caves, forests, and rugged hills, show that TASG-Explore achieves the best overall performance among six representative state-of-the-art planners. The proposed traversability analysis improves processing efficiency by 6.3 times while maintaining high accuracy, and the exploration planner improves exploration efficiency by 51% and increases coverage by up to 2.95 times in rugged hill scene. Large-scale real-world experiments further demonstrate the practical value of the proposed method.

AI.tldr: This paper presents TASG-Explore, a traversability-aware sector-guided exploration framework for ground robots on uneven terrain. It combines hierarchical traversability analysis (variable-voxel ground fitting and adaptive 8-bit obstacle encoding), sector-based exploration splitting with frontier extraction, and a sector-guided planner for efficient route generation. Benchmarks show a 6.3x improvement in traversability processing efficiency, 51% higher exploration efficiency, and up to 2.95x more coverage in rugged terrain versus six SOTA planners.
AI.motivation: Ground robot exploration on uneven terrain faces a trade-off between local reliability (achieved via detailed terrain reasoning) and large-scale efficiency (achieved via coarse region guidance). Existing methods struggle to balance these, often missing narrow passages or slowing down in challenging environments.
AI.method: TASG-Explore consists of three main components: (1) hierarchical traversability analysis via variable-voxel ground fitting and adaptive 8-bit obstacle encoding; (2) sector-based cost map partitioning with incremental cluster updates, terrain-coupled frontier viewpoint extraction, and a dynamic topological roadmap with unknown topological hypotheses; (3) a sector-guided planner that selects region targets and inserts local viewpoints to generate efficient exploration routes.
AI.result: Benchmark experiments in caves, forests, and rugged hills show TASG-Explore achieves the best overall performance among six SOTA planners. Traversability analysis improves processing efficiency 6.3x while maintaining high accuracy; exploration planner improves exploration efficiency by 51% and increases coverage up to 2.95x in rugged hill scenes. Large-scale real-world experiments validate practical applicability.
AI.conclusion: TASG-Explore effectively reconciles exploration efficiency, coverage completeness, and terrain safety by integrating hierarchical traversability analysis with sector-guided planning. The significant improvements in processing speed, exploration efficiency, and coverage—especially in rugged environments—demonstrate its strong practical value for autonomous ground robot exploration.

title: The Internal Anatomy of Strategic Choice in Large Language Models
summary: Large language models act as strategic agents and models of human choice, yet choosing like a strategic agent does not mean computing like one. We recorded activations from four open-weight models --- dense and mixture-of-experts, including a matched base--instruct pair --- in one-shot play of 144 strict ordinal $2\times2$ games.
