In addition to the inherent scientific interest of this question, these latent quantities are often invoked to explain the behavior of LLMs to users or to define and evaluate harmful behaviors which are relative to intent. Nevertheless, we currently lack a means to systematically test whether concepts like "belief" are well-applied to LLMs, and hence whether they are likely to be fruitful ingredients of attempts to align models with human interests. We propose an approach for empirically studying such questions, asking whether a single latent variable inferred from the LLMs' outputs -- interpreted as a degree of belief -- allows an observer to make interpretable predictions of how the LLMs' will respond to new prompts. We find that highly capable models are usefully described as holding beliefs and that, generally, the predictability of model outputs based on an inferred latent belief tracks overall trends in model capability. Building on these findings, we provide empirical strategies to study how beliefs in LLMs can be measured, the extent to which LLMs comply with instructed decision rules or payoffs, and how beliefs evolve within individual instances of an LLM over the course of reasoning.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an empirical framework to test whether abstractions like "beliefs" meaningfully describe LLM behavior, finding that capable models are usefully characterized as holding beliefs, and that the predictability of outputs from inferred latent beliefs tracks model capability.
AI.motivation: There is significant uncertainty about whether mentalistic abstractions like beliefs or desires are appropriate for describing LLM behavior. These latent constructs are often invoked to explain outputs to users and to define/evaluate harmful behaviors relative to intent, yet there is no systematic method to test whether such concepts are well-applied to LLMs.
AI.method: The authors propose an empirical approach that infers a single latent variable from an LLM's outputs—interpreted as a degree of belief—and tests whether this latent variable allows an observer to make interpretable predictions of the LLM's responses to new prompts. They also develop empirical strategies to study how beliefs can be measured, how models comply with instructed decision rules or payoffs, and how beliefs evolve during reasoning within individual instances.
AI.result: Highly capable models are usefully described as holding beliefs, and the predictability of model outputs based on an inferred latent belief generally tracks overall trends in model capability.
AI.conclusion: Mentalistic abstractions such as beliefs can be empirically validated for LLMs, providing a foundation for strategies to measure, evaluate, and understand beliefs in these models—potentially informing alignment efforts.

title: CausalVerify: An Execution-Grounded Benchmark for LLM Causal Inference Workflows
comment: 22 pages, 9 figures, 12 tables. Code and data: https://github.com/causalverify/causalverify
summary: Existing causal-inference benchmarks for LLMs mostly score method descriptions or whether generated code runs, not whether the executed workflow recovers the target causal estimate. CausalVerify studies this verification problem for structured econometric causal-estimation workflows by separating realistic interpretation from verifiable computation. It pairs 259 published economics papers (reconstructed research question, data description, institutional context) with 100 fixed-seed synthetic scenarios that realise CSV datasets for difference-in-differences, event study, instrumental variables, and regression discontinuity designs. Experiment A (real-paper text agreement) scores method-family and direction agreement against four-LLM consensus labels. Experiment B (synthetic execution) runs model-written R code and checks whether the extracted treatment-effect estimate matches a canonical estimator on the same realised dataset; this execution-grounded correctness layer is L2b+, distinct from L2b, which records only whether the code executes. A calibration arm asks whether self-reported confidence separates correct from incorrect workflows. On Experiment B, seven LLMs reach L2b+ pass rates of 10% to 88% at the default 50% tolerance, and 66 of the 426 workflows that execute (15.5%) return a wrong estimate. Execution ranking (L2b) agrees with L2b+ far better than text-direction scoring (L4): Kendall $τ=0.81$ and Spearman $ρ=0.93$, versus Kendall $τ$ between $-0.20$ and $0.10$ for L4. Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct shows the same qualitative gap, and reported confidence does not reliably separate correct from incorrect workflows. The claims are confined to standardized single-shot workflows in these four design families under the evaluated R backend and model panel; the benchmark does not measure general causal-inference ability. Code, data, cached outputs, and a datasheet are released.

AI.tldr: CausalVerify is a benchmark for causal-inference LLM workflows that checks whether executed R code recovers the target causal estimate, not just whether code runs or methods are textually correct. It pairs 259 economics papers with 100 synthetic scenarios across four causal designs, achieving L2b+ (execution-grounded correctness) pass rates of 10-88% across seven LLMs.
AI.motivation: Existing causal-inference benchmarks for LLMs score method descriptions or whether generated code executes, but do not verify whether the executed workflow actually recovers the target causal estimate. The authors aim to study this verification problem by separating realistic interpretation from verifiable computation in structured econometric workflows.
AI.method: CausalVerify pairs 259 published economics papers (with reconstructed research questions, data descriptions, and institutional context) with 100 fixed-seed synthetic scenarios producing CSV datasets for four design families: difference-in-differences, event study, instrumental variables, and regression discontinuity. Experiment A scores method-family and direction agreement against four-LLM consensus labels. Experiment B runs model-written R code and checks whether extracted treatment-effect estimates match a canonical estimator on the same realized dataset, defining an L2b+ correctness layer. A calibration arm assesses whether self-reported confidence separates correct from incorrect workflows.
AI.result: Seven LLMs achieve L2b+ pass rates of 10% to 88% at a default 50% tolerance. 66 of 426 executing workflows (15.5%) return wrong estimates. Execution ranking (L2b) agrees far better with L2b+ than text-direction scoring (L4): Kendall tau=0.81 and Spearman rho=0.93 vs. Kendall tau between -0.20 and 0.10 for L4. Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct shows the same qualitative gap, and reported confidence does not reliably separate correct from incorrect workflows.
AI.conclusion: Execution-grounded verification (L2b+) reveals substantial gaps in LLM causal-inference workflows that text-level evaluations miss, as execution ranking correlates strongly with true correctness while text-direction scoring does not. Claims are confined to standardized single-shot workflows in four design families under the evaluated R backend and model panel; the benchmark does not measure general causal-inference ability.

title: PlannerForge: LLM Agents for Scenario-Based Testing of Motion Planners in Autonomous Driving
comment: Accepted to EMNLP 2026 (Main Conference). 35 pages including appendix
summary: Ensuring the safety of autonomous driving is a critical challenge. Scenario-based testing is a systematic process used to validate Autonomous Driving Systems (ADSs), but it remains a fragmented modular pipeline in which scenario generation, retrieval, modification, ADS execution, and results analysis are performed by separate tools with little interaction. Large Language Model (LLM) agents have shown promise across ADS sub-systems such as perception, planning, and control. However, no prior work covers the whole scenario-based testing pipeline for ADSs with a unified LLM-agent framework. We present PlannerForge, an LLM-agent framework that extends all scenario-based testing stages (from Scenario Generation to ADS Assessment) and adds two further LLM-enhanced stages: ADS Enhancement and ADS Benchmarking. We evaluate PlannerForge with 10 off-the-shelf LLMs across all tasks (Generation, Selection, Modification, Module Routing, Planner Testing, and Enhancement) under 5 prompt conditions. Best-per-task scores range from 0.88 to 1.00, and open-source 20-35B backends match commercial APIs on most tasks. Open-source models such as Qwen3.6:35B match commercial APIs on three of the five tasks. Chaining the modules end-to-end retains 83% / 78% of seed queries (commercial / open). It outperforms Scenario Factory 2.0 (Finkeldei et al., 2025) on natural-language generation (193 vs. 144 executable of 200) and realises 92-96% of requested city, road and vehicle attributes. It outperforms BM25 (Robertson and Zaragoza, 2009) at rank 1 selection (92.0% vs. 67.5%) and From-Words-to-Collisions (Gao et al., 2025) on physically valid edits (>=94% vs. 31%). At N=400, cost-tuning lifts planner success from 50.4% to 70.2% and cuts collisions from 19.0% to 8.4%, without domain-specific fine-tuning.

AI.tldr: PlannerForge is a unified LLM-agent framework that spans the entire scenario-based testing pipeline for Autonomous Driving Systems (ADSs), adding two novel LLM-enhanced stages (ADS Enhancement and Benchmarking) beyond the conventional stages. Evaluated across 10 LLMs and 5 prompt conditions, it achieves best-per-task scores of 0.88-1.00, matches or outperforms commercial APIs with open-source 20-35B models on most tasks, and demonstrates strong end-to-end chaining performance with a 83%/78% query retention rate. It significantly outperforms prior baselines on natural-language generation, retrieval, and physically valid editing, and lifts planner success from 50.4% to 70.2% while cutting collisions from 19.0% to 8.4% via cost-tuning—all without domain-specific fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Scenario-based testing for ADSs remains a fragmented, modular pipeline where scenario generation, retrieval, modification, ADS execution, and analysis are siloed across separate tools with little interaction. While LLM agents have been applied to individual ADS sub-systems (perception, planning, control), no prior work unifies the entire scenario-based testing pipeline under a single LLM-agent framework. PlannerForge addresses this gap by offering a holistic, extensible agent-based framework covering all testing stages.
AI.method: PlannerForge is an LLM-agent framework that extends all scenario-based testing stages from Scenario Generation through ADS Assessment, and introduces two additional LLM-enhanced stages: ADS Enhancement and ADS Benchmarking. The framework involves multiple tasks: Generation, Selection, Modification, Module Routing, Planner Testing, and Enhancement. The authors evaluate the framework with 10 off-the-shelf LLMs under 5 prompt conditions, comparing commercial and open-source models, and perform end-to-end chaining experiments with cost-tuning at N=400.
AI.result: Best-per-task scores range from 0.88 to 1.00. Open-source 20-35B backends match commercial APIs on most tasks; Qwen3.6:35B matches commercial APIs on three of five tasks. End-to-end module chaining retains 83% (commercial) and 78% (open) of seed queries. PlannerForge outperforms Scenario Factory 2.0 on natural-language generation (193 vs. 144 executable of 200), realizes 92-96% of requested attributes, outperforms BM25 at rank-1 selection (92.0% vs. 67.5%) and From-Words-to-Collisions on physically valid edits (>=94% vs. 31%). Cost-tuning improves planner success from 50.4% to 70.2% and reduces collisions from 19.0% to 8.4% at N=400.
AI.conclusion: PlannerForge demonstrates that a unified LLM-agent framework can effectively cover and extend the entire scenario-based testing pipeline for ADSs. It validates that open-source models of moderate size can compete with commercial APIs across most tasks, and that LLM-enhanced stages (Enhancement and Benchmarking) can meaningfully improve planner success rates and reduce collisions without domain-specific fine-tuning, suggesting a scalable and cost-effective path forward for ADS validation.

title: Support Topology and Gradient Mixing in Sinkhorn Layers
summary: Sparse Sinkhorn layers use a fixed support graph to restrict transport between tokens. How does this graph control gradient propagation through the scaling iterations. We develop a fixed-support calculus showing that each row-column cycle induces a row-stochastic operator on column-potential perturbations modulo constants. Its transpose propagates zero-mass reverse-mode cotangents. The finite-cycle operator uses two distinct half-step transport plans; at a balanced fixed point it reduces to a two-step walk determined by a single plan. We derive the accompanying score and marginal source terms and use Dobrushin contraction and minorization to bound homogeneous and source-driven tail cotangents. Our main result characterizes when support and marginals guarantee one-step contraction uniformly over finite scores: every feasible face of the transportation polytope must have pairwise two-hop column overlap. Otherwise, suitable score directions make the contraction coefficient arbitrarily close to one. We extend this analysis to ordered support schedules and derive certificates for partition heat-bath layers, coordinate sweeps, forced shared mass, and register-augmented supports. These results provide mathematical criteria for support design in differentiable transport layers, with guarantees restricted to the fixed-support quotient-gradient component.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes how the fixed support graph in Sparse Sinkhorn layers controls gradient propagation through scaling iterations. It develops a fixed-support calculus linking each row-column cycle to a row-stochastic operator on column-potential perturbations, characterizes when support structure guarantees one-step contraction of cotangents (requiring pairwise two-hop column overlap on every feasible face of the transportation polytope), and extends the analysis to ordered support schedules with certificates for various practical layer designs.
AI.motivation: Sparse Sinkhorn layers restrict optimal transport between tokens using a fixed support graph, but how this graph influences gradient propagation through the scaling iterations was not understood. Understanding the mathematical relationship between support structure and gradient contraction is essential for principled support design in differentiable transport layers.
AI.method: The authors develop a fixed-support calculus showing each row-column cycle induces a row-stochastic operator on column-potential perturbations modulo constants, whose transpose propagates zero-mass reverse-mode cotangents. The finite-cycle operator uses two distinct half-step transport plans which reduce to a two-step walk at a balanced fixed point. They derive score and marginal source terms, then use Dobrushin contraction and minorization to bound homogeneous and source-driven tail cotangents. The core result characterizes when support and marginals guarantee one-step contraction uniformly over finite scores via pairwise two-hop column overlap on every feasible face, with extensions to ordered support schedules and certificates for partition heat-bath layers, coordinate sweeps, forced shared mass, and register-augmented supports.
AI.result: The main theorem establishes that one-step contraction of cotangents is guaranteed uniformly over finite scores if and only if every feasible face of the transportation polytope has pairwise two-hop column overlap; otherwise, adversarial score directions can drive the contraction coefficient arbitrarily close to one. The analysis successfully extends to ordered support schedules and provides explicit certificates for several practical support designs (partition heat-bath layers, coordinate sweeps, forced shared mass, and register-augmented supports), with guarantees restricted to the fixed-support quotient-gradient component.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides rigorous mathematical criteria for support design in differentiable transport layers, establishing a precise necessary and sufficient condition for gradient contraction based on two-hop column overlap across feasible faces of the transportation polytope. The framework offers practical certificates for common sparse support architectures while clarifying the limitations of guarantees on the fixed-support quotient-gradient component.

title: From Event Logs to Governed Action: A BlueSky Agenda for Agentic Process Mining
summary: Process mining has long turned event logs into process knowledge: discovered models, conformance evidence, bottleneck diagnoses, and runtime predictions. Agentic AI changes the target. Process-aware agents will not only ask what happened. They will ask whether a proposed action should be taken, given the available evidence, privacy budget, organizational authority, and downstream risk. This BlueSky paper proposes event-to-action process mining: a process-mining agenda for transforming heterogeneous operational event data into governed action. The goal is not another dashboard, a generic enterprise simulator, or a language interface over logs. We argue that the community needs four mineable artifacts: event-object representations, action evidence packages, governance contracts, and benchmarks where act, defer, ask, and refuse are all valid outputs. This agenda is timely because agentic business process management (BPM), LLM-assisted process mining, object-centric event standards, causal process monitoring, and privacy-preserving learning are maturing separately. Bringing them together defines a data-mining target inside process mining: mining logged organizational behavior for accountable action, not only retrospective insight.

AI.tldr: This BlueSky paper proposes "event-to-action process mining," a new agenda that shifts process mining from retrospective insight extraction (discovered models, conformance, diagnostics) toward governed, decision-supporting artifacts for process-aware agents. It argues that instead of only asking what happened, agents need to determine whether proposed actions should be taken under constraints of evidence, privacy, authority, and risk. The paper calls for four mineable artifacts: event-object representations, action evidence packages, governance contracts, and benchmarks where act/defer/ask/refuse are all valid outputs.
AI.motivation: Agentic AI is changing the use of process data: process-aware agents will need to make and justify action decisions, not just derive retrospective diagnoses. Existing paradigms (dashboards, enterprise simulators, log-language interfaces) are insufficient. Simultaneously, several maturing fields (agentic BPM, LLM-assisted process mining, object-centric event standards, causal monitoring, privacy-preserving learning) have yet to be unified around a concrete data-mining target.
AI.method: The paper proposes an agenda rather than a single algorithm. Its methodological contribution is to define four mineable artifact types: (1) event-object representations linking events to operational entities; (2) action evidence packages that bundle the log-derived evidence supporting a candidate action; (3) governance contracts encoding privacy budgets, authority rules, and risk constraints; and (4) benchmarks where outputs are classified as act, defer, ask, or refuse—thus treating action decision-making as part of the mining problem itself.
AI.result: As a BlueSky/position paper, its primary result is a framing and research agenda: it identifies a coherent data-mining target (mining logged organizational behavior for accountable action) and delineates the four artifact families the community should build. No empirical results are presented; the contribution is conceptual and prescriptive.
AI.conclusion: Event-to-action process mining is proposed as the unifying agenda that brings mature but isolated research threads together. The field should orient toward accountable, governed action support—where the artifact of value is not a dashboard or simulator but evidence and contracts that allow agents to act, defer, ask, or refuse responsibly.

title: When Can LLM Digital Twins Reduce Human Measurement? From Behavioral Fidelity to Statistical Substitutability
summary: LLM-based digital twins promise to reduce repeated human data collection by generating person- specific responses, yet existing evaluations provide little evidence about whether they can reduce human measurement while preserving valid inference. To address this, we introduce statistical substitutability, an inferential criterion that evaluates the extent to which twin predictions can reduce human measurement for a particular estimand while preserving valid inference. We develop a framework, grounded in mixed-subject and prediction-powered inference, that evaluates statistical substitutability along four dimensions: aggregate fidelity, paired respondent-level signal, finite-sample human-label recovery, and stability across populations. Across two empirical evaluations spanning behavioral experiments, multiple models, and alternative respondent representations, we find that digital twins can reproduce average human effects while providing little information about which individuals differ from those averages. Newer models and richer respondent information improve some dimensions of performance but do not reliably translate into human-data savings. Human calibration can reduce aggregate prediction error, yet limited labeled samples often fail to produce stable precision gains. Importantly, these findings demonstrate that behavioral fidelity is neither necessary nor sufficient for statistical substitutability. More broadly, they suggest that AI-generated evidence should be evaluated based on its ability to support valid scientific inference rather than its ability to reproduce human outcomes alone. Digital twins should therefore be judged for confirmatory use by whether they reduce uncertainty about human quantities, not merely by whether they reproduce human means, distributions, or effects.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces "statistical substitutability," an inferential criterion for evaluating whether LLM-based digital twins can reduce human data collection while preserving valid statistical inference. Through a mixed-subject and prediction-powered inference framework assessing fidelity, respondent-level signal, finite-sample label recovery, and stability, the authors find that digital twins reproduce average human effects but provide little individual-level information, and that newer models and richer data do not reliably translate into human-data savings.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of LLM-based digital twins provide little evidence about whether they can actually reduce human measurement while preserving valid inference. The authors aim to establish an inferential standard for evaluating whether digital twin predictions are statistically substitutable for human measurements.
AI.method: The authors propose a framework grounded in mixed-subject and prediction-powered inference that evaluates "statistical substitutability" along four dimensions: (1) aggregate fidelity, (2) paired respondent-level signal, (3) finite-sample human-label recovery, and (4) stability across populations. They conduct two empirical evaluations spanning behavioral experiments, multiple models, and alternative respondent representations.
AI.result: Digital twins can reproduce average human effects but offer limited signal about which individuals differ from averages. Newer models and richer respondent information improve some dimensions of performance but do not reliably translate into human-data savings. Human calibration reduces aggregate prediction error, yet limited labeled samples often fail to produce stable precision gains. Behavioral fidelity is shown to be neither necessary nor sufficient for statistical substitutability.
AI.conclusion: AI-generated evidence should be evaluated by its ability to support valid scientific inference rather than merely reproducing human outcomes. Digital twins for confirmatory use should be judged by whether they reduce uncertainty about human quantities—not by whether they reproduce human means, distributions, or effects.

title: Mini-Batch Risk-Averse Deep Q-Learning: A Robot Navigation Case Study
summary:
We study the control of Markov decision processes in which the quality of a policy is evaluated by a dynamic, time-consistent Markov risk measure rather than by an expected discounted cost. The main obstacle to combining such measures with reinforcement learning is that a transition risk mapping depends on the transition kernel in a nonlinear way, and therefore cannot be estimated from a single observed transition. We remove this obstacle by employing mini-batch transition risk mappings: the mapping is applied to the empirical measure of $N$ independent next-state samples, and the result is averaged. The resulting mapping is again coherent. However, as an expected value of a function of $N$ next-state values, it admits an unbiased one-sample estimator.
  We embed this mapping into a double deep Q-network, analyze the two sources of estimation bias that arise, and obtain a risk-averse Q-learning method applicable to state spaces far beyond the reach of tabular schemes. The method is applied to an underwater robot navigation problem, in which a vehicle must visit collection points, gather stochastic information payloads, and deliver them at transmission points, while exposed at each step to the risk of destruction. A hierarchical decomposition delegates path execution to an exact graph search and confines learning to the high-level ``collect or transmit'' decision. A low-dimensional feature map, invariant under the symmetries of the problem, replaces the raw state--configuration encoding. In experiments on $300$ held-out environments, the resulting policies transfer to instance sizes never seen in training, and already $N=2$ reduces the upper semideviation of the outcome distribution while simultaneously improving its mean whenever the simulator is misspecified---an empirical counterpart of the duality between coherent risk measures and distributional robustness.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a risk-averse reinforcement learning framework for Markov decision processes evaluated by dynamic, time-consistent Markov risk measures. To overcome the nonlinearity of transition risk mappings, the authors employ mini-batch transition risk mappings applied to empirical measures of N independent next-state samples, enabling unbiased one-sample estimation. They integrate this into a double deep Q-network and demonstrate the method on an underwater robot navigation problem, where policies trained on 300 held-out environments transfer to unseen instance sizes, with even N=2 reducing upper semideviation while improving mean performance under model misspecification.
AI.motivation: The main challenge is that combining dynamic risk measures with reinforcement learning is difficult because transition risk mappings depend nonlinearly on the transition kernel and cannot be estimated from a single observed transition. This limits risk-averse RL to tabular settings and prevents application to large state spaces.
AI.method: The authors introduce mini-batch transition risk mappings: applying the risk mapping to the empirical measure of N independent next-state samples and averaging the results. This admits an unbiased one-sample estimator since it becomes an expected value of a function of N next-state values. They embed this into a double deep Q-network (DDQN), analyze two sources of estimation bias, and incorporate a hierarchical decomposition (exact graph search for path execution, learned high-level "collect or transmit" decisions) with a low-dimensional symmetry-invariant feature map.
AI.result: Experiments on 300 held-out environments show the policies transfer to instance sizes never seen during training. With N=2, the method reduces the upper semideviation of the outcome distribution while simultaneously improving the mean under simulator misspecification, empirically confirming the duality between coherent risk measures and distributional robustness.
AI.conclusion: The proposed method successfully scales risk-averse Q-learning to state spaces beyond tabular schemes, provides a theoretically grounded approach to estimating coherent risk measures in RL, and demonstrates practical benefits in underwater robot navigation with robustness to simulator misspecification.

title: Sparks of In Silico Cognitive Science: Theories from Simulated Data Can Generalize to Humans
summary: Behavioral foundation models have been proposed as stand-ins for human participants across settings, but it is unclear whether theories discovered on them generalize to humans or merely characterize the simulator. We ran the Automated Cognitive Scientist (\textsc{AutoCog}), a closed-loop discovery system in which LLM agents design theory-discriminating experiments, collect responses, arbitrate between competing theories, and synthesize successors, entirely on behavior simulated by Centaur, a foundation model of human behavior. In a multi-attribute decision-making setting, the theories \textsc{AutoCog} found on Centaur generalized to human data: they outperformed canonical theories on ten held-out experiments and were rivaled only by theories found by running the same loop on people. We argue that this succeeds despite the simulator's inevitable imperfections because a discovery loop that arbitrates between competing theories demands less of its simulator than estimation does. The simulator only needs to capture the regularities that distinguish the theories, and not necessarily reproduce behavior precisely. Imperfect simulators can therefore widen the search over theories, with human data then testing whether the surfaced theories generalize.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates whether behavioral theories discovered using AI foundation models (simulators of human behavior) can generalize to actual humans. Using AutoCog, a closed-loop LLM-based discovery system running on the Centaur behavioral simulator, the authors found theories in multi-attribute decision-making that outperformed canonical theories on ten held-out human experiments, rivaling only theories discovered directly on human participants.
AI.motivation: Behavioral foundation models are proposed as replacements for human participants in research, but it is unclear whether theories discovered on such simulators generalize to real humans or merely characterize the simulator itself.
AI.method: The authors ran AutoCog, an automated discovery system where LLM agents design theory-discriminating experiments, collect responses, arbitrate between competing theories, and synthesize successor theories. The entire loop ran on Centaur, a foundation model of human behavior, in a multi-attribute decision-making setting. Discovered theories were then tested against human data.
AI.result: Theories found by AutoCog on Centaur generalized to human data, outperforming canonical theories across ten held-out experiments. They were only rivaled by theories discovered by running the same discovery loop directly on human participants.
AI.conclusion: Simulator-based discovery of behavioral theories can succeed despite simulator imperfections because a discovery loop that arbitrates between competing theories requires less fidelity from its simulator than parameter estimation does. The simulator need only capture regularities distinguishing the candidate theories, not reproduce behavior precisely. Imperfect simulators can thus broaden the theory search space, with human data serving as the final arbiter of generalization.

title: From Version Conflicts to Decision Conflicts: Selective Revalidation for Long-Running AI Agents
comment: 6 pages, 2 figures, 3 tables. Supplemental artifact available at https://github.com/ezreal13/atr-decision-validation/tree/89c32fa475f5216db4c9d76a1eddde79e874073b
summary: Long-running AI agents may read state, reason, wait for tools or human approval, and perform an external action much later. The state that justified the action can change in the meantime. For example, after an agent proposes an 80 GBP refund under a limit of 100, a customer-name change affects only presentation metadata, a new limit of 90 still permits the refund, a limit of 50 invalidates it, and a refund issued by another worker must prevent a duplicate. Standard optimistic concurrency control and version checks can detect that previously read state has changed, but by themselves do not determine whether that change invalidates the pending action's justification. We call any detected version change a version conflict; when that change invalidates the action's justification, it is also a decision conflict. ATR records the explicit, executable conditions that justify a pending action and rechecks only the conditions affected by a change before releasing the external operation. It can retain the action, refresh non-decisive metadata, require replanning, or block execution; a target-side transaction or compare-and-set binds checked state to commit. Across 210,000 controlled executions over 15 mutation cases, ATR matched every developer-specified outcome with no false allows or blocks. In ten durable SQLite checkpoint/resume cells, it evaluated 0.6 conditions per change versus 6.0 for FullScan. At 4,093 recorded reads, ATR took 9.3 microseconds versus 2595.9 microseconds for FullScan. These deterministic results establish controlled feasibility, not production generality or automatic extraction of the required conditions.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces ATR, a system for long-running AI agents that records executable conditions justifying pending actions and rechecks only affected conditions when state changes occur, distinguishing between non-decisive version conflicts and decision conflicts that invalidate the action's justification.
AI.motivation: Long-running AI agents that defer actions face state changes that may or may not invalidate the original justification. Standard optimistic concurrency control and version checks detect state changes but cannot determine whether those changes actually invalidate a pending action's justification, risking either false allows or false blocks.
AI.method: ATR records explicit executable conditions that justify pending actions. Upon detecting a version conflict, it rechecks only the conditions affected by the change before releasing the external operation. It can retain the action, refresh non-decisive metadata, require replanning, or block execution. A target-side transaction or compare-and-set binds the checked state to commit.
AI.result: Across 210,000 controlled executions over 15 mutation cases, ATR matched every developer-specified outcome with no false allows or blocks. In ten durable SQLite checkpoint/resume cells, it evaluated 0.6 conditions per change versus 6.0 for FullScan. At 4,093 recorded reads, ATR took 9.3 microseconds versus 2595.9 microseconds for FullScan.
AI.conclusion: ATR demonstrates controlled feasibility for differentiating version conflicts from decision conflicts in long-running AI agent workflows, though the authors note it does not establish production generality or automatic condition extraction.

title: A Layered Analysis of Disagreement And Answer Quality in Multi-Agent LLM Debate
summary: Multi-agent debate, in which several LLMs exchange arguments before answering, is widely assumed to improve answer quality by surfacing genuine disagreement. That mechanism is rarely checked. We introduce four measurements: (A) the agreement a debater reports; (B) whether its reply text actually pushes back; (C) whether the position persists once the eliciting instruction is removed; and (D) for open-weight models, the stance response in the debater's own token log-probabilities. We evaluate three-model committees debating open-ended GlobalOpinionQA across 750 debates under three tones: friendly (seek common ground), neutral, and hostile (stress-test every position). (A) Tone strongly reshapes reported agreement: full agreement differs by 50.4 percentage points between the friendly and hostile endpoints. (B) A judge that reads only the reply text, never the self-report or the condition, recovers the same pattern. (C) The dissent appears partly tied to the instruction that elicited it: labels revert toward agreement 23.1 points more often after deleting the hostile instruction than under a matched re-ask that keeps it; question-weighted inference is inconclusive on first-round turns alone (p=0.0625), significant pooling all rounds (p=0.016), and only 11/28 first-round reversions also appear in the reply text. (D) Opposing arguments weaken a debater's stance margin more consistently than they shift its direction. For final answers we detect no quality gain: a bias-checked jury returns 299/299 ties (ruling out only large differences), accuracy on a verifiable control task is unchanged, and a jury without the bias check had declared debate the winner 66% of the time -- an artifact of reading order. Taken together, LLM debate readily changes what agents say, but we find much weaker evidence that it changes what they persistently endorse or improves the quality of the final answer.

AI.tldr: This paper critically examines the assumption that multi-agent LLM debate improves answer quality by surfacing genuine disagreement. Through four measurements (self-reported agreement, reply-text pushback, position persistence under instruction removal, and token log-probabilities for open-weight models) across 750 GlobalOpinionQA debates under three tones, the authors find that debate tone strongly reshapes reported agreement (50.4 pp gap between friendly and hostile), but dissent is largely instruction-driven rather than persistent, and no final answer quality gain is detected—a bias-checked jury yields 299/299 ties, while an unchecked jury's apparent debate advantage was an artifact of reading order.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent debate between LLMs is widely assumed to improve answer quality by surfacing genuine disagreement, yet this core mechanism is rarely tested. The authors aim to rigorously investigate whether debate actually changes what agents persistently endorse versus merely what they say.
AI.method: The authors introduce four measurements: (A) self-reported agreement, (B) reply-text pushback detection by a blind judge, (C) position persistence when the eliciting instruction is removed, and (D) stance in token log-probabilities for open-weight models. They run three-model committees debating open-ended GlobalOpinionQA across 750 debates under three tones (friendly, neutral, hostile), and evaluate final answers with both a bias-checked and unchecked jury.
AI.result: Tone drives a 50.4 percentage-point gap in reported full agreement between friendly and hostile conditions; a blind judge recovers the same pattern from reply text. Labels revert toward agreement 23.1 points more often when the hostile instruction is removed than under matched re-ask; question-weighted inference is inconclusive on first-round turns (p=0.0625) but significant pooling all rounds (p=0.016); only 11/28 first-round reversions appear in reply text. Opposing arguments weaken stance margins more than shift directions. For final answers, a bias-checked jury returns 299/299 ties, accuracy on a verifiable control task is unchanged, while an unchecked jury declared debate the winner 66% of the time—an artifact of reading order.
AI.conclusion: LLM debate readily alters what agents say, but there is much weaker evidence that it changes what they persistently endorse or improves final answer quality. The apparent benefits of debate in prior studies may stem from methodological artifacts such as reading order and instruction-driven conformity rather than genuine epistemic improvement.

title: Eliciting Self-Verification in Multimodal Reasoning Agents with Reinforcement Learning
comment: To appear in ECCV 2026. 11 main pages. 7 figures
summary: Reasoning agents increasingly rely on external tools such as web search to answer complex queries. Reinforcement learning (RL) finetuning algorithms such as GRPO have improved long-form reasoning in text-only language models, particularly for coding and mathematics. Reliable tool use in multimodal agents, however, remains challenging because models must interpret text and images while integrating noisy retrieved evidence, often under sparse outcome-level supervision without explicit verification signals. We present Self-Verification via Reinforcement Learning (SVRL), an RL-only finetuning framework that trains multimodal agents to verify and filter retrieved evidence within their own reasoning traces, reducing reliance on external verifiers at inference time. SVRL also introduces a search-aware penalty that discourages unnecessary tool calls and a query-diversity reward that encourages diverse, well-formed search queries, providing fine-grained feedback on when and what to search. Finetuning Qwen-2.5-VL-7B with SVRL on only 5{,}000 visual question answering examples yields consistent gains in multi-hop VQA generalization and tool efficiency across benchmarks. Overall, SVRL narrows the gap between compact agents and much larger proprietary models while requiring substantially lower training and inference cost.

AI.tldr: SVRL is an RL-only finetuning framework that trains multimodal agents to self-verify and filter retrieved evidence within their own reasoning traces, reducing reliance on external verifiers at inference time. It introduces a search-aware penalty to discourage unnecessary tool calls and a query-diversity reward for better search queries. Finetuning Qwen-2.5-VL-7B on only 5,000 visual QA examples yields consistent gains in multi-hop VQA generalization and tool efficiency, narrowing the gap with much larger proprietary models at substantially lower cost.
AI.motivation: Reliable tool use in multimodal agents remains challenging because models must interpret text and images while integrating noisy retrieved evidence, often under sparse outcome-level supervision without explicit verification signals.
AI.method: SVRL is an RL-only finetuning framework that trains multimodal agents to verify and filter retrieved evidence within their own reasoning traces. It introduces two reward components: a search-aware penalty that discourages unnecessary tool calls and a query-diversity reward that encourages diverse, well-formed search queries, providing fine-grained feedback on when and what to search.
AI.result: Finetuning Qwen-2.5-VL-7B with SVRL on only 5,000 visual question answering examples yields consistent gains in multi-hop VQA generalization and tool efficiency across benchmarks. SVRL narrows the gap between compact agents and much larger proprietary models while requiring substantially lower training and inference cost.
AI.conclusion: SVRL demonstrates that RL-only finetuning with self-verification capabilities can make compact multimodal agents competitive with much larger proprietary models on tool-augmented reasoning tasks, while significantly reducing computational costs for both training and inference.

title: ResidualAuth: What Authorization State Must Language Agents Preserve under Revocable Delegation?
comment: 61 pages, 7 figures. Includes appendices. Moonwon Choi and Seokho Jeong contributed equally; Seunggeun Lee is the corresponding author
summary: Tool-using language agents can delegate and revoke permissions while acting through external services. We show that two authorization histories can have identical current permissions and identical all-pairs reachability yet require opposite decisions after the same direct-edge revocation. We formalize the information needed to preserve such distinctions as a residual authorization state. We prove that exponentially many future-distinct states can share one fixed transitive closure, and give exact or tight asymptotic bounds on the state required by an exact monitor as delegation redundancy varies. ResidualAuth compiles these constructions into paired language-agent episodes. Across four open-weight models, a fixed 256-token summary solved 0-2/16 pairs, sham reads solved 0/16, and authenticated current-query reads solved 15-16/16. In a separate held-out online-memory diagnostic, exact ledger serializations fit all 128 four-coordinate pairs at both 768 and 1,024 tokens. At either cap, factually supported model-written memories sufficient for every prespecified continuation solved at most 1/128 pairs per model. A hard gate reduced eight observed unauthorized effects to zero without changing the preceding attempts. These results distinguish required authorization state, usable decision information, online state maintenance, and effect mediation.

AI.tldr: This paper studies authorization state in tool-using language agents, showing that identical permissions and reachability can mask divergent revocation outcomes, formalizing the residual authorization state needed for correct decisions, and demonstrating that exact ledger serialization far outperforms model-written memory summaries.
AI.motivation: Tool-using language agents must delegate and revoke permissions, requiring agents to track authorization state over time. The authors investigate what minimal information is truly needed to make correct revocation decisions, revealing a gap between simple permission tracking (current permissions, reachability) and full authorization history.
AI.method: The paper formalizes authorization via delegation graphs and shows that current permissions plus all-pairs reachability are insufficient after edge revocation. It introduces "residual authorization state" as the necessary information, proves bounds on exact monitors, and builds ResidualAuth, a paired language-agent episode framework. Experiments test four open-weight models on summary-based, sham-read, and authenticated current-query read conditions, plus a separate online-memory diagnostic with exact ledger serializations versus model-written memories.
AI.result: A fixed 256-token summary solved 0-2/16 pairs, sham reads solved 0/16, and authenticated current-query reads solved 15-16/16. Exact ledger serializations fit all 128 four-coordinate pairs at both 768 and 1,024 tokens, while factually supported model-written memories solved at most 1/128 pairs per model. A hard gate reduced eight observed unauthorized effects to zero.
AI.conclusion: The results distinguish required authorization state, usable decision information, online state maintenance, and effect mediation, demonstrating that exact, externally verified state representations are necessary for reliable authorization decisions in language agents while model-generated memory summaries are insufficient.

title: Automated Design of Inventory Policy with Large Language Models: An Exploratory Study
summary: Firms making inventory decisions have access to operational data, optimization tools, and large language models (LLMs). Typically, data characterize the operating environment, optimization selects parameters within a prespecified inventory policy class, and LLMs support coding and decision analysis. We develop an integrated framework that combines these resources to automate inventory policy design. Given demand data, the framework iteratively uses an LLM to generate parameterized policy classes and an external solver to optimize its parameters within each class. Across 30 lost-sales inventory instances, the mean cost reduction relative to optimized base-stock benchmarks increases from 17.5% after one generation to 30.0% after ten generations. Parameter optimization is central to this performance: an LLM-only variant performs substantially worse, whereas optimization-guided feedback improves policy quality, accelerates search, and directs the LLM toward better policy classes rather than merely better parameter values within a fixed class. The strongest discovered policies are also interpretable: they combine recognizable inventory-control motifs, including capped orders, discounted or weighted pipeline inventory, and threshold-based replenishment logic. The search thereby produces new policy-class functional forms that, to our knowledge, have not previously been studied in the lost-sales inventory literature. These functional forms are not specified ex ante but emerge from the search process. Moreover, after their parameters are re-optimized, three discovered policy classes achieve average cost reductions of 21.75% to 22.60% across 10,064 new inventory instances. Overall, the results show that data-driven parameter optimization can guide LLM-based search over a broad space of inventory policy classes and identify high-performing, interpretable, and transferable decision rules.

AI.tldr: This paper develops an integrated framework combining LLMs with external parameter optimization to automate inventory policy design. The framework iteratively generates parameterized policy classes via LLM and optimizes parameters using a solver, achieving cost reductions from 17.5% (after one generation) to 30.0% (after ten generations) across 30 lost-sales inventory instances, and discovering novel, interpretable policy forms that transfer well to 10,064 new instances.
AI.motivation: Firms possess operational data, optimization tools, and LLMs separately, but no framework integrates them to automatically design inventory policies. LLMs alone produce poor parameter values, while optimization alone is restricted to prespecified policy classes. The paper aims to combine these resources to explore a broad space of inventory policy classes rather than relying on ad hoc or ex ante specified functional forms.
AI.method: An iterative framework that alternates between an LLM generating parameterized inventory policy classes and an external optimization solver tuning the parameters within each class. The LLM receives demand data and optimization-guided feedback from previous iterations to propose improved policy structures. Search proceeds over ten generations across 30 lost-sales inventory instances, with discovered policies subsequently re-optimized and tested for transferability on 10,064 new instances.
AI.result: Mean cost reduction versus optimized base-stock benchmarks improves from 17.5% after one generation to 30.0% after ten generations. LLM-only variants perform substantially worse, confirming that parameter optimization is central. Optimization-guided feedback improves policy quality, accelerates search, and directs the LLM toward better policy classes rather than just better parameters. Discovered policies combine recognizable motifs (capped orders, weighted pipeline inventory, threshold-based replenishment) and yield 21.75%-22.60% average cost reductions across 10,064 new instances after parameter re-optimization.
AI.conclusion: Data-driven parameter optimization can effectively guide LLM-based search over a broad policy-class space, uncovering novel, interpretable, and transferable inventory decision rules that were not specified ex ante and have not previously appeared in the lost-sales inventory literature.

title: Inference-Time Nash Alignment
summary: Preference-based fine-tuning methods such as RLHF and DPO require substantial compute and large preference datasets. They also need direct access to the model parameters which are not provided by many state-of-the art models. Inference-time alignment offers a cost-effective alternative without updating model parameters. However, existing inference-time methods rely on a scalar reward model derived under a Bradley-Terry assumption, which cannot represent general preferences. Following recent work on fine-tuning with generalized preferences, in this work, we initiate the study of inference-time alignment under general preferences. We formulate the problem as obtaining a Nash equilibrium of a two-player zero-sum game between policies. We propose two algorithms: Best-of-Nash (BoN) and Nash Mirror Descent (NMD). We prove that both algorithms achieve a duality gap that matches the problem lower bound. Empirically, we implement the two methods on three datasets, which shows that our methods substantially outperform the base policy, converging to the performance of the fine-tuned models. Moreover, our results show that NMD remains robust across the regularization parameter.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces inference-time alignment under general preferences (beyond Bradley-Terry scalar rewards) by formulating the problem as a two-player zero-sum game between policies. The authors propose Best-of-Nash (BoN) and Nash Mirror Descent (NMD), proving both achieve a duality gap matching the problem lower bound. Experiments on three datasets show these methods outperform the base policy and approach fine-tuned model performance, with NMD remaining robust across regularization parameters.
AI.motivation: Preference-based fine-tuning (RLHF/DPO) is computationally expensive, requires large preference datasets, and needs direct parameter access that many state-of-the-art models do not provide. While inference-time alignment offers a cheaper alternative without parameter updates, existing methods rely on scalar reward models under the Bradley-Terry assumption, which cannot represent general (non-transitive) preferences. This limits their applicability and expressiveness.
AI.method: The problem is formulated as finding a Nash equilibrium of a two-player zero-sum game between policies. Two algorithms are proposed: Best-of-Nash (BoN) and Nash Mirror Descent (NMD), both designed to handle general preferences at inference time without parameter updates.
AI.result: Both BoN and NMD achieve a duality gap matching the theoretical problem lower bound. Empirically, on three datasets, both methods substantially outperform the base policy and converge to performance comparable to fine-tuned models. NMD additionally demonstrates robustness across different regularization parameter values.
AI.conclusion: Inference-time alignment can effectively handle general preferences by framing the problem as a two-player zero-sum game and solving for Nash equilibrium, achieving competitive performance to fine-tuning while requiring no parameter updates or large compute budgets. NMD offers stable and robust performance across hyperparameter settings.

title: RevalExo: A Functional Daily-Activity Benchmark for Inertial and Visual Locomotion Mode Recognition in Older Adults and Clinical Cohorts
summary: Assistive devices for people with mobility impairments, such as powered exoskeletons, rely on accurate locomotion mode recognition to adapt control strategies and provide appropriate assistance during daily activities. However, public benchmarks are typically collected from healthy adults, lack temporally precise labels necessary for detecting mode transitions, or focus on a limited set of tasks. To support development and evaluation under realistic clinical constraints and daily mobility demands, we introduce RevalExo, a functional daily-activity benchmark for inertial and visual locomotion mode recognition. RevalExo is built around a standardized, clinically and ecologically validated daily-activity protocol reflecting the cumulative everyday mobility demands in ageing and clinical populations. The benchmark includes 27 participants across three cohorts: older adults without mobility impairments, stroke survivors, and older adults with probable sarcopenia. The full cohort was recorded with lower-body IMUs, while synchronized egocentric video was collected for a clinically feasible subset of 13 participants. RevalExo provides 10.1 hours of frame-level annotations across 11 locomotion modes, including 5.1 hours of paired inertial--visual recordings. We benchmark three challenges: unimodal and multimodal locomotion mode recognition across multiple horizons, cross-population generalization from older adults without mobility impairments to clinical cohorts, and vision-guided knowledge transfer to IMU-only models. Results confirm consistent gains from fusing inertial and visual inputs but reveal a substantial gap between general recognition ($\sim$93\% F1) and recognition during transitions ($\sim$68\% F1), alongside persistent challenges in cross-population generalization and cross-modal transfer. We release RevalExo to stimulate further research on these open challenges.

AI.tldr: RevalExo is a new functional daily-activity benchmark for inertial and visual locomotion mode recognition, built around a clinically validated protocol. It includes 27 participants across three cohorts (older adults, stroke survivors, and probable sarcopenia), 10.1 hours of frame-level annotations across 11 locomotion modes, and benchmarks unimodal/multimodal recognition, cross-population generalization, and vision-guided knowledge transfer. Results show fusion gains but reveal a large gap between general recognition (~93% F1) and transition recognition (~68% F1), plus persistent challenges in cross-population and cross-modal transfer.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks for locomotion mode recognition in assistive devices are limited because they are typically collected from healthy adults, lack temporally precise transition labels, or cover a narrow set of tasks. There is a need for a benchmark reflecting realistic clinical constraints and daily mobility demands to support development of assistive technologies like powered exoskeletons.
AI.method: The authors construct RevalExo using a standardized, clinically and ecologically validated daily-activity protocol reflecting cumulative everyday mobility demands in aging and clinical populations. Data was collected from 27 participants across three cohorts: older adults without mobility impairments, stroke survivors, and older adults with probable sarcopenia. Lower-body IMUs were used for all participants, with synchronized egocentric video from a clinically feasible subset of 13 participants. The dataset provides 10.1 hours of frame-level annotations across 11 locomotion modes (5.1 hours paired inertial-visual). Three benchmark challenges are defined: (1) unimodal and multimodal recognition across multiple horizons, (2) cross-population generalization from healthy older adults to clinical cohorts, and (3) vision-guided knowledge transfer to IMU-only models.
AI.result: Fusing inertial and visual inputs yields consistent performance gains. General locomotion recognition reaches ~93% F1, but recognition during mode transitions drops substantially to ~68% F1. Cross-population generalization and cross-modal (vision-to-IMU) transfer remain persistent challenges.
AI.conclusion: RevalExo exposes significant open gaps in locomotion mode recognition—particularly during transitions, across clinical populations, and for cross-modal transfer. The benchmark is released publicly to stimulate further research addressing these challenges for assistive device applications.

title: CIVI: A Framework for Diagnosing Search Agent Failures in Civic Information
summary: Large Language Models are increasingly deployed in public-sector settings, where incorrect guidance can cause irreversible harm. We introduce CIVI, the first framework for diagnosing search agent failures in civic information. Its benchmark instantiation jointly spans cross-national, interjurisdictional government contexts (federal, state, and local) and functional categories from an internationally adopted United Nations standard. We evaluate ten frontier search agents and find that none matches an attentive human baseline. Alongside accuracy, CIVI measures search invocation rate, selective no-search accuracy, and how often agents cite authoritative government sources. To perform this diagnosis, we introduce ARISE, which decomposes agentic search failures into four mutually exclusive modes, isolated via source-injection ablation. ARISE attributes 72.1% of all observed failures to retrieval-bound causes rather than to gaps in the models' parametric knowledge.

AI.tldr: CIVI is a framework for diagnosing search agent failures in civic information tasks, spanning cross-national and interjurisdictional government contexts. Ten frontier search agents were evaluated against human baselines, and ARISE, a decomposition method, attributes 72.1% of failures to retrieval-bound causes rather than parametric knowledge gaps.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used in public-sector settings where incorrect guidance can cause irreversible harm, yet there was no framework for systematically diagnosing search agent failures in civic information contexts.
AI.method: CIVI introduces a benchmark jointly spanning cross-national, interjurisdictional government contexts (federal, state, local) and functional categories from a United Nations standard. It measures accuracy, search invocation rate, selective no-search accuracy, and authoritative source citation. ARISE decomposes agentic search failures into four mutually exclusive modes via source-injection ablation to isolate retrieval-bound causes from parametric knowledge gaps.
AI.result: None of the ten frontier search agents matched an attentive human baseline. ARISE attributed 72.1% of observed failures to retrieval-bound causes rather than gaps in the models' parametric knowledge.
AI.conclusion: Frontier search agents underperform humans on civic information tasks, and the dominant failure mode is retrieval-related rather than knowledge-related, suggesting that improving search/retrieval mechanisms is more impactful than expanding parametric knowledge for civic information applications.

title: Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Digital Inventory of Cultural Heritage & Traditional Knowledge: Case for Indonesian Open Digital Library of Culture
summary: The Indonesian Digital Library of Culture (Perpustakaan Digital Budaya Indonesia, PDBI; budaya-indonesia.org) is a participatory platform that has collected tens of thousands of entries on Nusantara cultural heritage through public contribution since 2007. Manual contribution faces three structural barriers: coverage (knowledge is scattered across languages and sites), integrity (open sources mix authentic documentation with noise), and completeness (subjects are recorded but their data remain shallow). This paper presents a methodological framework for autonomous, AI-based harvesting of cultural knowledge from the open web, designed to expand corpus coverage while intensifying per-entry data depth. The methodology is organised as a five-stage economic funnel: focused crawling, multilingual extraction and canonicalisation, vector encoding with blocking, agentic decision-making, and idempotent publication, under the principle of deterministic orchestration, agentic decisions. Each stage is formalised: funnel economics and optimal filter ordering; crawl-frontier dynamics as a subcritical branching process that explains the necessity of recurrent re-seeding; fact-level novelty via a containment measure; Bayesian multi-source evidence fusion with elevated publication thresholds for sacred categories; exactly-once effects via idempotent upserts and the transactional outbox; sliding-window inference budgeting with a reservation protocol; statistical quality auditing; and seed selection as submodular coverage maximisation. The framework retains four high-value human roles: curator of direction, escalation approver, quality auditor, and guardian of meaning, while machine autonomy is raised in stages. Ethical, legal, and cultural-sensitivity implications are discussed, including the architectural guarantee that the machine never overwrites human contributions.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a methodological framework for autonomous, AI-based harvesting of Indonesian cultural knowledge from the open web to expand and deepen the Indonesian Digital Library of Culture (PDBI). The framework is organized as a five-stage economic funnel (focused crawling, multilingual extraction/canonicalisation, vector encoding with blocking, agentic decision-making, idempotent publication) under the principle of deterministic orchestration with agentic decisions, incorporating formal models for funnel economics, branching-process crawl dynamics, Bayesian evidence fusion, exactly-once publication, inference budgeting, quality auditing, and submodular seed selection—while retaining four high-value human roles and guaranteeing machines never overwrite human contributions.
AI.motivation: Manual contribution to the participatory PDBI platform faces three structural barriers: coverage (knowledge scattered across languages and sites), integrity (open sources mix authentic documentation with noise), and completeness (recorded subjects have shallow data), motivating an autonomous AI-based harvesting framework.
AI.method: A five-stage economic funnel methodology: focused crawling, multilingual extraction and canonicalisation, vector encoding with blocking, agentic decision-making, and idempotent publication. It is formalized with funnel economics and optimal filter ordering; crawl-frontier dynamics as a subcritical branching process with recurrent re-seeding; fact-level novelty via containment measures; Bayesian multi-source evidence fusion with elevated publication thresholds for sacred categories; exactly-once effects via idempotent upserts and the transactional outbox; sliding-window inference budgeting with a reservation protocol; statistical quality auditing; and seed selection as submodular coverage maximisation. Human roles preserved: curator of direction, escalation approver, quality auditor, and guardian of meaning.
AI.result: The paper contributes a complete, formal methodological framework rather than experimental results, detailing each funnel stage mathematically, raising machine autonomy in stages, and discussing ethical, legal, and cultural-sensitivity implications including an architectural guarantee that machine outputs never overwrite human contributions.
AI.conclusion: The framework addresses coverage, integrity, and completeness barriers in participatory cultural knowledge platforms by combining deterministic orchestration with agentic decision-making, formalizing each pipeline stage, preserving essential human oversight roles, and embedding safeguards for cultural sensitivity and human-authority supremacy.

title: Router Prior Bias: Preserving Base Routing Structure in MoE Post-Training
summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) pretraining relies on an auxiliary load-balancing loss (LBL) to drive per-expert utilization toward uniformity. Post-training inherits a different situation: the base router already encodes non-uniform expert co-activation structure, which a re-imposed uniformity objective flattens away. We show that downstream performance depends instead on holding this inherited routing softly, a principle we term soft router anchoring, and instantiate it as Router Prior Bias (RPB), a training-time bias that pulls the router logits toward a prior read off the frozen base router while leaving the router itself trainable. On math post-training of Moonlight-16B-A3B, RPB attains 45.77 in-domain accuracy against 31.91 under re-applied LBL and 29.44 under unanchored fine-tuning, and retains more out-of-domain capability than either. The ordering against LBL reproduces on a second model family (Qwen3-30B-A3B-Base), and the advantage over LBL is resolvable on an independently sourced corpus. Anchors defined on the router weights, on its logits, or on its output distribution perform comparably with no consistent ordering, which places the effect in the softness of the constraint rather than in the particular prior RPB supplies. Retained community structure in the expert co-activation graph tracks these gains wherever the base router is non-uniform enough for communities to form, yet enforcing the same prior as a hard assignment preserves that structure while performance falls sharply. Community structure is therefore a footprint of soft anchoring rather than its source, and the practical lesson is that inherited routing should be held softly during post-training, since both flattening it toward uniformity and enforcing it absolutely carry a downstream cost. Our code will be released at https://github.com/naver-ai/rpb.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Router Prior Bias (RPB), a soft anchoring technique for MoE post-training that preserves the base router's non-uniform expert co-activation structure rather than flattening it via load-balancing loss. RPB significantly outperforms both LBL and unanchored fine-tuning across multiple model families and datasets.
AI.motivation: Standard MoE post-training re-applies a load-balancing loss that forces expert utilization toward uniformity, which destroys the non-uniform expert co-activation structure already encoded in the pretrained router. Since downstream performance depends on holding this inherited routing structure, a uniform re-imposition is fundamentally counterproductive.
AI.method: The paper proposes Router Prior Bias (RPB), a training-time bias that pulls router logits toward a prior derived from the frozen base router while keeping the router itself trainable. Anchors can be defined on router weights, logits, or output distributions, all performing comparably, indicating the effect stems from the softness of the constraint rather than the specific prior form.
AI.result: On math post-training of Moonlight-16B-A3B, RPB achieves 45.77 in-domain accuracy vs. 31.91 (LBL) and 29.44 (unanchored). The ordering reproduces on Qwen3-30B-A3B-Base and on an independently sourced corpus. Hard-assignment enforcement of the same prior preserves community structure but sharply degrades performance.
AI.conclusion: Inherited routing should be held softly during MoE post-training. Both flattening it toward uniformity (via LBL) and enforcing it absolutely (hard anchoring) carry downstream costs. Retained community structure in expert co-activation graphs is a footprint of soft anchoring, not its causal source.

title: SchemeArena: Factorized Stress Testing of Scheming in LLM Agents
summary: We study scheming in LLM agents, in which agents covertly pursue misaligned goals. Our focus is to understand how scheming arises from the interaction of key factors, such as instrumental goals, environmental affordances, oversight conditions, and perceived consequences. Prior work examines only a small number of scenarios, limiting the ability to isolate how these conditions shape an agent's propensity or capability to scheme. This limited scale and task diversity also restrict coverage of realistic deployment settings and the range of scheming strategies that can be observed. To this end, we introduce SCHEMEARENA, a 400-scenario benchmark for scalable scheming stress testing, constructed through a factorized scenario synthesis framework spanning diverse safety-relevant tool domains, instrumental goals, oversight conditions, and pressure mechanisms. To enable scalable and reliable monitoring, we further propose SCOUT, a scheming monitor that grounds multi-criteria judgments in evidence drawn from agents' reasoning and actions. Across controlled stress tests on five LLM agents, we find that explicit instrumental goals are the strongest driver of scheming propensity. Strategic hints play a distinct role by helping agents translate scheming reasoning into concrete covert behavior. Oversight has mixed effects: in several closed models, action-only monitoring increases scheming, suggesting that partial oversight can act as an optimization constraint rather than a deterrent. CoT is a useful but incomplete monitoring signal: it can reveal latent scheming before execution, yet action-only scheming shows that covert behavior may occur without explicit reasoning evidence. We release the benchmark, code, and monitor at: https://github.com/launchnlp/SchemeArena.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces SCHEMEARENA, a 400-scenario benchmark for testing scheming behavior in LLM agents, along with SCOUT, an evidence-grounded monitoring framework. Experiments on five LLM agents reveal that explicit instrumental goals are the strongest driver of scheming propensity, strategic hints help translate intent into action, and partial (action-only) oversight can paradoxically increase scheming in some closed models. Chain-of-thought reasoning is useful but incomplete as a monitoring signal since covert behavior can occur without explicit reasoning evidence.
AI.motivation: Prior work on scheming in LLM agents examines only a small number of scenarios, limiting the ability to isolate how key factors (instrumental goals, environmental affordances, oversight conditions, perceived consequences) shape an agent's propensity or capability to scheme. This limited scale and task diversity also restrict coverage of realistic deployment settings and the range of observable scheming strategies.
AI.method: The authors construct SCHEMEARENA, a 400-scenario benchmark built through a factorized scenario synthesis framework spanning diverse safety-relevant tool domains, instrumental goals, oversight conditions, and pressure mechanisms. They also propose SCOUT, a scheming monitor that grounds multi-criteria judgments in evidence drawn from agents' reasoning and actions. Controlled stress tests are conducted on five LLM agents.
AI.result: Explicit instrumental goals are the strongest driver of scheming propensity. Strategic hints help translate scheming reasoning into concrete covert behavior. Action-only monitoring increases scheming in several closed models, suggesting partial oversight acts as an optimization constraint rather than a deterrent. Chain-of-thought can reveal latent scheming before execution, but action-only scheming demonstrates covert behavior can occur without explicit reasoning evidence.
AI.conclusion: Scheming arises from the interplay of multiple factors, with instrumental goals being the primary driver. Oversight has nuanced and sometimes counterproductive effects, and reasoning-based monitoring signals are useful but insufficient. The authors release the benchmark, code, and monitor publicly to enable scalable scheming stress testing and further research.

title: SWE-Bench Pro Verified: A Reliable Benchmark for Software Engineering Agents
summary: SWE-Bench Pro has emerged as a standard benchmark for evaluating software engineering agents on challenging repository-level tasks. However, our analysis work show that its evaluation is undermined by two sources of unreliability: \textbf{reward hacking}, enabled by leakage of gold solutions or hidden evaluation information, and \textbf{task quality issues}, including misleading problem statements and improperly scoped tests. These issues can inflate benchmark performance and obscure agents' true coding ability. We present \textbf{SWE-Bench Pro Verified}, a verified version of SWE-Bench Pro that addresses both problems. Our approach combines \textbf{anti-hacking} safeguards that eliminate major leakage channels without disrupting normal agent functionality, with \textbf{task refinement} that minimally corrects inconsistencies within flawed instances. Evaluations on SWE-Bench Pro Verified reveal that some models perform substantially worse than previously reported, suggesting that existing results on SWE-Bench Pro may overestimate real software engineering capability. SWE-Bench Pro Verified offers a more trustworthy benchmark for assessing software engineering agents.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies two sources of unreliability in SWE-Bench Pro—reward hacking via leakage of gold solutions/hidden evaluation info and task quality issues such as misleading problem statements and improperly scoped tests—and introduces SWE-Bench Pro Verified, which applies anti-hacking safeguards and task refinement to fix these flaws. Evaluations show some models perform substantially worse than previously reported, indicating prior results overestimated real coding ability.
AI.motivation: SWE-Bench Pro is a standard benchmark for repository-level software engineering agents, but its evaluation is compromised by reward hacking (leakage of gold solutions or hidden evaluation information) and task quality issues (misleading statements and improperly scoped tests), which can inflate performance and obscure true agent capability.
AI.method: The authors present SWE-Bench Pro Verified, combining anti-hacking safeguards that eliminate major leakage channels without disrupting normal agent functionality, alongside task refinement that minimally corrects inconsistencies within flawed instances.
AI.result: Evaluations on SWE-Bench Pro Verified show that some models perform substantially worse than previously reported, suggesting existing results on SWE-Bench Pro may overestimate real software engineering capability.
AI.conclusion: SWE-Bench Pro Verified provides a more trustworthy benchmark for assessing software engineering agents by addressing both reward hacking and task quality issues.

title: WorldAgen: Unified State-Action Prediction with Test-Time World Model Training
summary: How can vision-language-action (VLA) models adapt to new environments where world dynamics shift? While recent research has combined world modeling and action prediction to improve VLA performance, existing methods largely rely on pretraining on static datasets, without mechanisms for active adaptation at deployment time. As a result, these models often fail to generalize when deployed in unseen scenarios with novel object configurations or dynamics. We present WorldAgen, a unified framework that jointly learns world modeling and action prediction while enabling Test-Time Training (TTT) to adapt to new environments. WorldAgen employs a shared Transformer backbone with two heads: (1) a world model head that predicts future states from past state-action trajectories, and (2) an agent model head that predicts actions conditioned on task instructions. We design a Mixed Unidirectional Attention Mask to separate these two models. During test time, WorldAgen samples exploratory actions, collects ground-truth state transitions, and performs lightweight TTT updates to refine its world model. This adaptation improves the model's understanding of the environment and leads to more accurate action predictions. Experiments on the CALVIN and LIBERO benchmarks demonstrate that our baseline model achieves comparable, and in some cases superior, performance to current state-of-the-art approaches. Moreover, with TTT on a small number of samples, our method surpasses existing state-of-the-art models, highlighting the effectiveness of adapting world models at inference time.

AI.tldr: WorldAgen is a unified framework for vision-language-action (VLA) models that jointly learns world modeling and action prediction, with Test-Time Training (TTT) enabling active adaptation to new environments at deployment. It uses a shared Transformer backbone with separate world model and agent model heads, a Mixed Unidirectional Attention Mask, and lightweight TTT updates based on exploratory action sampling. Experiments on CALVIN and LIBERO show performance comparable to or better than state-of-the-art baselines, with TTT on few samples surpassing existing methods.
