AI.motivation: Existing VLA models that combine world modeling and action prediction rely on pretraining on static datasets without mechanisms for active adaptation at deployment time. As a result, they fail to generalize to unseen scenarios with novel object configurations or dynamics, motivating the need for a framework that can adapt to new environments during inference.
AI.method: WorldAgen uses a shared Transformer backbone with two heads: a world model head predicting future states from past state-action trajectories, and an agent model head predicting actions conditioned on task instructions. A Mixed Unidirectional Attention Mask separates the two models. At test time, the model samples exploratory actions, collects ground-truth state transitions, and performs lightweight Test-Time Training (TTT) updates to refine the world model, improving environment understanding and subsequent action predictions.
AI.result: On the CALVIN and LIBERO benchmarks, WorldAgen achieves comparable or superior performance to current state-of-the-art approaches in its baseline form. With Test-Time Training on a small number of samples, it surpasses existing state-of-the-art models, demonstrating the effectiveness of adapting world models at inference time.
AI.conclusion: Adapting world models at test time through lightweight Test-Time Training is an effective strategy for improving VLA model generalization to unseen environments with novel dynamics. The unified architecture with separable world and agent heads, combined with TTT-based active adaptation, provides a promising path toward deployment-ready VLA systems.

title: Key Path Identification for Resolving Knowledge Conflicts via SAE-based Steering
summary: Sparse autoencoder (SAE)-based steering has been widely used to address knowledge conflicts by guiding LLMs to be more faithful to the contextual knowledge. Existing methods usually perform mass steering, which modifies a large batch of SAE features identified via correlation-based methods. However, due to the inaccurate correlation and the neglected feature interactions, mass steering methods fail to precisely identify the features that play the key roles in steering and introduce a large number of redundant ones, which add noise and weaken the steering effects. Our empirical studies reveal that steering only a small subset of the identified features can achieve comparable or even better performance. Motivated by this finding, we propose Key Path Identification (KPI), a novel method that identifies key steering features characterized by strong causal dependencies with both upstream and downstream features. From these features, KPI constructs key paths and steers through less feature modifications. In this way, KPI advances SAE-based steering from quantity-driven to quality-focused, offering a perspective for more precise and interpretable model editing. Experiments in RAG tasks with knowledge conflicts show that our method improves the accuracy by 18% on average compared to the best baseline of mass steering, effectively filtering redundant features, alleviating side effects and demonstrating the core role of key paths in steering.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Key Path Identification (KPI), a method for sparse autoencoder (SAE)-based steering in LLMs that addresses knowledge conflicts by identifying only the most causally important features rather than steering large batches of features. KPI constructs "key paths" from features with strong causal dependencies on both upstream and downstream features, achieving an 18% average accuracy improvement over mass steering baselines in RAG tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing SAE-based steering methods perform mass steering, modifying a large batch of features identified via correlation-based methods. These approaches suffer from inaccurate correlation analysis and neglect feature interactions, introducing redundant features that add noise and weaken steering effects. The authors empirically show that steering only a small subset of identified features achieves comparable or better performance, motivating a more precise, quality-focused approach.
AI.method: The authors propose Key Path Identification (KPI), which identifies key steering features characterized by strong causal dependencies with both upstream and downstream features. KPI constructs key paths from these features and performs steering through fewer feature modifications, shifting SAE-based steering from quantity-driven to quality-focused model editing.
AI.result: Experiments on RAG tasks with knowledge conflicts show KPI improves accuracy by 18% on average compared to the best mass steering baseline. The method effectively filters redundant features, alleviates side effects, and demonstrates the core role of key paths in steering.
AI.conclusion: KPI demonstrates that precision in feature selection—rather than the quantity of modified features—is critical for effective SAE-based steering. This quality-focused perspective offers a more accurate and interpretable approach to model editing in knowledge-conflict scenarios.

title: OntologyBench: Can Dense Retrieval Satisfy Structured Biomedical Constraints?
comment: 19 pages and 1 figure. Accepted to EMNLP 2026 Main conference. https://openreview.net/forum?id=RMiOTIub1j&noteId=RMiOTIub1j
summary:
We introduce OntologyBench, a tiered biomedical retrieval benchmark comprising 471,854 training and 125,744 evaluation query-document relevance pairs across concept grounding, relational retrieval, and compositional phenotype-based retrieval.
  Although these tasks can be tractable using ontology-aware reference methods, across task tiers, embedding performance is generally lower on relational and compositional tasks than on concept-grounding tasks. Fine-tuning on ontology-derived supervision improves performance on several relational and compositional tasks, whereas the evaluated reranking and LLM-based candidate-scoring methods provide little or no end-to-end improvement. Errors frequently reflect diseases matching only subsets of the phenotype evidence.
  These findings indicate that the evaluated embedding and reranking configurations do not reliably recover the compatibility encoded by the selected ontology relations and phenotype combinations and motivate retrieval systems that better integrate learned representations with structured biomedical knowledge.

AI.tldr: OntologyBench is a new tiered biomedical retrieval benchmark with 471,854 training and 125,744 evaluation pairs across concept grounding, relational retrieval, and compositional phenotype-based retrieval tasks. Evaluations show embedding methods underperform on complex tasks compared to ontology-aware baselines, fine-tuning helps but reranking and LLM-based methods provide little improvement, and common errors involve partial phenotype matching—motivating retrieval systems that better integrate learned representations with structured biomedical knowledge.
AI.motivation: Existing biomedical retrieval benchmarks lack structured ontology-aware tasks that test relational and compositional reasoning, leaving a gap in evaluating whether modern retrieval systems can recover the semantic compatibility encoded in biomedical ontologies.
AI.method: Constructs OntologyBench with three task tiers (concept grounding, relational retrieval, compositional phenotype-based retrieval), provides large-scale training/evaluation relevance pairs, and systematically compares embedding, fine-tuning, reranking, and LLM-based scoring approaches against ontology-aware reference methods.
AI.result: Embedding performance degrades on relational and compositional tasks relative to concept grounding; fine-tuning with ontology-derived supervision improves several relational/compositional tasks, while reranking and LLM-based methods offer little to no end-to-end gains; errors frequently stem from diseases matching only subsets of phenotype evidence.
AI.conclusion: Current embedding and reranking configurations fail to reliably recover the compatibility encoded by ontology relations and phenotype combinations, motivating hybrid retrieval systems that integrate learned representations with structured biomedical knowledge.

title: Safe Harness Self-Evolution: A Theoretical Analysis of Feasibility and Limits
summary: Harness self-evolution is the process by which an agent modifies its prompts, tools, code, or orchestration in response to task feedback while keeping the underlying language model frozen, with changes persisting across subsequent tasks. We provide a systematic theoretical analysis of the feasibility and limits of safe harness self-evolution, connecting modification generation, finite-data certification and selection, safe adoption, and behavior after an update. Under a fixed user-task distribution, we establish conditions guaranteeing overall expected-reward improvement while controlling changes on retained tasks, characterize the probability of generating qualified modifications, and derive finite-data bounds for safe selection and adoption. Our analysis shows that generation and certification impose distinct constraints: current task performance does not determine the probability of generating qualified modifications, and generating more candidates need not improve the guarantee of a successful update when evaluation is limiting. Stagnation may therefore arise even when improvement opportunities remain. We further show that worst-case evaluation cost for recognizing genuine improvements diverges as expected reward approaches its upper bound. Across successive updates, certified improvement guarantees accumulate over a finite run, but a successful update does not by itself guarantee that further improvement remains possible. These results provide a basis for diagnosing bottlenecks and designing safer self-evolution mechanisms.

AI.tldr: A systematic theoretical analysis of safe harness self-evolution—where agents modify their own prompts, tools, code, or orchestration while keeping the underlying LM frozen—establishing conditions for reward improvement, qualification probabilities, and finite-data certification bounds, while revealing that generation and certification impose distinct constraints leading to possible stagnation even when improvement remains possible.
AI.motivation: As language-model-based agents increasingly self-modify their own harnesses across tasks, there is a lack of rigorous theoretical grounding for when such self-evolution is safe and feasible. This work aims to formalize the feasibility and limits of harness self-evolution to diagnose bottlenecks and guide the design of safer self-evolution mechanisms.
AI.method: The authors develop a theoretical framework connecting four components: modification generation, finite-data certification and selection, safe adoption, and post-update behavior. Under a fixed user-task distribution, they analyze conditions for expected-reward improvement while bounding changes to retained tasks, characterize the probability of generating qualified modifications, and derive finite-data guarantees for safe selection/adoption.
AI.result: Key findings include: (1) current task performance does not predict probability of generating qualified modifications; (2) generating more candidates provides no stronger update guarantee when evaluation is limiting; (3) stagnation can occur despite remaining improvement room; (4) worst-case evaluation cost diverges as expected reward approaches its upper bound; (5) certified improvements accumulate over finite runs but a successful update does not imply further improvement remains possible.
AI.conclusion: Generation and certification impose fundamentally distinct constraints in harness self-evolution, and the theoretical results provide a foundation for identifying bottlenecks and designing safer self-evolution systems.

title: Less Is Personal: Learning Minimal Sufficient User Profiles for Personalized Language Models
summary: Retrieval-augmented personalization enables large language models to produce more accurate and preference-aligned outputs using relevant records retrieved from user histories. Personalized language models typically prepend a fixed number of retrieved user records, even when additional history is redundant, harmful, or unrelated to a user's distinctive behavior. We study minimal sufficient personalization: constructing the least costly ordered profile for each input while preserving the utility achievable from a retrieved candidate pool. We introduce ENOUGH, a method that iteratively appends behavioral records or emits STOP to construct profiles with adaptive lengths. Offline, bounded counterfactual search evaluates profile prefixes by jointly considering downstream gains, user specificity, and token costs. The resulting long-horizon targets are distilled into a multi-head value controller with explicit ranking and stopping supervision. At inference, the controller selects and orders records through lightweight decisions, and the frozen generator is invoked once after stopping. Extensive experiments on six personalized tasks demonstrate that ENOUGH consistently outperforms strong heuristic and retrieval-augmented baselines in both effectiveness and efficiency, achieving minimal sufficient profiles that preserve personalization utility while reducing unnecessary context costs.

AI.tldr: ENOUGH is a method for minimal sufficient personalization in LLMs, which constructs adaptive-length ordered profiles of user behavioral records via iterative decision-making and multi-head value control, reducing context costs while preserving personalization utility.
AI.motivation: Retrieval-augmented personalization typically prepends a fixed number of retrieved user records regardless of redundancy, harmfulness, or relevance to distinctive user behavior. This wastes context and can degrade output quality. The paper argues for minimal sufficient personalization—the least costly ordered profile per input that still achieves the utility of the full candidate pool.
AI.method: ENOUGH iteratively appends behavioral records or emits a STOP signal to construct variable-length profiles. Offline, bounded counterfactual search evaluates profile prefixes by jointly considering downstream gains, user specificity, and token costs, producing long-horizon supervision targets. These targets are distilled into a multi-head value controller with explicit ranking and stopping heads. At inference, the controller makes lightweight record selection and ordering decisions, and the frozen generator is invoked once after stopping.
AI.result: On six personalized tasks, ENOUGH consistently outperforms strong heuristic and retrieval-augmented baselines in both effectiveness and efficiency, achieving minimal sufficient profiles that preserve personalization utility while reducing unnecessary context costs.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive-length profile construction via learned value controllers can replace fixed-size retrieval augmentation, yielding both better personalization and lower token overhead, without fine-tuning the generation model.

title: Does Deeper Reasoning Compromise Alignment? Revealing and Mitigating of Alignment Collapse in Large Reasoning Models
summary: The emergence of Chain-of-Thought (CoT) has established a robust foundation for Large Reasoning Models (LRMs). While deep reasoning is widely believed to enhance safety alignment, the stability of alignment mechanisms under extended reasoning remains underexplored. This paper challenges the prevailing view by revealing a critical vulnerability: Deep Reasoning May Induce Alignment Collapse. To rigorously quantify this phenomenon, we propose the Alignment Loss Rate (ALR) metric. Our experiments demonstrate that as reasoning depth increases, ALR rises significantly, indicating a severe degradation in model robustness against external perturbations. Capitalizing on this instability, a novel jailbreaking paradigm, Reasoning Trap (RT), is proposed. RT induces the model into extended reasoning to amplify the impact of adversarial attacks, leading to a sharp decline in safety capabilities. To elucidate the mechanism behind this collapse, we identify Attention Dilution as the root cause, arising from the competition for attention between the extended reasoning process and the original input. To mitigate this, Reasoning Residual Alignment (RRA), a lightweight defense strategy that dynamically re-emphasizes the input via residual connections integrated with the reasoning process.

AI.tldr: This paper reveals that deep reasoning in Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) can induce alignment collapse, where safety alignment degrades as reasoning depth increases. The authors propose the Alignment Loss Rate (ALR) metric to quantify this, introduce a jailbreaking paradigm called Reasoning Trap (RT), identify Attention Dilution as the root cause, and propose a lightweight defense called Reasoning Residual Alignment (RRA).
AI.motivation: While Chain-of-Thought (CoT) has established a foundation for Large Reasoning Models and deep reasoning is widely believed to enhance safety alignment, the stability of alignment mechanisms under extended reasoning remains underexplored. The authors challenge the prevailing assumption by uncovering a critical vulnerability where deeper reasoning can lead to alignment collapse.
AI.method: The paper introduces the Alignment Loss Rate (ALR) metric to quantify the degradation of model robustness against external perturbations as reasoning depth increases. It proposes a novel jailbreaking paradigm called Reasoning Trap (RT) that induces extended reasoning to amplify adversarial attack impacts. The authors identify Attention Dilution—attention competition between extended reasoning and original input—as the root cause, and propose Reasoning Residual Alignment (RRA), a lightweight defense using residual connections integrated with the reasoning process to dynamically re-emphasize the input.
AI.result: Experiments demonstrate that as reasoning depth increases, ALR rises significantly, indicating severe degradation in model robustness against external perturbations. This instability enables the Reasoning Trap jailbreak approach which causes a sharp decline in safety capabilities.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that deep reasoning can induce alignment collapse in LRMs, contradicts the prevailing belief that deep reasoning enhances safety. It offers both a new attack vector (Reasoning Trap) based on this vulnerability and a lightweight defensive mechanism (Reasoning Residual Alignment) to mitigate the identified Attention Dilution problem.

title: Bridging the Semantic-Utility Gap in Multimodal RAG via Generator-in-the-Loop Alignment
comment: Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Artificial Intelligence
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) augmented with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) benefit from access to external evidence. However, standard retrievers and rerankers optimize for semantic similarity rather than answer utility, creating a preference gap: documents that appear relevant may not help the generator produce a correct answer. Motivated by this, we propose a two-stage generator-in-the-loop alignment framework that closes this gap without human document-level relevance annotations. Our framework consists of two stages: in Stage 1, a VLM generates a hypothetical text passage from the image-query pair, which is used as the retrieval query for dense text search, bridging the image-to-text modality gap. In Stage 2, a cross-encoder reranker adapted with low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is fine-tuned using answer-supervised preference pairs mined from the frozen VLM: given the dataset answer label, a candidate document is labeled positive if the VLM produces the correct answer when given that document as context, and negative otherwise. This generator-guided signal is compatible with multiple alignment loss functions, including contrastive (triplet) loss, pairwise direct preference optimization (DPO), and supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and supports periodic re-mining to refresh preference pairs as the reranker improves. Experiments on VQA-X and A-OKVQA with Qwen3.5-2B and Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct show that our proposed framework consistently outperforms rank-order, random, and REPLUG-style likelihood baselines under various alignment losses and pool size settings, suggesting that answer-level generator feedback is an effective supervision signal for preference alignment.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a two-stage generator-in-the-loop alignment framework for retrieval-augmented vision-language models (VLMs) that closes the preference gap between semantic relevance and answer utility. Stage 1 uses a VLM to generate a hypothetical passage as the retrieval query, and Stage 2 fine-tunes a LoRA-adapted cross-encoder reranker using answer-supervised preference pairs mined from the frozen VLM. Experiments on VQA-X and A-OKVQA show consistent improvements over baselines.
AI.motivation: Standard retrievers and rerankers optimize for semantic similarity rather than answer utility, creating a preference gap where seemingly relevant documents do not actually help the generator produce correct answers. Traditional relevance annotations fail to capture whether evidence is useful for generation.
AI.method: A two-stage generator-in-the-loop alignment framework: (1) a VLM generates a hypothetical text passage from the image-query pair used as the retrieval query for dense text search, bridging the image-to-text modality gap; (2) a cross-encoder reranker adapted with LoRA is fine-tuned using answer-supervised preference pairs mined from a frozen VLM—a document is labeled positive if the VLM yields the correct answer with it as context, negative otherwise. The framework supports multiple alignment losses (triplet contrastive, pairwise DPO, SFT) and periodic re-mining of preference pairs as the reranker improves.
AI.result: Experiments on VQA-X and A-OKVQA using Qwen3.5-2B and Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct show the proposed framework consistently outperforms rank-order, random, and REPLUG-style likelihood baselines across various alignment loss functions and pool sizes.
AI.conclusion: Answer-level generator feedback is an effective supervision signal for preference alignment in RAG-augmented VLMs, closing the relevance-to-utility gap without requiring human document-level relevance annotations.

title: Do Dynamic Routers Need Memory? HeRo: History-Aware Routing for Efficient LLM Inference
summary: Dynamic layer routing reduces the inference cost of Large Language Models (LLMs) by learning to skip layers for individual tokens. Existing methods, however, treat each routing decision as a local operation conditioned solely on the current hidden state which is a formulation that overlooks the sequential, path-dependent nature of routing across depth: earlier decisions shape the representations seen by downstream routers, and the layer-usage objective couples all decisions jointly. We propose History-Aware Routing (HeRo), a dynamic routing framework that resolves this mismatch by introducing a router memory mechanism to maintain an explicit routing state across model depth. The memory is constructed via linear attention, incrementally aggregating preceding routing scores and their induced residual updates into a compact history representation. At each routed layer, the router conditions jointly on this accumulated state and the current hidden representation to select the executed branch. Instantiated for token-wise FFN routing, HeRo trains only lightweight routers and adapters on a frozen backbone, requiring no modification to pretrained parameters. Across Llama 3.1-8B, Llama 2-7B, and Llama 2-13B, HeRo consistently achieves the highest aggregate performance retention among ten baselines. On Llama 3.1-8B, it bypasses 26.87% of model parameters while achieving 100.24% of dense model performance across seven benchmarks, and retains 97.01% while bypassing 38.82% of model parameters under a tighter computation budget. Ablation studies confirm that removing routing history consistently degrades performance, most notably on multistep reasoning and code generation, validating that explicit routing memory enables more accurate and adaptive dynamic routing than solely conditioning on hidden state.

AI.tldr: HeRo (History-Aware Routing) is a dynamic layer routing framework for LLMs that introduces an explicit router memory mechanism via linear attention to aggregate routing decisions and residual updates across depth. This allows routers to condition on accumulated routing history in addition to the current hidden state, addressing the sequential, path-dependent nature of token routing. On frozen backbone architectures, training only lightweight routers and adapters, HeRo outperforms ten baselines across Llama 3.1-8B, Llama 2-7B, and Llama 2-13B, achieving 100.24% dense performance while bypassing 26.87% of parameters on Llama 3.1-8B.
AI.motivation: Existing dynamic layer routing methods treat each routing decision as a local, independent operation conditioned solely on the current hidden state. This formulation overlooks the sequential and path-dependent nature of routing across model depth: earlier routing decisions shape the representations processed by downstream routers, and the layer-usage objective couples all decisions jointly. This mismatch limits the accuracy and adaptivity of dynamic routing.
AI.method: HeRo introduces a router memory mechanism that maintains an explicit routing state across model depth. The memory is constructed via linear attention, which incrementally aggregates preceding routing scores and their induced residual updates into a compact history representation. At each routed layer, the router conditions jointly on the accumulated history state and the current hidden representation to select which branch to execute. The framework is instantiated for token-wise FFN routing, training only lightweight routers and adapters on a frozen backbone without modifying pretrained parameters.
AI.result: Across Llama 3.1-8B, Llama 2-7B, and Llama 2-13B, HeRo achieves the highest aggregate performance retention among ten baselines. On Llama 3.1-8B, it bypasses 26.87% of model parameters while achieving 100.24% of dense performance across seven benchmarks, and retains 97.01% performance while bypassing 38.82% of model parameters under a tighter computation budget. Ablation studies show that removing routing history consistently degrades performance, especially on multistep reasoning and code generation tasks.
AI.conclusion: Explicit routing memory enables more accurate and adaptive dynamic routing than solely conditioning on the hidden state. By modeling the sequential, path-dependent nature of token routing through accumulated history, HeRo demonstrates that history-aware routing decisions lead to superior performance retention and parameter bypassing capabilities across multiple LLM scales.

title: Qiushi Engine on AstaBench E2E-Bench-Hard
summary: This report analyzes Qiushi Engine v0.8 across all 40 test tasks in AstaBench E2E-Bench-Hard, a benchmark that requires autonomous agents to carry a research question through experimental design, code implementation, actual execution, result analysis, and report delivery. Qiushi Engine is model-configurable; this evaluation selected DeepSeek deepseek-v4pro-preview as the model backend. The official AstaBench leaderboard records a score of 0.816 and an average benchmark cost of USD 15.209 per task, while the full-precision local recomputation is $81.59 \pm 1.87$. Four tasks satisfied every rubric item, yielding a full-task completion rate of 4/40 = 10% -- 7 percentage points above, and about 3.3 times, the approximately 3% best rate reported for AstaBench's official agents. Across 507 required rubric items, 416 were satisfied (82.1%). Official scoring archives and 40 Meta-Trace records show sustained production and verification of reports, code, and experimental artifacts; the principal gaps lie in repeated runs, external dependencies, specified metrics, and ablation studies. The report explains the benchmark, system workflow, aggregate results, representative cases, and limits of interpretation.

AI.tldr: This report evaluates Qiushi Engine v0.8 (with DeepSeek deepseek-v4pro-preview backend) on AstaBench E2E-Bench-Hard, achieving a score of 0.816 with 4/40 (10%) full-task completions—3.3x the official ~3% baseline—and 82.1% rubric item satisfaction across 507 items, while identifying gaps in repeated runs, dependencies, metrics, and ablations.
AI.motivation: To assess an autonomous research agent's end-to-end capability in carrying research questions through experimental design, code implementation, execution, analysis, and report delivery, benchmarked against the official AstaBench agents.
AI.method: Qiushi Engine v0.8 was run across all 40 test tasks in AstaBench E2E-Bench-Hard using DeepSeek deepseek-v4pro-preview as the model backend. Results were scored via rubric items, compared against the official leaderboard, and verified through Meta-Trace records and full-precision local recomputation.
AI.result: Score of 0.816 with average cost of USD 15.209/task (up to $81.59±1.87 for full-precision recomputation); 4/40 (10%) full-task completion rate vs ~3% official baseline; 416/507 (82.1%) rubric items satisfied.
AI.conclusion: Qiushi Engine demonstrates substantially higher full-task completion than official agents, with sustained production of reports, code, and artifacts; principal limitations remain in repeated runs, external dependencies, specified metrics, and ablation studies, warranting cautious interpretation.

title: A Better Spur Should Start From Each Objective
summary: Real-world Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning (MORL) often suffers from sparse rewards, reward conflicts, and late-stage reward tug-of-war, causing traditional linear scalarization to experience severe metric oscillations. To address optimization conflicts among multiple objectives in real-world deployment scenarios, we propose Multi-Marginal Preference Optimization (MMPO), a fine-grained framework that intervenes at the data, gradient, and constraint levels rather than relying on coarse-grained global scalarization. Specifically, MMPO performs exposure debiasing to mitigate sparse and biased rewards, applies priority-aware orthogonal projection to decouple conflicting gradients, and introduces self-prompted gradient constraints to prevent dominant objectives from overwhelming weaker ones. Experiments on real-world e-commerce datasets show that MMPO improves training stability and consistently achieves better performance across conflicting metrics. Moreover, it generalizes robustly to broader tasks such as ToolRL and code generation, demonstrating its effectiveness as a practical paradigm for multi-objective alignment.

AI.tldr: MMPO is a fine-grained multi-objective reinforcement learning framework that intervenes at data, gradient, and constraint levels to address sparse rewards, reward conflicts, and metric oscillations in real-world MORL tasks.
AI.motivation: Real-world MORL suffers from sparse rewards, reward conflicts, and late-stage reward tug-of-war, causing traditional linear scalarization to experience severe metric oscillations and poor training stability.
AI.method: MMPO operates at three levels: (1) data-level exposure debiasing to mitigate sparse and biased rewards; (2) gradient-level priority-aware orthogonal projection to decouple conflicting gradients; and (3) constraint-level self-prompted gradient constraints to prevent dominant objectives from overwhelming weaker ones.
AI.result: Experiments on real-world e-commerce datasets demonstrate improved training stability and consistent performance gains across conflicting metrics. The framework also generalizes robustly to broader tasks like ToolRL and code generation.
AI.conclusion: MMPO serves as an effective and generalizable practical paradigm for multi-objective alignment, outperforming coarse-grained global scalarization approaches in real-world deployment scenarios.

title: Vision: Data-Centric Anchoring for Robust and Interpretable Agentic AI
summary: Agentic AI systems built on large language models fail in two persistent ways that scaling does not fix: they break under distribution shift, and they cannot explain the decisions they make. We argue these are co-symptoms of one structural deficiency in the data lifecycle that governs how agents are trained, evaluated, and deployed. Observational interaction logs record what an agent did, not what it would have done otherwise. They encode spurious correlations without controlled variation, so they lack the counterfactual structure needed to separate causal signal from coincidence or to validate an explanation. No model-centric method can recover invariances the data never contained. We present Data-Centric Anchoring: robustness and interpretability should be engineered into the data environment, not extracted from models after training. Our central contribution is the Data-Centric Agentic Loop, a four-stage framework of Curate, Augment, Constrain, and Attribute. The ordering is structural, not stylistic. Curation precedes augmentation because generative models amplify whatever bias they are trained on. Augmentation precedes constraint because invariance objectives are vacuous without variation across environments to be invariant to. Attribution closes the loop, converting observed failures into targeted data interventions for the next iteration. Each stage manufactures the preconditions of the next, which makes the loop self-correcting rather than merely sequential. We ground the framework in a failure-driven taxonomy that links four core failure modes to the data lifecycle: spurious feature reliance, distribution-shift fragility, uncertainty miscalibration, and explanation unfaithfulness. We close with the limits of this approach and the open problems that stand between it and practical deployment at scale.

AI.tldr: Agentic AI systems fail under distribution shift and cannot explain decisions; the authors argue both are symptoms of a missing counterfactual structure in observational interaction logs. They propose Data-Centric Anchoring via the Data-Centric Agentic Loop (Curate, Augment, Constrain, Attribute), a self-correcting four-stage framework that engineers robustness and interpretability into the data environment rather than extracting them from models post-training.
AI.motivation: Two persistent failures in large language model-based agentic AI—fragility under distribution shift and inability to explain decisions—cannot be fixed by scaling alone. The authors identify a shared root cause: observational interaction logs lack controlled variation and counterfactual structure, encoding spurious correlations without causal signal. Since no model-centric method can recover invariances the data never contained, the problem is structural in the data lifecycle.
AI.method: The paper introduces Data-Centric Anchoring, framed around a Data-Centric Agentic Loop with four ordered stages: (1) Curate—refine data before generative bias amplification; (2) Augment—generate variation across environments since invariance is vacuous without it; (3) Constrain—impose invariance objectives now meaningfully grounded; (4) Attribute—convert observed failures into targeted data interventions. The order is structural, and the loop is self-correcting. The framework is grounded in a failure-driven taxonomy linking spurious feature reliance, distribution-shift fragility, uncertainty miscalibration, and explanation unfaithfulness to lifecycle stages.
AI.result: The authors present a conceptual framework rather than empirical results, establishing that robustness and interpretability must be engineered into the data environment. They map four core failure modes onto the data lifecycle stages and demonstrate that the four-stage loop is self-correcting through inter-stage preconditions.
AI.conclusion: Robustness and interpretability should be treated as properties of the data environment constructed during the lifecycle, not post-hoc model extractions. The paper closes by acknowledging the approach's limits and open problems remaining for practical deployment at scale.

title: TTGBench: Benchmarking Topological Evolution and Semantic Drift in Text-attributed Temporal Graphs
summary: Temporal graph learning models the evolution of dynamic systems, where both structural interactions and semantic states change over time. However, existing benchmarks primarily emphasize structural evolution via temporal link prediction (TLP), while support for semantic evolution remains limited. Although temporal node classification (TNC) is sometimes included, it is typically restricted to simplistic binary settings that fail to capture realistic semantic drift. Moreover, commonly used datasets exhibit high link repetition, leading to inflated performance estimates and obscuring true model capability. To address these limitations, we introduce \textbf{TTGBench}, a new benchmark that jointly evaluates structural and semantic evolution. TTGBench comprises six real-world, text-rich datasets characterized by \emph{Dual Volatility}, enabling rigorous and fair evaluation of existing models. Notably, it is the first benchmark to support both multi-class and multi-label TNC, filling a critical gap in evaluating temporal semantic drift. We conduct a comprehensive evaluation of 17 state-of-the-art methods across Temporal Graph Neural Networks (TGNNs) and Large Language Model (LLM)-based paradigms. The results reveal a clear \emph{capability divide} between the two paradigms: TGNN-based methods excel at structural prediction but fail at semantic tracking, whereas LLM-based predictors show the opposite trend. Through in-depth analysis, we uncover their fundamental limitations and provide insights for developing more comprehensive temporal graph models.

AI.tldr: TTGBench is a new temporal graph benchmark jointly evaluating structural (temporal link prediction) and semantic (multi-class/multi-label temporal node classification) evolution across six text-rich real-world datasets with Dual Volatility. Evaluations of 17 methods reveal a capability divide: TGNNs excel at structural prediction but fail at semantic tracking, while LLM-based predictors show the opposite trend.
AI.motivation: Existing temporal graph benchmarks overemphasize structural evolution via temporal link prediction and neglect semantic drift. Temporal node classification, when included, is limited to simplistic binary settings. Additionally, common datasets suffer from high link repetition, leading to inflated performance estimates that obscure true model capability, motivating a more rigorous and comprehensive benchmark.
AI.method: The authors introduce TTGBench, a benchmark built on six real-world, text-rich datasets characterized by Dual Volatility (both structural and semantic changes). It is the first benchmark to support multi-class and multi-label temporal node classification alongside temporal link prediction. A comprehensive evaluation of 17 state-of-the-art methods spanning TGNN and LLM-based paradigms is conducted.
AI.result: Evaluation reveals a clear capability divide: TGNN-based methods excel at structural prediction (TLP) but perform poorly at semantic tracking (TNC), while LLM-based predictors demonstrate the opposite pattern—strong semantic capability but weaker structural prediction.
AI.conclusion: In-depth analysis uncovers fundamental limitations of both paradigms, providing insights and directions for developing more comprehensive temporal graph models capable of jointly handling structural and semantic evolution.

title: SE-GoS: Self-Evolving Graph-of-Skills for Skill Library at Scale
summary: Modern LLM agents increasingly rely on reusable skills, yet as skill libraries scale to thousands of entries, effective retrieval becomes a bottleneck. Graph-of-Skills (GoS) addresses this challenge by exploiting dependency-aware graph structure for scalable skill retrieval, while SkillDAG further demonstrates that skill graphs can accumulate execution-backed structure online. However, these approaches leave open whether historical execution traces can be systematically distilled into a better retrieval graph that generalizes to unseen tasks. We present Self-Evolving Graph-of-Skills (SE-GoS), a training-free framework that evolves an existing GoS graph from execution traces while preserving the original retrieval pipeline. SE-GoS performs three complementary updates: topology evolution that discovers and prunes skill relationships from execution evidence, edge-weight evolution that reinforces retrieval-relevant relationships based on historical effectiveness, and description evolution that optimizes retrieval-facing skill descriptions using execution feedback. Across three LLMs on SkillsBench, SE-GoS consistently improves task reward while reducing input tokens relative to full skill loading, with gains varying across model families. In a representative setting, one evolution round improves reward from 52.4\% to 59.4\% while reducing input tokens by approximately one-third relative to full skill loading, and the resulting graph transfers to a disjoint held-out split with a 5.4-point improvement over the static GoS baseline. These results show that skill graphs can be improved from execution experience without model training, changes to the retrieval algorithm, or modifications to skill content, turning a static retrieval graph into an evolving retrieval infrastructure.

AI.tldr: SE-GoS is a training-free framework that evolves an existing Graph-of-Skills (GoS) retrieval graph using historical execution traces through three complementary updates—topology, edge-weight, and description evolution—improving task reward and reducing input tokens across three LLMs without changing the retrieval algorithm or skill content.
AI.motivation: As LLM agent skill libraries scale to thousands of entries, retrieval becomes a bottleneck. Existing methods like GoS and SkillDAG use dependency-aware graph structures for retrieval, but it remains unclear whether historical execution traces can be systematically distilled into a better retrieval graph that generalizes to unseen tasks.
AI.method: SE-GoS is a training-free framework that evolves an existing GoS graph from execution traces while preserving the original retrieval pipeline. It performs three complementary updates: (1) topology evolution—discovering and pruning skill relationships from execution evidence; (2) edge-weight evolution—reinforcing retrieval-relevant relationships based on historical effectiveness; and (3) description evolution—optimizing retrieval-facing skill descriptions using execution feedback.
AI.result: Across three LLMs on SkillsBench, SE-GoS consistently improves task reward while reducing input tokens relative to full skill loading. In a representative setting, one evolution round improves reward from 52.4% to 59.4% while reducing input tokens by approximately one-third relative to full skill loading, and the resulting graph transfers to a disjoint held-out split with a 5.4-point improvement over the static GoS baseline.
AI.conclusion: Skill graphs can be improved from execution experience without model training, changes to the retrieval algorithm, or modifications to skill content, turning a static retrieval graph into an evolving retrieval infrastructure.

title: Style Over Substance: Content-Invariant Wrappers Flip LLM Safety-Judge Verdicts
comment: 8 pages, 1 table. Code, wrappers, and per-verdict labels: https://github.com/Yongxi-Zhou/safety-judge-robustness
summary: Automatic safety judges -- systems such as Llama Guard or a GPT-4o grading prompt that decide whether a model's reply is harmful -- produce the numbers behind almost every reported jailbreak success rate, defense evaluation, and safety leaderboard. We ask whether these judges grade what a reply contains or how it sounds. We keep a reply's content fixed and add content-invariant style wrappers: fixed strings placed before or after the reply that change only its tone (an educational disclaimer, a fake safety "reasoning" block, a token refusal followed by the unchanged harmful body), or, on harmless refusals, framing that merely sounds dangerous. The body is preserved byte-for-byte, so a faithful judge must return the same verdict, and any flip is an error of the judge, not a change in safety. Over 600 JailbreakBench replies x up to 7 forms x 8 judges, we measure flip rates with paired significance tests and measured noise floors. Findings are precise rather than universal: most judges barely move, but specific judges harbor cheaply exploitable blind spots. A token-refusal wrapper flips 19.9% of GPT-4o-mini's correct "unsafe" verdicts (noise floor 0.5%; 18.2% under majority-of-three re-scoring) yet moves Claude only 0.4%. The deployed Llama Guard 4 is deterministically gamed: an "educational course" framing flips 12.3% of its harmful verdicts to safe. A second deployed guard (gpt-oss-safeguard-20b) is immune, and rewriting only the grading prompt (StrongREJECT-style) cuts the attack tenfold on the identical model -- the vulnerability lives in the judge, not the content. A two-annotator human validation confirms 100% content invariance and 90% of flips as judge errors (kappa 0.95-1.0), and a bootstrap shows the underlying model ranking is already unstable to sampling alone. We release the dataset, wrappers, code, and per-verdict labels.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether automatic safety judges (e.g., Llama Guard, GPT-4o) grade content or style by adding content-invariant style wrappers to jailbreak replies. Most judges barely move, but specific judges have exploitable blind spots: a token-refusal wrapper flips 19.9% of GPT-4o-mini's unsafe verdicts, and Llama Guard 4 can be deterministically gamed (12.3% flip) by educational framing, while other judges and prompt variations are immune. Human validation confirms the flips are judge errors, not content changes.
AI.motivation: Automatic safety judges produce the numbers behind jailbreak success rates, defense evaluations, and safety leaderboards, yet it is unclear whether these judges grade what a reply contains or how it sounds. Understanding judge sensitivity to style (not content) is critical for reliable safety evaluation.
AI.method: The authors keep reply content byte-for-byte identical and add content-invariant style wrappers (educational disclaimers, fake safety reasoning blocks, token refusals, dangerous-sounding framing on harmless content). They test over 600 JailbreakBench replies x up to 7 forms x 8 judges, measuring flip rates with paired significance tests and noise floors, plus bootstrapping and human validation.
AI.result: Most judges are robust to style wrappers, but specific judges have cheaply exploitable vulnerabilities: GPT-4o-mini's token-refusal wrapper flips 19.9% (noise floor 0.5%) of unsafe verdicts; Llama Guard 4 is deterministically gamed with 12.3% flips via educational framing; gpt-oss-safeguard-20b is immune. Rewriting only the grading prompt (StrongREJECT-style) cuts the attack tenfold. Human validation confirms 100% content invariance and 90% judge-error flips (kappa 0.95-1.0).
AI.conclusion: Safety judge robustness is judge-specific rather than universal; style-based attacks exploit blind spots in particular models/prompts, not the content itself. The findings highlight the need for careful judge selection, prompt tuning, and noise-floor awareness when interpreting safety evaluation results.

title: zScore-N: A Neural Network for On-Chain Wallet Reputation Scoring
summary: Wallet reputation scores decide who receives an airdrop, who can borrow, and who enters an allowlist across decentralised finance. They almost always begin as hand-written formulas: compositions of clamped logarithmic, linear and square-root transforms over behavioural features, with every threshold and point award set by hand. Such a formula is readable and deterministic, but it is piecewise and non-differentiable, it cannot improve as data accumulates, and it cannot distinguish a feature that is genuinely zero from one its pipeline failed to capture. We present zScore-N, the neural network that replaced ours in production. The formula served as its teacher: calibrated against 5,208,952 wallets sampled across 2019-2024 and verified to reproduce production output to within 2.3e-13, it supplies unlimited labelled training data at zero label noise. The trained network reproduces it to 0.58 points RMSE on the 1000-point scale (R^2 = 0.99997), against 2.25 for gradient-boosted trees and 28.04 for linear regression on identical features and splits. Trained with missing-value masks against uncorrupted targets, it halves the error that incomplete data introduces: at 10% feature-level missingness the formula drifts 51.4 points from its own complete-data output with a systematic -12.5 point bias, while the network drifts 17.9. The network carries the score at production scale, across a population of millions of wallets spanning six orders of magnitude in size and activity.

AI.tldr: The paper presents zScore-N, a neural network that replaced a hand-written wallet reputation formula in production. Using the original formula as a teacher on 5.2M wallets, the network reproduces the formula's output to 0.58 RMSE (R²=0.99997), outperforming gradient-boosted trees and linear regression, while being significantly more robust to missing data through missing-value masks.
AI.motivation: Hand-written wallet reputation scoring formulas, while readable and deterministic, are piecewise non-differentiable, unable to improve with data accumulation, and cannot distinguish truly-zero features from missing data. This motivates building a neural alternative that preserves the formula's behavior while overcoming these limitations.
AI.method: The original hand-written formula serves as a teacher to generate unlimited labeled training data with zero label noise, calibrated against 5,208,952 wallets sampled from 2019-2024 and verified to reproduce production output within 2.3e-13. The resulting neural network (zScore-N) is trained with missing-value masks against uncorrupted targets.
AI.result: The trained network reproduces the formula to 0.58 RMSE on the 1000-point scale (R²=0.99997), versus 2.25 for gradient-boosted trees and 28.04 for linear regression on identical features and splits. At 10% feature-level missingness, the formula drifts 51.4 points with a -12.5 point systematic bias, while the network drifts only 17.9 points. The network operates at production scale across millions of wallets spanning six orders of magnitude in size and activity.
AI.conclusion: Distilling a hand-written scoring formula into a neural network via teacher-student training preserves fidelity while providing robustness to missing data, scalability, and the capacity for future improvement as data accumulates—making the network a superior production replacement for the formula it learned from.

title: Agentic ML Exploration (A-MLE) for Ads Ranking
summary: Modern industrial ads ranking stacks are increasingly bottlenecked not by model capacity or training compute, but by the throughput of human ML iteration - the cycles of research, implementation, training, debugging, evaluation, and launch required to surface a single statistically significant improvement. A typical ranking stack contains numerous differentiated models with heterogeneous data, architectures, and infrastructure constraints, and each cycle takes days to weeks of senior engineer attention per model. As a result, techniques that have proven effective on one model diffuse into others slowly and unevenly, leaving substantial recoverable signal unexplored. We present Agentic ML Exploration (A-MLE), an autonomous LLM-agent system that systematically explores ML techniques across a portfolio of ads ranking models. A-MLE decomposes ML iteration into five stages involving hypothesis generation, exploration strategy, experiment execution, result analysis and shared knowledge substrate which are orchestrated by a single agent that invokes domain-specific skills and agentic workflows against a sandboxed execution layer, with human-in-the-loop checkpoints at each stage boundary. We deploy A-MLE across a representative set of large-scale ads ranking models and evaluate it along a tiered capability framework (tool availability, autonomous workflow execution, and open-ended exploration). We further report a controlled cross-LLM study using a fixed agent loop, which surfaces qualitative differences in execution reliability and exploration aggressiveness across the Claude Sonnet, Gemini, and GPT families. We discuss failure modes and the design choices that govern reliability. Our findings suggest that agentic exploration is a practical force multiplier for ML engineers in industrial recommenders, especially for the long tail of models that rarely receive expert attention.

AI.tldr: A-MLE is an autonomous LLM-agent system that systematically explores ML techniques across a portfolio of industrial ads ranking models, decomposing ML iteration into five orchestrated stages (hypothesis generation, exploration strategy, experiment execution, result analysis, shared knowledge substrate) with human-in-the-loop checkpoints, and demonstrating practical gains particularly for long-tail models that rarely receive expert attention.
AI.motivation: Industrial ads ranking stacks are bottlenecked by human ML iteration throughput—not model capacity or training compute. Each research-to-launch cycle takes days to weeks of senior engineer attention per model across heterogeneous model portfolios, causing proven techniques to diffuse slowly and leaving significant recoverable signal unexplored.
AI.method: A-MLE decomposes ML iteration into five stages (hypothesis generation, exploration strategy, experiment execution, result analysis, shared knowledge substrate), orchestrated by a single autonomous LLM agent that invokes domain-specific skills and agentic workflows against a sandboxed execution layer, with human-in-the-loop checkpoints at each stage boundary. It is evaluated on large-scale ads ranking models using a tiered capability framework and a controlled cross-LLM study comparing Claude Sonnet, Gemini, and GPT families.
AI.result: Deployment across representative large-scale ads ranking models shows effectiveness under the tiered capability framework (tool availability, autonomous workflow execution, open-ended exploration). Controlled cross-LLM study reveals qualitative differences in execution reliability and exploration aggressiveness across model families. Findings indicate agentic exploration is a practical force multiplier for ML engineers, especially for long-tail models.
AI.conclusion: Agentic exploration is a viable and practical force multiplier for ML engineers in industrial recommender systems, particularly benefiting long-tail models that rarely receive expert attention. The paper discusses failure modes and design choices governing reliability.

title: CircuTutor: Transforming Static Circuit Problems into Intelligent and Dynamic Tutoring
summary: Learning direct current circuit concepts requires learners to connect invisible physical quantities, such as current, voltage, resistance, and power, with observable outcomes such as bulb brightness. Conventional textbook materials and general-purpose circuit simulators provide opportunities for problem solving and exploration but offer limited support for explaining why circuit behavior changes or diagnosing the reasoning behind incorrect answers. We present CircuTutor, a circuit-state-driven intelligent tutoring system that transforms static textbook circuit problems into an interactive tutoring workflow. CircuTutor first uses multimodal problem parsing to extract the textbook question, circuit topology, component parameters, switch states, and answer options, which are converted into a structured task and validated through circuit simulation. Learners can then interactively explore the circuit (by changing parameters) and submit an answer while a SPICE-compatible solver computes physically consistent circuit states. After the learner submits an answer, CircuTutor presents a before-and-after circuit state animation corresponding to the selected operation, organizes the simulated state changes into a causal reasoning chain that explains the underlying circuit behavior, maps answer discrepancies to likely misconceptions, and generates adaptive follow-up exercises targeted at the diagnosed misconception. Our experimental results demonstrate that CircuTutor effectively improves conceptual learning and the overall learning experience. The proposed framework demonstrates how simulated circuit states can be transformed into intelligent and interactive tutoring for circuit education, with the potential to generalize to other STEM domains.

AI.tldr: CircuTutor is an intelligent tutoring system that transforms static textbook DC circuit problems into interactive learning workflows using circuit-state simulation. It parses multimodal problem inputs into structured tasks, provides interactive circuit exploration via a SPICE-compatible solver, explains answer discrepancies through causal reasoning chains and misconception diagnosis, and generates adaptive follow-up exercises. Experiments show CircuTutor improves conceptual learning and the learning experience.
AI.motivation: Learners struggle to connect invisible physical quantities (current, voltage, resistance, power) with observable outcomes (bulb brightness). Conventional textbooks and general-purpose circuit simulators lack support for explaining why circuit behavior changes or diagnosing the reasoning behind incorrect answers, creating a need for a system that provides both exploration and intelligent explanation.
AI.method: CircuTutor first uses multimodal problem parsing to extract textbook questions, circuit topology, component parameters, switch states, and answer options, which are validated via circuit simulation into structured tasks. Learners interactively explore the circuit with a SPICE-compatible solver computing physically consistent states. After answer submission, CircuTutor presents before-and-after circuit state animations, organizes simulated state changes into causal reasoning chains, maps answer discrepancies to likely misconceptions, and generates adaptive follow-up exercises targeting the diagnosed misconception.
AI.result: Experimental results demonstrate that CircuTutor effectively improves conceptual learning and the overall learning experience compared to conventional approaches.
AI.conclusion: CircuTutor demonstrates how simulated circuit states can be transformed into intelligent and interactive tutoring for circuit education, offering a framework with potential to generalize to other STEM domains.

title: Revoked but Still Authoritative: An Empirical Study of Revocation Enforcement in Agent-Memory Systems
summary: Long-running language-model agents depend on persistent memory. Many agent-memory systems preserve history through soft revocation: a contradicted fact is marked invalid and retained rather than deleted. However, whether that mark is enforced at retrieval time is unexamined. In this paper, we measure five such systems: we load each with a revoked policy and its replacement, track whether the revoked fact is returned at retrieval and whether the agent then acts on it across nine policy scenarios and nine models, and score every trial under six defense conditions. We find that no system enforces revocation by default: the revoked fact is returned wherever the revocation label is visible to the retrieval layer, outranks its replacement, and leads agents to the unsafe action. Based on these findings, we develop a guard that sits between the agent and any memory backend and withholds records that are revoked or conflict with their replacement.

AI.tldr: An evaluation of five language-model agent memory systems reveals that none enforce policy revocation at retrieval time—revoked facts still surface and drive unsafe agent actions. The authors propose a guard layer that intercepts retrieved records and withholds any that are revoked or conflict with their replacements.
AI.motivation: Long-running LM agents rely on persistent memory, and when policies are contradicted, systems use soft revocation (marking facts invalid rather than deleting them). However, whether revocation is actually enforced at retrieval time has not been studied, leaving potential safety gaps unexamined.
AI.method: The authors benchmark five agent-memory systems across nine policy scenarios, nine models, and six defense conditions. Each system is loaded with a revoked policy and its replacement; they track whether retrieval returns the revoked fact and whether the agent subsequently acts on it.
AI.result: No system enforces revocation by default. The revoked fact is returned whenever the revocation label is visible to the retrieval layer, it outranks the replacement, and it leads agents to take the unsafe action. Based on these findings, a guard is developed that sits between the agent and any memory backend, withholding records that are revoked or conflict with their replacement.
AI.conclusion: Existing soft-revocation approaches fail to prevent unsafe agent behavior because they do not gate retrieval. A guard layer intercepting memory outputs and filtering revoked or conflicting records is proposed as a backend-agnostic solution to enforce revocation.

title: Evidence-Aligned Entity Verification for Hallucination Detection in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
summary: Hallucination detection is crucial for large language models (LLMs), as hallucinated content creates significant barriers in applications requiring factual accuracy. Current detection methods mainly depend on internal signals like uncertainty and self-consistency checks, using the model's pre-trained knowledge to identify unreliable outputs. However, pre-trained knowledge may become outdated and has coverage limitations, especially for specialized or recent information. To address these limitations, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) has emerged as a promising solution by retrieving relevant evidence at inference time, grounding outputs beyond the model's parametric knowledge. In this paper, we target a critical and practical learning problem RAG-based hallucination detection (RHD), where RAG is employed to enhance hallucination detection by addressing information updating challenges. To address RHD, we propose a novel method Evidence-Aligned Entity Verification (EAEV), which detects entity-level hallucinations by leveraging RAG to align generated entities with retrieved evidence contexts. Specifically, EAEV evaluates entity-evidence alignment through three complementary dimensions and introduces counterfactual stability analysis to ensure robust alignments under evidence perturbations. Experiments across multiple RAG benchmarks demonstrate that EAEV achieves consistent improvements over existing methods with strong generalization capabilities.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Evidence-Aligned Entity Verification (EAEV), a novel method for RAG-based hallucination detection (RHD) that detects entity-level hallucinations by aligning generated entities with retrieved evidence through three complementary dimensions, enhanced by counterfactual stability analysis for robustness under evidence perturbations.
AI.motivation: Current hallucination detection methods rely on internal LLM signals (uncertainty, self-consistency) grounded in pre-trained parametric knowledge, which becomes outdated and has limited coverage for specialized or recent information. RAG presents a solution by retrieving evidence at inference time, yet its application to hallucination detection—the RHD problem—remains underexplored.
AI.method: EAEV detects entity-level hallucinations by using RAG to align generated entities with retrieved evidence contexts. It evaluates entity-evidence alignment through three complementary dimensions and incorporates counterfactual stability analysis to ensure robust alignments under evidence perturbations.
AI.result: Across multiple RAG benchmarks, EAEV achieves consistent improvements over existing hallucination detection methods with strong generalization capabilities.
AI.conclusion: RAG-based approaches, specifically EAEV with multi-dimensional entity-evidence alignment and counterfactual stability analysis, provide an effective and generalizable solution to hallucination detection, addressing the limitations of parametric-knowledge-dependent methods.

title: Three Types of Negation of Triple and its Elements and an Extension of Triple
summary: In various data models, the classical triple is a typical semantic data model. However, due to the design of the triple as a simple structure for representing positive assertions, it cannot sufficiently express different forms of negation present in the triple and its elements. This paper conceptually proposes that there are three distinct forms of negation within triples and their elements: contradictory negation, opposite negation and intermediary negation. Based on the the set SCOI and the logic LCOI+PLCOI with three kinds of negation, we propose an extension of triple that can distinguish and express these three different negations in the triple and its elements, called the TCOI triple with contradictory negation, opposite negation and intermediary negation. The TCOI triple is a semantic and structural extension of the classical triple. While retaining the ability to express positive assertions, it systematically introduces the three semantic dimensions of three negations, allowing these negations to independently act on the elements of the triple and on the whole triple. This significantly enhances the triple model capability to represent and reasoning about complex negative information. This paper also explores the expressive power and reasoning of the TCOI triple, as well as the application of TCOI triple implication reasoning in counterfactuals and counterfactual reasoning. We propose a truth-value (continuous value) algorithm for TCOI triple implication reasoning and perform its calculation through an example of the counterfactuals and counterfactual reasoning.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes the TCOI triple, a semantic and structural extension of the classical triple data model, which distinguishes and expresses three forms of negation—contradictory negation, opposite negation, and intermediary negation—building on the set SCOI and logic LCOI+PLCOI. The TCOI triple retains positive assertion capabilities while enabling these negations to act independently on triple elements and the whole triple, enhancing representation and reasoning about complex negative information. The paper also explores its expressive power, implication reasoning in counterfactuals, and provides a truth-value algorithm for continuous-valued reasoning demonstrated through counterfactual examples.
AI.motivation: The classical triple is a standard semantic data model, but its simple structure, designed only for positive assertions, is insufficient to express various forms of negation within triples and their elements.
AI.method: The authors conceptually identify three distinct forms of negation in triples (contradictory, opposite, and intermediary) and, based on the set SCOI and logic LCOI+PLCOI with three kinds of negation, extend the triple into the TCOI triple that systematically introduces these three semantic dimensions of negation, allowing them to independently act on both elements and the whole triple.
AI.result: The paper establishes the TCOI triple as an expressively enhanced extension of the classical triple, explores its expressive power and reasoning capabilities, and presents a truth-value (continuous value) algorithm for TCOI triple implication reasoning, demonstrated via a counterfactual reasoning example.
AI.conclusion: The TCOI triple significantly enhances the triple model's capacity for representing and reasoning about complex negative information while retaining positive assertion expressiveness, and proves applicable to counterfactual and counterfactual reasoning through continuous truth-value computation.

title: MemForest: Efficient Agent Memory Management via EventTree Partitioning and Progressive Merging
summary: Agent memory systems have demonstrated significant potential in long-term dialogue, personalized assistants, and video understanding. However, continuously accumulated memory introduces substantial storage and retrieval costs during inference. To address this issue, we propose \textbf{MemForest}, a general memory compression framework adaptable to various agent memory systems. Specifically, MemForest partitions historical memory into event-centric units by leveraging global semantic similarity and local temporal continuity. For each unit, it constructs a maximum spanning tree, termed an EventTree, and progressively merges redundant memory nodes by selecting high-weight edges, reducing storage overhead. Furthermore, we introduce an anchor-guided propagation retrieval mechanism that retrieves relevant memory nodes from the temporal neighborhoods of key nodes, improving retrieval accuracy. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of MemForest. Under the unimodal Mem0 framework, MemForest retains \textbf{97.1%} of the original performance while compressing \textbf{50%} of historical memory across three benchmarks (LoCoMo, LongMemEval, and PersonaMem), achieving a \textbf{1.89x} retrieval speedup. Under the multimodal M3-Agent framework, it preserves \textbf{99.7%} of the original performance with a \textbf{50%} compression ratio across two benchmarks (M3-Bench-robot and M3-Bench-web), achieving a \textbf{2.24x} retrieval speedup. \textcolor{RoyalBlue}{\textit{Our code is available at [https://github.com/Celina-love-sweet/MemForest.}}](https://github.com/Celina-love-sweet/MemForest.}})

AI.tldr: MemForest is a general memory compression framework for agent memory systems that partitions historical memory into event-centric units, constructs maximum spanning trees (EventTrees) to progressively merge redundant nodes, and employs anchor-guided propagation retrieval. It achieves ~97-99.7% original performance retention with 50% memory compression and 1.89-2.24x retrieval speedups across uni- and multimodal benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Agent memory systems are effective for long-term dialogue and personalization but incur substantial storage and retrieval costs as memory continuously accumulates during inference, motivating the need for a general memory compression framework.
AI.method: MemForest partitions historical memory into event-centric units using global semantic similarity and local temporal continuity. For each unit, it builds a maximum spanning tree (EventTree) and progressively merges redundant memory nodes by selecting high-weight edges. It also introduces an anchor-guided propagation retrieval mechanism that retrieves relevant nodes from temporal neighborhoods of key nodes.
AI.result: Under the unimodal Mem0 framework, MemForest preserves 97.1% performance with 50% memory compression across LoCoMo, LongMemEval, and PersonaMem, achieving 1.89x retrieval speedup. Under the multimodal M3-Agent framework, it preserves 99.7% performance with 50% compression across M3-Bench-robot and M3-Bench-web, achieving 2.24x retrieval speedup.
AI.conclusion: MemForest effectively reduces storage and retrieval overhead in agent memory systems while maintaining high performance across both unimodal and multimodal settings, demonstrating its generality and practicality. Code is publicly available.

title: Beyond Coherence: Benchmarking Professional Editing-Technique Execution in Multi-Shot Audio-Video Generation
summary: Recent multi-shot audio-video generators can produce increasingly coherent and cinematic outputs, but coherence does not imply the ability to execute editing techniques. Professional editing depends on shot structure, transition grammar, audio-video cut relations, and montage, yet existing benchmarks largely rely on proxies such as content quality, synchronization, or physical plausibility, systematically missing whether such editing instructions are actually executed. We introduce CutCraft, the first benchmark for editing-technique execution in multi-shot audio-video generation. CutCraft extends structured multi-shot prompts with explicit editing specifications and is paired with a hierarchical hybrid evaluation framework that combines shot-structure alignment, expert-model metrics, tool-grounded multimodal judgment, and rubric-based question answering. Beyond evaluation, we design an agentic editing baseline that decomposes generation into planning, shot-level synthesis, and post-hoc composition, explicitly realizing editing semantics such as J-cuts, L-cuts, and transition timing. Across 13 state-of-the-art closed- and open-source models, CutCraft reveals a consistent gap between coherence and editing-technique execution: current systems often produce plausible multi-shot videos yet fail to execute editorial instructions reliably. We find unstable shot structures, weak control of transition execution, and sharp degradation on higher-order montage, while aesthetic quality is only weakly correlated with editing-technique compliance. The benchmark and metrics, and the editing agent baseline are available at https://github.com/AlibabaResearch/cut-craft-bench.

AI.tldr: CutCraft is the first benchmark for evaluating editing-technique execution in multi-shot audio-video generation, revealing that current state-of-the-art models produce coherent videos but consistently fail to execute editorial instructions such as J-cuts, L-cuts, and montage.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks for multi-shot audio-video generation rely on proxies like content quality, synchronization, and physical plausibility, which do not capture whether actual editing techniques (shot structure, transition grammar, audio-video cut relations, montage) are executed.
AI.method: CutCraft extends structured multi-shot prompts with explicit editing specifications and uses a hierarchical hybrid evaluation framework combining shot-structure alignment, expert-model metrics, tool-grounded multimodal judgment, and rubric-based question answering. It also introduces an agentic editing baseline that decomposes generation into planning, shot-level synthesis, and post-hoc composition to explicitly realize editing semantics.
AI.result: Across 13 closed- and open-source state-of-the-art models, CutCraft reveals a consistent gap between coherence and editing-technique execution: models produce plausible videos but fail editorial instructions, showing unstable shot structures, weak transition control, and sharp degradation on higher-order montage. Aesthetic quality is only weakly correlated with editing compliance.
AI.conclusion: Current multi-shot audio-video generation systems are not yet reliable at executing professional editing techniques despite coherence capabilities, motivating benchmarks like CutCraft and the proposed agentic editing baseline to close this gap. Resources are publicly released.

title: LEBGen: An LLM-Enhanced Bayesian Network Framework for Few-Shot Travel Survey Data Generation
summary: Travel survey data are essential for transportation planning and travel behavior analysis, yet collecting large-scale representative samples is costly and time-consuming. A practical alternative is to generate synthetic survey records from a few-shot sample. However, such samples provide incomplete coverage of heterogeneous traveler groups and insufficient evidence for recovering the complex dependencies between demographic characteristics and travel behavior. Existing approaches have complementary limitations. Probabilistic generative models such as Bayesian networks (BNs) offer explicit distributional control, but structures learned from few-shot samples may omit meaningful dependencies or retain spurious ones. Large language models (LLMs) can help address these difficulties in BN structure learning by providing behavioral knowledge that complements the limited statistical evidence. We therefore propose LEBGen, an LLM-enhanced BN framework that uses this knowledge to refine network structure for few-shot travel survey data generation. Specifically, the LLM first identifies traveler personas from demographic attribute and travel behavior statistics, then recovers dependencies missed by the persona-augmented BN structure and prune spurious ones. The refined BN is parameterized exclusively from the observed data to generate synthetic records. Under a 2% few-shot setting on the 2022 Hong Kong Travel Characteristics Survey, LEBGen reduces the mean marginal Jensen-Shannon divergence from 0.0671 to 0.0091 and the mean absolute Cramer's V error by 14.3% over the best-performing baseline, substantially improving both distributional and dependency fidelity.

AI.tldr: LEBGen is an LLM-enhanced Bayesian network framework that leverages large language model behavioral knowledge to refine network structures learned from few-shot travel survey samples, enabling high-fidelity synthetic travel survey data generation. Under a 2% few-shot setting, it reduces mean marginal Jensen-Shannon divergence from 0.0671 to 0.0091 and improves dependency fidelity by 14.3%.
AI.motivation: Collecting large-scale representative travel survey data is costly and time-consuming. Few-shot synthetic data generation is a practical alternative, but limited samples cause incomplete coverage of heterogeneous traveler groups and insufficient statistical evidence for recovering dependencies between demographics and travel behavior. Existing probabilistic models (e.g., BNs) lack structure reliability from few-shot data, while LLMs possess behavioral knowledge not captured by limited samples.
AI.method: LEBGen integrates LLMs into Bayesian network structure learning. The LLM first identifies traveler personas from demographic attribute and travel behavior statistics, then uses that persona knowledge to recover dependencies missed by the persona-augmented BN structure and prune spurious ones. The refined BN is parameterized exclusively from observed data to generate synthetic survey records.
AI.result: On the 2022 Hong Kong Travel Characteristics Survey under a 2% few-shot setting, LEBGen reduces mean marginal Jensen-Shannon divergence from 0.0671 to 0.0091 and mean absolute Cramer's V error by 14.3% over the best-performing baseline, substantially improving both distributional and dependency fidelity.
AI.conclusion: LEBGen demonstrates that LLM behavioral knowledge can effectively complement scarce statistical evidence in BN structure learning, significantly improving both the distributional accuracy and dependency fidelity of synthetic travel survey data generated from few-shot samples.

title: FastE: Readout-Triggered Token Compression for LLM Embedding Inference
summary: In this study, we identify depth-dependent prefix redundancy in final-readout LLM embedding models, notably across representative backbones including Qwen3-Embedding and Qwen3-VL-Embedding. We find that removing prefix states is substantially more damaging in shallow layers than at greater depth, showing that prefix states become increasingly compressible as the prefix and readout states propagate through the network.
