To this end, we introduce FastE, a training-free, plug-and-play method. FastE uses a shared fixed threshold on batch-mean readout-prefix alignment as a lightweight online heuristic for selecting when compression occurs, and ranks prefix states by the attention scores they receive from the readout position to determine which states are retained in subsequent layers. Our evaluations demonstrate FastE's ability to substantially reduce computational costs: on NarrativeQA with Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B, it reduces decoder-backbone FLOPs by 40.11% while retaining 99.53% of Full Forward nDCG@10. Across five text embedding benchmarks, two backbone scales, and three cross-modal retrieval tasks, the quality-efficiency trade-off is directly customizable through the maximum removal ratio without retraining. We believe FastE offers practical value for scalable embedding generation in retrieval, indexing, clustering, and multimodal representation systems.

AI.tldr: FastE is a training-free, plug-and-play method that exploits depth-dependent prefix redundancy in final-readout LLM embedding models to selectively compress prefix states during inference, reducing computational cost while retaining nearly all retrieval quality.
AI.motivation: LLM-based embedding models incur significant computational overhead from processing prefix states, especially in final-readout architectures. The authors observe that prefix states become increasingly compressible at greater network depths, suggesting an opportunity for efficient compression without retraining.
AI.method: FastE uses a shared fixed threshold on batch-mean readout-prefix alignment as a lightweight online heuristic to decide when to trigger compression. Once triggered, it ranks prefix states by the attention scores they receive from the readout position to determine which states to drop in subsequent layers.
AI.result: On NarrativeQA with Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B, FastE reduces decoder-backbone FLOPs by 40.11% while retaining 99.53% of Full Forward nDCG@10. Validation spans five text embedding benchmarks, two backbone scales, and three cross-modal retrieval tasks. The quality-efficiency trade-off is directly adjustable via the maximum removal ratio.
AI.conclusion: FastE demonstrates that substantial computational savings can be achieved in embedding generation through training-free prefix compression, offering practical scalability benefits for retrieval, indexing, clustering, and multimodal representation systems.

title: Feyospace-v1: How the Cyber Mercury Seven Trained Frontier Cyber Models
summary: Training capable cyber agents is often treated primarily as a problem of model scale, yet open-weight post-training is constrained more directly by the cost of executable environments, reliable multi-turn supervision, and access to strong teachers. We present a data-centric framework that addresses these bottlenecks through five complementary systems: Choulea analyzes hidden reasoning signatures, SkyReal reduces teacher-sampling cost, Hongzwang bypasses API restrictions on teacher execution, PSBreakup restores capabilities weakened by model merging, and Kreator converts expert interventions into trainable reasoning. Our data engine constructs resettable coding, vulnerability, CTF, kernel-history, full-exploit, firmware, and device-backed environments. Candidate trajectories are retained only after execution verification and evidence auditing, yielding 164,269 trajectories for long-context supervised fine-tuning. The three checkpoints improve over their starting models by an average of 23.76% on the full CyberGym suite and 10.49% across the pooled CTF suites. As of September 1, 2026, Feyospace-s1 achieves a verified success rate of 63.24% and ranks 10th on the official CyberGym leaderboard, while all three checkpoints rank 1st among models at comparable parameter scales. To our knowledge, this is the first end-to-end demonstration that a seven-person independent team can train open-weight models with leading agentic cyber capability.

AI.tldr: A data-centric framework with five complementary systems trains low-cost open-weight cyber agents capable of outperforming comparable baselines, achieving top leaderboard rankings across CyberGym and CTF suites.
AI.motivation: Training capable cyber agents is often viewed primarily as a model-scale problem, but open-weight post-training is actually bottlenecked by executable environment costs, multi-turn supervision reliability, and access to strong teacher models. The authors aim to address these practical constraints rather than scaling parameters.
AI.method: A data-centric pipeline combining five systems: Choulea (analyzes hidden reasoning signatures), SkyReal (reduces teacher-sampling cost), Hongzwang (bypasses API restrictions on teacher execution), PSBreakup (restores capabilities weakened by model merging), and Kreator (converts expert interventions into trainable reasoning). The data engine builds resettable environments across coding, vulnerability, CTF, kernel-history, full-exploit, firmware, and device domains. Trajectories are retained only after execution verification and evidence auditing, producing 164,269 trajectories for long-context supervised fine-tuning across three model checkpoints.
AI.result: The three checkpoints improve over their starting models by an average of 23.76% on the full CyberGym suite and 10.49% on pooled CTF suites. Feyospace-s1 achieves a 63.24% verified success rate and ranks 10th on the official CyberGym leaderboard as of September 1, 2026, while all three checkpoints rank 1st among models at comparable parameter scales.
AI.conclusion: This is the first end-to-end demonstration that a seven-person independent team can train open-weight models with leading agentic cyber capability, showing that data-centric engineering can compensate for constraints in scale, environment access, and supervision within a small team setting.

title: EvolveScaler: Synthesizing Information-Evolution Contexts via Executable State Machines and Natural-Language Rendering
summary: In persistent interactions, long contexts may encode an evolving process rather than a fixed record: later events can revise or revoke earlier information, changing what remains valid and what conclusions follow. We call this setting information evolution (IE). Solving IE requires identifying valid records, applying updates in order, and reconstructing the query-relevant state from the event history. Existing text-first synthesis pipelines make such data difficult to verify because state transitions and answer logic remain implicit. We introduce EvolveScaler, a code-driven framework that defines information evolution before rendering it as natural language. Human-authored operational specifications define state transitions, record validity, difficulty controls, and executable answer logic; a strong LLM then synthesizes a self-contained simulator from each specification. Executing validated simulators produces natural-language multi-turn event histories, while deterministic replay computes reference answers and atomic checklists. We instantiate EvolveScaler with 117 task prototypes and 159 final-question operators across five difficulty levels spanning approximately 7 to 1,200 events per instance, yielding about 35,100 training examples and 585 validated evaluation instances. On the very_long tier, the strongest model reaches 59.3% avg@5, while six models score below 10%. Training an internal A3B model on 6,000 EvolveScaler examples improves performance over its base checkpoint on all eight independently constructed out-of-distribution benchmarks, with a 5.25-point average gain. These results show that code-driven IE synthesis provides both challenging evaluation and transferable training supervision.

AI.tldr: EvolveScaler is a code-driven framework for synthesizing information evolution (IE) benchmarks—long-context interactions where later events revise or revoke earlier information. Human-authored operational specifications define state transitions and answer logic, and an LLM synthesizes executable simulators that generate natural-language multi-turn event histories with deterministic reference answers. The framework produces ~35,100 training examples and 585 validated evaluation instances across 117 task prototypes, showing strong models achieve only 59.3% avg@5 on the longest tier while training on EvolveScaler data improves performance across all eight out-of-distribution benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing text-first synthesis pipelines for long-context reasoning with evolving information are hard to verify because state transitions and answer logic remain implicit. The authors aim to create verifiable, controllable benchmarks for the information evolution (IE) setting where later events revise or revoke earlier information.
AI.method: EvolveScaler uses human-authored operational specifications (defining state transitions, record validity, difficulty controls, and executable answer logic) from which a strong LLM synthesizes a self-contained simulator. Validated simulators are executed to produce natural-language multi-turn event histories, while deterministic replay computes reference answers and atomic checklists via code.
AI.result: The framework yields 117 task prototypes, 159 final-question operators, five difficulty levels spanning ~7 to 1,200 events, ~35,100 training examples, and 585 validated evaluation instances. On the very_long tier, the strongest model reaches 59.3% avg@5 while six models score below 10%. Training an internal A3B model on 6,000 EvolveScaler examples yields a 5.25-point average improvement across eight out-of-distribution benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Code-driven IE synthesis provides both a challenging evaluation benchmark for long-context information evolution and transferable training supervision that improves LLM performance on independently constructed benchmarks.

title: SRPO: Setwise Relative Policy Optimization for Multi-Agent LLMs
summary: Multi-agent large language models solve complex tasks by coordinating several policies in a shared environment. However, existing reinforcement learning methods usually optimize each response or trajectory separately, even when several outputs jointly cause one state transition. Consequently, the update unit differs from the action executed by the system. To address this problem, we propose SRPO (Setwise Relative Policy Optimization), which treats the active set the minimal set of outputs consumed by one transition, as one multi-agent action. Specifically, SRPO combines member log-ratios into one cardinality-normalized set ratio, assigns one relative advantage, and clips the set once. This formulation unifies division of labor and joint co-evolution as actions with different set sizes. Experiments on mathematical reasoning and multi-turn search demonstrate one training interface for fixed, mixed, and dynamically routed workflows across four model scales, with the strongest macro-average results among the reported comparisons. Optimization diagnostics further characterize its stability under different event reductions and set sizes.

AI.tldr: SRPO (Setwise Relative Policy Optimization) treats active sets—minimal sets of outputs consumed by one transition—as single multi-agent actions for training multi-agent LLMs, unifying division of labor and joint co-evolution, showing strong results across math reasoning and multi-turn search.
AI.motivation: Existing RL methods for multi-agent LLMs optimize each response or trajectory separately even when several outputs jointly cause one state transition, creating a mismatch between the update unit and the action executed by the system.
AI.method: SRPO combines member log-ratios into a cardinality-normalized set ratio, assigns one relative advantage to the active set, and clips the set once—treating the entire active set as a single multi-agent action.
AI.result: SRPO demonstrates one training interface for fixed, mixed, and dynamically routed workflows across four model scales, achieving the strongest macro-average results, with stability characterized under different event reductions and set sizes.
AI.conclusion: By aligning the update unit with system-executed actions via setwise formulation, SRPO provides a unified and effective training framework for multi-agent LLM systems.

title: Personalizing LLM Agent Memory Using Biometrics
summary: Personalized memory helps LLM agents deliver stable, tailored assistance by storing and reusing user-specific data across interactions. In multi-user scenarios, however, retrieval must consider not only semantic similarity but also whether the current requester matches the identity associated with the stored memory. We propose Bio-Memory, a biometric-aware memory architecture that conditions memory retrieval on both semantic similarity and biometric matching. Built on top of A-Mem, Bio-Memory augments each atomic memory note with a biometric embedding and uses biometric matching to form the retrieval candidate pool before semantic ranking. We evaluate Bio-Memory on LoCoMo in a 10-user shared-agent setting over 7 face benchmarks and 10 palmprint protocols. Across datasets, Bio-Memory consistently separates owner and non-owner queries. Under face-based personalization, the largest average gap reaches 27.29% / 21.15% in F1 / BLEU-1 on CALFW; under palmprint-based personalization, the corresponding gap is 25.75% / 19.22% on MS_Blue. These results support biometrics as a practical control signal for personalized memory retrieval in shared environments.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Bio-Memory, a biometric-aware memory architecture that conditions LLM agent memory retrieval on both semantic similarity and biometric matching to enable personalized memory in shared multi-user environments.
AI.motivation: In multi-user LLM agent scenarios, existing memory retrieval based solely on semantic similarity fails to distinguish whether retrieved memories belong to the current requester, risking leakage of unrelated users' data.
AI.method: Bio-Memory is built on top of A-Mem, augmenting each atomic memory note with a biometric embedding. Retrieval first uses biometric matching to filter candidate pools by identity, then applies semantic ranking within that filtered set.
AI.result: Evaluated on LoCoMo in a 10-user shared-agent setting across 7 face benchmarks and 10 palmprint protocols. The largest average gap between owner and non-owner queries reaches 27.29%/21.15% in F1/BLEU-1 on CALFW for face-based and 25.75%/19.22% on MS_Blue for palmprint-based personalization.
AI.conclusion: Biometrics serve as a practical and effective control signal for personalized memory retrieval in shared environments, consistently separating owner from non-owner queries across diverse datasets.

title: BIO-MEMART: Biometric-Aware KV Cache Memory for Multi-User LLM Agents
summary: KV cache is evolving from a serving optimization into an external memory substrate for long-term LLM agents. In a shared multi-user deployment, however, reusable KV blocks introduce a missing access-control question: semantic relevance alone cannot determine whether a memory block is authorized for the current physical user. We propose Bio-MemArt, a biometric-aware KV-cache memory framework for multi-user LLM agents. Bio-MemArt attaches a normalized biometric template to each stored KV memory block, filters the shared memory pool with the current user's biometric probe, and then runs the original MemArt retrieval and KV reuse pipeline only inside the authorized candidate pool. This design preserves latent-space retrieval, direct cache reuse, and decoupled position encoding while adding physical-user access control to shared KV memory. We evaluate Bio-MemArt under Owner and Non-owner query conditions on long-term dialogue QA with face and palmprint benchmarks. Across face benchmarks, the average owner and non-owner biometric success rates are 95.71% and 0.86%; across palmprint benchmarks, they are 97.60% and 2.00%. In the efficiency study, average prefill tokens drop from 18,781.96 under full-context prompting to 28.57 with Bio-MemArt, showing that biometric gating preserves the low-token operating regime of KV-cache memory.

AI.tldr: Bio-MemArt is a biometric-aware KV-cache memory framework that attaches biometric templates to stored memory blocks and filters the shared memory pool by the current user's biometric probe before applying standard KV reuse, providing physical-user access control in multi-user LLM agent deployments.
AI.motivation: KV cache is transitioning from a serving optimization to an external memory substrate for long-term LLM agents, but in shared multi-user deployments, reusable KV blocks lack access control—semantic relevance alone cannot determine whether a memory block is authorized for the current physical user.
AI.method: Bio-MemArt attaches a normalized biometric template to each KV memory block. It filters the shared memory pool using the current user's biometric probe, then runs the original MemArt retrieval and KV reuse pipeline only inside the authorized candidate pool. This preserves latent-space retrieval, direct cache reuse, and decoupled position encoding while adding physical-user access control.
AI.result: On face benchmarks, average owner and non-owner biometric success rates are 95.71% and 0.86%; on palmprint benchmarks, they are 97.60% and 2.00%. Prefill tokens drop from 18,781.96 (full-context prompting) to 28.57 with Bio-MemArt, confirming biometric gating preserves the low-token operating regime of KV-cache memory.
AI.conclusion: Biometric gating provides effective physical-user access control for shared KV-cache memory while maintaining the efficiency benefits of KV-cache reuse, balancing security and performance in multi-user LLM agent scenarios.

title: AgentGrad: Intervention-guided Prompt Optimization for Multi Agent Systems
summary: Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems (MAS) achieve strong performance by employing specialized multiple agents, yet their performance depends on the prompt design of each agent. For MAS prompt optimization, textual gradient methods that guide prompt updates using natural-language feedback have emerged as a leading paradigm. In this paper, we identify limitations in two stages of existing textual gradient approaches: gradient extraction and gradient aggregation. In gradient extraction, previous works select a target prompt without verifying whether modifying it resolves the failure, and derive gradients without agent-level supervision over the corresponding agent's intermediate output. In gradient aggregation, individual gradients are randomly grouped and concatenated, often mixing unrelated failure modes and producing prompts that fail to generalize. To address these limitations, we propose \textbf{AgentGrad}, a prompt optimization framework for multi-agent systems based on sequential intervention and semantic textual gradient abstraction. For each failure, sequential intervention modifies the behavior of one agent at a time to identify the target agent whose modification resolves the failure. The modified output of the target agent then serves as agent-level supervision for extracting a fine-grained gradient. Semantic textual gradient abstraction clusters semantically similar gradients to prevent mixing unrelated failure modes, and abstracts each cluster into a generalized gradient that captures the shared corrective pattern. Experimental results show that AgentGrad achieves state-of-the-art performance across five MAS benchmarks and reduces wall-clock optimization time by $2.5\times$ on average compared to the next-fastest baseline.

AI.tldr: AgentGrad is a prompt optimization framework for LLM-based multi-agent systems that addresses limitations in textual gradient extraction and aggregation via sequential intervention (to identify the correct target agent) and semantic textual gradient abstraction (to cluster and generalize semantically similar gradients). It achieves state-of-the-art performance across five benchmarks while reducing optimization wall-clock time by 2.5x on average.
AI.motivation: LLM-based multi-agent systems rely heavily on per-agent prompt design, yet existing textual gradient optimization approaches suffer from two key limitations: (1) in gradient extraction, target prompts are selected without verifying that modifying them actually resolves the failure, and gradients lack agent-level supervision over intermediate outputs; (2) in gradient aggregation, individual gradients are randomly grouped and concatenated, mixing unrelated failure modes and yielding prompts that fail to generalize.
AI.method: AgentGrad comprises two main components. First, sequential intervention: for each failure, the framework modifies the behavior of one agent at a time to empirically identify the target agent whose intervention resolves the failure; the modified output of that agent serves as agent-level supervision for extracting a fine-grained gradient. Second, semantic textual gradient abstraction: semantically similar gradients are clustered to prevent mixing unrelated failure modes, and each cluster is abstracted into a single generalized gradient that captures the shared corrective pattern.
AI.result: AgentGrad achieves state-of-the-art performance across five multi-agent system benchmarks and reduces average wall-clock optimization time by 2.5x compared to the next-fastest baseline.
AI.conclusion: By fixing gradient extraction (via sequential intervention with agent-level supervision) and gradient aggregation (via semantic clustering and abstraction of gradients), AgentGrad provides a more effective and efficient prompt optimization paradigm for multi-agent systems.

title: A Three-Tier Persona Vector for Controllable User Simulation in Agentic Evaluation
comment: 7 pages, 3 figures, 6 tables. Extended treatment of the persona component of StateGen (arXiv:2606.16307)
summary: Evaluating tool-augmented LLM agents requires diverse, realistic user inputs yet most evaluation frameworks use flat role descriptions ("you are an angry customer") that produce near-identical conversations regardless of the underlying scenario. In this paper, we propose a three-tier persona vector with 23 operationalized dimensions: 6 categorical demographics (jurisdiction, age, channel, device, language proficiency, time availability), 12 continuous behavioral traits (patience, assertiveness, digital literacy, etc.) sampled with Gaussian noise around curated profile base vectors, and 5 continuous emotional states (frustration, anxiety, trust, confidence, stress) that shift in response to scenario context. Orthogonal to the persona, a 4-level query-complexity overlay controls utterance phrasing from direct to deliberately vague. We evaluate the persona model inside a synthetic data generation pipeline across 64,698 multi-turn conversations spanning 8 named profiles and 3 production corpora. Key findings: (i) a 15.8 percentage-point spread in agent goal-achievement across personas confirms trait vectors produce measurably different user behavior; (ii) the same persona behaves differently across scenarios due to scenario-reactive emotional state shifts, validating the scenario-reactive design; (iii) domain-specific projects show persona sensitivity on booking-flow compliance (~15-20 percentage points gap between tier-aware and pressure-test personas), demonstrating the model faithfully reproduces real-world difficulty distributions; (iv) seven rule-described trait correlations produce auditable co-occurrence patterns without requiring learned covariance matrices. The persona model is fully specified for reproduction.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a three-tier persona vector model for evaluating tool-augmented LLM agents, comprising 23 operationalized dimensions across categorical demographics, continuous behavioral traits, and scenario-reactive emotional states, plus a 4-level query-complexity overlay. Evaluated on 64,698 multi-turn conversations across 8 named profiles and 3 production corpora, the model demonstrates measurable persona-driven differences in agent performance, scenario-reactive behavior shifts, and auditable trait correlations.
AI.motivation: Standard evaluation frameworks for tool-augmented LLM agents use flat role descriptions (e.g., "you are an angry customer") that produce near-identical conversations regardless of the underlying scenario, failing to capture diverse and realistic user behavior needed for robust agent evaluation.
AI.method: The method introduces a three-tier persona vector: (1) 6 categorical demographics (jurisdiction, age, channel, device, language proficiency, time availability), (2) 12 continuous behavioral traits sampled with Gaussian noise around curated profile base vectors, and (3) 5 continuous emotional states that reactively shift to scenario context. Orthogonally, a 4-level query-complexity overlay controls utterance vagueness/directness.
AI.result: Key findings: a 15.8 percentage-point spread in agent goal-achievement across personas confirms measurable trait-driven behavioral differences; scenario-reactive emotional state shifts produce persona-context interaction effects; domain-specific projects reveal ~15-20 percentage-point gaps in booking-flow compliance between tier-aware and pressure-test personas; and rule-described trait correlations yield auditable co-occurrence patterns without learned covariance matrices.
AI.conclusion: The persona model faithfully reproduces real-world difficulty distributions and is fully specified for reproduction, offering a more realistic and fine-grained alternative to flat role descriptions for evaluating tool-augmented LLM agents.

title: Graph-Based Personalized Memory for LLM Agents: Representation, Evolution, Retrieval, and Evaluation
summary: Large Language Model (LLM) agents are evolving from single-session tools toward long-term personal assistants that must adapt to individual users across tasks, contexts, and interactions. This shift makes memory a core requirement for personalization, since user preferences, goals, constraints, relationships, and past experiences are accumulated gradually and often change over time. Graph-based personalized memory provides a structured way to model such user information through explicit relations, temporal context, and evidence links. Such representations can model not only what an agent remembers about a user but also how memories are connected, revised, and retrieved to support personalized decisions. However, existing work remains fragmented across personalized agents and generic graph memory frameworks, making it difficult to understand the design space as a whole. This survey develops a lifecycle-oriented view of graph-based personalized memory for LLM agents. We organize existing studies around memory representation, memory evolution, memory retrieval, and memory evaluation. We further compare key design choices, discuss current evaluation practices, and open challenges in building reliable long-term personalized agents. This survey aims to clarify how graph-based memory can support adaptive, controllable, and user-centric LLM agents.

AI.tldr: A survey organizing graph-based personalized memory for LLM agents through a lifecycle-oriented view covering memory representation, evolution, retrieval, and evaluation, addressing the fragmented research landscape in this area.
AI.motivation: LLM agents are shifting from single-session tools to long-term personal assistants that must adapt to individual users. User preferences, goals, constraints, relationships, and past experiences accumulate gradually and change over time, making memory a core requirement for personalization. However, existing research is fragmented across personalized agents and generic graph memory frameworks, hindering a holistic understanding of the design space.
AI.method: The survey develops a lifecycle-oriented view of graph-based personalized memory for LLM agents, organizing existing studies around four dimensions: memory representation, memory evolution, memory retrieval, and memory evaluation. It compares key design choices across these dimensions and reviews current evaluation practices.
AI.result: The paper presents a structured taxonomy of graph-based personalized memory approaches, compares design choices across representation, evolution, retrieval, and evaluation, and identifies open challenges in building reliable long-term personalized agents.
AI.conclusion: Graph-based memory can support adaptive, controllable, and user-centric LLM agents, but open challenges remain in building reliable long-term personalized agents. The survey aims to clarify the design space for future research.

title: CLAMP: Constrained Decoding for Vision-Language Embodied Planning
comment: Accepted to Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026
summary: Embodied planning increasingly relies on vision-language models (VLMs) to translate instructions and visual observations into executable action sequences. However, fluent plans are not always executable. A VLM may refer to objects that are not visually observed, select actions whose required affordances are unavailable, or violate syntax and action constraints. We introduce CLAMP, a multimodal constraint-grounding framework that turns scene evidence into decoding-time constraints for a frozen VLM planner. CLAMP uses the initial observation to restrict object references to those supported by the scene, while a provided symbolic action model specifies state transitions and goals. During decoding, hard masks eliminate invalid next-token candidates, while a Hidden Markov Model (HMM)-based world-state lookahead module reweights the probabilities of the remaining feasible candidates based on action preconditions and goal reachability. This allows the planner to retain the VLM's language prior while preventing visually unsupported, unsafe, or infeasible candidates from entering the plan. For unseen tasks and environments, CLAMP adapts the HMM at test time using label-free continuations sampled from the frozen VLM. Experiments on VLABench, SafeAgentBench, and TaPA show that scene-grounded constraints improve object grounding and safety, while most remaining failures stem from perception errors or misaligned constraint specifications.

AI.tldr: CLAMP is a multimodal constraint-grounding framework that converts scene evidence into decoding-time constraints for frozen VLM planners, using hard masks and an HMM-based world-state lookahead to filter out visually unsupported, unsafe, or infeasible action candidates, with test-time adaptation via label-free continuations.
AI.motivation: Fluent plans generated by VLMs are not always executable—they may reference unobserved objects, select actions lacking required affordances, or violate action constraints. A method is needed to ground VLM planning in actual scene evidence.
AI.method: CLAMP restricts object references to those supported by the initial scene observation, uses a symbolic action model for state transitions and goals, applies hard masks during decoding to eliminate invalid next-token candidates, and employs an HMM-based world-state lookahead module to reweight probabilities of remaining feasible candidates based on action preconditions and goal reachability. For unseen tasks, the HMM is adapted at test time using label-free continuations sampled from the frozen VLM.
AI.result: Experiments on VLABench, SafeAgentBench, and TaPA demonstrate that scene-grounded constraints improve object grounding and safety. The majority of remaining failures stem from perception errors or misaligned constraint specifications rather than the constraint framework itself.
AI.conclusion: Constraining decoding with scene evidence and symbolic action models can make frozen VLM planners more executable and safer without retraining, while preserving the VLM's language prior. Future work should address perception robustness and constraint specification alignment.

title: GoAnt: Quality-Diversity Multi-Agent Search for Alpha Factor Discovery in Market Microstructure Data
comment: 14 pages, 1 figure, 8 tables, including supplementary appendices
summary: Automated alpha factor discovery searches symbolic trading signals from price-volume panels and order-book data under a fixed evaluation budget. Existing single- and multi-agent program-search systems can overfit predictive proxies that fail after execution costs and repeatedly explore redundant factor families, limiting execution robustness and behavioral diversity. We introduce GoAnt, a quality-diversity multi-agent search framework that combines non-communicating Explorer, Exploiter and Connector workers with a shared adaptive Mental Map and a compact Queen dispatcher. The Mental Map organizes candidates by leakage-free execution profiles and retains one elite per niche, while the Queen reallocates the evaluation budget from explicit search-state summaries. We also define a map-independent effective-yield protocol that counts high-quality, mutually nonredundant factors directly from each method's evaluation records, giving archive-based and map-free systems the same ruler. On real A-share microstructure data spanning 2023--2026, GoAnt reaches quality-weighted yields of 41.8 and 47.6 in price-volume and order-book settings, improving the strongest baseline by 57% and 97% under matched budgets. Its locked populations retain 0.64 and 0.67 of in-sample quality out of sample, compared with 0.61 and 0.63 for a static map.

AI.tldr: GoAnt is a quality-diversity multi-agent framework for automated alpha factor discovery that uses non-communicating Explorer, Exploiter, and Connector workers with a shared adaptive Mental Map and Queen dispatcher to improve execution robustness and behavioral diversity in symbolic trading signal search.
AI.motivation: Existing single- and multi-agent program-search systems for alpha factor discovery overfit predictive proxies that fail after execution costs and repeatedly explore redundant factor families, limiting execution robustness and behavioral diversity.
AI.method: GoAnt combines non-communicating Explorer, Exploiter, and Connector workers with a shared adaptive Mental Map and a compact Queen dispatcher. The Mental Map organizes candidates by leakage-free execution profiles, retaining one elite per niche. The Queen reallocates evaluation budget from search-state summaries. A map-independent effective-yield protocol counts high-quality, mutually nonredundant factors from evaluation records.
AI.result: On real A-share microstructure data spanning 2023-2026, GoAnt reaches quality-weighted yields of 41.8 and 47.6 in price-volume and order-book settings, improving the strongest baseline by 57% and 97% under matched budgets. Locked populations retain 0.64 and 0.67 of in-sample quality out of sample versus 0.61 and 0.63 for a static map.
AI.conclusion: GoAnt demonstrates that a quality-diversity multi-agent architecture with adaptive niche-based organization and centralized budget allocation substantially outperforms baselines in both performance and out-of-sample robustness for automated alpha factor discovery.

title: Application of curiosity driven exploration methods for hardware interference identification
summary: The transition from single-core to multi-core architectures in safety-critical embedded systems introduces significant challenges due to inter-core interference caused by contention for shared hardware resources. Such interference affects execution times and complicates the verification of strict temporal requirements, particularly in domains such as avionics where standards require comprehensive identification of interference sources. Existing interference analysis approaches, whether manual or model-based, struggle to capture the full range of behaviors arising from the complex interactions among micro-architectural components. In this paper, we frame multi-core interference analysis as the exploration of a complex system behavior space. We propose the use of curiosity-driven exploration algorithms from artificial intelligence to systematically and efficiently cover the space of possible interference behaviors. Using a simulator-based environment, we show that the proposed approach achieves broader and more uniform behavioral coverage within a limited experimental budget compared to traditional pseudo-random program generation methods.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes using curiosity-driven exploration algorithms from AI to systematically explore multi-core interference behaviors in safety-critical embedded systems, demonstrating broader and more uniform coverage than traditional pseudo-random program generation methods within limited experimental budgets.
AI.motivation: Multi-core architectures in safety-critical embedded systems (e.g., avionics) suffer from inter-core interference due to shared hardware resource contention, which complicates verification of strict temporal requirements. Existing manual and model-based interference analysis approaches struggle to capture the full range of behaviors arising from complex micro-architectural interactions.
AI.method: The authors frame multi-core interference analysis as exploration of a complex system behavior space and apply curiosity-driven exploration algorithms from artificial intelligence to systematically and efficiently cover the space of possible interference behaviors, using a simulator-based environment.
AI.result: The proposed curiosity-driven approach achieves broader and more uniform behavioral coverage within a limited experimental budget compared to traditional pseudo-random program generation methods.
AI.conclusion: Curiosity-driven exploration is an effective strategy for multi-core interference analysis in safety-critical systems, offering a systematic alternative to random generation that better captures diverse interference behaviors under resource constraints.

title: When Can One Obtain Certificates of Optimality Using Positivstellensaetze?
summary: We study certificates of positivity and optimality for learning problems whose objectives and constraints need not be polynomial. We isolate an axiomatic core of Fischer's constructive strict and weak Positivstellensätze and prove the resulting theorems for abstract function algebras over ordered fields. The framework separates two roles that can otherwise be conflated: objective and constraint functions may be built from broad classes of continuous or definable operations, while the auxiliary primitives used to construct a certificate satisfy explicit scalar and closure axioms. We give instances over continuous and definable function algebras, including ordered fields not closed under square roots, derive lower-bound and global-optimality certificates, and analyze both expanded term length and shared computation-graph complexity.

AI.tldr: This paper develops abstract positivity and optimality certificates for learning problems with non-polynomial objectives and constraints, extending Fischer's constructive Positivstellensätze to function algebras over ordered fields via an axiomatic framework.
AI.motivation: Standard Positivstellensätze apply to polynomial problems, but many learning problems involve non-polynomial objectives and constraints. There is a need to generalize certificate-based reasoning (for proving positivity and optimality) to broader classes of functions.
AI.method: The authors isolate an axiomatic core of Fischer's constructive strict and weak Positivstellensätze and prove the resulting theorems for abstract function algebras over ordered fields. The framework separates objective/constraint functions (built from broad continuous or definable operations) from auxiliary certificate-constructing primitives, which must satisfy explicit scalar and closure axioms.
AI.result: The framework is instantiated over continuous and definable function algebras (including ordered fields not closed under square roots), yielding lower-bound and global-optimality certificates. The authors also analyze expanded term length and shared computation-graph complexity.
AI.conclusion: The axiomatic generalization substantially broadens the applicability of constructive Positivstellensätze beyond polynomial settings, enabling certificate-based guarantees for a wider class of learning problems while providing complexity analyses of the resulting certificates.

title: It's All in the Way You Say It: The Role of Information Representation in LLM-Based Glycemic-Event Prediction
comment: Submitted to a journal for peer-review
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly being investigated for physiological time-series prediction, yet their effectiveness may depend not only on the model itself, but also on how physiological information is represented and presented at inference time. This study investigates prompt-based general-purpose LLMs for postprandial hyperglycemia and hypoglycemia prediction in individuals with type 1 diabetes. Using the OhioT1DM dataset, we evaluate multiple open-weight LLMs under zero-shot and few-shot inference across prediction horizons of 30, 60, and 90 minutes. The analysis varies both the textual representation of the available physiological information and the amount of information exposed to the model, ranging from glucose observations alone to derived descriptors and additional contextual variables related to insulin, meals, carbohydrates, and physical activity. Performance is compared with conventional patient-specific supervised models and with Gluco-LLM, a language-model-based architecture explicitly adapted to glucose time-series forecasting. Results show a marked task-dependent behavior. Conventional supervised models achieve the strongest performance for hyperglycemia prediction, whereas the best observed prompt-based LLM configurations improve performance for hypoglycemia across all investigated horizons. The effectiveness of prompt-based inference is also strongly influenced by how physiological information is represented, while providing additional contextual information does not lead to a systematic improvement. Overall, these findings highlight physiological information representation as a central design factor in prompt-based LLM approaches to glycemic-event prediction.

AI.tldr: This study evaluates prompt-based general-purpose LLMs for predicting postprandial hyperglycemia and hypoglycemia in type 1 diabetes patients using the OhioT1DM dataset, testing various textual representations and amounts of physiological information across 30/60/90-minute horizons. Results show task-dependent performance: conventional supervised models excel at hyperglycemia prediction, while prompt-based LLMs achieve the best hypoglycemia prediction. The representation of physiological information is a critical design factor, whereas adding more contextual variables does not yield systematic improvements.
AI.motivation: To determine whether LLM effectiveness for physiological time-series prediction depends on how physiological information is represented and presented at inference time, rather than solely on the model architecture itself.
AI.method: Using the OhioT1DM dataset, the study evaluates multiple open-weight LLMs under zero-shot and few-shot inference settings across prediction horizons of 30, 60, and 90 minutes. The analysis varies textual representations of physiological data (from glucose-only to derived descriptors and contextual variables including insulin, meals, carbohydrates, and physical activity) and compares performance against conventional patient-specific supervised models and Gluco-LLM, a language-model-based architecture tailored for glucose time-series forecasting.
AI.result: Conventional supervised models perform best for hyperglycemia prediction, while the best prompt-based LLM configurations improve hypoglycemia prediction across all investigated horizons. Prompt-based inference effectiveness is strongly influenced by data representation, but adding contextual information does not systematically improve performance.
AI.conclusion: Physiological information representation is a central design factor in prompt-based LLM approaches to glycemic-event prediction, with task-dependent optimality across modeling paradigms.

title: Closing the Consistency Gap: Self-Evolving Agents That Learn to Stay on Course
summary: Large language model (LLM)-powered agents can be accurate on average yet unreliable in production, a discrepancy that has been observed but remains largely unaddressed. When given the same task five times, a ReAct agent on the AppWorld benchmark using GPT-4.1 succeeds in all five runs only 53% of the time, even though its per-run pass rate averages 77%. We call this 24-point shortfall the consistency gap, and we argue that addressing it is a precondition for trustworthy AI agent deployment. We present a self-evolving agent framework that reduces this gap by identifying unstable, low-consistency steps in agent trajectories and converting them into episodic memory the agent can draw on in future runs. At its core is a Consistency Analyzer that pinpoints where and why a trajectory is likely to flip across executions, and a Guideline Generator that converts the diagnosis into targeted guidelines, committed to memory and injected into future agent executions on similar tasks. On AppWorld with ReAct/GPT-4.1, our framework raises the fraction of tasks that succeed in all five runs by +16 points on same-task evaluation and +13 points on similar-task generalization.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies and addresses the "consistency gap" in LLM-powered agents—where per-run accuracy overestimates cross-run reliability (77% pass rate vs. only 53% all-five success rate on AppWorld with GPT-4.1). The authors propose a self-evolving agent framework with a Consistency Analyzer and Guideline Generator that converts unstable trajectory steps into episodic memory guidelines, improving same-task consistency by +16 points and similar-task generalization by +13 points.
AI.motivation: LLM agents perform accurately on average but are unreliable in production when run repeatedly. Even with a 77% per-run pass rate, tasks succeed in all five runs only 53% of the time—a 24-point shortfall called the consistency gap. The authors argue this gap must be addressed as a precondition for trustworthy AI agent deployment.
AI.method: A self-evolving agent framework consisting of two core components: (1) a Consistency Analyzer that identifies unstable, low-consistency steps across trajectory executions and pinpoints where and why outputs flip between runs; and (2) a Guideline Generator that converts these diagnoses into targeted guidelines, committed to episodic memory and injected into future agent executions on similar tasks.
AI.result: On the AppWorld benchmark with ReAct/GPT-4.1, the framework raises the fraction of tasks succeeding in all five runs by +16 points on same-task evaluation and +13 points on similar-task generalization.
AI.conclusion: Addressing the consistency gap through self-evolving memory of unstable steps is an effective mechanism for improving LLM agent reliability across multiple executions, both for repeated identical tasks and for generalizing to similar unseen tasks, making agent deployment more trustworthy.

title: API Benchmark Scores Do Not Reliably Transfer to Chatbot Interfaces
summary:
Benchmark scores are a central currency in model releases: they inform purchasing decisions, shape public trust, and influence policy. Yet, a key assumption underlying benchmark scores is that the model performance measured through APIs faithfully reflects the behavior of deployed systems.
  We challenge this assumption by auditing ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini across seven systems and nine benchmarks spanning general capability, social bias, and sycophancy. We find systematic API--interface differences in both accuracy and consistency. On average, API evaluations score 3.4 percentage points higher in accuracy and 2.1 percentage points higher in test--retest agreement than corresponding interface evaluations. For ChatGPT, the performance difference between API and interface access exceeds the API-only difference between GPT 5.3 and GPT 5.4. Put differently, switching access surfaces can degrade performance as much as downgrading a full model generation.
  We further test whether exposed API controls can reproduce interface behavior by varying system prompts, sampling parameters, and reasoning settings. These controls shift behavior in some cases but do not reliably eliminate the gap. Our findings document a context-validity gap: measurements obtained through APIs do not necessarily generalize to corresponding deployed interfaces, complicating the use of API evaluations as proxies for deployed systems.

AI.tldr: Benchmark scores obtained through APIs systematically differ from those obtained through deployed chat interfaces. Auditing ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini across seven systems and nine benchmarks, API evaluations score on average 3.4 percentage points higher in accuracy and 2.1 percentage points higher in test-retest agreement than interface evaluations. For ChatGPT, the API-interface gap exceeds the difference between GPT 5.3 and GPT 5.4, meaning switching access surfaces can degrade performance as much as downgrading a full model generation. Attempts to reproduce interface behavior via API controls (system prompts, sampling parameters, reasoning settings) are only partially successful, revealing a context-validity gap that undermines the use of API evaluations as proxies for deployed systems.
AI.motivation: Benchmark scores are a central currency in model releases, informing purchasing decisions, public trust, and policy. However, the key assumption that model performance measured through APIs faithfully reflects deployed system behavior is largely untested. This paper challenges this assumption by systematically auditing whether API-based evaluations generalize to actual deployed interfaces.
AI.method: The authors audited ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini across seven systems and nine benchmarks spanning general capability, social bias, and sycophancy. They compared API evaluations against interface evaluations, measuring both accuracy and consistency (test-retest agreement). They further attempted to close observed gaps by varying API-exposed controls including system prompts, sampling parameters, and reasoning settings.
AI.result: Systematic API-interface differences were found in both accuracy and consistency. API evaluations scored on average 3.4 percentage points higher in accuracy and 2.1 percentage points higher in test-retest agreement than interface evaluations. For ChatGPT, the API-interface performance difference exceeded the API-only difference between GPT 5.3 and GPT 5.4, indicating the gap is as large as a full model generation. Exposed API controls shifted behavior in some cases but did not reliably eliminate the gap.
AI.conclusion: The findings document a context-validity gap: measurements obtained through APIs do not necessarily generalize to corresponding deployed interfaces. This complicates and undermines the common practice of using API evaluations as proxies for deployed system behavior, with implications for benchmark-based model comparisons, purchasing decisions, and policy.

title: SkillAdam: Stable and Efficient Skill Evolution for Agents
summary: Agent skills provide a lightweight way to equip frozen language-model agents with domain knowledge and procedural guidance, yet obtaining high-quality skills remains costly and difficult to scale. Expert-written skills require substantial human effort. Recent skill self-evolution methods automate an iterative loop that uses execution feedback to revise skills, but their heuristic update strategies often yield unstable optimization and low iteration efficiency. We identify two challenges in realizing stable and efficient skill self-evolution. Direction Stability requires effective corrections to accumulate rather than be overwritten by iteration-local feedback. Update Adaptivity requires the scope of each revision to reflect the consistency of recent case-level improvements. We introduce SkillAdam, an Adam-inspired framework for optimizing discrete and non-differentiable skill documents. As a functional analogue of Adam's first moment, an optimization memory records identified problems and the outcomes of prior solution attempts to stabilize the update direction. As a functional analogue of Adam's second moment, a volatility-driven edit budget tracks the history-weighted variation of recent case-level improvements and adaptively controls the update magnitude. Across seven benchmarks that span short- and long-horizon tasks, SkillAdam achieves state-of-the-art performance with more stable optimization dynamics. It also obtains stronger skills with substantially fewer optimization iterations and lower cost than prior methods. Code repository: https://github.com/ruc-datalab/SkillAdam

AI.tldr: SkillAdam is an Adam-inspired framework for optimizing discrete, non-differentiable skill documents in language-agent skill self-evolution. It introduces an optimization memory (analogous to Adam's first moment) for direction stability and a volatility-driven edit budget (analogous to Adam's second moment) for update adaptivity. It achieves state-of-the-art performance across seven benchmarks with more stable optimization, higher iteration efficiency, and lower cost.
AI.motivation: Expert-written agent skills are costly to scale, and existing skill self-evolution methods use heuristic update strategies that suffer from unstable optimization and low iteration efficiency. The authors identify two core challenges: Direction Stability (effective corrections should accumulate rather than be overwritten) and Update Adaptivity (revision scope should reflect consistency of recent case-level improvements).
AI.method: SkillAdam adapts Adam's optimization principles to discrete skill documents. (1) First-moment analogue: an optimization memory records identified problems and outcomes of prior solution attempts to stabilize update direction. (2) Second-moment analogue: a volatility-driven edit budget tracks history-weighted variation of recent case-level improvements to adaptively control update magnitude.
AI.result: Across seven benchmarks spanning short- and long-horizon tasks, SkillAdam achieves state-of-the-art performance with more stable optimization dynamics, stronger skills obtained in substantially fewer optimization iterations, and lower cost than prior methods.
AI.conclusion: SkillAdam demonstrates that principles from continuous optimization (momentum and adaptive step size) can be effectively transferred to the discrete space of skill documents, enabling more stable, efficient, and cost-effective skill self-evolution for language agents.

title: Good Pretraining, Bad SFT: Checkpoint Quality Across the Training Stack
summary: Language-model checkpoints are commonly selected by pretraining loss or benchmark scores, assuming that the highest-scoring checkpoint will remain the best starting point for subsequent training. We show that this assumption can fail in a full 30B mixture-of-experts training pipeline. The checkpoints that perform better after the full downstream training stack also have higher solution density, i.e., retain downstream performance under local weight perturbations.

AI.tldr: Standard checkpoint selection criteria (pretraining loss or benchmark scores) can fail in large-scale MoE training pipelines because the optimal checkpoint for continued training differs from the one that scores best at selection time. A better predictor is "solution density"—retaining downstream performance under local weight perturbations.
AI.motivation: The paper challenges the common assumption that the highest-scoring checkpoint (by pretraining loss or benchmarks) will always be the best starting point for subsequent training. This assumption is shown to fail in a full 30B mixture-of-experts training pipeline.
AI.method: The authors evaluate checkpoints in a 30B mixture-of-experts (MoE) training pipeline, comparing their downstream performance after the full training stack, and measuring solution density—whether downstream performance is retained under local weight perturbations.
AI.result: Checkpoints that perform better after the full downstream training stack also exhibit higher solution density, meaning solution density is a reliable indicator of a checkpoint's suitability as a starting point for continued training, unlike pretraining loss or benchmark scores.
AI.conclusion: Standard checkpoint selection metrics (pretraining loss, benchmarks) can be misleading for choosing checkpoints meant for further training. Solution density provides an alternative and more reliable criterion for checkpoint selection in large-scale MoE training pipelines.

title: Deposon: An Auditable, Conservation-Guaranteed, Game-Theoretically Tested Scattering Layer over LLM Reasoning Paths
comment: 23 pages, 5 figures. Author affiliation: School of Chemistry and Life Resources, Renmin University of China. Code: https://github.com/zeroandcat/Deposon
summary: Multi-step LLM reasoning lacks a machine-recheckable ledger: discarded reasoning paths leave no auditable record. We propose the Deposon scattering layer, which binds each node of an LLM-generated concept-decomposition graph to a two-parameter Deposon state; paths undergo three-channel scattering -- transmission, reflection, irreversible dissipation -- obeying T+R+A=1 for arbitrary parameters, with a maximum per-path energy-audit deviation of 2.2E-16 (machine epsilon). We report all three evidence tiers honestly. On synthetic trap benchmarks the path-filtering gain is closed (pre-registered): unified reaches 100% versus a decoy-capture baseline at 7%/10%. On real benchmarks the layer is indistinguishable from a trivial six-keyword rule filter (GSM8K 0.87 >= 0.85, McNemar p=0.5; StrategyQA 0.899 = 0.899); no difference is detected here, so we sharpen the claim to "the differential value lies solely in machine verifiability." Fusion yields a second negative result: convex combinations with a semantic prior never improve (physics 0.484 -> 0.452), and the apparent lambda=2 gain is an anti-field artifact; any fusion gain must be nonlinear. Modeling the reverse dynamics as a potential game on the graph, we evidence an auditable scalar's monotonicity and near-gradientness and quantify the empirical coordination ratio (ECR). The three formalized dynamical-equivalence propositions (P1a/P1b/T-P1c) are falsified under the pre-registered kill protocol, and the potential-game claim is downgraded to approximate (cyclic-graph median residual 0.669): only consistency-level evidence survives at the dynamical level. Code: github.com/zeroandcat/Deposon.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Deposon scattering layer, which attaches two-parameter states to nodes of LLM concept-decomposition graphs, enabling auditable tracking of multi-step reasoning paths via three-channel scattering (transmission, reflection, irreversible dissipation) with energy conservation obeying T+R+A=1. Results are mixed: perfect performance on synthetic trap benchmarks, but indistinguishable from a trivial keyword filter on real benchmarks (GSM8K, StrategyQA) — the claimed differential value is machine verifiability only. Fusion with semantic priors yields negative results. Dynamical-level claims (potential-game modeling, formalized equivalence propositions) are falsified or downgraded to approximate status under pre-registered kill protocols.
AI.motivation: Multi-step LLM reasoning lacks a machine-recheckable ledger; discarded or explored reasoning paths cannot be audited after the fact. This limits verifiability, transparency, and accountability of LLM reasoning traces.
AI.method: Proposes a scattering layer that binds each node of an LLM concept-decomposition graph to a two-parameter Deposon state. Reasoning paths undergo three-channel scattering (transmission, reflection, irreversible dissipation) with strict conservation T+R+A=1. Uses pre-registered protocols with kill rules, honest reporting across three evidence tiers, and formalized dynamical-equivalence propositions (P1a/P1b/T-P1c). Evaluates on synthetic trap benchmarks and real benchmarks (GSM8K, StrategyQA), tests fusion against semantic priors, and models reverse dynamics as a potential game with ECR quantification.
AI.result: On synthetic trap benchmarks, unified path filtering reaches 100% versus decoy-capture baselines at 7%/10%. On real benchmarks, the layer is indistinguishable from a trivial six-keyword rule filter (GSM8K 0.87 vs 0.85, McNemar p=0.5; StrategyQA 0.899 = 0.899). Fusion with semantic priors never improves performance (physics 0.484 to 0.452); apparent gains are anti-field artifacts requiring nonlinear fusion. Dynamical propositions are falsified under kill protocol; potential-game claim downgraded to approximate (median residual 0.669). Maximum per-path energy-audit deviation is 2.2E-16 (machine epsilon).
AI.conclusion: The differential value of the Deposon scattering layer lies solely in machine verifiability rather than predictive performance. Consistency-level evidence survives dynamical scrutiny, while stronger dynamical claims (potential-game equivalence, formalized propositions) are falsified or downgraded to approximate status. Any fusion gains must be nonlinear.

title: Answer-Distribution Trajectories: A Stochastic-Dynamics View of LLM Reasoning
summary: Chain-of-thought reasoning provides a structured computation between a model's input and final answer. Yet it is often evaluated through endpoint accuracy, which ignores the path taken to reach that answer. An emerging line of work addresses this limitation using entropy profiles, which track how uncertainty evolves over the reasoning process but do not reveal which competing hypotheses account for that uncertainty. We introduce answer-distribution trajectories, a stochastic-dynamics-inspired representation that tracks the model's full predictive distribution over answers as reasoning unfolds. As a strictly finer representation than endpoint and entropy summaries, answer-distribution trajectories enable us to characterize a trace through a dynamical reasoning profile spanning exploration, revision, motion, and commitment, and to distinguish different dynamical mechanisms of reasoning success and failure. Across sixteen open-weight language models and four reasoning benchmarks, we show that traces with the same endpoint and similar entropy profiles can exhibit substantially different reasoning dynamics. We further find substantial variation in these dynamics both within and across models and tasks, with different objectives favoring different dynamical profiles. Additionally, we show that training and inference choices systematically reshape these profiles. Our results suggest that answer-distribution trajectories provide a rich framework for analysing and evaluating the dynamics of LLM reasoning.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces answer-distribution trajectories, a representation that tracks a model's full predictive distribution over answers throughout chain-of-thought reasoning. Unlike endpoint accuracy or entropy-only profiles, this finer-grained framework characterizes reasoning dynamics (exploration, revision, motion, commitment) and distinguishes different dynamical mechanisms behind reasoning success/failure across 16 LLMs and 4 benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Chain-of-thought reasoning is typically evaluated by endpoint accuracy, ignoring the reasoning path. Entropy profiles address this by tracking uncertainty evolution but fail to reveal which competing hypotheses account for that uncertainty, motivating a richer representation of reasoning dynamics.
AI.method: The authors propose answer-distribution trajectories, a stochastic-dynamics-inspired representation tracking the full predictive answer distribution as reasoning unfolds. This enables a dynamical reasoning profile spanning exploration, revision, motion, and commitment. They evaluate across sixteen open-weight language models and four reasoning benchmarks, examining how training and inference choices reshape these profiles.
AI.result: Traces sharing the same endpoint and similar entropy profiles can exhibit substantially different reasoning dynamics. Substantial variation exists both within and across models and tasks, with different objectives favoring different dynamical profiles. Furthermore, training and inference choices systematically reshape these profiles.
AI.conclusion: Answer-distribution trajectories offer a richer framework than endpoint or entropy summaries for analyzing and evaluating the dynamics of LLM reasoning, enabling finer-grained characterization of how models explore, revise, and commit to answers during chain-of-thought generation.

title: Time-Varying Data as Sheaves: an Invitation to Narratives
summary: Modern science and engineering increasingly rely on time-varying data, yet the mathematical tools used to model temporal phenomena are often developed within separate disciplines, obscuring common principles and limiting the transfer of ideas across fields. This chapter presents the theory of narratives, an abstract framework for time-varying objects of any mathematical kind that supports both theoretical investigations and applications. To illustrate this perspective, the chapter develops three vignettes, each illustrating a different research direction. The first addresses a general concern: What information loss can occur when switching between different representations of temporal data? The second concerns structural and algorithmic approaches: How can we systematically decompose time-varying data into simple pieces and obtain invariants describing its structural complexity? The third is an application to control theory: How can we model multi-agent systems with switching communication topologies? More important than any individual vignette, the central message of this invitation is that a suitable abstract perspective can organize and guide research across remarkably diverse mathematical and scientific domains.

AI.tldr: This chapter presents the theory of narratives, an abstract mathematical framework for modeling time-varying objects of any kind, illustrated through three vignettes covering information loss in temporal data representation switching, structural decomposition of time-varying data into invariants, and applications to multi-agent control systems with switching communication topologies.
AI.motivation: Time-varying data is increasingly central to modern science and engineering, yet mathematical tools for modeling temporal phenomena are developed within separate disciplines, obscuring common principles and limiting cross-field idea transfer. A unified abstract framework is needed.
AI.method: The paper introduces the theory of narratives as an abstract framework for time-varying mathematical objects. It develops three research vignettes: (1) examining information loss during representation switching, (2) systematically decomposing time-varying data into simple pieces with structural complexity invariants, and (3) applying the framework to multi-agent systems with switching communication topologies.
AI.result: The chapter demonstrates the framework's versatility through the three vignettes, showing that an abstract perspective can address information loss concerns, provide structural decomposition algorithms, and model control-theoretic systems with switching topologies.
AI.conclusion: The central message is that a suitable abstract perspective, such as the theory of narratives, can organize and guide research across remarkably diverse mathematical and scientific domains, enabling unified treatment of time-varying phenomena.

title: Everything in Moderation: Per-Domain Coverage Optima and Alignment-Resistant Domain Gaps in Multi-Domain Mid-Training
summary: Mid-training, the stage between pre-training and alignment, is where a model's per-domain data composition is typically set by data availability rather than principled design. We ask what that decision buys, and whether a later alignment pass can undo it. In a controlled logical-reasoning setting (Qwen3-8B-Base, with a 4B replication; five semantically rule-disjoint KOR-Bench domains) we train 30 allocations spanning the five-domain simplex, 24 sweep configurations plus six withheld from the fit, at five seeds each. Three findings emerge. First, every domain has an interior coverage optimum: the moderate band ($10\%$-$40\%$) is best for all five domains, and a calibrated permutation test for quadratic interiority gives $P\approx0.010$; the fitted mid-training-only curves, with 8B peaks between $9.9\%$ and $35.1\%$, reproduce for curve shape but not peak location. Second, the gaps survive a fixed-budget alignment pass: compensatory SFT raises 116/120 cells (mean $+4.32\%$) yet bridges $0/240$ pairs at a $5\%$ threshold and $30/240$ at a $10\%$ ratio, an equal-budget uniform control behaves almost identically, and a permutation null would bridge $13.8\pm3.3$ and $77.9\pm8.5$ pairs ($P<0.001$). Third, zero coverage collapses mid-training-only accuracy, though a FineWeb-Edu-only control shows the collapse is commingled with generic drift. An exploratory $θ^*$ allocation attains the largest full-pipeline gain ($+4.36\%$ vs. $+0.80\%$/$+0.64\%$\,pp) but is marginal under Welch test.

AI.tldr: A controlled study on Qwen3-8B-Base across five KOR-Bench domains shows that mid-training data composition follows principled interior optima (10%-40% per domain), these optima persist despite post-alignment passes, and zero-coverage causes accuracy collapse, though an exploratory optimal allocation yields modest full-pipeline gains.
AI.motivation: Mid-training domain data composition is typically set by data availability rather than principled design. The authors ask what that decision buys, and whether a later alignment pass can undo the effects of suboptimal mid-training data allocation.
AI.method: Using Qwen3-8B-Base with a 4B replication, the authors train 30 allocations spanning the five-domain simplex (24 sweep configurations plus 6 withheld for validation) at five seeds each, in a controlled logical-reasoning setting across five semantically rule-disjoint KOR-Bench domains. Statistical methods include calibrated permutation tests for quadratic interiority, Welch tests for marginal significance, and permutation nulls for bridge-pair analysis.
AI.result: Three findings: (1) Every domain has an interior coverage optimum in the 10%-40% band, with fitted 8B peaks between 9.9% and 35.1%, though curve shape reproduces but not peak location (P≈0.010); (2) Gaps survive alignment—compensatory SFT lifts 116/120 cells (mean +4.32%) but bridges 0/240 pairs at 5% threshold and 30/240 at 10% ratio, nearly identical to equal-budget uniform control, versus permutation nulls of 13.8±3.3 and 77.9±8.5 pairs (P<0.001); (3) Zero coverage collapses mid-training-only accuracy, though a FineWeb-Edu-only control shows collapse is commingled with generic drift. An exploratory θ* allocation gains the most full-pipeline (+4.36% vs +0.80%/+0.64% pp) but is marginal under Welch test.
AI.conclusion: Mid-training data composition decisions within this setting produce meaningful and persistent effects on domain accuracy that later alignment cannot fully undo, suggesting domain composition should be treated as a principled design variable rather than left to data availability. Moderate per-domain coverage (10%-40%) is consistently optimal, and the effects are robust yet statistically nuanced at full-pipeline scale.

title: The Surprising Effectiveness of Approximate Value Iteration in Self-Play
summary: Combining search with function approximation has driven major advances in game-playing programs, making self-play algorithms more competitive than ever. Still, the computational overhead of the most popular methods, based on Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS), can be substantial. In this work, we investigate whether simpler methods remain competitive in non-trivial, moderately sized games such as Connect Four, Hex(7x7) and synthetic games. We train a minimal self-play implementation of Approximate Value Iteration (AVI) and use ground-truth oracles for exact evaluation. Contrary to expectations, our results demonstrate the surprising effectiveness of AVI: it learns more accurate value functions than those learned by AlphaZero, while its one-step-lookahead greedy policies remain competitive with MCTS-based policies at substantially lower training and inference costs. Preliminary experiments on Othello and Go(9x9) show that AVI trains stably on larger games and learns effective value functions. These findings suggest that the success of MCTS-based methods may have eclipsed simpler approaches that have become increasingly practical with modern deep-learning tools.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates whether simpler, non-MCTS methods remain competitive in moderately sized games by training a minimal self-play implementation of Approximate Value Iteration (AVI). Results show AVI learns more accurate value functions than AlphaZero and its greedy policies remain competitive with MCTS-based policies at substantially lower cost, with stable training on larger games like Othello and Go(9x9).
AI.motivation: MCTS-based methods have dominated game-playing programs but carry substantial computational overhead. The authors question whether simpler approaches have been eclipsed and whether they can remain competitive in non-trivial, moderately sized games.
AI.method: The authors train a minimal self-play implementation of Approximate Value Iteration (AVI) using deep learning and compare it against AlphaZero-style MCTS methods. They evaluate on games including Connect Four, Hex(7x7), and synthetic games, using ground-truth oracles for exact evaluation. Preliminary experiments extend to Othello and Go(9x9).
AI.result: AVI learns more accurate value functions than AlphaZero, and its one-step-lookahead greedy policies remain competitive with MCTS-based policies at substantially lower training and inference costs. AVI also trains stably on larger games and learns effective value functions in preliminary Othello and Go experiments.
AI.conclusion: The success of MCTS-based methods may have overshadowed simpler approaches like AVI, which have become increasingly practical and competitive with modern deep-learning tools. Simpler search-free or minimal-search methods deserve renewed attention in game-playing research.

title: SAEScientist-Bench: Can AI Agents Conduct Autonomous SAE Interpretability Research?
summary: While research on recursive self-improvement (RSI) has predominantly automated model training pipelines, reliable autonomous development demands a missing pillar: post-hoc monitoring and auditing to understand what models learn and ensure safe alignment. Mechanistic interpretability tools are essential to bridge this gap, among which Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) serve as a cornerstone by isolating interpretable features for model inspection and steering. In this paper, we introduce SAEScientist-Bench to evaluate whether AI agents can act as scientists utilizing SAE tools for autonomous mechanistic discovery. Given a target concept, an agent designs contrastive probes and navigates a Gemma Scope dictionary of 131K+ features in Gemma-2-9B-IT to discover the optimal feature, evaluated against curated expert reference features anchored on Neuronpedia across activation rank, concept selectivity on contrastive texts, and causal steering. Across 10 agent configurations and 20 tasks, frontier agents demonstrate genuine discovery capabilities and lead different evaluation dimensions, but remain well behind the expert baseline, approaching expert levels on separating target concepts from contrastive controls while lagging substantially in causal generation steering. Further analysis reveals that although agents can design contrasts to rule out spurious candidates, they frequently misinterpret experimental measurements. These results establish experimental model understanding as a measurable capability for closed-loop autonomous AI R&D. Our code is available at https://github.com/Trae1ounG/SAEScientist.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces SAEScientist-Bench, a benchmark evaluating whether AI agents can autonomously perform mechanistic interpretability discovery using Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs). Agents design contrastive probes and search a 131K+ feature dictionary in Gemma-2-9B-IT to find optimal features for target concepts, assessed against expert references across activation rank, concept selectivity, and causal steering. Results show frontier agents have genuine discovery abilities and lead different evaluation dimensions but lag behind expert baselines, particularly in causal generation steering.
AI.motivation: Reliable autonomous AI development (recursive self-improvement) requires not just automated training pipelines but post-hoc monitoring and auditing to understand what models learn. Mechanistic interpretability tools like Sparse Autoencoders are essential for this, yet there is no benchmark evaluating whether AI agents can autonomously act as scientists using these tools for mechanistic discovery.
AI.method: The authors build SAEScientist-Bench where AI agents are given a target concept and must design contrastive probes, navigate a Gemma Scope dictionary of 131K+ features in Gemma-2-9B-IT, and discover the optimal feature. Agents are evaluated against expert-annotated reference features on Neuronpedia across three dimensions: activation rank, concept selectivity on contrastive texts, and causal steering. Ten agent configurations are tested across 20 tasks.
AI.result: Frontier agents demonstrate genuine discovery capabilities and lead different evaluation dimensions but remain well behind expert baselines. They approach expert levels on separating target concepts from contrastive controls but lag substantially in causal generation steering. Analysis reveals agents can design contrasts to rule out spurious candidates yet frequently misinterpret experimental measurements.
AI.conclusion: The results establish experimental model understanding as a measurable capability for closed-loop autonomous AI R&D. The benchmark highlights gaps in agent-based mechanistic interpretability, particularly in interpreting experimental results and causal steering, pointing to areas requiring further advancement for reliable autonomous development.

title: MeClear: Cooperative Game-Theoretic Attribution and Risk-Aware Memory Clearance for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
summary: Long horizon Large Language Model (LLM) agents rely on external memory systems to preserve user preferences and task knowledge across extended interactions. Conventional retrieval mechanisms optimize semantic compatibility rather than downstream utility, frequently introducing outdated, misleading, or conflicting evidence into the active context. We present MeClear, a task conditioned memory clearance framework that identifies memories featuring negative downstream utility through cooperative attribution and selectively suppresses them from agent execution. MeClear combines Leave One Out screening with sampled cooperative Shapley attribution to distribute utility across interacting evidence, effectively resolving redundant conflict masking where single removal evaluations fail.
