Utilizing attribution rankings, MeClear executes a query scoped minimal clearance strategy over a nested filtration, verifying task recovery on the cleared context without permanently altering the persistent memory bank. Comprehensive experimental evaluations across ten long dialogue memory pools demonstrate that MeClear achieves a target recall of 85.9% and an overall task recovery rate of 82.3%, representing a 25.5 percentage point improvement over Leave One Out (LOO) baselines.

AI.tldr: MeClear is a task-conditioned memory clearance framework for long-horizon LLM agents that identifies and suppresses memories with negative downstream utility using cooperative attribution (Leave One Out screening combined with sampled cooperative Shapley values), achieving 85.9% target recall and 82.3% task recovery—25.5 points above LOO baselines.
AI.motivation: Conventional retrieval mechanisms in LLM memory systems optimize for semantic compatibility rather than downstream task utility, often introducing outdated, misleading, or conflicting evidence into the active context, degrading long-horizon agent performance.
AI.method: MeClear combines Leave One Out (LOO) screening with sampled cooperative Shapley attribution to distribute utility across interacting evidence, resolving redundant conflict masking where single-removal evaluations fail. It then executes a query-scoped minimal clearance strategy over a nested filtration, verifying task recovery on the cleared context without permanently modifying the persistent memory bank.
AI.result: Across ten long dialogue memory pools, MeClear achieves 85.9% target recall and 82.3% overall task recovery rate, a 25.5 percentage point improvement over LOO baselines.
AI.conclusion: Cooperative attribution-based memory clearance effectively removes harmful memories while preserving persistent memory integrity, significantly outperforming conventional single-removal attribution methods for long-horizon LLM agents.

title: A Generalization of Amari's Bayesian Duality
summary: Amari's contributions to information geometry and machine learning are well known. Here, we revisit Amari's work on Bayesian duality which has not received as much attention. We connect Amari's Bayesian duality to a convex duality of Bayes' rule. Using this connection, we present a generalization of Amari's Bayesian duality and discuss its relevance for modern artificial intelligence.

AI.tldr: This paper revisits Amari's underappreciated work on Bayesian duality, connects it to a convex duality of Bayes' rule, generalizes Amari's original formulation, and discusses the implications of this generalized Bayesian duality for modern artificial intelligence.
AI.motivation: While Amari's contributions to information geometry and machine learning are widely recognized, his work on Bayesian duality has received comparatively little attention. The authors aim to shed light on this overlooked topic, establish fresh connections to convex duality, and demonstrate its relevance to contemporary AI.
AI.method: The authors establish a connection between Amari's Bayesian duality and a convex duality formulation of Bayes' rule. Building on this relationship, they derive a generalization of Amari's original Bayesian duality framework.
AI.result: A generalization of Amari's Bayesian duality is presented, formulated through the lens of convex duality of Bayes' rule, offering a broader theoretical framework than the original.
AI.conclusion: The generalized Bayesian duality is argued to be relevant for modern artificial intelligence, suggesting it can inform or improve contemporary AI approaches through this deeper theoretical perspective on Bayesian inference.

title: ExecCritic: Learn to Test, Test to Improve for Coding Agents
summary: Execution feedback can guide coding agents toward correct repository repairs, but only when the tests capture the behavior requested by the issue. Agent-generated tests can encode incomplete or incorrect behavioral targets; when the same trajectory writes both the patch and the test, their errors can agree and create false confidence. We introduce ExecCritic, combining a test--verify--revise scaffold with a role-specific reinforcement learning recipe for training agents within it. The scaffold separates test construction from source-code repair: a Test agent independently generates repository-native tests, a fail-closed harness qualifies and freezes them, and a Repair agent revises source code from their execution feedback without changing the tests. Both roles use Qwen-3.5-35B-A3B as the backbone and are trained separately. In Learn to Test, the Test agent learns to produce behaviorally valid tests that distinguish correct from incorrect patches. In Test to Improve, the Repair agent learns both direct task resolution and feedback-guided revision. On SWE-bench Verified, test quality determines whether feedback helps: holding the base Repair agent fixed, tests from the base Test agent reduce resolved rate from a no-test baseline of 61.2% to 57.3%, whereas tests from GPT-5.6-sol raise it to 65.3%. Role-specific post-training raises the Qwen Test agent's Base-to-Gold success from 22.2% to 62.2%; composing the two post-trained Qwen agents reaches 72.6%, an 11.4-point gain over the original no-test baseline without stronger-model or Oracle feedback at evaluation time. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/MSR-Orchard/execcritic.

AI.tldr: ExecCritic is a framework for training coding agents to use execution feedback effectively by separating test generation from code repair. It uses a test-verify-revise scaffold where a Test agent independently generates repository-native tests that are validated and frozen before a Repair agent revises source code based on execution feedback. Role-specific reinforcement learning post-training improves both agents, reaching 72.6% on SWE-bench Verified—an 11.4-point gain over the 61.2% no-test baseline without stronger models or Oracle feedback.
AI.motivation: Execution feedback only helps coding agents when the tests used actually capture the behavior described in the issue. Since agent-generated tests can encode incomplete or wrong behavioral targets, and when the same trajectory produces both the patch and the test, their errors can align and create false confidence, a decoupled approach is needed where test generation quality is independently validated before guiding repair.
AI.method: ExecCritic introduces a test-verify-revise scaffold with two roles: a Test agent that independently generates repository-native tests, and a fail-closed harness that qualifies and freezes them before a Repair agent revises source code using execution feedback. Both roles use Qwen-3.5-35B-A3B as the backbone with separate role-specific reinforcement learning recipes: "Learn to Test" trains the Test agent to produce behaviorally valid tests that distinguish correct from incorrect patches, while "Test to Improve" trains the Repair agent in both direct task resolution and feedback-guided revision.
AI.result: On SWE-bench Verified, test quality directly determines whether feedback helps: with the base Repair agent fixed, base Test agent tests reduce resolved rates from 61.2% to 57.3%, while GPT-5.6-sol tests raise it to 65.3%. Role-specific post-training improves the Qwen Test agent's Base-to-Gold success from 22.2% to 62.2%, and composing the two post-trained agents reaches 72.6%—an 11.4-point improvement over the no-test baseline without stronger-model or Oracle feedback at evaluation time.
AI.conclusion: The results demonstrate that (1) separating test generation from repair prevents self-consistent errors from creating false confidence, (2) test quality is the critical determinant of whether execution feedback aids repair, and (3) role-specific reinforcement learning enables open-weight models to produce high-quality tests and effectively leverage them, closing much of the gap to stronger models.

title: Co-Evolving Harnesses and Models: On-Policy Correction Helps Weaker Models Catch Up Where Imitation Fails
summary: Agent harnesses (the system prompt, tool set, execution hooks, and context-management scaffolding around a model) are a critical determinant of agentic task success. Automated harness evolution can enable smaller models to perform well on domain-specific tasks at a fraction of frontier-model cost. Since both the harness and model weights shape behavior, we ask how harness evolution and lightweight fine-tuning should be combined. Across seven enterprise agent tasks, we first evolve a harness with the weaker model, then find that a stronger expert often uses it more effectively, suggesting expert supervision could close the remaining gap. However, training the weaker model on the expert's complete trajectories under the evolved harness backfires: performance regresses on all seven tasks by 4 to 30 points across Qwen3-Coder and Gemma 4, even though the same procedure helps under the unevolved harness. Our analysis shows that imitation transfers knowledge and increases scaffold usage, but disrupts model-harness fit: the weaker model adopts the expert's planning strategy without the competence to execute it and no longer matches the harness evolved around its native planning style. We therefore develop an on-policy expert-correction pipeline, automated by a meta-level MLE agent, that localizes the failing turn in the weaker model's own rollout and asks the expert to rewrite only that turn. This preserves the model's planning style and combines the gains of harness evolution and model adaptation. Our results identify and resolve a source of contention between harness and weight updates, yielding a compatibility-preserving recipe for economical co-evolution on domain-specific enterprise tasks.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how to combine automated harness evolution with lightweight fine-tuning for domain-specific agentic tasks. The authors find that imitating an expert's full trajectories under an evolved harness backfires (4-30 point regression across seven tasks) because it disrupts the fit between the weaker model's planning style and the harness evolved around it. They propose an on-policy expert-correction pipeline, automated by a meta-level MLE agent, that only rewrites the failing turn in the weaker model's own rollout, preserving planning style while combining the gains of harness evolution and model adaptation.
AI.motivation: Agent harnesses (system prompts, tools, execution hooks, context management) are critical for agentic task success, and automated harness evolution can enable smaller models to perform well at lower cost than frontier models. However, since both harness and model weights shape behavior, the key question is how harness evolution and lightweight fine-tuning should be combined—especially whether expert supervision can close the remaining performance gap after harness evolution.
AI.method: (1) Evolve a harness with a weaker model across seven enterprise agent tasks. (2) Test whether fine-tuning the weaker model on a stronger expert's complete trajectories under the evolved harness improves performance (it does under the unevolved harness but backfires under the evolved one). (3) Analyze why this fails: imitation transfers knowledge and increases scaffold usage but disrupts model-harness fit, as the weaker model adopts the expert's planning strategy without the competence to execute it. (4) Develop an on-policy expert-correction pipeline, automated by a meta-level MLE agent, that localizes the failing turn in the weaker model's own rollout and asks the expert to rewrite only that turn, preserving the model's native planning style.
AI.result: Off-policy imitation of expert full trajectories under an evolved harness causes performance regression of 4 to 30 points across all seven tasks on both Qwen3-Coder and Gemma 4. The proposed on-policy expert-correction pipeline resolves this by preserving the model's planning style while combining the gains of harness evolution and model adaptation, providing a compatibility-preserving recipe for economical co-evolution.
AI.conclusion: There is a fundamental contention between harness and weight updates: naive imitation of expert trajectories can disrupt the harmony between a model's planning style and its evolved harness. The solution is to make model adaptation on-policy—correcting only the failing turns in the model's own rollouts rather than transplanting the expert's full behavior—yielding an economical recipe for co-evolving harness and model on domain-specific enterprise tasks.

title: A Data-Driven Framework for Identifying and Prioritizing RPA Opportunities in Healthcare Processes
summary: Robotic Process Automation (RPA) is widely used to reduce administrative burden in United States hospitals, yet an estimated 30-50% of RPA initiatives underperform because processes are selected informally, without a repeatable method to catalogue candidates, prioritize them, match each to an automation tier -- a Python bot, an open-source orchestrator such as n8n, or an enterprise platform such as UiPath -- and forecast financial return before committing resources. We propose a four-module, data-driven framework unifying these decisions: a Process Taxonomy of twenty recurring hospital processes across five value streams; a Prioritization module deriving an Automation Suitability Index from an Analytic Hierarchy Process matrix with an explicit consistency check; a Tool-Tier Selection module recommending the least-cost technology sufficient for a process complexity, integration, and compliance profile; and a Return-on-Investment module quantifying labor savings, error-cost avoidance, payback, and net present value. Applied to a synthetic portfolio spanning all twenty processes, plus a reference data-flow architecture linking it to hospital EHR/payer/ERP systems: 12 of 20 clear the prioritization threshold; the ranking is robust to +/-20% weight perturbation (Spearman correlation 0.83, top-5 set preserved 97.7%, 2,000 Monte Carlo trials); an Automation Risk Index flags four qualifying processes as Critical risk; a budget-constrained portfolio optimization shows diminishing marginal NPV as spend scales from $400K to $1.03M; and a second Monte Carlo analysis shows portfolio NPV stays positive at its 5th percentile. The framework is a conceptual synthesis of the literature rather than an instrument calibrated on primary hospital data; we discuss HIPAA governance and a research agenda for empirical validation. A supplementary Python implementation accompanies the paper.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a four-module, data-driven framework for hospital RPA selection that unifies process cataloguing, prioritization, tool-tier selection, and ROI forecasting. Applied to a synthetic portfolio of 20 hospital processes, the framework shows robust prioritization under weight perturbation, identifies risk-critical processes, and demonstrates diminishing returns in budget-constrained portfolio optimization, with a supplementary Python implementation provided.
AI.motivation: An estimated 30-50% of RPA initiatives in US hospitals underperform because process selection is done informally—without a repeatable method to catalogue candidates, prioritize them, match each to an appropriate automation tier (Python bot, open-source orchestrator, or enterprise platform), and forecast financial return before committing resources.
AI.method: A four-module framework: (1) Process Taxonomy cataloguing twenty recurring hospital processes across five value streams; (2) Prioritization module using an Automation Suitability Index derived from an Analytic Hierarchy Process matrix with consistency checking; (3) Tool-Tier Selection module recommending the least-cost technology matched to process complexity, integration, and compliance profile; (4) Return-on-Investment module quantifying labor savings, error-cost avoidance, payback, and net present value. Validation uses Monte Carlo simulations (2,000 trials for weight perturbation) and a reference data-flow architecture linking to EHR/payer/ERP systems.
AI.result: Of 20 processes, 12 clear the prioritization threshold. Rankings are robust to +/-20% weight perturbation (Spearman correlation 0.83, top-5 set preserved 97.7%). An Automation Risk Index flags four qualifying processes as Critical risk. Budget-constrained portfolio optimization shows diminishing marginal NPV as spend scales from $400K to $1.03M, and portfolio NPV remains positive at its 5th percentile in a second Monte Carlo analysis.
AI.conclusion: The framework is a conceptual synthesis of the literature rather than an instrument calibrated on primary hospital data. The authors discuss HIPAA governance considerations and outline a research agenda for empirical validation, noting that a supplementary Python implementation accompanies the paper.

title: Procedural Graphs: Self-Evolving Execution Structures for LLM Agents
comment: 36 pages including references and appendices, 6 figures, 11 tables
summary: Large language models are increasingly deployed as agents that plan over long horizons and act through external tools. Most agents select actions through unconstrained generation over an accumulating history, leaving implicit the procedural knowledge of what to do, in what order, and under which conditions. As trajectories lengthen, agents can lose track of their objectives, invoke tools out of order, and repeat unproductive actions. We introduce the Procedural Graph: just as a knowledge graph organizes factual knowledge into (entity, relation, entity) triplets for what-is questions, a Procedural Graph organizes procedural knowledge into (procedure, relation, procedure) triplets for what-to-do questions. At each decision step, the framework localizes the agent's active node, and a guidance model translates the surrounding subgraph into step-level situational guidance that biases the solver's next action without dictating it. The graph is self-evolving: an LLM refiner contrasts failed trajectories with successful ones and edits the graph's topology and attributes, committing edits that preserve or improve held-out validation performance while retaining rejected ones to discourage repetition. Starting from a minimal skeleton, the loop builds graphs that match or surpass hand-designed ones. It can also repair a flawed expert prior. Across multiple datasets, task types, and LLMs, the Procedural Graph delivers consistent gains over memory-based baselines, and self-evolution further improves performance without manual engineering.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Procedural Graph, a framework that organizes an AI agent's procedural knowledge into (procedure, relation, procedure) triplets—analogous to how knowledge graphs organize factual knowledge—so agents can plan over long horizons and use tools correctly. A guidance model converts the graph subgraph around the agent's current node into step-level guidance that biases action selection, and the graph self-evolves via an LLM refiner that contrasts failed and successful trajectories to edit the graph, retaining only edits that improve held-out validation performance. Starting from a minimal skeleton, the framework builds graphs matching hand-designed ones, can repair flawed expert priors, and consistently outperforms memory-based baselines across datasets, task types, and LLMs.
AI.motivation: LLM agents that act over long horizons via external tools rely on unconstrained generation over an accumulating history, which lacks explicit procedural knowledge of what to do, in what order, and under which conditions. As trajectories lengthen, agents lose track of objectives, invoke tools out of order, and repeat unproductive actions. The paper addresses this by imposing an explicit, learnable procedural structure on agent decision-making.
AI.method: The Procedural Graph organizes procedural knowledge as (procedure, relation, procedure) triplets, analogously to a knowledge graph's (entity, relation, entity) structure. At each decision step, the framework localizes the agent's active node; a guidance model translates the surrounding subgraph into step-level situational guidance that biases (but does not dictate) the solver's next action. The graph is self-evolving: an LLM refiner contrasts failed trajectories with successful ones, proposes edits to graph topology and attributes, and commits only those edits that preserve or improve held-out validation performance, while retaining rejected edits to discourage repetition. The process starts from a minimal skeleton and iteratively builds the graph, and can also repair flawed expert priors.
AI.result: Starting from a minimal skeleton, the loop builds graphs that match or surpass hand-designed ones, and can repair flawed expert priors. Across multiple datasets, task types, and LLMs, the Procedural Graph delivers consistent gains over memory-based baselines, and self-evolution further improves performance without manual engineering.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly organizing procedural knowledge in a graph structure with self-evolving refinement improves long-horizon agent performance over memory-based approaches. The Procedural Graph provides a general, automatic mechanism to encode what-to-do procedural knowledge, matching or exceeding hand-crafted structures while requiring minimal manual engineering.
